tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result always begins with two meta columns, then adds one column per indexed source field (from the explicit `fields` spec, or the introspected index mapping when `fields` is omitted). The per-field DuckDB type follows the `es_type_mapping` reference view.

## Always-present meta columns

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `_id` | VARCHAR | The Elasticsearch/OpenSearch document `_id`. Always present. |
| `_score` | DOUBLE | The relevance score for the hit; NULL when sorting suppresses scoring. Always present. |

## Source columns (example: `fields => 'name:keyword,price:double,created:date,meta:object'`)

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | An ES `keyword`/`text` field. |
| `price` | DOUBLE | An ES `double`/`float` field. |
| `created` | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | An ES `date`/`date_nanos` field, parsed to a UTC microsecond timestamp. |
| `meta` | VARCHAR | An ES `object`/`nested`/`geo_*` field, surfaced as raw JSON text. |

workers.doc_md:
# Local Text Embeddings & Semantic Search in SQL

![fastembed logo](https://qdrant.tech/images/logo_with_text.png)

**Turn text into vector embeddings directly in DuckDB SQL** — generate fixed-length `FLOAT[]` embedding vectors and score them with cosine similarity for semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and nearest-neighbor ranking, all without leaving your query and without sending a single byte to an external API.

The **embed** extension brings sentence-transformer text embeddings to SQL for data engineers, RAG builders, and search teams who want vector search inside the database instead of a separate embedding service. Embeddings are computed **entirely in-process and offline** — there is no torch dependency, no GPU requirement, and no network call after the one-time model download — so the same query runs identically on a laptop, in CI, and in production.

Under the hood it is powered by [fastembed](https://github.com/qdrant/fastembed) from [Qdrant](https://qdrant.tech) (Apache-2.0), which runs quantized sentence-transformer models through [ONNX Runtime](https://onnxruntime.ai) ([source](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime)). The default model is [`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`](https://huggingface.co/BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5) (384-dimensional, MIT licensed), downloaded on first use and cached locally; larger `bge` models and `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` are also supported. Vectors are returned over Apache Arrow as native DuckDB `FLOAT[]` lists, ready to index and rank with the [DuckDB VSS extension](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/vss.html).

## How it works

There are two embedding modes. *Symmetric* embedding maps any text to a vector for text-to-text comparison (dedup, clustering, classification). *Asymmetric* retrieval follows the query/passage convention these models are trained on: a short search query and a longer document are embedded with slightly different instruction prefixes so they land in the same space, which improves recall over plain symmetric embedding. Ranking is then just cosine similarity between vectors -- pure arithmetic, no model load. Model discovery and dimension lookups let you size a vector column or VSS index ahead of time.

```sql
-- A sentence is more similar to itself than to an unrelated one
SELECT embed.similarity(embed.embed('cat'), embed.embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

NULL or empty input text yields a NULL vector, and the model is loaded once and amortized across every row in a scan.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## embed.main schema

The single schema of the embed worker. It groups the local text-embedding and vector-similarity surface into a few concepts: symmetric text-to-text embedding, the asymmetric query/passage convention used for retrieval, a pure-arithmetic cosine-similarity score, and model-discovery/dimension helpers for sizing vector columns and indexes.

Everything runs in-process via fastembed/ONNX (no torch, no network after the one-time model download). Use it to build semantic search and RAG pipelines that store and rank vectors with DuckDB VSS, all in SQL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embed.main

Local text-embedding and cosine-similarity functions over Apache Arrow, for semantic search and RAG with DuckDB.

## Overview

This schema holds the worker's scalar embedding and similarity helpers plus a model-discovery table. Embeddings are generated locally with fastembed on ONNX Runtime; the default model is `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` (384-dim). Symmetric embedding is for text-to-text comparison; the query/passage pair is for asymmetric retrieval.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT embed.similarity(embed.embed('cat'), embed.embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

## Notes

- Use the query/passage pair for retrieval; use plain symmetric embedding for text-to-text comparison.
- NULL or empty text yields a NULL vector.

## supported_models()

List every embedding model the worker can use, one `(model, dim)` pair per row. Takes no arguments.

**When to use.** Use it to discover the valid values for the second argument of `embed(text, model)` (and for `embedding_dim(model)`) and to see each model's output dimension before you size a vector column or VSS index.

**Output.** Columns: `model` (`VARCHAR` -- the name to pass to `embed`/`embedding_dim`) and `dim` (`INTEGER` -- the `FLOAT[]` length the model produces). One row per supported model.

**Edge cases.** This is a discovery table function -- reference it in the query's table position, `embed.main.supported_models()`, rather than as a scalar. A parenthesis-free `supported_models` view exposes the same rows for plain browsing. Runnable, catalog-qualified examples are attached as example queries.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## embedding_dim(model)

Return the output dimension (the `FLOAT[]` length) a model produces, **without** loading the model or embedding anything. Pass `''` or NULL to get the default model's dimension.

**When to use.** Use it to size a vector column or index ahead of time (e.g. an `ARRAY[FLOAT, N]` / VSS HNSW index), or to validate that a chosen model matches an existing index width before re-embedding a corpus.

**Input/output.** Input: a `VARCHAR` model name (`''`/NULL = default). Output: `INTEGER` dimension, or NULL for an unknown model name (it does not raise).

**Edge cases.** Unknown model names return NULL rather than erroring, so a dirty model column won't abort a scan.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embedding_dim(model)

Output dimension (vector length) for a model name -- `''`/NULL = the default model. No model is loaded.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT embed.embedding_dim('BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5');  -- 384
SELECT embed.embedding_dim('');                        -- default model dim
```

## Notes

- Unknown model name -> NULL (no error).
- Use to size a vector column / VSS index before embedding.

## embed(text, model)

The two-argument arity overload of `embed`: embed text into a `FLOAT[]` vector using an *explicit* model name instead of the default. Call `supported_models()` to discover valid model names and their output dimensions.

**When to use.** Use this when you need a specific model -- a larger model for higher recall, or a model whose dimension matches an existing vector index. Otherwise use the one-argument `embed(text)`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## embed_passage(text)

Embed a *document/passage* for retrieval. For bge-style retrieval models, passages get **no** instruction prefix (only queries do), and this function mirrors that convention exactly.

**When to use.** Use `embed_passage` for the corpus side of asymmetric retrieval and `embed_query` for the user query, then rank with `similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc))`. Pre-compute passage vectors once and store them (e.g. in a DuckDB VSS HNSW index).

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` passage per row. Output: one `FLOAT[]` per row (NULL/empty -> NULL), same dimension as `embed`.

**Edge cases.** Numerically this equals plain `embed` for bge (passages have no prefix); it exists as a named counterpart to `embed_query` so retrieval pipelines read symmetrically.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embed_passage(text)

Embed a document/passage for retrieval (the corpus side of asymmetric retrieval -- no query prefix).

## Usage

Materialize passage vectors once with `embed_passage(body)` into a stored column (e.g. a DuckDB VSS HNSW index over the resulting `FLOAT[]`), then at query time score them against `embed_query(q)`. Runnable, catalog-qualified examples are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- Pair with `embed_query` for the query side.
- For bge, passages get no instruction prefix (by design).
- NULL or empty input returns NULL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## embed_query(text)

Embed a *search query* for retrieval, applying the default model's recommended query instruction prefix (for bge: `Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: `). This is the query side of asymmetric retrieval.

**When to use.** Use `embed_query` for the short user query and `embed_passage` for the corpus documents, then rank passages by `similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc))`. The prefix nudges the query vector toward the passages that answer it, improving recall over a plain symmetric `embed`.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` query per row. Output: one `FLOAT[]` per row (NULL/empty -> NULL), same dimension as `embed`.

**Edge cases.** Pair only with `embed_passage` (not `embed`) so query and passage live in the same trained retrieval space.

## Notes

- Pair with `embed_passage` for the documents, not plain `embed`.

functions.name: similarity
functions.comment: Cosine similarity of two FLOAT[] vectors, in [-1, 1] (pure arithmetic, no model). NULL/empty/length-mismatch -> NULL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## similarity(a, b)

Compute the **cosine similarity** of two `FLOAT[]` vectors, a value in `[-1, 1]` where 1 means identical direction. This is pure arithmetic -- it loads no model and does no I/O -- so it is cheap to call over large joins.

**When to use.** Use it to rank or threshold embedding pairs: `ORDER BY similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc)) DESC` for retrieval, or a `WHERE similarity(...) > 0.8` cutoff for dedup/near-duplicate detection.

**Input/output.** Inputs: two `FLOAT[]` vectors (typically from `embed*`). Output: one `DOUBLE` per row. NULL, empty, or length-mismatched vector pairs yield NULL rather than an error.

**Edge cases.** A zero vector has undefined direction and yields NULL; vectors must be the same length to be comparable.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# similarity(a, b)

Cosine similarity of two `FLOAT[]` vectors, in `[-1, 1]` (pure arithmetic, no model).

## Usage

Feed two `FLOAT[]` vectors (typically from the `embed*` functions) to `similarity(a, b)` to get a `DOUBLE` in `[-1, 1]`; order retrieval candidates by it descending, or threshold it (e.g. `> 0.8`) for near-duplicate detection. Runnable, catalog-qualified examples are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- 1.0 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal, -1 = opposite.
- NULL / empty / length-mismatch returns NULL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Score how similar two embeddings are (rounded for stable output).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('dog'), embed.main.embed('puppy')), 3) AS related

vgi.example_queries.description: Confirm a related pair ranks above an unrelated pair.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('dog'), embed.main.embed('puppy')) > embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('dog'), embed.main.embed('airplane')) AS related_wins

tags.vgi.title: Cosine Similarity Score

## First Trust ETFs

First Trust US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables and a table function.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `FTCS`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund's deeper facts or its holdings. Holdings are the current published portfolio (First Trust does not publish historical holdings).

Data is provided for informational use; review First Trust's terms before redistribution.

It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (~300 funds — slow, so prefer a filter). First Trust publishes CURRENT holdings only, so there is no historical as-of date; as_of_date is the page's own date. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (2.59 = 2.59%). Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.

## holdings

Detailed fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'FTCS'` for one fund's holdings (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('FTCS','AIRR')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (~300 partitions — slow). First Trust publishes **current holdings only** (no historical dates). `weight_percent` is in percent points (2.59 = 2.59%).

workers.doc_md:
## Global X ETFs

Global X US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `QYLD`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund's holdings. Holdings are the current published portfolio (Global X does not publish historical holdings).

Data is provided for informational use; review Global X's terms before redistribution.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed portfolio holdings for Global X ETFs as a hive-partitioned table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (~116 funds — slow, so prefer a filter). Global X publishes CURRENT holdings only, so there is no historical as-of date; as_of_date is the published file's own date. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (0.74 = 0.74%). Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'QYLD'` for one fund's holdings (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('QYLD','COPX')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (~116 partitions — slow). Global X publishes **current holdings only** (no historical dates). `weight_percent` is in percent points (0.74 = 0.74%).

vgi.example_queries.description: Two funds at once (partition fan-out)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fund_ticker, name, weight_percent FROM globalx.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker IN ('QYLD', 'COPX')

## products

The Global X US ETF catalog as a base table — one row per fund. It takes no arguments; query it directly and filter with a WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE theme = 'Fixed Income' ORDER BY net_assets DESC`; see the example queries). workers.doc_md:
## Invesco ETFs

Invesco US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables and table functions.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `RSP`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund. Fund holdings are **current-only**: Invesco reports a single effective date per fund, so there is no historical time travel (unlike some other providers).

Data is provided for informational use; review Invesco's terms before redistribution.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Functions that return Invesco ETF data at two levels. At the catalog level you screen the whole lineup on key facts and resolve a fund's key. At the fund level you drill into one fund — its current holdings, its characteristics, and its distribution and NAV history. A fund is keyed by its exchange `ticker` (e.g. `RSP`); resolve the key at the catalog level first. Holdings are current-only (no historical as-of).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Invesco fund data

Work happens at two levels. **Catalog level:** screen the lineup on key facts and find a fund's key. **Fund level:** drill into a single fund — its current constituents, characteristics, and time series. A fund is keyed by its exchange `ticker` (e.g. `RSP`).

Holdings are current-only: Invesco reports one effective date per fund, with no historical time travel.

vgi.example_queries.description: Cheapest Invesco ETFs by expense ratio
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, name, expense_ratio_percent FROM invesco.main.products ORDER BY expense_ratio_percent LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Top holdings of RSP
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, name, weight_percent FROM invesco.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'RSP' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent NAV history for RSP
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, nav FROM invesco.main.nav_history('RSP', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Screen the catalog, then drill into a fund's holdings (join on fund_ticker = products.ticker)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.ticker, p.name, p.expense_ratio_percent, h.ticker AS holding, h.weight_percent FROM invesco.main.products p JOIN invesco.main.holdings h ON h.fund_ticker = p.ticker WHERE p.ticker = 'RSP' ORDER BY h.weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed current portfolio holdings for Invesco ETFs as a hive-partitioned table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (a couple hundred funds — slow, so prefer a filter). Holdings are current-only — Invesco reports a single effective date (the as_of_date column), with no historical time travel. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (0.33 = 0.33%); bond funds also fill coupon/maturity/rating. Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed **current** fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'RSP'` for one fund, or scan with no filter to stream every fund (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('RSP','SPHQ')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (a couple hundred partitions — slow). Holdings are **current-only** (Invesco reports one effective date; no time travel). `weight_percent` is in percent points (0.33 = 0.33%).

vgi.example_queries.description: Top 10 current holdings of RSP
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, name, weight_percent FROM invesco.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'RSP' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Two funds at once (partition fan-out)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fund_ticker, ticker, weight_percent FROM invesco.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker IN ('RSP', 'SPHQ')

vgi.example_queries.description: A bond fund also fills coupon / maturity / rating
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, coupon_percent, maturity_date, rating, weight_percent FROM invesco.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'BSCR' LIMIT 5

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## products

The Invesco US ETF catalog as a base table — one row per fund. It takes no arguments; query it directly and filter with a WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE asset_class = 'Equity' ORDER BY expense_ratio_percent`; see the example queries). Percent columns (`*_percent`) are in **percent points** (an expense ratio of 0.2 means 0.20%). The ticker column is the key for the other functions.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Daily NAV time series for a fund, back to inception. Each row carries the valuation date and the net asset value per share. Bound the range with start_date/end_date. Use it for NAV-based return series. This is fund NAV, not intraday candles.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## nav_history

Daily NAV history back to inception, one row per valuation day. Bound the range with `start_date`/`end_date` (inclusive SQL `DATE`s; omit for the full history). This is **fund NAV**, not an intraday candle series (see the example queries).

vgi.example_queries.description: Daily RSP NAV since a start date
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, nav FROM invesco.main.nav_history('RSP', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: NAV range over a bounded window
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT min(nav), max(nav) FROM invesco.main.nav_history('RSP', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01', end_date := DATE '2025-12-31')

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: as_of_date
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Valuation date.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: nav
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Net asset value per share.

arguments.name: fund
arguments.description: The fund to look up, given as an exchange ticker like 'RSP' (a raw CUSIP also works). Required, first positional argument.

arguments.name: end_date
arguments.description: Optional inclusive upper bound on the valuation-day range — omit for no upper bound. Named end_date because END is a reserved SQL keyword.

arguments.name: start_date
arguments.description: Optional inclusive lower bound on the valuation-day range — omit for the full history back to inception. Filters client-side.

examples: SELECT as_of_date, nav FROM invesco.main.nav_history('RSP', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC
SELECT min(nav), max(nav) FROM invesco.main.nav_history('RSP', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01', end_date := DATE '2025-12-31')

workers.doc_md:
## iShares ETFs

iShares (BlackRock) US fund data, exposed as DuckDB tables and table functions.

Two ideas run through everything. First, the **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `IVV`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund. Second, fund holdings are **point-in-time**: you can ask for a fund's constituents as of any past business day, which makes day-over-day portfolio comparison possible.

Data is provided for informational use; review iShares' terms before redistribution.

example_queries.title: largest_etfs
example_queries.description: The largest iShares ETFs by net assets
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, net_assets FROM ishares.main.products ORDER BY net_assets DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.title: top_holdings

example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, name, weight_percent FROM ishares.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'IVV' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Join holdings to the catalog: a fund's top holdings alongside its fund-level facts (holdings.fund_ticker = products.ticker)
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.fund_name, p.expense_ratio_percent, h.ticker, h.name, h.weight_percent FROM ishares.main.holdings h JOIN ishares.main.products p ON h.fund_ticker = p.ticker WHERE h.fund_ticker = 'IVV' ORDER BY h.weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Recent daily NAV history for IVV

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed portfolio holdings for iShares funds as a hive-partitioned, time-travel table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (hundreds of funds — slow, so prefer a filter). The as-of date is a time-travel coordinate: omit it for the latest holdings, or read a past day with `AT (TIMESTAMP => DATE '2025-12-31')` — any business day back to ~inception, not just the featured holding_dates. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (7.38 = 7.38%); fixed-income funds also fill coupon/maturity/duration/ytm. Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned, time-travel table**. Partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker) with the as-of date as the **time-travel version**. `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'IVV'` for one fund's latest holdings, or read a past date with `AT (TIMESTAMP => DATE '2025-12-31')` (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('IVV','AGG')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (hundreds of partitions — slow). `weight_percent` is in percent points (7.38 = 7.38%).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## products

The iShares US product catalog as a base table — one row per fund. It takes no arguments; query it directly and filter with a WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE product_view = 'etf' ORDER BY net_assets DESC`; see the example queries). The ticker column is the key for the other functions.

workers.doc_md:
## J.P. Morgan ETFs

J.P. Morgan Asset Management US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables and a table function.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `JEPI`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund. Fund holdings are **current-only**: J.P. Morgan reports a single effective date per fund, so there is no historical time travel, and no distribution or NAV time series is published.

Data is provided for informational use; review J.P. Morgan's terms before redistribution.

example_queries.title: largest_etfs
example_queries.description: The largest J.P. Morgan ETFs by assets
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, name, net_assets FROM jpmorgan.main.products ORDER BY net_assets DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.title: top_holdings
example_queries.description: The top holdings of the JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, name, weight_percent FROM jpmorgan.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'JEPI' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.sql: SELECT p.ticker, p.name, p.net_assets, h.ticker AS holding, h.weight_percent FROM jpmorgan.main.products p JOIN jpmorgan.main.holdings h ON h.fund_ticker = p.ticker WHERE p.ticker = 'JEPI' ORDER BY h.weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

## J.P. Morgan fund data

Work happens at two levels. **Catalog level:** screen the lineup on key facts and find a fund's key. **Fund level:** drill into a single fund — its full current constituents and its characteristics. A fund is keyed by its exchange `ticker` (e.g. `JEPI`).

Holdings are current-only: J.P. Morgan reports one effective date per fund, with no historical time travel.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed current portfolio holdings for J.P. Morgan ETFs as a hive-partitioned table — the FULL published position list per fund. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (75 funds — slow, so prefer a filter). Holdings are current-only — J.P. Morgan reports a single effective date (the as_of_date column), with no historical time travel. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (1.71 = 1.71%); bond funds also fill coupon/maturity/rating. Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed **current** fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table** (the full published position list per fund), partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'JEPI'` for one fund, or scan with no filter to stream every fund (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('JEPI','JPST')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (75 partitions — slow). Holdings are **current-only** (J.P. Morgan reports one effective date; no time travel). `weight_percent` is in percent points (1.71 = 1.71%).

vgi.example_queries.description: A bond fund also fills coupon / maturity

## products

The J.P. Morgan US ETF catalog as a base table — one row per fund. It takes no arguments; query it directly and filter with a WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE asset_class = 'U.S. Equity' ORDER BY net_assets DESC`; see the example queries). ## Schwab Asset Management ETFs

Schwab Asset Management US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `SCHD`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund's holdings. Holdings are the current published portfolio (Schwab does not publish historical holdings).

Data is provided for informational use; review Schwab's terms before redistribution.

## Schwab fund data

Work happens at two levels. **Catalog level:** screen the lineup on key facts and find a fund's key. **Fund level:** drill into a single fund's constituents. A fund is keyed by its exchange `ticker` (e.g. `SCHD`).

Holdings are the current published portfolio; Schwab does not publish historical holdings.

vgi.example_queries.description: Top holdings of SCHD

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed portfolio holdings for Schwab ETFs as a hive-partitioned table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (~35 funds — slow, and a broad bond fund can list thousands of constituents, so prefer a filter). Schwab publishes CURRENT holdings only, so there is no historical as-of date; as_of_date is the published page's own date. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own symbol). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'SCHD'` for one fund's holdings (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('SCHD','SCHF')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (~35 partitions — slow). Schwab publishes **current holdings only** (no historical dates). `weight_percent` is in percent points (4.49 = 4.49%); `market_value` is approximate (abbreviated on the page).

vgi.example_queries.description: Top 10 current holdings of SCHD
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, ticker, weight_percent FROM schwab.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'SCHD' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: The largest positions of the International Equity ETF
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, weight_percent, market_value FROM schwab.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'SCHF' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Two funds at once (partition fan-out)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fund_ticker, name, weight_percent FROM schwab.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker IN ('SCHD', 'SCHF')

vgi.example_queries.description: Join holdings to the catalog for fund-level facts (name + expense ratio)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.fund_name, p.expense_ratio_percent, h.name, h.weight_percent FROM schwab.main.holdings h JOIN schwab.main.products p ON h.fund_ticker = p.ticker WHERE h.fund_ticker = 'SCHD' ORDER BY h.weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

## holdings_scan

The backing scan for the **`holdings` table** — prefer the table. Hive-partitioned by `fund_ticker`: pass a fund's ticker as the argument (`holdings_scan(fund_ticker => 'SCHD')`) for one fund, or omit it and filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'SCHD'` so the filter is pushed down (see the example queries). `fund_ticker` is distinct from the constituent `ticker` column.

workers.doc_md:
## SPDR ETFs

SPDR / State Street (SSGA) US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables and a table function.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `SPY`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund's holdings or NAV history. Holdings are the current published portfolio (SSGA does not publish historical holdings).

Data is provided for informational use; review SSGA's terms before redistribution.

example_queries.title: largest_etfs
example_queries.description: The largest SPDR ETFs by net assets
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, net_assets FROM spdr.main.products ORDER BY net_assets DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.title: top_holdings
example_queries.description: The top holdings of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, ticker, weight_percent FROM spdr.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'SPY' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Ten largest SPDR ETFs by net assets
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, net_assets FROM spdr.main.products ORDER BY net_assets DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Top holdings of SPY
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, ticker, weight_percent FROM spdr.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'SPY' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Recent daily NAV history for SPY
example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, nav FROM spdr.main.nav_history('SPY', start_date := DATE '2026-01-01') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC

example_queries.description: A bond fund fills coupon / maturity / par value
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, coupon_percent, maturity_date, par_value FROM spdr.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'BIL' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Two funds at once (partition fan-out)
example_queries.sql: SELECT fund_ticker, name, weight_percent FROM spdr.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker IN ('SPY', 'BIL')

example_queries.description: Cheapest equity ETFs by expense ratio
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, expense_ratio_percent FROM spdr.main.products WHERE asset_class = 'Equity' ORDER BY expense_ratio_percent LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Look up a single fund by ticker
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, expense_ratio_percent FROM spdr.main.products WHERE ticker = 'SPY'

example_queries.description: Recent daily total net assets for SPY
example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, total_net_assets FROM spdr.main.nav_history('SPY') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Position count and summed weight for two funds (partition fan-out)
example_queries.sql: SELECT fund_ticker, count(*) AS positions, round(sum(weight_percent), 2) AS total_weight FROM spdr.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker IN ('SPY', 'BIL') GROUP BY fund_ticker ORDER BY positions DESC

workers.doc_md:
## Vanguard ETFs

Vanguard US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables and table functions.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `VOO`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund. Fund holdings are **current-only**: Vanguard reports a single as-of date per fund, so there is no historical time travel (unlike some other providers).

Data is provided for informational use; review Vanguard's terms before redistribution.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed current portfolio holdings for Vanguard ETFs as a hive-partitioned table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (over a hundred funds — slow, so prefer a filter). Holdings are current-only — Vanguard reports a single as-of date (the as_of_date column), with no historical time travel. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (7.89 = 7.89%); bond funds also fill coupon/maturity/face. Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed **current** fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'VOO'` for one fund, or scan with no filter to stream every fund (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('VOO','BND')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (over a hundred partitions — slow). Holdings are **current-only** (Vanguard reports one as-of date; no time travel). `weight_percent` is in percent points (7.89 = 7.89%).

functions.name: distributions
functions.comment: Recent distribution history for a fund — one row per distribution with record, reinvestment, and payable dates, the distribution type, the per-share amount, and the reinvestment price. `fund` is a ticker; bound the record-date range with start_date/end_date.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Distribution (dividend / capital-gain) history for a fund: record / reinvestment / payable dates, the distribution type, the per-share amount, and the reinvestment price. Amounts are per-share dollars, not percents. Bound the record-date range with start_date/end_date. Vanguard publishes only a rolling recent window — about the trailing 18 months (roughly 6 payouts for a quarterly payer, 18 for a monthly one) — so bounds outside it return no rows; derive them from CURRENT_DATE rather than hard-coding a calendar year.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## distributions

Recent distribution history, one row per distribution. Amounts are **per-share** dollars (not percentages). Bound the record-date range with `start_date`/`end_date` (see the example queries). Vanguard publishes only a rolling window of about the trailing 18 months, so bounds outside it return no rows.

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent VOO distributions
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT record_date, per_share_amount FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO') ORDER BY record_date DESC LIMIT 8

vgi.example_queries.description: Total distributions over the trailing year
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(per_share_amount) AS total FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE)

vgi.example_queries.description: Distributions within a bounded record-day window
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT record_date, per_share_amount FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE, end_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 3 MONTH)::DATE) ORDER BY record_date

functions.name: holdings_scan
functions.comment: Backing scan for the holdings table — prefer the `holdings` table. Detailed current fund holdings, hive-partitioned by fund_ticker: pass a single fund as holdings_scan(fund_ticker := 'VOO'), or filter WHERE fund_ticker = 'VOO' (or fund_ticker IN (…)) for specific funds, or scan with no filter to stream every fund's holdings. weight_percent is in percent points; bond funds also fill coupon/maturity/face.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The backing scan for the `holdings` table. Prefer querying the `holdings` table. Takes an optional single fund_ticker argument: holdings_scan(fund_ticker := 'VOO') scans just that fund. Hive-partitioned by fund_ticker (the fund's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): pass the fund as the argument, or filter WHERE fund_ticker = '…' (or fund_ticker IN (…)) for specific funds, or scan with no argument/filter to stream every fund (over a hundred partitions — slow). Holdings are current-only (no historical as-of). weight_percent is in percent points (7.89 = 7.89%); bond funds also fill coupon/maturity/face.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings_scan

The backing scan for the **`holdings` table** — prefer the table. Takes an optional `fund_ticker` argument: `holdings_scan(fund_ticker := 'VOO')` scans one fund. Hive-partitioned by `fund_ticker`: pass the fund as the argument, filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'VOO'`, or scan with no argument to stream every fund (see the example queries). `fund_ticker` is distinct from the constituent `ticker` column. Holdings are current-only (no historical as-of).

vgi.example_queries.description: Top 10 holdings of VOO via the backing scan (fund passed as an argument)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, name, weight_percent FROM vanguard.main.holdings_scan(fund_ticker := 'VOO') ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Two partitions at once via a pushdown filter (fan-out)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fund_ticker, count(*) FROM vanguard.main.holdings_scan() WHERE fund_ticker IN ('VOO', 'BND') GROUP BY fund_ticker

functions.name: nav_history
functions.comment: Net-asset-value and market-price history for a fund over a look-back window — one row per observation with the NAV and the market (exchange) price. `fund` is a ticker; `period` picks the window (1M/1Y/5Y/10Y, default 1Y). Longer windows return coarser (weekly/monthly) points.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: NAV and market-price time series for a fund over a look-back window (period = 1M/1Y/5Y/10Y, default 1Y). Each row carries the NAV and the market (exchange) price for a date. Use it for NAV-based return series and NAV-vs-price comparison. Shorter windows are daily; 5Y thins to weekly and 10Y to monthly. This is fund NAV, not intraday candles.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## nav_history

NAV and market-price history over a look-back window. Pick the window with `period` (`1M`/`1Y`/`5Y`/`10Y`, default `1Y`); longer windows return coarser points (5Y weekly, 10Y monthly). This is **fund NAV**, not an intraday candle series (see the example queries).

vgi.example_queries.description: Daily VOO NAV over the past year
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, nav FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '1Y') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: 10-year NAV vs market-price series (monthly points)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, nav, market_price FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '10Y') ORDER BY as_of_date

SELECT as_of_date, nav, market_price FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '10Y') ORDER BY as_of_date

workers.doc_md:
## WisdomTree ETFs

WisdomTree US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `DGRW`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund's holdings. Holdings are the current published portfolio (WisdomTree does not publish historical holdings).

Data is provided for informational use; review WisdomTree's terms before redistribution.

example_queries.title: etf_lineup
example_queries.description: The WisdomTree US ETF lineup
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, asset_class FROM wisdomtree.main.products ORDER BY ticker LIMIT 5;

example_queries.title: top_holdings
example_queries.description: The top holdings of the WisdomTree U.S. Quality Dividend Growth Fund
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, ticker, weight_percent FROM wisdomtree.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'DGRW' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 5;

tables.name: holdings
tables.comment: Detailed current fund holdings, hive-partitioned by fund_ticker (filter WHERE fund_ticker = … for one fund, or scan unfiltered for all). WisdomTree publishes current holdings only (no historical dates).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed portfolio holdings for WisdomTree ETFs as a hive-partitioned table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (~85 funds — slow, so prefer a filter). WisdomTree publishes CURRENT holdings only, so there is no historical as-of date; as_of_date is the fund page's own date. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (7.38 = 7.38%). Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'DGRW'` for one fund's holdings (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('DGRW','EPS')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (~85 partitions — slow). WisdomTree publishes **current holdings only** (no historical dates). `weight_percent` is in percent points (7.38 = 7.38%).

workers.title: Windows Event Log Parser
workers.tagline: Parse Windows Event Logs (.evtx) into rows for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.summary: Windows Event Log (.evtx) parsing for defensive DFIR — turn event-log files into queryable rows.
workers.doc_md:
# Windows Event Log (.evtx) Parsing in SQL

Query Windows Event Logs directly in DuckDB: this VGI extension turns binary `.evtx` files into Apache Arrow rows so you can run digital-forensics and incident-response (DFIR) analysis, threat hunting, and log triage entirely in SQL — no external tooling, no network access, no scripting.

## What it does

The Windows Event Log (`.evtx`, the binary `ElfFile` format that backs the Security, System, Application, PowerShell, and Sysmon channels) is the primary evidence source for Windows DFIR. This extension reads those files — including logs pulled from potentially compromised hosts — and exposes every event record as a queryable row, with convenience columns for the event id, provider, channel, source computer, severity level, and creation time, plus the complete original event preserved as JSON. It is built for incident responders, threat hunters, detection engineers, SOC analysts, and anyone who would rather join, filter, and aggregate event logs in SQL than wrangle them in a GUI.

## How it works

Parsing is powered by the battle-tested [`evtx`](https://github.com/omerbenamram/evtx) Rust crate (API docs on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/evtx)), which decodes the BinXML chunks of the [Windows event-logging](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/eventlog/event-logging) format. Everything runs offline inside the worker — it never touches the network — and every entry point is hardened against hostile input: malformed, truncated, or deliberately corrupted files yield `NULL` / `false` / no rows and never crash the worker. Input may be supplied either inline as a `BLOB` (for example from `read_blob()`) or as a `VARCHAR` filesystem path.

## Working in SQL

Because every event becomes an ordinary row, you build timelines by filtering on provider and creation time, surface the noisiest activity by grouping and counting event ids, and pivot from triage to detection: the preserved event JSON composes with the companion `vgi-sigma` worker to run Sigma detection rules straight against your logs. The curated `windows_event_id_reference` view lets you look up what a given event id means and join it onto parsed records for readable timelines. Runnable, catalog-qualified queries for every function and the reference view are attached to each object and to this schema as example queries.

example_queries.description: Validate that a file's bytes are a parseable .evtx before loading it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT evtx.main.is_valid_evtx((SELECT content FROM read_blob('Security.evtx')));

example_queries.description: Count how many event records a .evtx file contains.
example_queries.sql: SELECT evtx.main.evtx_record_count((SELECT content FROM read_blob('Security.evtx')));

example_queries.description: Explode a .evtx file into one row per event record, ordered by record id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_id, event_id, provider, time_created FROM evtx.main.evtx_records('Security.evtx') ORDER BY record_id;

example_queries.description: Rank event ids by how often they occur to surface the noisiest activity.
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_id, count(*) AS n FROM evtx.main.evtx_records('Security.evtx') GROUP BY event_id ORDER BY n DESC;

example_queries.description: Look up the meaning and DFIR relevance of a single Windows event id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, dfir_use FROM evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference WHERE event_id = 4688

example_queries.description: List the curated Security-channel event ids in numeric order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_id, name FROM evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference WHERE channel = 'Security' ORDER BY event_id

example_queries.description: Explode a .evtx file at the given path into one row per event record, ordered by record id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_id, event_id, provider, time_created FROM evtx.main.evtx_records('test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx') ORDER BY record_id;

example_queries.description: Rank event ids by frequency to surface the noisiest activity in a log.
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_id, count(*) AS n FROM evtx.main.evtx_records('test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx') GROUP BY event_id ORDER BY n DESC;

example_queries.description: Non-evtx bytes yield zero rows from evtx_records (hostile input is handled, never an error).
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM evtx.main.evtx_records('not a real evtx'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Non-evtx bytes are reported as not valid (false), never an error.
example_queries.sql: SELECT evtx.main.is_valid_evtx('not a real evtx'::BLOB) AS valid;

example_queries.description: Non-evtx bytes count as zero event records (hostile input is handled).
example_queries.sql: SELECT evtx.main.evtx_record_count('not a real evtx'::BLOB) AS records;

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## evtx.main

Windows Event Log (`.evtx`) parsing and inspection over Apache Arrow. This schema turns a `.evtx` file — supplied as inline `BLOB` bytes or a `VARCHAR` filesystem path — into queryable event rows so a whole log can be joined, filtered, and aggregated in SQL.

Alongside parsing, it lets you validate and size a log before loading it, and each event's full JSON is preserved so results compose with downstream detection tooling such as `vgi-sigma`.

Everything runs offline. All entry points tolerate hostile input — malformed, truncated, or non-evtx data yields empty or false results rather than an error — because event logs are routinely pulled from potentially compromised hosts.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A curated, browsable registry of well-known Windows Event IDs and what they mean for digital-forensics and incident-response work. Columns: event_id (`INTEGER`), channel (`VARCHAR`), name (short label), dfir_use (why it matters). Scan it to discover which event ids to look for, or LEFT JOIN it onto evtx_records.event_id to label parsed records with human-readable meanings. It is static reference data — no .evtx input and no network access.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## windows_event_id_reference

A curated lookup of well-known Windows Event IDs (Security auditing, the System service-control log, Sysmon, and PowerShell script-block logging) with a short name and a DFIR relevance note for each. Browse it to learn which ids matter — for example 4624 (successful logon), 4625 (failed logon), 4688 (process creation), or 7045 (service installed) — or join it onto parsed records by `event_id` to turn a raw timeline into a readable one. It is static data: it needs no `.evtx` file and touches no network.

workers.summary: SHAP explanations for scikit-learn / XGBoost models as SQL functions.
workers.doc_md:
# SHAP Model Explanations in SQL

![SHAP logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shap/shap/master/docs/artwork/shap_logo.png)

**Explainable AI for machine learning predictions, right inside DuckDB — compute SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) feature attributions for fitted scikit-learn and XGBoost models with plain SQL.**

The `explain` catalog turns model interpretability into a set of DuckDB/SQL table functions, so you can answer *why* a model made a prediction without leaving your database or writing any Python. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and ML practitioners who need transparent, auditable, per-prediction explanations — for model debugging, regulatory and fair-lending reviews, feature selection, or simply building trust in a model's output. Every explanation is computed over your data in place via Apache Arrow, so it composes naturally with joins, filters, and aggregates in ordinary SQL.

Under the hood the worker is powered by [SHAP](https://github.com/shap/shap), the reference implementation of Shapley-value feature attribution ([documentation](https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)), grounded in cooperative game theory's [Shapley values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shapley_value). Importantly, vgi-explain does **not** train models — it *interprets* the self-contained *model* `BLOB` produced by the sibling `vgi-sklearn` ([scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)) and `vgi-xgboost` ([XGBoost](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/)) workers. SHAP automatically selects an appropriate explainer (e.g. TreeExplainer for tree ensembles), so explanations are exact and fast for the supported model families. Because a DuckDB table function accepts only one subquery argument (reserved for the feature relation), the model travels as a scalar `model` argument, usually held in a session variable and read with `getvariable('m')` — see the schema's and each function's example queries for ready-to-run SQL.

Three functions make up the surface. `shap_values` streams a feature relation and emits per-row, per-feature signed contributions in long format (with a contribution per class for multi-class classifiers), aligning input columns to the model's fitted features by name. `shap_base_value` returns the explainer's expected value — the model's baseline output that the per-feature contributions add onto, so that base value + sum(contributions) reproduces the prediction (SHAP's additivity property). `feature_importance` aggregates `mean(|SHAP|)` across a relation to produce a global, ranked importance of which features matter most, falling back to the model's native importances when no rows are supplied. Together they cover local (single-prediction) and global (whole-dataset) interpretability for the models you already serve from VGI.

example_queries.description: Read the model's baseline output (one row per class for a binary classifier).
example_queries.sql: ["SET VARIABLE m = (SELECT model FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/models.parquet') WHERE name = 'rf_clf')", "SELECT class, base_value FROM explain.main.shap_base_value(model := getvariable('m')) ORDER BY class"]

example_queries.description: Explain each row's prediction feature by feature (long-format SHAP contributions).
example_queries.sql: ["SET VARIABLE m = (SELECT model FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/models.parquet') WHERE name = 'rf_clf')", "SELECT id, feature, class, shap_value FROM explain.main.shap_values((SELECT id, signal, noise_a, noise_b FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/features.parquet')), model := getvariable('m'), id := 'id') ORDER BY id, feature, class LIMIT 6"]

# SHAP Explanations

Model-interpretability table functions that turn a fitted scikit-learn or XGBoost model into per-prediction and dataset-wide **SHAP** feature attributions. Every explanation is computed in place over Apache Arrow, so it composes with ordinary SQL joins, filters, and aggregates.

## What it covers

*Local* interpretability answers **why did the model predict this row?** by attributing the output to each input feature; *global* interpretability ranks **which features matter most** across a whole dataset. Multi-class classifiers report a contribution per class, and every attribution obeys SHAP additivity — a row's base value plus its feature contributions reconstruct the model's output.

## How models arrive

This schema does **not** train models: it *interprets* the self-contained model `BLOB` packed by the sibling `vgi-sklearn` / `vgi-xgboost` workers. Because a DuckDB table function reserves its single subquery slot for the feature relation, the model travels as a scalar `model` argument — typically held in a session VARIABLE and read with `getvariable('m')`.

functions.name: shap_values
functions.comment: Per-row, per-feature SHAP contributions in long format (one row per row x feature [x class])

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `shap_values`

Compute **per-row, per-feature SHAP contributions** for a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model, returned in **long format** — one output row per (input row x feature [x class]).

**When to use it.** Answer *why did the model predict this for this row?* — the signed `shap_value` for each feature shows how much that feature pushed the model's output up (positive) or down (negative), relative to the model's base value (see `shap_base_value`). Summing a row's contributions and the base value reconstructs the model's raw output (SHAP additivity).

**Inputs.** A feature relation as the single subquery argument; a `model` `BLOB` (scalar, produced by vgi-sklearn / vgi-xgboost), typically a session VARIABLE or an inline subquery; and an optional `id` column name to carry through (excluded from features). Features are aligned to the model's fitted columns **by name**, so input column order does not matter; the input must contain every feature the model expects.

**Outputs.** Columns `id`, `feature`, `class`, `shap_value`. For a multi-class classifier with K>2 classes there is one row per class (the `class` column carries the label); regression and binary classification collapse to a single output with `class = NULL`.

**Edge cases.** An empty input relation yields zero rows. A missing feature column is an input-alignment failure and raises a clear `input is missing feature column(s) …` error (listing the model's expected features and the input's columns); a separate `invalid model: …` error is raised only for a malformed, truncated, or untrusted model `BLOB`. Neither crashes the worker.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# shap_values

Per-row, per-feature **SHAP contributions** for a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model, in **long format** (one row per input row x feature, and per class for multi-class classifiers).

## Usage

The model travels as the scalar `model` argument (a DuckDB table function allows only one subquery, reserved for the feature relation); it is usually held in a session VARIABLE and read with `getvariable('m')`. Pass the feature relation as the single table argument, the model as `model := getvariable('m')`, and optionally the id column as `id := 'row_id'`. Features are aligned to the model's fitted columns by name, so input order is irrelevant. A runnable end-to-end demonstration ships in this function's `vgi.executable_examples`.

## Notes

- Each row's contributions plus the model base value (`shap_base_value`) reconstruct the prediction (SHAP additivity).
- `class` is the label for multi-class classifiers, `NULL` for regression / binary.
- A missing feature column raises an `input is missing feature column(s) …` error; a malformed or untrusted model `BLOB` raises an `invalid model: …` error.

functions.name: shap_base_value
functions.comment: The SHAP base (expected) value of a model -- one row, or one row per class

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `shap_base_value`

Return the **SHAP base (expected) value** of a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model — the explainer's *expected output* over the background distribution. This is the anchor that every row's per-feature SHAP contributions (`shap_values`) add onto to reconstruct that row's prediction (SHAP additivity).

**When to use it.** Establish the model's baseline before reading local explanations: a row's prediction = base value + sum of its SHAP contributions. Pair it with `shap_values` whenever you present a per-row attribution.

**Inputs.** Just the scalar `model` `BLOB` (produced by vgi-sklearn / vgi-xgboost) — no feature relation. It is typically a session VARIABLE or an inline subquery.

**Outputs.** Columns `class`, `base_value`. A multi-class classifier returns one row per class (the `class` column carries the label); regression and binary classification return a single row with `class = NULL`.

**Edge cases.** The model `BLOB` does not carry a background sample, so the base value is computed from a single zero feature vector — exact for tree / linear explainers, an approximation for models that require real background data. An invalid / untrusted `BLOB` raises a clear `invalid model: …` error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# shap_base_value

The **SHAP base (expected) value** of a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model: the explainer's expected output — the anchor that a row's SHAP contributions add onto to reach its prediction.

## Usage

Takes only the scalar `model` `BLOB` (no feature relation), usually held in a session VARIABLE and read with `getvariable('m')` — pass it as `model := getvariable('m')`. A runnable end-to-end demonstration ships in this function's `vgi.executable_examples`.

## Notes

- One row per class for multi-class classifiers; a single `class = NULL` row otherwise.
- Computed from a zero background vector (exact for tree / linear explainers).
- `base_value + sum(shap_value)` reconstructs a row's model output.

SELECT class, base_value FROM explain.main.shap_base_value(model := getvariable('m')) ORDER BY class

functions.name: feature_importance
functions.comment: Global feature importance: mean(|SHAP|) over the relation (or native importances if empty)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `feature_importance`

Rank a fitted model's features by **global importance** — by default the **mean absolute SHAP value** (`mean(|SHAP|)`) of each feature over the feature relation you pass. This aggregates the per-row, per-feature attributions of `shap_values` into one number per feature: how much, on average, the feature moves the model's output.

**When to use it.** Answer *which features matter most overall?* — for model summaries, feature selection, or dashboards. SHAP-based importance is consistent and model-agnostic, unlike split-count / Gini heuristics.

**Inputs.** A feature relation (the single subquery argument) to average over; the scalar `model` `BLOB`; and an optional `id` column name to exclude from features. Features are aligned to the model's fitted columns by name.

**Outputs.** Columns `feature`, `importance`, `rank` (1 = most important), and `method` (`'mean_abs_shap'` or `'native'`).

**Edge cases.** If the passed relation has **zero rows**, the function falls back to the model's *native* importances (`feature_importances_`, or `|coef_|` for linear models) and sets `method = 'native'`; if the model exposes neither, that empty-relation call raises a clear error. An invalid / untrusted model `BLOB` raises `invalid model: …`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# feature_importance

**Global feature importance** for a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model: `mean(|SHAP|)` over the relation you pass, or the model's native importances when the relation is empty.

## Usage

Pass the feature relation as the single table argument and the model as the scalar `model` argument (usually a session VARIABLE read with `getvariable('m')`, passed as `model := getvariable('m')`); order the output by `rank`. A runnable end-to-end demonstration ships in this function's `vgi.executable_examples`.

## Notes

- `method = 'mean_abs_shap'` when rows are supplied; `'native'` when the relation is empty (uses `feature_importances_` / `|coef_|`).
- `rank` is 1-based, most important first.
- Features are aligned to the model's fitted columns by name.

workers.doc_md:
# Formula 1 results, standings, and timing

Query Formula 1 from SQL. Current tables cover this season's championships, calendar, and latest result. Parameterized functions reach back to 1950 for results and standings, and into 2023+ sessions for lap, stint, pit, weather, and race-control detail.

## Data model

Jolpica-F1 functions are keyed by `season`, `round`, and text ids (`driver_id`, `constructor_id`, `circuit_id`). OpenF1 functions are keyed by `session_key` and car `driver_number`; use `session_drivers()` to map numbers to names.

## Licence

Both sources publish their data under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: attribute them, do not use the data commercially, and share derived datasets alike. This worker fetches on demand and does not rehost data. It is not affiliated with Formula 1 or the FIA.

example_queries.title: current_driver_standings_are_populated
example_queries.description: The current drivers' championship has driver rows with stable identifiers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AND count(driver_id) = count(*) AS populated FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings;

example_queries.title: championship_points_are_ordered
example_queries.description: A higher championship position never has more points than a lower one.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(points <= prev_points) AS ordered FROM (SELECT points, lag(points) OVER (ORDER BY position) AS prev_points FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings WHERE position IS NOT NULL) WHERE prev_points IS NOT NULL;

example_queries.title: verstappen_2023_wins
example_queries.description: Max Verstappen won 19 Grands Prix in 2023.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS wins FROM f1.main.race_results(2023) WHERE position = 1 AND driver_id = 'max_verstappen';

example_queries.description: The current championship top ten.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, constructor_name, points, wins FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings ORDER BY position LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Points gap from each driver to the leader.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name, points, max(points) OVER () - points AS gap_to_leader FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Seasons held so far.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS seasons, max(season) AS latest FROM f1.main.seasons

example_queries.description: Podium of the latest Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT race_name, position, driver_name, constructor_name, race_time FROM f1.main.last_race_results WHERE position <= 3 ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Biggest gainers from grid to finish in the latest race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name, grid, position, grid - position AS places_gained FROM f1.main.last_race_results WHERE classified AND grid > 0 ORDER BY places_gained DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Remaining races this season.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round, race_name, country, race_start_utc FROM f1.main.current_schedule WHERE race_date >= current_date ORDER BY round

example_queries.description: Current constructors' table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, constructor_name, points, wins FROM f1.main.current_constructor_standings ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Sprint winners in 2024.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round, race_name, driver_name FROM f1.main.sprint_results(2024) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY round

example_queries.description: Session keys for every 2024 race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT session_key, country_name, location, date_start FROM f1.main.sessions(2024, session_name := 'Race') ORDER BY date_start

example_queries.description: Track temperature range during the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT min(track_temperature) AS coolest, max(track_temperature) AS hottest, bool_or(rainfall) AS any_rain FROM f1.main.session_weather(9472)

example_queries.description: Fastest race laps in the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_number, lap_number, lap_duration FROM f1.main.session_laps(9472) WHERE lap_duration IS NOT NULL ORDER BY lap_duration LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: The 2024 calendar in round order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round, race_name, country, race_date FROM f1.main.schedule(2024) ORDER BY round

example_queries.description: Current constructors' leader from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT constructor_name, points FROM f1.main.all_current_constructor_standings() WHERE position = 1

example_queries.description: Flags shown in the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT date, lap_number, flag, scope, message FROM f1.main.race_control(9472) WHERE category = 'Flag' ORDER BY date

example_queries.description: Pole sitters in 2024.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round, race_name, driver_name, q3 FROM f1.main.qualifying_results(2024) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY round

example_queries.description: 2024 race weekends on street circuits.
example_queries.sql: SELECT meeting_name, location FROM f1.main.meetings(2024) WHERE circuit_type LIKE '%Street%' ORDER BY date_start

example_queries.description: Quickest pit-lane visits in the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_number, lap_number, lane_duration FROM f1.main.session_pits(9472) ORDER BY lane_duration LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Circuits on the 2024 calendar by country.
example_queries.sql: SELECT circuit_name, locality, country FROM f1.main.circuits(season := 2024) ORDER BY country

example_queries.description: Max Verstappen's laps in the 2024 Chinese Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT lap, position, lap_time FROM f1.main.lap_times(2024, 5, driver_id := 'max_verstappen') ORDER BY lap

example_queries.description: Current championship top five from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, points FROM f1.main.all_current_driver_standings() ORDER BY position LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Podium of the most recent race from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, constructor_name FROM f1.main.all_last_race_results() WHERE position <= 3 ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Compound usage in the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT compound, count(*) AS stints, sum(lap_end - lap_start + 1) AS laps FROM f1.main.session_stints(9472) GROUP BY compound ORDER BY laps DESC

example_queries.description: Top ten of the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix with driver names.
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.position, d.full_name, r.points, r.gap_to_leader FROM f1.main.session_result(9472) r JOIN f1.main.session_drivers(9472) d USING (driver_number) WHERE r.position <= 10 ORDER BY r.position

example_queries.description: Final 2024 constructors' championship.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, constructor_name, points, wins FROM f1.main.constructor_standings(2024) ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Final 2024 drivers' championship.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, constructor_name, points, wins FROM f1.main.driver_standings(2024) ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: The 2024 championship after round 10.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, points FROM f1.main.driver_standings(2024, round := 10) ORDER BY position LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Lewis Hamilton's career wins and podiums.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE position = 1) AS wins, count(*) FILTER (WHERE position <= 3) AS podiums FROM f1.main.driver_results('hamilton')

example_queries.description: The 2024 constructors.
example_queries.sql: SELECT constructor_id, constructor_name, nationality FROM f1.main.constructors(season := 2024)

example_queries.description: The 2024 grid.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_id, driver_code, driver_name, nationality FROM f1.main.drivers(season := 2024) ORDER BY family_name

example_queries.description: Entry list for the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix (session 9472).
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_number, name_acronym, full_name, team_name FROM f1.main.session_drivers(9472) ORDER BY driver_number

example_queries.description: Winners of every 2024 Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round, race_name, driver_name, constructor_name FROM f1.main.race_results(2024) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY round

example_queries.description: Full classification of the 2024 Chinese Grand Prix (round 5).
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, grid, status, points FROM f1.main.race_results(2024, round := 5) ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Fastest pit-lane times in the 2024 Chinese Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_id, lap, duration_seconds FROM f1.main.pit_stops(2024, 5) ORDER BY duration_seconds LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Number of championship seasons from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS seasons FROM f1.main.all_seasons()

example_queries.description: Sprint weekends this season from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round, race_name FROM f1.main.all_current_schedule() WHERE is_sprint_weekend

example_queries.description: Radio clips per driver in the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_number, count(*) AS clips FROM f1.main.team_radio(9472) GROUP BY driver_number ORDER BY clips DESC

workers.summary: Fetch and parse RSS / Atom / JSON feeds into rows.
workers.doc_md:
# RSS, Atom & JSON Feed Parser for DuckDB

Parse RSS, Atom, and JSON feeds directly in SQL — turn any syndication feed into queryable DuckDB rows over Apache Arrow, with zero glue code and automatic format detection.

This VGI extension brings **feed parsing to SQL** for data engineers, analysts, and anyone who needs to ingest news, blog, or podcast feeds without writing a custom scraper. Point it at an `http(s)` URL and it fetches the feed over HTTP, or hand it a raw RSS / Atom / JSON Feed document inline — either way the format is auto-detected, so a single query handles RSS 2.0, Atom, and JSON Feed alike. Missing or unparseable publish dates surface as `NULL` timestamps, absent text fields as empty strings, and malformed feeds raise a clean, actionable error rather than crashing your session.

Feed parsing and format auto-detection are powered by [gofeed](https://github.com/mmcdole/gofeed), a robust, widely-used Go feed parser (see the [gofeed API documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/mmcdole/gofeed)). It understands the [RSS 2.0 specification](https://www.rssboard.org/rss-specification), the [Atom Syndication Format (RFC 4287)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4287), and the [JSON Feed format](https://www.jsonfeed.org/), normalizing their differences into one consistent row shape. HTTP fetches are bounded by a timeout and a maximum response size so a query can never hang or exhaust memory on a hostile feed.

## SQL use cases & functions

Use `feed_items(input [, timeout_ms, max_items])` to get **one row per feed entry**, with `seq`, `guid`, `title`, `link`, `published`, `updated`, `author`, a `categories` list, `summary`, and `content` columns — ideal for monitoring news and blog feeds, building a podcast episode catalog, deduplicating items by GUID, or `UNNEST`-ing categories for tag analytics. Use `feed_info(input [, timeout_ms])` for a **single row of feed-level metadata**: `title`, `description`, `link`, detected `feed_type` (rss / atom / json), `language`, last `updated` time, and `item_count` — perfect for cataloging or health-checking a set of feeds.

New to the data? Browse the `feed_registry` view for a curated set of real, public feeds across all three formats, pick a `url`, and hand it to either table function. Runnable, network-free example queries are attached to each function and to the `main` schema.

Source code and issues: [github.com/Query-farm/vgi-feed](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-feed).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Curated Feed Registry

A browsable, zero-argument view listing well-known public **RSS / Atom / JSON** feeds — a starting point for discovery when you do not already have a feed URL in hand.

### Columns

- **`name`** — human-friendly feed name.
- **`url`** — the feed URL to hand to `feed_items(input)` or `feed_info(input)`.
- **`feed_type`** — the feed format (`rss`, `atom`, or `json`).
- **`category`** — a broad topic (Technology, News, Science, Security, Comics).
- **`description`** — a one-line summary of the feed.

### Notes

The registry is a static list, so it returns instantly with no network access. Pick a `url` here, then parse it with the feed table functions.

workers.summary: Query HL7 FHIR R4 REST servers and return resources as rows
workers.doc_md:
# FHIR R4 in SQL

![HL7 FHIR logo](https://hl7.org/fhir/assets/images/fhir-logo-www.png)

**Query live HL7 FHIR R4 healthcare APIs directly from SQL** — turn any FHIR REST server into DuckDB tables and run analytics over patients, clinical observations, and server capabilities without writing a line of integration code.

The `fhir` catalog connects to any [HL7 FHIR R4](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/) endpoint over plain REST/JSON and streams the resources back as DuckDB rows over Apache Arrow. FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is the modern HL7 standard that powers EHR, EMR, and health-data interoperability across hospitals, payers, and digital-health platforms. This connector is for analysts, data engineers, and clinical-informatics teams who want to explore, validate, or extract FHIR data with familiar SQL instead of bespoke API clients — point a function at a service base URL (for example `https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR4`) and start querying.

Under the hood the worker speaks the FHIR R4 [RESTful API](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/http.html) using nothing but the Go standard library, so it stays light and dependency-free while remaining faithful to the published [FHIR R4 specification](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/) (build source at [HL7/fhir on GitHub](https://github.com/HL7/fhir)). It follows FHIR [search](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/search.html) Bundle pagination automatically — every `link[].relation == "next"` page is fetched up to a safety cap — so a single query transparently spans many result pages. An optional OAuth bearer `token` argument unlocks protected endpoints, and non-2xx responses (including FHIR `OperationOutcome` bodies) surface as clean SQL errors rather than panics.

The connector turns a FHIR endpoint's core capabilities into SQL: pull clinical resources with their most-used fields flattened into typed columns, run a generic search across any resource type (Condition, Encounter, MedicationRequest, …) with an optional raw query string and `_count` page size, read an individual resource by its logical id, and discover which resource types and REST interactions a server supports from its [CapabilityStatement](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/capabilitystatement.html). Flattened results always carry the untouched resource JSON alongside the typed columns, so nothing is lost — anything not surfaced as a column is still reachable with `json_extract`. Built on the [vgi-go](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-go) SDK.

Not sure which endpoint to point at? Browse the built-in `fhir_servers` directory view for a curated list of public FHIR R4 base URLs, then hand one to any `fhir_*` function. Worked, runnable statements ship as each function's examples.

example_queries.sql: SELECT resource FROM fhir.main.fhir_read('https://r4.smarthealthit.org', 'Patient', '45a69bf0-7116-4f9f-a1d9-29700439b4a4');

## FHIR R4 Query Functions

This schema groups every table function exposed by the **vgi-fhir** connector. Each function takes a FHIR R4 service *base URL* as its first argument and returns resources as DuckDB rows over Apache Arrow.

The functions cover the common ways to pull data from a FHIR R4 endpoint: listing clinical resources with their most-used fields flattened into typed columns, running a generic search across any resource type, reading an individual resource by its logical id, and inspecting the server's CapabilityStatement for the resource types and REST interactions it supports.

### Notes

- Bundle pagination (`link[].relation == "next"`) is followed automatically up to a safety cap.
- The flattened functions also expose the untouched resource JSON (`raw` / `resource`) so nothing is lost.
- An optional `token` named argument supplies an OAuth bearer token for protected endpoints.
