## fhir_servers

A curated, credential-free directory of well-known **public HL7 FHIR R4** endpoints. It is a static list (no network access), so it always returns instantly and is the natural starting point for discovery: pick a `base_url` here and hand it to any `fhir_*` table function as its first argument.

### Columns

- `name` — human-friendly server name.
- `base_url` — the FHIR R4 service base URL (e.g. `https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR4`).
- `fhir_version` — the FHIR version served (all `4.0.1`).
- `requires_auth` — whether an OAuth bearer token is needed (all listed servers are open).
- `description` — what the endpoint is and what data it holds.

## fhir_search

Run a FHIR R4 [search](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/search.html) over a single resource type and return one row per matched resource.

### Usage

Call it with a FHIR R4 base URL and a resource type (for example `Condition`) to return one row per matched resource; runnable statements are attached as this function's examples.

Pass a raw `query` (e.g. `name=smith&_count=50`) and/or `count` to refine the search, and `token` for protected servers.

### Notes

- Follows Bundle `next` links across pages until exhausted or the safety cap is reached.
- The `resource` column holds the complete resource JSON, so any field not surfaced by the flattened functions is still reachable via `json_extract`.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## fhir_capabilities

Read a server's [CapabilityStatement](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/capabilitystatement.html) (`GET /metadata`) and list each resource type it exposes together with the REST interactions supported for that type.

### Usage

Call it with a FHIR R4 base URL to list every resource type the server exposes and the REST interactions it supports for each; runnable statements are attached as this function's examples.

### Notes

- `interactions` is a `VARCHAR[]`; `UNNEST` it to get one row per (resource type, interaction) pair.
- Use this first to discover what an unfamiliar EHR/FHIR endpoint supports before querying specific resource types.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT resource_type, UNNEST(interactions) AS interaction FROM fhir.main.fhir_capabilities('https://r4.smarthealthit.org');

workers.title: Fixed-Width Records
workers.tagline: Read and write fixed-width / flat-file / mainframe data in DuckDB with SQL — Perl unpack / Python struct / COBOL copybooks (COMP-3, EBCDIC, OCCURS, REDEFINES). A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Fixed-width / Perl-unpack / Python-struct / COBOL-copybook record parsing and formatting for SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# fixed

Fixed-width / flat-file record parsing and formatting over Apache Arrow. Brings Perl-`unpack`, Python-`struct`, and COBOL-copybook style layouts to SQL so you can ingest and emit mainframe and legacy flat-file data without an external ETL step.

A layout spec is given in one of three auto-detected formats — a Perl/Python `unpack` **template** string (e.g. `A10 N s>`), a **JSON** field list, or a COBOL **copybook** — and maps each field to a typed column (`BIGINT` / `REAL` / `DOUBLE` / `VARCHAR` / `BOOLEAN`, `DECIMAL(p,s)` for COMP-3 / zoned / implied-point numbers, `LIST` for `OCCURS` / `OCCURS … DEPENDING ON`, `STRUCT` for groups, nested JSON `fields`, and REDEFINES). Encodings are `ascii` (default) or `ebcdic` (CP037); record framing is `newline` (default), `fixed`, `rdw`, or `rdw_blocked`. The spec format is auto-detected from the spec text; on the table functions you can force it with `format =>` ('template' / 'json' / 'copybook') when a layout would otherwise be ambiguous. With the defaults (newline framing, ascii encoding) the common call is just `(record, spec)`.

Decoding a record into a `STRUCT` and re-encoding that `STRUCT` back to bytes are exact inverses, and whole files can be scanned, written, or introspected — including heterogeneous multi-record-type files (a UNION per record type) — without leaving SQL.

example_queries.description: Decode a fixed-width record into a typed struct with a template spec.
example_queries.sql: SELECT fixed.main.unpack_fixed('JohnDoe  00042', 'A8 N')

example_queries.description: Encode a struct back into a fixed-width record blob.
example_queries.sql: SELECT fixed.main.pack_fixed({'name': 'Jo', 'id': 7}, 'A2 N')

example_queries.description: Introspect how a layout spec resolves — fields, types, byte offsets — without reading data.
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM fixed.main.describe_fixed('name:A10 qty:9(5)')

example_queries.description: Write a relation out to a fixed-width file and report the write summary.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rows_written, bytes_written FROM fixed.main.write_fixed((FROM (VALUES ('ALICE', 5)) AS v(name, qty)), '/tmp/fixed_example.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')

example_queries.description: Scan the file just written back into typed rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('/tmp/fixed_example.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')

example_queries.title: unpack_pack_roundtrip
example_queries.description: Decode a fixed-width record into a typed struct, then encode that struct back into the original record bytes — pack_fixed and unpack_fixed are exact inverses.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT fixed.main.unpack_fixed('JohnDoe  00042', 'name:A8 qty:9(5)') AS decoded;
SELECT fixed.main.pack_fixed(fixed.main.unpack_fixed('JohnDoe  00042', 'name:A8 qty:9(5)'), 'name:A8 qty:9(5)')::VARCHAR = 'JohnDoe  00042' AS round_trips;

example_queries.title: describe_a_layout
example_queries.description: Introspect how a layout spec resolves — one row per field with its dotted path, DuckDB type, byte offset, and width — without reading any data.
example_queries.sql: SELECT path, sql_type, byte_offset, width FROM fixed.main.describe_fixed('name:A10 qty:9(5)') ORDER BY byte_offset;

example_queries.title: write_then_read_fixed
example_queries.description: Write a relation out to a fixed-width file and scan it straight back into typed rows.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT rows_written FROM fixed.main.write_fixed((FROM (VALUES ('ALICE', 5), ('BOB', 7)) AS v(name, qty)), '/tmp/fixed_executable_example.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)');
SELECT name, qty FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('/tmp/fixed_executable_example.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)') ORDER BY name;

example_queries.description: List the record-framing modes the worker accepts, with their meanings.
example_queries.sql: SELECT token, description FROM fixed.main.spec_reference WHERE topic = 'framing' ORDER BY token

example_queries.description: Show how each layout field kind maps to a DuckDB column type.
example_queries.sql: SELECT token AS field_kind, maps_to AS duckdb_type FROM fixed.main.spec_reference WHERE topic = 'field_kind' ORDER BY token

example_queries.description: Round-trip a heterogeneous flat file: read it into a UNION column and write it back out to a new multi-record file, reporting the counts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rows_written, bytes_written FROM fixed.main.write_multi((FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}')), 'data/_example_multi_out.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}')

example_queries.description: Write two accounts to a newline-framed fixed-width file (10-char name, 5-digit quantity) and report how much was written.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rows_written, bytes_written FROM fixed.main.write_fixed((FROM (VALUES ('ALICE', 5), ('BOB', 999)) AS v(name, qty)), 'data/_example_write.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')

example_queries.description: Write back-to-back fixed-length records (no newline) by forcing the framing named argument, returning just the record count.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rows_written FROM fixed.main.write_fixed((FROM (VALUES ('ALICE', 5), ('BOB', 999)) AS v(name, qty)), 'data/_example_write.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)', framing => 'fixed')

example_queries.description: Read a header/detail/trailer flat file into a UNION column and project the detail rows' sku and qty.
example_queries.sql: SELECT union_extract(record, 'D').sku AS sku, union_extract(record, 'D').qty AS qty FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}') WHERE union_tag(record) = 'D' ORDER BY sku

example_queries.description: Count records of each type in a heterogeneous multi-record file.
example_queries.sql: SELECT union_tag(record) AS record_type, count(*) AS n FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}') GROUP BY record_type ORDER BY record_type

example_queries.description: Profile a newline-delimited fixed-width feed of 7-digit ids: count the rows and report the id range.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS records, min(id) AS min_id, max(id) AS max_id FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/large.dat', 'id:9(7)')

example_queries.description: Glob several account files (10-char name, 5-digit qty) and total the quantity across every record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(qty) AS total_qty FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/acct*.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')

example_queries.description: Resolve a header/detail multi-record spec and show each record type's fields with their DuckDB types and byte offsets.
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_type, path, sql_type, byte_offset FROM fixed.main.describe_multi('{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}') ORDER BY record_type, byte_offset

example_queries.description: Count how many fields each record type declares in a multi-record layout.
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_type, count(*) AS field_count FROM fixed.main.describe_multi('{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}') GROUP BY record_type ORDER BY record_type

example_queries.description: Resolve a COBOL copybook (forcing the copybook format) and list only the repeating OCCURS fields.
example_queries.sql: SELECT path, sql_type, occurs FROM fixed.main.describe_fixed('01 REC. 05 SKU PIC X(8). 05 QTY PIC 9(3) OCCURS 4.', format => 'copybook') WHERE occurs IS NOT NULL

example_queries.description: Unpack an ASCII record by passing 'ascii' explicitly (the default).
example_queries.sql: SELECT fixed.main.unpack_fixed('JohnDoe 12345', 'A8 A5', 'ascii')

example_queries.description: Unpack an EBCDIC (CP037) record; the encoding also governs zoned/COMP-3 sign nibbles.
example_queries.sql: SELECT fixed.main.unpack_fixed(rec, 'A8 N', 'ebcdic') FROM (SELECT 'JohnDoe \x00\x00\x00\x2A'::BLOB AS rec)

example_queries.description: Pack a struct into an EBCDIC (CP037) record blob; the encoding also governs zoned/COMP-3 sign nibbles.
example_queries.sql: SELECT fixed.main.pack_fixed({'name': 'Jo', 'id': 7}, 'A2 N', 'ebcdic')

example_queries.description: EBCDIC round-trip: pack with the same encoding that unpack used.
example_queries.sql: SELECT fixed.main.pack_fixed(fixed.main.unpack_fixed(rec, 'A2 N', 'ebcdic'), 'A2 N', 'ebcdic') FROM (SELECT 'Jo\x00\x00\x00\x07'::BLOB AS rec)

example_queries.description: Decode one detail record into a UNION and read its tag + a field.
example_queries.sql: SELECT union_tag(u) AS kind, union_extract(u, 'D').sku AS sku FROM (SELECT fixed.main.unpack_multi('DWIDGET    00042', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"pad","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"pad","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}') AS u)

agent_tasks: I have one fixed-width record 'JOHN      00042' where the first 10 characters are an account name and the next 5 are a zero-padded quantity. Parse it and return the quantity as a single integer column named qty.

The file data/large.dat is a newline-delimited fixed-width feed where each record is a single 7-digit zero-padded id. Profile it: return one row with a column named records (the record count), a column named min_id, and a column named max_id.

A nightly job drops one or more fixed-width account files into data/, named acct1.dat, acct2.dat, and so on. Each record is a 10-character account name followed by a 5-digit zero-padded quantity. Read all of the acct*.dat files at once and return the total quantity across every record as a single column named total_qty.

We received a mainframe extract at data/ebcdic_comp3.dat. It is EBCDIC-encoded and fixed-length (no line delimiters between records). Each record is a 5-byte name (PIC X(5)) followed by a signed packed-decimal amount PIC S9(3)V99 COMP-3. Decode the file and return the largest amount as a single column named max_amount.

We need to emit a single fixed-width record for an export. The layout is a 10-character left-justified, space-padded account name followed by a 5-digit zero-padded quantity. Build the record for account name 'ALICE' with quantity 5 and return the resulting record text as a single column named record.

A mainframe ingest job needs an account record encoded the way the host expects it: the name as a 5-byte EBCDIC field (PIC X(5)) followed by a signed packed-decimal amount PIC S9(3)V99 COMP-3. Encode name 'ACME' with amount 123.45 and return the resulting record bytes as an uppercase hex string in a single column named record_hex.

Export two accounts to a newline-delimited fixed-width file at data/_agent_write.dat, where each record is a 10-character left-justified name followed by a 5-digit zero-padded quantity: ALICE with quantity 5 and BOB with quantity 999. Return the write summary with a column named rows_written and a column named bytes_written.

I have the fixed-width layout 'name:A10 qty:9(5)' — a 10-character name followed by a 5-digit zero-padded quantity. Without reading any data, work out the byte offset at which the qty field begins and return it as a single column named qty_offset.

This multi-record layout has a 1-byte record-type discriminator at offset 0 and two record types: a header 'H' with one field, and a detail 'D' with a 10-char sku and a 5-digit qty. The spec is {"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}. Without reading any data, return how many fields the 'D' record type declares, as a single column named field_count.

The file data/multi.dat is a heterogeneous fixed-width feed whose records have a 1-byte record-type tag at offset 0: 'H' header, 'D' detail, 'T' trailer. Each record's first byte is the tag; a detail record is the tag plus a 10-char sku and a 5-digit qty. The layout spec is {"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}. Read the file and return how many detail ('D') records it contains, as a single column named detail_count.

I have one heterogeneous record 'DWIDGET    00042'. Its first byte is a record-type tag; 'D' means a detail record laid out as the tag byte, a 10-character sku, then a 5-digit zero-padded qty. The multi-record spec is {"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}. Decode the record and return its qty as a single column named qty.

Round-trip the heterogeneous file data/multi.dat: read it into its UNION representation and write it straight back out to data/_task_multi_out.dat using the same multi-record layout, then report how many records were written as a single column named rows_written. The layout spec (for both the read and the write) is {"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}.
Using the fixed-format worker's built-in reference table, list how many record-framing modes it supports. Return the count as a single column named framing_modes.

# fixed.main

The single (and only) schema for the `fixed` worker — the catalog name matches the `ATTACH` name, so qualify calls as `fixed.main.<fn>(...)`.

It provides functions for parsing a record into a `STRUCT` and encoding a `STRUCT` back to bytes (an exact inverse pair), scanning and emitting whole fixed-width files (including heterogeneous multi-record-type files as a UNION per record type), and introspecting a layout — one row per field with its dotted path, type, byte offset, width, and OCCURS info — without reading data.

Layouts are given as Perl/Python `unpack` templates, JSON field specs (which may nest a `fields` array for `STRUCT`/`LIST`-of-`STRUCT` sub-records), or COBOL copybooks (auto-detected; override with `format =>` on the table functions). Encodings are `ascii` (default) or `ebcdic` (CP037); record framing is `newline` (default), `fixed`, `rdw`, or `rdw_blocked`.

Field kinds map to columns as:

- text / hex → `VARCHAR`
- integers → `BIGINT`
- COMP-3 / zoned / implied-point → `DECIMAL(p,s)`
- OCCURS and OCCURS … DEPENDING ON → `LIST`
- group / nested-fields / REDEFINES → `STRUCT`

tables.name: spec_reference
tables.comment: Reference registry of the worker's spec formats, encoding / framing / compression option tokens, and field-kind to DuckDB-type mappings.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A static lookup table of the fixed-format worker's own vocabulary, so an agent can discover the valid option tokens and type mappings before building a `spec`. One row per (topic, token): the `topic` column groups the rows into `spec_format` (the three auto-detected layout formats — template, json, copybook), `encoding` (ascii / ebcdic), `framing` (newline / fixed / rdw / rdw_blocked), `compression` (auto / none / gzip / zstd), and `field_kind` (how each layout field kind maps to a DuckDB column type). The `token` column is the accepted value (or field-kind name), `maps_to` is the resulting DuckDB type for field_kind rows (empty otherwise), and `description` explains it. Query it to enumerate the legal `encoding =>` / `framing =>` / `compression =>` / `format =>` values, or to see which DuckDB type a COMP-3 or OCCURS field becomes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# spec_reference

A browsable, credential-free registry of the `fixed` worker's own vocabulary — query it to discover valid option values and type mappings before constructing a layout `spec`.

Each row is a (topic, token) pair:

- **topic** — one of `spec_format`, `encoding`, `framing`, `compression`, or `field_kind`.
- **token** — the accepted value for that topic (or the field-kind name).
- **maps_to** — for `field_kind` rows, the DuckDB column type the kind maps to; empty otherwise.
- **description** — a one-line explanation.

For example, filter `topic = 'framing'` to list the record-framing modes, or `topic = 'field_kind'` to see how a COMP-3 or OCCURS field is typed.

vgi.example_queries.description: List the record-framing modes the worker accepts, with their meanings.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT token, description FROM fixed.main.spec_reference WHERE topic = 'framing' ORDER BY token

vgi.example_queries.description: Show how each layout field kind maps to a DuckDB column type.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT token AS field_kind, maps_to AS duckdb_type FROM fixed.main.spec_reference WHERE topic = 'field_kind' ORDER BY token

functions.name: copy_fixed
functions.comment: Read a fixed-width / flat-file / COBOL-copybook file into the COPY target table (the COPY-FROM counterpart of read_fixed)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Load a fixed-width / flat-file / COBOL-copybook file straight into a DuckDB table — the COPY-FROM counterpart of read_fixed. It is invoked as a COPY statement (not called directly):

```sql
COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed', spec '<layout>');
```

The format name is catalog-qualified by the ATTACH name (e.g. 'fixed.fixed'). Each record is decoded per the `spec` option (a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook; auto-detected unless `format` is given) and the decoded columns are assigned to the COPY target table's columns BY POSITION and cast to each target column's type, so the spec must produce the same number of columns in the same order. Options are named: `spec` (required), `format`, `encoding` ('ascii'/'ebcdic'), `framing` ('newline'/'fixed'/'rdw'/'rdw_blocked'), `record_length` (bytes, 'fixed' framing only), plus `endpoint`/`region`/`url_style`/`use_ssl` for `s3://` sources. `path` may be local, `s3://`, or `http(s)://`. Use it to ingest mainframe or legacy flat-file data into an existing table without a read_fixed call.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Load a fixed-width file into a table:

```sql
COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed', spec '<layout>');
```

Decoded columns map to the target table's columns by position (cast to each type). Named options: `spec` (required), `format`, `encoding`, `framing`, `record_length`, and S3 overrides. The COPY-FROM counterpart of `read_fixed`.
tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
`copy_fixed` is invoked through `COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed', …)`, not as a table function, so it returns **no result set of its own**. The rows decoded from the file are inserted into the COPY **target table**, and DuckDB reports the number of rows loaded as the statement's `Count`. The materialized columns are therefore the target table's own columns — each decoded field is mapped to a target column **by position** and cast to that column's type, so the `spec` must produce the same number of columns, in the same order, as the table.

For a target table `accounts(name VARCHAR, qty INTEGER)` loaded with the spec `name:A10 qty:9(5)`, the loaded columns are:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | The target column populated from the first decoded field (bytes 0–9). |
| `qty` | INTEGER | The target column populated from the second decoded field, cast from the 5-digit value. |

functions.name: write_multi
functions.comment: Write a relation's UNION column to a multi-record-type file (inverse of read_multi)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Write a relation whose single UNION column holds heterogeneous records back out to a multi-record-type fixed-width / flat file — the inverse of read_multi. The `data` relation (passed as a subquery, e.g. `(FROM read_multi(...))` or a `(SELECT ...)`) must have exactly ONE column: a sparse UNION whose variant names are the discriminator tags of the `spec` (the exact shape read_multi emits). For each row the active variant gives its record type and its `STRUCT` field values; the matching variant layout encodes those fields, the discriminator field is stamped with the tag, the records are framed per the named `framing =>` argument ('newline' the default, 'fixed', 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'), encoded under named `encoding =>` ('ascii' the default, or 'ebcdic'/CP037), optionally compressed via `compression =>`, and streamed to `path` (overwritten if it exists). The `spec` is the SAME multi-record JSON as read_multi: a `discriminator` ({offset,width}) plus a `records` map of tag → JSON field list. `encoding`, `framing`, and `compression` are NAMED arguments. Use it to emit header/detail/trailer or other heterogeneous mainframe flat files from SQL. Returns exactly one summary row: `rows_written BIGINT` and `bytes_written BIGINT`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Write a relation's single UNION column out to a heterogeneous multi-record-type fixed-width file — the inverse of read_multi. The relation is a subquery with one UNION column whose variant names are the spec's discriminator tags. The `spec` is the same multi-record JSON (`discriminator` + `records`). Each row's active variant is encoded with its layout and the discriminator stamped with the tag. Optional NAMED args: `encoding =>` ('ascii'/'ebcdic'), `framing =>` ('newline'/'fixed'/'rdw'/'rdw_blocked'), `compression =>`. Returns one row `(rows_written BIGINT, bytes_written BIGINT)`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Round-trip a heterogeneous flat file: read it into a UNION column and write it back out to a new multi-record file, reporting the counts.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rows_written, bytes_written FROM fixed.main.write_multi((FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}')), 'data/_example_multi_out.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}')

functions.name: read_multi
functions.comment: Read a heterogeneous (multi-record-type) flat file into a UNION column

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan a heterogeneous fixed-width / flat file whose records have DIFFERENT layouts — e.g. a header, many detail rows, and a trailer — selected by a 'record type' discriminator field. The `spec` is a JSON object: a `discriminator` ({offset, width} of the bytes that identify each record's type) and a `records` map of tag → field list (each field list uses the same JSON field syntax as `read_fixed`'s JSON spec, so every field type / group / OCCURS works per record type). Each record is framed per `framing =>` ('newline' the default, 'fixed', 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'), its discriminator bytes pick the matching variant, and it is decoded with that variant's layout. The result is a single column `record` of type UNION — one `STRUCT` variant per record type, the variant names being the discriminator tags. Use `union_tag(record)` to get a row's record type and `union_extract(record, 'D')` to pull out a given variant's `STRUCT`. An unmatched discriminator value is an error unless the spec gives a `default` tag. `path` may glob and may be a cloud URL. `framing`, `encoding`, `compression`, and `record_length` are NAMED arguments.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Scan a heterogeneous flat file whose records have different layouts selected by a discriminator field. The JSON `spec` declares a `discriminator` ({offset,width}) and a `records` map of tag → JSON field list; the result is one UNION column `record` with a `STRUCT` variant per record type. Use `union_tag(record)` / `union_extract(record, 'TAG')`. Named args: `framing =>`, `encoding =>`, `compression =>`, `record_length =>`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Read a header/detail/trailer flat file into a UNION column and project the detail rows' sku and qty.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT union_extract(record, 'D').sku AS sku, union_extract(record, 'D').qty AS qty FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}') WHERE union_tag(record) = 'D' ORDER BY sku

vgi.example_queries.description: Count records of each type in a heterogeneous multi-record file.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT union_tag(record) AS record_type, count(*) AS n FROM fixed.main.read_multi('data/multi.dat', '{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}],"T":[{"type":"filler","width":1},{"name":"cnt","type":"int","digits":6}]}}') GROUP BY record_type ORDER BY record_type

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result is always a **single** column, `record`, whose UNION variants are determined by the multi-record `spec` argument — one `STRUCT` variant per record type, named by that record type's discriminator tag. Read a row's record type with `union_tag(record)` and pull a variant's `STRUCT` with `union_extract(record, '<tag>')`.

For example, the header/detail/trailer spec used in the examples below (record types `H`, `D`, `T`) yields:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `record` | UNION(H STRUCT(co VARCHAR), D STRUCT(sku VARCHAR, qty BIGINT), T STRUCT(cnt BIGINT)) | A sparse UNION with one `STRUCT` variant per record type in the spec — here `H` (header), `D` (detail), and `T` (trailer). |

functions.name: read_fixed
functions.comment: Read a fixed-width file (template / JSON / copybook spec) into rows

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan a fixed-width / flat-file data file into typed rows. `path` may be a glob (e.g. '/data/*.dat'); matching files are read in sorted order and their rows concatenated. Each record is framed per the named `framing =>` argument ('newline' the default, 'fixed', 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked') and decoded into a row of typed columns according to the layout `spec` — a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook (format auto-detected unless you pass `format =>` 'template' / 'json' / 'copybook'). In a template spec, prefix each field with a name to set its column name, e.g. `'name:A10 qty:9(5)'`; unnamed fields become positional `field_1`, `field_2`, …. The named `encoding =>` argument is 'ascii' (default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037). The named `record_length =>` argument is the per-record length in BYTES; it is only used for 'fixed' framing (back-to-back records of equal length) and defaults to the length implied by the `spec`; it is ignored for the other framings. `format`, `encoding`, `framing`, and `record_length` are all NAMED arguments. The returned column set is dynamic: it is determined by the spec, with OCCURS becoming `LIST` columns and groups / REDEFINES becoming `STRUCT` columns. Use it to ingest mainframe or legacy flat-file data into SQL. This is the file-scanning counterpart of unpack_fixed and the inverse of write_fixed.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Scan a fixed-width file into rows, decoding each record per the layout `spec` (template, JSON, or COBOL copybook). `path` may glob (e.g. `read_fixed('/data/*.dat', 'A10 N')`), reading matching files in sorted order. Optional NAMED args: `format =>`, `encoding =>` ('ascii'/'ebcdic'), `framing =>` ('newline'/'fixed'/'rdw'/'rdw_blocked'), and `record_length =>` (per-record length in bytes, used only for `fixed` framing). The returned columns are dynamic — they depend on the spec, with OCCURS → `LIST` and group/REDEFINES → `STRUCT`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Profile a newline-delimited fixed-width feed of 7-digit ids: count the rows and report the id range.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS records, min(id) AS min_id, max(id) AS max_id FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/large.dat', 'id:9(7)')

vgi.example_queries.description: Glob several account files (10-char name, 5-digit qty) and total the quantity across every record.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(qty) AS total_qty FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/acct*.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The returned columns are **dynamic** — determined by the layout `spec`, one column per top-level field. Column names come from the field names in the spec — name your fields (e.g. `name:A10 qty:9(5)`); **unnamed** template fields become positional `field_1`, `field_2`, …. Column types follow the field kind: text/hex → `VARCHAR`, integer → `BIGINT`, float/double → `REAL`/`DOUBLE`, COMP-3 / zoned / implied-point decimal → `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `?` boolean → `BOOLEAN`, OCCURS / repeat → `LIST` of the element type, and group / REDEFINES → `STRUCT` of the child fields.

For the spec `name:A10 qty:9(5)` the result columns are:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `VARCHAR` | The 10-byte text field decoded from bytes 0–9. |
| `qty` | `BIGINT` | The 5-digit zoned integer decoded from bytes 10–14. |

For the single-field spec `id:9(7)` the result is one column:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `BIGINT` | The 7-digit zoned integer decoded from bytes 0–6. |
tags.vgi.title: Read Fixed-Width File

arguments.name: path
arguments.description: Path(s) to the fixed-width file(s) to read: a single path, or a list of paths to read several files in one call (their rows are concatenated in order). A path may be a glob (e.g. 'data/*.dat') to scan matching files in sorted order, or a cloud URL: 's3://bucket/key' (AWS S3, or R2/MinIO/GCS-HMAC via a `CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, …, ENDPOINT …)`) or 'https://host/file'. Credentials come from the matching DuckDB secret, resolved per path scope — so a list spanning several buckets picks the right secret for each.

arguments.name: spec
arguments.description: The record layout to decode each row with: a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook. Determines the output column names and types; format is auto-detected unless `format` is given.

arguments.name: format
arguments.description: Force how `spec` is interpreted: 'template', 'json', or 'copybook'. Omit to auto-detect.

arguments.name: encoding
arguments.description: Byte encoding of the file: 'ascii' (the default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037).

arguments.name: framing
arguments.description: How records are delimited in the file: 'newline' (the default), 'fixed' (back-to-back records of equal length), 'rdw', or 'rdw_blocked'.

arguments.name: record_length
arguments.description: The length of each record in BYTES. Used only for 'fixed' framing (back-to-back equal-length records); ignored for the other framings. Defaults to the length implied by the layout `spec`.

arguments.name: compression
arguments.description: Input compression: 'auto' (the default — detect gzip/zstd from the file's magic bytes, else read raw), 'none', 'gzip', or 'zstd'. Applies to local and cloud paths alike; decompression happens before framing/decoding.

arguments.name: max_decompressed_bytes
arguments.description: Safety cap on total DECOMPRESSED bytes per file (a decompression-bomb backstop; default 16 GiB). Only applies to gzip/zstd input — uncompressed files are unbounded. Raise it to read a legitimately huge compressed file.

arguments.name: endpoint
arguments.description: Custom S3 endpoint for an `s3://` path (e.g. MinIO/R2 'host:9000'); a scheme is inferred from `use_ssl` when omitted. Overrides any endpoint from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: region
arguments.description: AWS region for an `s3://` path. Overrides the region from a CREATE SECRET.

arguments.name: url_style
arguments.description: S3 addressing for an `s3://` path: 'path' (path-style, e.g. MinIO) or 'vhost' (the default). Overrides a CREATE SECRET's URL_STYLE.

arguments.name: use_ssl
arguments.description: Whether to use TLS for an `s3://` path's custom endpoint (default true). Set false for a plain-HTTP endpoint such as a local MinIO.

examples: SELECT count(*) AS records, min(id) AS min_id, max(id) AS max_id FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/large.dat', 'id:9(7)')
SELECT sum(qty) AS total_qty FROM fixed.main.read_fixed('data/acct*.dat', 'name:A10 qty:9(5)')

result_columns.name: name
result_columns.description: The 10-byte text field decoded from bytes 0–9.

result_columns.name: qty
result_columns.description: The 5-digit zoned integer decoded from bytes 10–14.

result_columns.name: id
result_columns.description: The 7-digit zoned integer decoded from bytes 0–6.

functions.name: describe_multi
functions.comment: Describe a multi-record spec (each record type's fields) without reading data

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Introspect a multi-record `spec` without reading any data: returns one row per (record type, field), describing how every variant's layout resolves. The leading `record_type` column is the discriminator tag; the remaining columns mirror describe_fixed — `path` (dotted field path), `depth`, `kind` (codec label), `sql_type` (the DuckDB type the field maps to), `byte_offset` and `width`, `occurs` (OCCURS maximum, else NULL), and `depending_on` (the OCCURS … DEPENDING ON controller, else NULL). The `spec` is the same multi-record JSON object as read_multi (a `discriminator` plus a `records` map of tag → field list). Use it to debug a multi-record layout or document each record type before running read_multi / unpack_multi.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Describe how a multi-record `spec` resolves — one row per (record type, field) with its dotted path, codec kind, DuckDB type, byte offset, width, and OCCURS info. Reads no data. The multi-record counterpart of describe_fixed.

vgi.example_queries.description: Resolve a header/detail multi-record spec and show each record type's fields with their DuckDB types and byte offsets.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT record_type, path, sql_type, byte_offset FROM fixed.main.describe_multi('{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}') ORDER BY record_type, byte_offset

vgi.example_queries.description: Count how many fields each record type declares in a multi-record layout.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT record_type, count(*) AS field_count FROM fixed.main.describe_multi('{"discriminator":{"offset":0,"width":1},"records":{"H":[{"name":"co","type":"str","width":20}],"D":[{"name":"sku","type":"str","width":10},{"name":"qty","type":"int","digits":5}]}}') GROUP BY record_type ORDER BY record_type

functions.name: describe_fixed
functions.comment: Describe a fixed-width layout spec (fields, types, offsets) without reading data

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Introspect a fixed-width layout `spec` without reading any data: returns one row per field (group items and their children included) describing how the spec resolves. Columns: `path` (dotted field path, e.g. `item.sku`), `depth` (nesting level), `kind` (codec label, e.g. `text`, `int32 LE`, `comp-3`), `sql_type` (the DuckDB column type the field maps to, e.g. `VARCHAR`, `DECIMAL(9,2)`, `STRUCT`, `BIGINT[]`), `byte_offset` and `width` (static byte position and per-occurrence width), `occurs` (declared repeat / OCCURS maximum, else NULL), and `depending_on` (the controlling field for `OCCURS … DEPENDING ON`, else NULL). `spec` is a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook (auto-detected unless you pass `format =>` 'template'/'json'/'copybook'). Use it to debug a spec, document a layout, or check field offsets before running `read_fixed`. For a variable-length layout (OCCURS DEPENDING ON) the reported offsets are the static positions before the table.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Describe how a fixed-width layout `spec` resolves — one row per field with its dotted path, codec kind, DuckDB type, byte offset, width, OCCURS count, and DEPENDING ON controller. Reads no data. `format =>` forces template/json/copybook.

vgi.example_queries.description: Introspect a two-field template layout: show each field's DuckDB type, byte offset, and width.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT path, sql_type, byte_offset, width FROM fixed.main.describe_fixed('name:A10 qty:9(5)') ORDER BY byte_offset

vgi.example_queries.description: Resolve a COBOL copybook (forcing the copybook format) and list only the repeating OCCURS fields.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT path, sql_type, occurs FROM fixed.main.describe_fixed('01 REC. 05 SKU PIC X(8). 05 QTY PIC 9(3) OCCURS 4.', format => 'copybook') WHERE occurs IS NOT NULL

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: kind

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The controlling field name for an `OCCURS … DEPENDING ON` table, else NULL.

functions.name: copy_to_fixed
functions.comment: Write the COPY source out to a fixed-width / flat-file / COBOL-copybook file (the COPY-TO counterpart of write_fixed)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Write a query or table out to a fixed-width / flat-file / COBOL-copybook file — the COPY-TO counterpart of write_fixed. It is invoked as a COPY statement (not called directly):

```sql
COPY (<query>|<table>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed_out', spec '<layout>');
```

The writer uses a DISTINCT format name 'fixed.fixed_out' (catalog-qualified by the ATTACH name) because the VGI SDK advertises FROM and TO as separate formats. Each input column is matched to a layout field BY NAME, encoded to record bytes per the `spec` option (a Perl/Python `unpack` template, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook; auto-detected unless `format` is given), framed per `framing`, and written to `<path>` (overwritten if it exists). Options are named: `spec` (required), `format`, `encoding` ('ascii'/'ebcdic'), `framing` ('newline'/'fixed'/'rdw'/'rdw_blocked'), plus `endpoint`/`region`/`url_style`/`use_ssl` for `s3://` destinations. NOTE: CREATE SECRET credentials are NOT forwarded on the COPY-TO path — use named S3 overrides, ambient credentials, or write_fixed for secret-backed cloud writes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Write a relation to a fixed-width file:

```sql
COPY (<query>|<table>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed_out', spec '<layout>');
```

Input columns map to layout fields by name. Named options: `spec` (required), `format`, `encoding`, `framing`, and S3 overrides. The COPY-TO counterpart of `write_fixed`.
tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
`copy_to_fixed` is invoked through `COPY (<query>|<table>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT 'fixed.fixed_out', …)`, not as a table function, so it returns **no result set of its own**. The COPY source rows are encoded to fixed-width records and written to `<path>` (overwritten if it exists); each input column is matched to a layout field **by name** before encoding. DuckDB reports only a single value — the number of rows written:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Count` | BIGINT | The number of source rows written to the file, reported by DuckDB as the `COPY … TO` statement's result. |
tags.vgi.title: Write Fixed-Width File (COPY TO)

functions.name: unpack_fixed
functions.comment: Parse a fixed-width record into a `STRUCT` using the given layout spec (template / JSON / copybook), assuming ASCII bytes

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a single fixed-width / flat-file record (a `VARCHAR` or `BLOB`) into a typed `STRUCT` whose fields are named and typed by the layout spec, controlling the byte `encoding`. This 3-argument overload adds a positional `encoding` argument: 'ascii' (the default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037). EBCDIC affects not only character fields but also the sign nibbles of zoned and COMP-3 (packed-decimal) numbers. The spec is a Perl/Python `unpack` template string, a JSON field list, or a COBOL copybook (auto-detected), and supports packed/zoned decimals, OCCURS lists (→ `LIST`), groups and REDEFINES (→ `STRUCT`). In a template spec, prefix each field with a name to set its `STRUCT` field name, e.g. `'name:A10 qty:9(5)'`; unnamed fields become `field_1`, `field_2`, …. The spec is a bind-time constant so the `STRUCT` output type is known at plan time. This is the inverse of pack_fixed when the same encoding is supplied to both.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Parse a fixed-width record into a `STRUCT` under an explicit byte encoding, e.g. `unpack_fixed(rec, 'A8 N', 'ebcdic')`. The third argument is `encoding` — 'ascii' (default) or 'ebcdic' (CP037), which also governs zoned/COMP-3 sign nibbles. It is positional, not named.

vgi.example_queries.description: Unpack an ASCII record by passing 'ascii' explicitly (the default).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fixed.main.unpack_fixed('JohnDoe 12345', 'A8 A5', 'ascii')

vgi.example_queries.description: Unpack an EBCDIC (CP037) record; the encoding also governs zoned/COMP-3 sign nibbles.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fixed.main.unpack_fixed(rec, 'A8 N', 'ebcdic') FROM (SELECT 'JohnDoe \x00\x00\x00\x2A'::BLOB AS rec)

tags.vgi.title: Unpack Fixed-Width Record (with encoding)

arguments.name: spec

examples: SELECT fixed.main.unpack_fixed('JohnDoe 12345', 'A8 A5', 'ascii')
SELECT fixed.main.unpack_fixed(rec, 'A8 N', 'ebcdic') FROM (SELECT 'JohnDoe \x00\x00\x00\x2A'::BLOB AS rec)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a single record from a heterogeneous (multi-record-type) feed into a DuckDB UNION value — the scalar counterpart of read_multi. The `spec` is the same multi-record JSON object (a `discriminator` of {offset, width} plus a `records` map of record-type tag → JSON field list); the record's discriminator bytes pick the variant to decode it with. The result is a UNION with one `STRUCT` variant per record type, named by the discriminator tag — use `union_tag(...)` for the record type and `union_extract(..., 'TAG')` to pull a variant's `STRUCT`. An unmatched discriminator value errors unless the spec gives a `default` tag. The 3-argument overload adds a positional `encoding` ('ascii' default, or 'ebcdic'/CP037, which also governs the discriminator bytes). The spec is a bind-time constant so the UNION type is known at plan time.

workers.summary: Offline reverse geocoding: lat/lon -> place, country, admin regions, timezone, plus haversine distance
workers.doc_md:
# Offline Reverse Geocoding in SQL

**Turn latitude/longitude coordinates into the nearest city, country, admin regions and IANA timezone -- entirely offline, with no API keys, no rate limits and no network calls -- directly in DuckDB.**

`geocode` is a VGI worker that brings fast, hermetic **reverse geocoding** to SQL. Point it at any column of `(lat, lon)` coordinates and it enriches each row with the nearest known place name, its ISO-3166 country code, first- and second-level administrative regions (state/region, county/district), and the local IANA timezone. Because every lookup runs against bundled spatial databases rather than a hosted geocoding API, it works on air-gapped hosts, scales to millions of rows without per-request billing, and returns deterministic results. It is built for data engineers, analysts and GIS practitioners who need to attach human-readable geography and time zones to coordinate data sets -- IoT and GPS traces, telemetry, event logs, store/asset locations -- without leaving the database.

Under the hood, place lookups are powered by [`reverse_geocoder`](https://github.com/thampiman/reverse-geocoder) ([PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/reverse_geocoder/)), which queries a [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/) cities KD-tree to find the nearest populated place in sub-millisecond time. Timezone resolution uses [`timezonefinder`](https://github.com/jannikmi/timezonefinder) ([documentation](https://timezonefinder.readthedocs.io/)), which maps a point to its [IANA time-zone](https://www.iana.org/time-zones) polygon offline. Distances are computed with the great-circle [haversine formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haversine_formula). Every function is total and NULL-safe: a NULL or out-of-range coordinate yields `NULL` rather than an error, so the functions are safe to drop into large batch queries.

## What you can do

The worker groups its capabilities into three areas:

- **Place lookup** -- resolve a coordinate to the nearest city, its ISO-3166 country, and first- and second-level administrative regions (state/region and county/district), either one attribute at a time or as a single combined `STRUCT` record for the whole place.
- **Timezone** -- map a coordinate to its IANA timezone name (e.g. `America/New_York`) for localizing timestamps.
- **Distance** -- measure the great-circle (haversine) distance in kilometers between two coordinates.

Every operation is a per-row scalar you can use inline in any projection or predicate, so enriching a whole coordinate column -- or filtering it by proximity -- is a single `SELECT` with no joins, staging tables, or API round-trips.

Backed by GeoNames cities (`reverse_geocoder`, LGPL-3.0, used as an unmodified dependency) and offline IANA timezone polygons (`timezonefinder`, MIT).
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'geocode' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-geocode@v0.2.0 vgi-geocode-worker');

SELECT geocode.nearest_city(40.7128, -74.0060);          -- 'New York City'
SELECT geocode.country_code(48.8566, 2.3522);            -- 'FR'
SELECT geocode.admin1(35.6762, 139.6503);                -- 'Tokyo'
SELECT geocode.admin2(34.0522, -118.2437);               -- county / district
SELECT geocode.timezone(40.7128, -74.0060);              -- 'America/New_York'
SELECT geocode.reverse_geocode(40.7128, -74.0060);       -- STRUCT(...)
SELECT geocode.reverse_geocode(40.7128, -74.0060).city;  -- 'New York City'
SELECT geocode.distance_km(40.7128, -74.0060, 51.5074, -0.1278);  -- ~5570 km

example_queries.description: Enrich a set of coordinates with nearest city and ISO-3166 country code.
example_queries.sql: SELECT lat, lon, geocode.main.nearest_city(lat, lon) AS city, geocode.main.country_code(lat, lon) AS country FROM (VALUES (40.7128, -74.0060), (48.8566, 2.3522), (35.6762, 139.6503)) AS t(lat, lon)

example_queries.description: Count coordinates per country by reverse-geocoding to a country code.
example_queries.sql: SELECT geocode.main.country_code(lat, lon) AS country, count(*) AS n FROM (VALUES (40.7, -74.0), (34.0, -118.2), (48.8, 2.35)) AS t(lat, lon) GROUP BY country ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: Keep only points within 1000 km of Paris using the haversine distance.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, round(geocode.main.distance_km(lat, lon, 48.8566, 2.3522)) AS km_to_paris FROM (VALUES ('London', 51.5074, -0.1278), ('New York', 40.7128, -74.0060)) AS t(name, lat, lon) WHERE geocode.main.distance_km(lat, lon, 48.8566, 2.3522) < 1000

## Reverse-geocoding scalars

Per-row scalar functions over Apache Arrow that turn a `(lat, lon)` coordinate into human-readable geography: the nearest city, its ISO-3166 country code, the first- and second-level administrative regions, and a single combined nearest-place record. All take coordinates positionally.

## Timezone and distance

The schema also resolves a coordinate to its IANA timezone name (for localizing timestamps) and computes the great-circle (haversine) distance in kilometers between two points.

## Semantics

Every function returns `NULL` for a `NULL` or out-of-range input, never an error, so it is safe to drop into large batch queries. Lookups are backed by GeoNames cities and offline IANA timezone polygons -- no API keys or network required.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Resolve a latitude/longitude to the **full nearest-place record** in a single call, returning a `STRUCT(city, admin1, admin2, country_code, place_lat, place_lon)` computed **entirely offline**.

## When to use
Prefer this over the single-field helpers (`nearest_city`, `country_code`, `admin1`, `admin2`) when you need several attributes at once -- it does the KD-tree lookup once and lets you pluck fields with dot access.

## Inputs / outputs
- `lat` `DOUBLE` in `[-90, 90]`, `lon` `DOUBLE` in `[-180, 180]`.
- Returns a `STRUCT` with `city`, `admin1`, `admin2` (`VARCHAR`), `country_code` (`VARCHAR`), and `place_lat`/`place_lon` (`DOUBLE`, the coordinates of the matched GeoNames place).

## Behavior & edge cases
- For a `NULL` or out-of-range coordinate the **entire struct is `NULL`**.
- Individual fields may be `NULL` (notably `admin2`) even for a valid match.
- Access fields with `reverse_geocode(lat, lon).city`, etc.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# reverse_geocode

Full nearest-place record for `(lat, lon)` as a `STRUCT`, computed offline.

## Columns (struct fields)

| field | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `city` | VARCHAR | Nearest city / place name. |
| `admin1` | VARCHAR | First-level admin region (state / region). |
| `admin2` | VARCHAR | Second-level admin region (county / district). |
| `country_code` | VARCHAR | ISO-3166 alpha-2 country code. |
| `place_lat` | DOUBLE | Latitude of the matched place. |
| `place_lon` | DOUBLE | Longitude of the matched place. |

## Usage

```sql
SELECT geocode.main.reverse_geocode(40.7128, -74.0060);        -- STRUCT(...)
SELECT geocode.main.reverse_geocode(35.6762, 139.6503).city;   -- 'Tokyo'
```

## Notes

Whole struct is `NULL` for `NULL`/out-of-range inputs; `admin2` is often `NULL`.

Return the **first-level administrative region** -- state, province, or region -- of the nearest known place to a latitude/longitude, computed **offline** from the bundled GeoNames index.

## When to use
Use it to roll coordinate data up to a state/province for regional reporting, territory assignment, or joins to administrative reference data.

## Inputs / outputs
- `lat` `DOUBLE` in `[-90, 90]`, `lon` `DOUBLE` in `[-180, 180]`.
- Returns the admin1 name as `VARCHAR`, or `NULL`.

- Names follow GeoNames conventions (e.g. `New York`, `Tokyo`, `Bavaria`) and can vary in spelling/transliteration between snapshots.
- `NULL` or out-of-range coordinates return `NULL` (never an error).

Use it for finer-grained geographic rollups than `admin1` (state): county- or district-level reporting, routing, or joins.

## Inputs / outputs
- `lat` `DOUBLE` in `[-90, 90]`, `lon` `DOUBLE` in `[-180, 180]`.
- Returns the admin2 name as `VARCHAR`, or `NULL`.

## Behavior & edge cases
- admin2 is **frequently empty** in GeoNames for many countries, so `NULL` results are common and expected -- not an error.
- `NULL` or out-of-range coordinates also return `NULL`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Compute the **great-circle (haversine) distance in kilometers** between two `(lat, lon)` points on a spherical Earth. Pure arithmetic -- no index, no lookup, no network.

## When to use
Use it for proximity filtering ('within N km of'), nearest-of ranking, trip length, or any straight-line distance between coordinate pairs in SQL.

## Inputs / outputs
- Four `DOUBLE` arguments: `lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2`, each in the usual lat `[-90, 90]` / lon `[-180, 180]` ranges.
- Returns the distance as a `DOUBLE` in kilometers, or `NULL`.

## Behavior & edge cases
- Uses a mean Earth radius (~6371 km); it is a sphere approximation, not a geodesic on the WGS-84 ellipsoid, so expect sub-percent error.
- If **any** of the four coordinates is `NULL` or out of range the result is `NULL` (never an error).
- Distance is symmetric and zero for identical points.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# distance_km

Great-circle (haversine) distance in kilometers between two points.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT geocode.main.distance_km(40.7128, -74.0060, 51.5074, -0.1278);  -- ~5570
```

## Notes

Spherical approximation (~6371 km radius), sub-percent error vs. WGS-84. Returns `NULL` if any coordinate is `NULL`/out of range.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the name of the nearest known populated place (city/town) to a given latitude/longitude, **entirely offline** using a GeoNames cities KD-tree.

## When to use
Reach for this when you have raw coordinate columns (GPS pings, device telemetry, store/asset locations) and want a human-readable place label to group, filter, or display by.

## Inputs / outputs
- `lat` `DOUBLE` in `[-90, 90]`, `lon` `DOUBLE` in `[-180, 180]`.
- Returns a `VARCHAR` city name, or `NULL`.

## Behavior & edge cases
- This is a *nearest-land-place* lookup: the index has no notion of water, so a point in the ocean resolves to the closest coastal city.
- A `NULL` coordinate or one out of range yields `NULL` (never an error).
- City labels track the bundled GeoNames snapshot and can drift slightly between releases.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **IANA timezone name** (e.g. `America/New_York`, `Europe/Paris`, `Asia/Tokyo`) for a latitude/longitude, computed **offline** from bundled IANA timezone polygons (`timezonefinder`).

## When to use
Use it to localize timestamps, derive local time, or bucket coordinate data by timezone -- the returned string drops straight into DuckDB's `timezone(name, ts)` / `AT TIME ZONE`.

## Inputs / outputs
- `lat` `DOUBLE` in `[-90, 90]`, `lon` `DOUBLE` in `[-180, 180]`.
- Returns the IANA tz name as `VARCHAR`, or `NULL`.

## Behavior & edge cases
- Uses true timezone *polygons*, not a nearest-place lookup, so it is exact at borders on land.
- Points outside every tz polygon return `NULL`; some uninhabited ocean cells resolve to a valid `Etc/GMT±N` name instead.
- `NULL` or out-of-range coordinates return `NULL` (never an error).

workers.title: GitHub API
workers.tagline: GitHub as ordinary DuckDB tables — a read-only VGI worker. Repositories, issues, pull requests, commits, releases, contributors and Actions runs, over SQL with LATERAL joins.
workers.summary: Read-only GitHub: repositories, issues, PRs, code, people, Actions, Projects and Discussions
workers.doc_md:
GitHub's REST and GraphQL APIs, read-only, as SQL.

Use `main` for curated typed tables, `rest` for all pinned REST GET operations, and `api` for endpoint discovery and GraphQL queries. REST pages retain complete JSON and binary bodies. GraphQL mutation documents are rejected before transport.

### Key concepts

- **A repository is written `'owner/name'`.** That one string is the key for everything repository-scoped, and every row that belongs to a repository carries it in a `repo` or `full_name` column — so the output of one function is the input of the next.
- **Search starts a question; lookups answer it.** The search functions take GitHub's own query syntax and stream results, so they drive a query. The keyed functions take a repository or a login and are built to sit inside a correlated `LATERAL`.
- **List functions are capped.** A function under `LATERAL` has to fetch everything for its input before it returns, so the keyed list functions take `max_rows`, default 100 — one page per input row. Discussion lists default to recently updated first; comments, replies and Projects retain GitHub's connection/listing order. `max_rows => 0` fetches everything, up to 10,000 rows per input row. The two search functions stream instead, take no `max_rows`, and stop at GitHub's 1,000-result cap.
- **Filter with arguments.** DuckDB applies a WHERE clause after the rows are fetched, so it cannot reach past `max_rows`. Named arguments such as `state =>` and `since =>` are sent to GitHub and narrow before the cap.

### A typical shape

A search drives, and a keyed function fans out from each row it returns:

```sql
FROM github.main.search_repositories('org:duckdb') r,
     LATERAL github.main.issues(r.full_name, state => 'open') i
```

### Authentication and rate limits

A token raises the budget from 60 requests an hour to 5,000 and makes private repositories visible. Without one, a private repository is indistinguishable from a missing one: both return no rows. Supply it as a DuckDB secret of type `github`; the `rate_limit` table shows what remains and whether a token is in use.

attach_options.name: reporting
attach_options.description: Reporting: complete validated keyed listings with max_rows=0; no result caching.

attach_options.name: operation_timeout_seconds
attach_options.description: Reporting operation deadline across a blended input batch, in seconds (1..3600).

attach_options.name: cache_ttl
attach_options.description: Default result cache seconds; 0 uses GitHub policy. Per-call cache_ttl overrides this.

attach_options.name: auth
attach_options.description: How to treat the optional 'github' secret: 'auto' (default) authenticates when one is present and goes anonymous otherwise; 'required' fails the query when none resolves; 'off' never authenticates.

attach_options.name: token_source
attach_options.description: Where to find your GitHub identity when no 'github' secret resolves: 'gh' uses the GitHub CLI's login (gh auth token), 'env' uses GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN. Only when DuckDB launches the worker locally; refused by a shared HTTP server.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Curated GitHub tables with typed columns. Discover with search_repositories() or search_issues(), then pass each repository's full_name ('owner/name') to the per-repository functions — under LATERAL to cover many repositories in one query. List functions return at most max_rows (default 100) rows per input row; check each function's documented ordering. Projects use REST and Discussions use automatically paged GraphQL. Search functions stream instead and stop at 1,000 results; filter with their named arguments (state =>, since =>, ...) rather than WHERE, which only sees fetched rows. Set max_rows => 0 for complete history.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Typed datasets from GitHub's read-only REST and GraphQL APIs.

### Finding your way in

If you know the repository, call its function directly: `issues('duckdb/duckdb')`. If you do not, `search_repositories()` finds it, and its `full_name` column feeds every per-repository function.

### The traps

- GitHub's issue listing includes pull requests. `issues()` removes them by default.
- A merged pull request has `state = 'closed'`; test `merged_at IS NOT NULL`.
- `stargazers()` is oldest first, so its default cap returns the *first* stars.
- A WHERE clause filters what was already fetched; it cannot reach rows past `max_rows`, and DuckDB does not push it into these functions. Filter with the named arguments (`state =>`, `labels =>`, `since =>`, `branch =>`, `status =>`, ...), which GitHub applies before the cap.

vgi.example_queries.description: The most starred repositories about DuckDB
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT full_name, stargazers_count, language FROM github.main.search_repositories('duckdb', sort => 'stars') LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Open issues with the most thumbs-up in one repository, ranked by search
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT number, title, reactions_plus_one FROM github.main.search_issues('repo:duckdb/duckdb is:issue is:open', sort => 'reactions-+1') LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Open issues for an organization's top repositories, via LATERAL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT r.full_name, count(i.number) AS open_issues FROM (SELECT full_name FROM github.main.search_repositories('org:duckdb', sort => 'stars') LIMIT 5) r, LATERAL github.main.issues(r.full_name, state => 'open') i GROUP BY r.full_name ORDER BY open_issues DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Profiles of a repository's top contributors, via LATERAL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.login, c.contributions, u.company, u.location FROM github.main.contributors('duckdb/duckdb', max_rows => 10) c, LATERAL github.main.user(c.login, cache_ttl => 3600) u ORDER BY c.contributions DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: CI failure rate per workflow
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE conclusion = 'failure') / count(*) AS failure_rate FROM github.main.workflow_runs('duckdb/duckdb', status => 'completed') GROUP BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: How much API budget is left
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT resource, remaining, request_limit, reset_at FROM github.main.rate_limit

tables.name: rate_limit
tables.comment: Remaining GitHub API budget for the credentials in use

tags.vgi.doc_llm: How many GitHub API requests remain in each budget, and when each resets. Check it before a large LATERAL fan-out, or to confirm a token is in use: authenticated core budgets are 5,000 an hour, anonymous ones 60. Reading it is free.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per budget GitHub tracks for the current credentials.

### Which budget applies

`core` is an hourly window covering every function in this catalog except `search_repositories()` and `search_issues()`, which spend `search` — a per-minute window. The other resources are for APIs this worker does not call and can be ignored. The column is `request_limit`, not `limit`, because LIMIT is an SQL keyword.

### Planning a LATERAL

A list function costs ceil(rows / 100) requests per input row — the default max_rows of 100 is exactly one — and a point lookup one per distinct key. Compare that with `remaining` before running something wide.

vgi.example_queries.description: Remaining budget and reset time
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT resource, remaining, request_limit, reset_at FROM github.main.rate_limit WHERE resource IN ('core', 'search')

vgi.example_queries.description: Is a token being used?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT authenticated, request_limit FROM github.main.rate_limit WHERE resource = 'core'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read top-level comments through GraphQL with GitHub credentials, in GitHub connection order. Replies are a separate connection: use discussion_replies(node_id) to read them. A missing discussion yields no rows in exploratory mode and fails in reporting mode. Composes under LATERAL; max_rows caps each input key, not the whole SQL result.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Read top-level comments through GraphQL with GitHub credentials, in GitHub connection order. Replies are a separate connection: use discussion_replies(node_id) to read them. A missing discussion yields no rows in exploratory mode and fails in reporting mode.

Pagination is automatic. Default `max_rows=100`; `max_rows=0` walks all pages, bounded at 100, and fails if more remain. Filter with named arguments before the cap. GitHub errors fail the query. Reporting mode requires `max_rows=0`, validates complete rows before projection, and disables result caching. Cache TTLs follow ATTACH unless overridden; GraphQL has no automatic response caching.

functions.comment: One GitHub user or organization profile by login

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A GitHub account's public profile — name, company, location, follower counts, account age — by login. Works for organizations too (type = 'Organization'). An unknown login yields no row rather than an error. Use it under LATERAL to turn any column of logins (issue authors, contributors, stargazers) into profiles; pass cache_ttl so repeated logins are fetched once.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per account. Users and organizations share an endpoint, so this is also the organization lookup; `type` says which you got.

### Enriching other results

Every function that names a person returns a login column (`user_login`, `login`, `author_login`), and each feeds this directly under LATERAL. Repeated logins inside one batch are fetched once; `cache_ttl` extends that across batches and queries.

### Free-text fields

`company`, `location` and `blog` are whatever the account typed — useful for grouping, not reliable for joining.

functions.name: stargazers
functions.comment: Stars on a GitHub repository with when each was given, oldest first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Stars on a repository with their timestamps (up to 10,000), OLDEST first — the raw data behind a star-history chart. Only works for repositories your token can administer: GitHub refuses the listing for anyone else's, and this raises an error rather than reporting zero stars. The default max_rows of 100 returns the first hundred stars; pass max_rows => 0 for the full history. For anyone else's repository, use repo() and its stargazers_count instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per star, in the order they were given.

### Only for repositories you administer

GitHub restricts who may list a repository's stargazers. For repositories the token does not administer it refuses the listing even though the repository exists — 404 for a user token, 403 for a GitHub App or Actions token, 401 anonymously — so this function raises an explanatory error instead of returning an empty result that would read as 'no stars'. For anyone else's repository, `repo()` still reports `stargazers_count`.

### Oldest first

GitHub lists stargazers chronologically and offers no reverse order, so `max_rows` keeps the *earliest* stars. For a star-history chart pass `max_rows => 0` and bucket `starred_at`; the walk stops with an error past 10,000 rows rather than returning a silently truncated history.

vgi.example_queries.description: A repository's first stargazers
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT starred_at, login FROM github.main.stargazers('Query-farm/vgi-kalshi', max_rows => 10)

vgi.example_queries.description: Stars per month
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT date_trunc('month', starred_at) AS month, count(*) AS stars FROM github.main.stargazers('Query-farm/vgi-kalshi', max_rows => 0) GROUP BY month ORDER BY month

functions.name: search_repositories
functions.comment: Search GitHub repositories with GitHub's query syntax

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Find repositories with GitHub's search syntax — topic words plus qualifiers like org:NAME, user:NAME, language:rust, stars:>1000, topic:database, pushed:>2026-01-01. The discovery entry point when you do not already know a repository's name. It must be the DRIVING side of a join: feed each row's full_name into the per-repository functions with a LATERAL on the right. Streams pages, so it has no max_rows; GitHub returns at most 1,000 results per query.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Repositories matching a search, streamed one page of 100 at a time — a `LIMIT` stops the walk early.

### Query syntax

The argument is passed to GitHub untouched, so every qualifier GitHub documents works: `org:duckdb`, `language:python`, `stars:>1000`, `topic:sql`, `archived:false`, `pushed:>2026-01-01`. Put qualifiers in the query rather than a WHERE clause: a WHERE filters the results GitHub chose to return, and search returns at most 1,000.

### Driving other functions

Same columns as `repo()` and `repos()`. Being a streaming scan it cannot sit *inside* a LATERAL, but it is the natural thing to drive one:

```sql
FROM github.main.search_repositories('org:duckdb') r,
     LATERAL github.main.issues(r.full_name, state => 'open') i
```

### Budget

Search has its own rate limit: 30 requests a minute with a token, 10 without.

vgi.example_queries.description: The most starred repositories about DuckDB
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT full_name, stargazers_count, language FROM github.main.search_repositories('duckdb', sort => 'stars') LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Open issue counts for an organization's most starred repositories, via LATERAL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT r.full_name, count(i.number) AS open_issues FROM (SELECT full_name FROM github.main.search_repositories('org:duckdb', sort => 'stars') LIMIT 5) r, LATERAL github.main.issues(r.full_name, state => 'open') i GROUP BY r.full_name ORDER BY open_issues DESC

functions.name: search_issues
functions.comment: Search GitHub issues and pull requests with GitHub's query syntax

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Find issues and pull requests across GitHub with its search syntax: text plus qualifiers like repo:OWNER/NAME, org:NAME, is:issue or is:pr, is:open, label:bug, author:LOGIN, involves:LOGIN, created:>2026-01-01. The way to search across many repositories at once, or by text. Same columns as issues(), but pull requests are INCLUDED unless the query says is:issue (is_pull_request tells them apart). Streams pages, so it has no max_rows; GitHub returns at most 1,000 results per query. Drive a LATERAL from it — it cannot be the inner side of one.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Issues and pull requests matching a search, streamed one page of 100 at a time.

### Issues and pull requests together

Search covers both unless the query says `is:issue` or `is:pr`; `is_pull_request` tells them apart in the result. This differs from `issues()`, which drops pull requests by default.

### Query, not WHERE

Qualifiers are evaluated by GitHub across everything; a WHERE clause only filters the at-most-1,000 results it returned. `repo:`, `org:`, `label:`, `is:open` and date ranges belong in the query.

### Budget

Search has its own rate limit: 30 requests a minute with a token, 10 without.

functions.name: releases
functions.comment: Releases of a GitHub repository, newest first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A repository's published releases, newest first: tag, title, pre-release flag, publish date, release notes and download_count (summed over attached assets). Use it for release cadence, version history or download counts. Capped at max_rows (default 100). A repository with no releases, or none at all, yields no rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per release, newest first.

### Releases are not tags

A release is a GitHub object attached to a tag, with notes and assets. Projects that only push tags have no releases, and this returns nothing for them.

### Download counts

`download_count` sums the release's attached assets. The source archives GitHub generates for every tag are not assets and are not counted, so a project that ships no binaries shows zero.

### Drafts

Draft releases are visible only to tokens with push access, so the result can differ with credentials.

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent releases and how long apart they were
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tag_name, published_at, published_at - lag(published_at) OVER (ORDER BY published_at) AS gap FROM github.main.releases('duckdb/duckdb', max_rows => 20) WHERE NOT is_prerelease ORDER BY published_at DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Most downloaded releases
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tag_name, download_count FROM github.main.releases('duckdb/duckdb') ORDER BY download_count DESC LIMIT 5

functions.name: all_rate_limit
functions.comment: GitHub API rate-limit budgets (the scan backing the `rate_limit` table)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: How many GitHub API requests remain in each budget and when it resets. Prefer the `rate_limit` table, which scans this. Check it before a large LATERAL, or to confirm a token is in use (core limit 5,000 with one, 60 without). Free: GitHub does not charge for reading it.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per budget GitHub tracks.

### Prefer the table

The `rate_limit` catalog table is backed by this function and returns the same rows; query the table.

### The budgets that matter

`core` (hourly) covers every function here except `search_repositories()` and `search_issues()`, which draw on `search` — a per-MINUTE window of 30 with a token, 10 without. `reset_at` is a UTC instant. The column is `request_limit` rather than GitHub's `limit` because LIMIT is an SQL keyword. Other resources (graphql, ...) are for APIs this worker does not call and can be ignored.

vgi.example_queries.description: Remaining core and search budget
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT resource, remaining, request_limit, reset_at FROM github.main.all_rate_limit() WHERE resource IN ('core', 'search')

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: resource
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Which budget this row describes: 'core' (most endpoints), 'search', 'graphql', ...

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: request_limit

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: used
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Requests spent in the current window.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: remaining
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Count of requests left before the window resets.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: reset_at
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: When the window resets and remaining returns to request_limit.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: authenticated
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Whether these figures are for a token (true) or this IP's anonymous budget (false).

functions.name: pulls
functions.comment: Pull requests in a GitHub repository, newest first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A repository's pull requests, newest first, open and closed, with branches, draft flag, reviewers and merge time. A merged PR has state 'closed' and a non-NULL merged_at — test merged_at, not state, for 'merged'. Capped at max_rows per repository (default 100).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per pull request, newest first.

### Merged is not a state

GitHub's `state` is only `open` or `closed`. A merged pull request is closed with a `merged_at`; one closed without merging has `merged_at` NULL. Time to merge is `merged_at - created_at`.

### Forks

`head_repo` is where the branch lives. When it differs from `repo`, the change came from a fork.

### The row cap

`max_rows` (default 100, one request) caps what is fetched per repository, newest first. `state` and `base` are sent to GitHub and narrow before the cap; a WHERE clause only filters what was fetched.

vgi.example_queries.description: Median hours to merge for recent pull requests
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT median(date_diff('hour', created_at, merged_at)) AS median_hours FROM github.main.pulls('duckdb/duckdb', state => 'closed') WHERE merged_at IS NOT NULL

vgi.example_queries.description: Open pull requests that came from forks
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT number, title, user_login, head_repo FROM github.main.pulls('duckdb/duckdb', state => 'open') WHERE head_repo <> repo ORDER BY number DESC

functions.name: repos
functions.comment: Repositories owned by a GitHub user or organization

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every repository an account owns, most recently pushed first, with the same columns as repo(). The way to go from an organization or user to its repositories — and, under LATERAL, from a set of accounts to all of theirs. Capped at max_rows per account (default 100); pass max_rows => 0 for all. type => 'owner' (default) lists what the account owns; 'member' and 'all' add repositories it collaborates on. An unknown owner yields no rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per repository owned by the account.

### Ordering and the row cap

`max_rows` (default 100) caps what is *fetched* per account, and `sort` decides which rows survive it: by default the most recently pushed, which is usually what 'their repositories' means. A WHERE clause filters what was fetched — it cannot reach repositories past the cap, so raise `max_rows` (or pass 0) when filtering for something rare.

### Private repositories

This lists what the account shows publicly. A token adds private repositories only for your own account; for a private organization's repositories, use `search_repositories('org:NAME')` with a token that can see them.

vgi.example_queries.description: An organization's most starred repositories
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT full_name, stargazers_count, language FROM github.main.repos('duckdb') ORDER BY stargazers_count DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Repositories across several organizations, via LATERAL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT r.owner_login, count(*) AS repos, sum(r.stargazers_count) AS stars FROM (VALUES ('duckdb'), ('apache')) o(name), LATERAL github.main.repos(o.name, max_rows => 50) r GROUP BY r.owner_login
