functions.name: commits
functions.comment: Commit history of a GitHub repository, newest first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A repository's commit history, newest first, with git author and committer identities, dates, messages, parents and signature verification. Defaults to the default branch; pass sha => 'branch' for another, path => 'dir/' to follow one part of the tree, author => 'login-or-email', since/until (ISO 8601, e.g. '2026-01-01'; an unparseable value is an error) for a window. Capped at max_rows (default 100).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per commit reachable from `sha` (the default branch unless given), newest first.

### Two identities per commit

`author_*` is who wrote the change and `committer_*` who applied it; they differ after a rebase, a cherry-pick or a web merge. `author_login` is GitHub's match from the email to an account, and is NULL when the email maps to none — group by `author_email` when completeness matters more than identity.

### Filtering at the source

`sha`, `path`, `author`, `since` and `until` are sent to GitHub, so they narrow before `max_rows` applies. A WHERE clause on the output filters only what was fetched.

### Empty repositories

A repository with no commits answers 409; that returns zero rows, not an error.

vgi.example_queries.description: The ten most recent commits on the default branch
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sha[:10] AS sha, author_login, committer_date, split_part(message, chr(10), 1) AS summary FROM github.main.commits('duckdb/duckdb', max_rows => 10)

vgi.example_queries.description: Commits per author over the last week
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT coalesce(author_login, author_email) AS who, count(*) AS commits FROM github.main.commits('duckdb/duckdb', since => strftime(now() - INTERVAL 7 DAY, '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ'), max_rows => 500) GROUP BY who ORDER BY commits DESC

functions.name: repo
functions.comment: One GitHub repository by 'owner/name'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A single repository's current metadata — stars, forks, language, license, activity timestamps — by its exact 'owner/name'. Use it as a point lookup, or under LATERAL to enrich any column of repository names (from search results, say). Returns no row for a repository that does not exist or that the current credentials cannot see.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per repository, with the same columns `search_repositories()` and `repos()` return, so the three are interchangeable downstream.

### Renamed and transferred repositories

GitHub redirects an old name to the new one, and the row comes back with the *current* `full_name` — it may differ from what you passed.

### Not found means no row

GitHub answers both 'does not exist' and 'private, and you are not allowed' with 404. Either way this returns zero rows for that input rather than failing the query, which is what a LATERAL over many names needs.

### Counts to read carefully

`open_issues_count` includes open pull requests, and `watchers_count` is the star count under an old name — both are GitHub's own quirks, kept for fidelity.

vgi.example_queries.description: One repository's headline numbers
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT full_name, stargazers_count, forks_count, language, license_spdx_id FROM github.main.repo('duckdb/duckdb')

functions.name: contributors
functions.comment: Contributors to a GitHub repository, most commits first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Who has contributed to a repository and how many commits each, largest first. Counts only commits on the default branch that GitHub can attribute to an account; anonymous (unlinked-email) contributors are not included. Feed login to user() under LATERAL for profiles. Capped at max_rows (default 100). GitHub may refuse to compute the list for an enormous history and answer with an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per contributing account, ordered by commit count.

### What is counted

Commits on the default branch whose author email maps to a GitHub account. Commits from unlinked emails are not attributed to anyone here; use `commits()` and group by `author_email` for a complete count.

### Very large repositories

GitHub may decline to compute the list for repositories with an enormous history, and answers with an error rather than a partial list.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT login, contributions FROM github.main.contributors('duckdb/duckdb', max_rows => 10) ORDER BY contributions DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: How concentrated a project's commits are
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(contributions) FILTER (WHERE rn <= 5) / sum(contributions) AS top5_share FROM (SELECT contributions, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY contributions DESC) AS rn FROM github.main.contributors('duckdb/duckdb', max_rows => 0))

functions.name: issue_comments
functions.comment: Comments on a GitHub issue or pull request

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The comment thread on one issue or pull request, oldest first. Takes the repository AND the number — the repo and number columns of issues() and pulls() output — so it composes directly under LATERAL (i.repo, i.number). max_rows (default 100) keeps the EARLIEST comments of a long thread. Pull request review comments on code lines are a different thing and are not included.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per comment, in posting order.

### Issues and pull requests share this

A pull request's conversation tab is an issue thread underneath, so the same function serves both. Inline review comments attached to lines of a diff are a separate API and are not returned.

### Driving it from issues()

Both positional arguments are columns `issues()` and `pulls()` return, so a LATERAL needs no reshaping. Each input row costs at least one request.

vgi.example_queries.description: Who comments most on the busiest recent issues
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.user_login, count(*) AS comments FROM (SELECT repo, number FROM github.main.issues('duckdb/duckdb', max_rows => 20) ORDER BY comments DESC LIMIT 5) i, LATERAL github.main.issue_comments(i.repo, i.number) c GROUP BY c.user_login ORDER BY comments DESC

functions.name: workflow_runs
functions.comment: GitHub Actions workflow runs for a repository, newest first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A repository's GitHub Actions runs, newest first: workflow name, trigger event, branch, status and conclusion, timing. Use it for CI reliability (failure rate by workflow), duration, or what is running now. Narrow at the source with branch =>, event => and status => (which also accepts a conclusion such as 'failure'); a WHERE clause only sees the max_rows (default 100) runs fetched, so a failure rate over the default is over the last 100 runs. For a longer window raise max_rows (GitHub caps a filtered listing at 1,000 runs).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per workflow run, newest first.

### Status versus conclusion

`status` is where the run is in its lifecycle; `conclusion` is how it ended and is NULL until `status = 'completed'`. Failure rate is `count(*) FILTER (WHERE conclusion = 'failure') / count(*)` over completed runs.

### Filter with arguments

`branch`, `event` and `status` are GitHub's own filters and narrow before `max_rows` applies. `status` takes either a lifecycle status (`completed`) or a conclusion (`failure`) — GitHub has one parameter for both. GitHub caps any filtered listing at 1,000 runs.

### Duration

For a completed run, `updated_at - run_started_at` approximates wall-clock time of the last attempt.

vgi.example_queries.description: Failure rate per workflow over the last 100 runs
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, count(*) AS runs, count(*) FILTER (WHERE conclusion = 'failure') AS failures FROM github.main.workflow_runs('duckdb/duckdb') WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY name ORDER BY failures DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent failed runs on main
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, head_sha[:10] AS sha, created_at, html_url FROM github.main.workflow_runs('duckdb/duckdb', branch => 'main', status => 'failure', max_rows => 30) ORDER BY created_at DESC

functions.name: issues
functions.comment: Issues in a GitHub repository, newest first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A repository's issues, newest first by creation — state defaults to 'all' (GitHub's own default is open-only) — with author, labels, assignees, comment and reaction counts. Pull requests are excluded by default (GitHub mixes them in); use pulls() for those. Capped at max_rows per repository (default 100), newest first. Filter with the named arguments (state => 'open', labels => 'bug', since => '2026-01-01' — since filters on UPDATED time), not WHERE: a WHERE clause only sees fetched rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per issue, newest first.

### Pull requests are not issues here

GitHub's issue listing returns pull requests too. They are dropped by default, and `max_rows` counts only the issues kept; pass `include_pull_requests => true` to keep them, flagged by `is_pull_request`.

### Filter with arguments, not WHERE

`max_rows` (default 100, one request) caps what is fetched per repository, newest first, and a WHERE clause is applied *after* that — so `WHERE state = 'closed'` over the newest 100 issues of a busy repository can return nothing even though thousands are closed. `state`, `labels` and `since` are sent to GitHub and narrow *before* the cap; use them. For anything else, raise `max_rows` and then filter.

### Ranking across the whole history

To find the most-reacted or most-commented issues ever, ask search to rank them — `search_issues('repo:OWNER/NAME is:issue is:open', sort => 'reactions-+1')` — rather than fetching every issue with `max_rows => 0`. A function under LATERAL cannot stream, so a walk of thousands of issues blocks the query, uncancellably, until it finishes.

### Open and closed

Unlike GitHub's own default of open-only, `state` defaults to `all`.

vgi.example_queries.description: The most discussed of the latest 100 open issues
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT number, title, comments, reactions_plus_one FROM github.main.issues('duckdb/duckdb', state => 'open') ORDER BY comments DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Labels on recent open issues, across several repositories via LATERAL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT repo, label, count(*) AS issues FROM (SELECT i.repo, unnest(i.labels) AS label FROM (VALUES ('duckdb/duckdb'), ('duckdb/duckdb-wasm')) t(name), LATERAL github.main.issues(t.name, state => 'open') i) GROUP BY repo, label ORDER BY issues DESC

functions.name: languages
functions.comment: Bytes of code per language in a GitHub repository

tags.vgi.doc_llm: How much code a repository has in each language, in bytes, largest first — the breakdown behind the language bar on a repository page. One request per repository, so it is cheap under LATERAL. The repo's single `language` column is just the largest of these.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per language GitHub's linguist detected.

### Shares

Rows come back largest first. Divide `bytes` by the repository's total for a share — the first example does it with a window function. A byte share is not a line count, so it can differ from other 'language share' measures.

### What linguist excludes

Vendored code, generated files and documentation are excluded by linguist's own rules, and a repository can override them, so this measures what GitHub considers the project's code.

vgi.example_queries.description: A repository's language mix as percentages
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT language, round(100.0 * bytes / sum(bytes) OVER (), 1) AS pct FROM github.main.languages('duckdb/duckdb') ORDER BY bytes DESC

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT l.language, sum(l.bytes) AS bytes FROM github.main.repos('duckdb', max_rows => 20) r, LATERAL github.main.languages(r.full_name) l GROUP BY l.language ORDER BY bytes DESC

workers.summary: Read-only professional golf leaderboards, schedules, statistics and world rankings
workers.doc_md:
# Professional golf

Leaderboards, schedules, hole-by-hole scorecards, PGA Tour season statistics and the Official World Golf Ranking, fetched on demand.

## Data model

Tournaments are keyed by ESPN `event_id` and golfers by ESPN `player_id`, shared across tours. The ranking uses OWGR's own `owgr_player_id`. Scores to par are integers (E = 0); round scores are strokes.

Data comes from ESPN's undocumented golf endpoints and OWGR's public backend. This worker is not affiliated with ESPN, Disney, any tour or OWGR.

example_queries.title: six_tours_supported
example_queries.description: The catalog covers six tours.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS tours FROM golf.main.tours;

example_queries.title: masters_2026_champion
example_queries.description: Rory McIlroy won the 2026 Masters at 12 under par.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, score_to_par FROM golf.main.leaderboard(event_id := 401811941) WHERE sort_order = 1;

example_queries.title: scorecard_matches_round_totals
example_queries.description: Scottie Scheffler's 2026 Masters hole scores sum to his round totals.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(total = round_strokes) AS consistent FROM (SELECT round, sum(strokes) AS total, any_value(round_strokes) AS round_strokes FROM golf.main.player_scorecard(401811941, 9478) GROUP BY round);

example_queries.title: world_rankings_are_populated
example_queries.description: The OWGR table has a world number one.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) >= 1 AS has_leader FROM golf.main.current_world_rankings WHERE rank = 1;

example_queries.description: Current PGA Tour top ten.

functions.name: leaderboard
functions.comment: Full tournament leaderboard for a tour and ESPN event id

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per entry in a golf tournament: position, score to par, per-round strokes, status (Finish, Missed Cut, Withdrawn), earnings and FedExCup points. Pass tour => 'pga'|'eur'|'liv'|'lpga'|'champions-tour'|'ntw' and an event_id from schedule(). Without event_id it returns the current or most recent event. Order by sort_order for leaderboard order; position is text with a T tie prefix and position_number is the numeric rank. Team events have entry_type = 'team'. in_playoff marks players who went to a playoff.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Leaderboard for one tournament, one row per player (or pairing in team events). `score_to_par` is an integer (E = 0); `round_1`..`round_4` are strokes per round. Missed-cut players keep their two rounds and have status `Missed Cut`.

vgi.example_queries.description: The final 2026 Masters leaderboard.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT position, player_name, score_to_par, round_1, round_2, round_3, round_4, earnings FROM golf.main.leaderboard(event_id := 401811941) ORDER BY sort_order

vgi.example_queries.description: Top ten at LIV Golf Indianapolis 2026.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT position, player_name, score_to_par, total_strokes FROM golf.main.leaderboard(tour := 'liv', event_id := 401811430) ORDER BY sort_order LIMIT 10

workers.doc_md:
# Google APIs for SQL

![Google logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Google_2015_logo.svg/250px-Google_2015_logo.svg.png)

**Query the entire Google REST API surface directly from DuckDB SQL** — read Google Sheets ranges, list Google Drive files, pull Google Calendar events, search YouTube videos, and reach any other Google API as ordinary SQL table functions, no glue code required.

This extension turns Google's APIs into a relational data source. It is built on the official [google-api-python-client](https://github.com/googleapis/google-api-python-client) library and Google's [API Discovery Service](https://developers.google.com/discovery), so any service Google publishes a discovery document for is reachable — not just a hand-picked few. Curated READ adapters give first-class, typed columns for the high-demand surfaces (Sheets, Drive, Calendar, YouTube), while a generic escape hatch covers everything else. Authentication is service-account-first (or an API key for public data), resolved securely through the VGI secret provider — credentials are never inlined in SQL. See the [client library documentation](https://googleapis.github.io/google-api-python-client/docs/) for the full API catalog and auth model.

It is built for data engineers and analysts who want spreadsheet data, file metadata, calendar schedules, and video statistics in their warehouse without standing up a separate ETL service. Three kinds of access work together: **curated data adapters** provide typed columns for the high-demand surfaces (Sheets, Drive, Calendar, YouTube), **generic API access** reaches any other Google REST method by name and returns its JSON response as rows, and **API discovery** lets you introspect which APIs and methods are reachable — all from inside SQL.

A typical query loads a spreadsheet range straight into SQL by naming a spreadsheet ID and an A1 range; the per-function example queries show the exact call shapes for Sheets, Drive, Calendar, YouTube, and the generic hatch. Pagination (Google's `nextPageToken`) is handled automatically and a `count` argument caps total rows. The connector is **READ-only**; data, quotas, billing and compliance with Google's Terms of Service remain the responsibility of the operator whose credentials are used.

example_queries.description: Discover the Sheets API's reachable versions via the Discovery Service.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version, title FROM google.main.google_apis() WHERE name LIKE '%sheets%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Browse the Drive v3 methods you can invoke through google_call.
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, http_method FROM google.main.google_methods('drive', 'v3') ORDER BY method LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Read a header sheet range, projecting a named column from each row.
example_queries.sql: SELECT row_number, record ->> '$.name' AS name FROM google.main.google_sheet('1AbC...', 'Sheet1!A1:Z', header := true) WHERE row_number <= 100 ORDER BY row_number

example_queries.description: List up to 100 PDF files in Google Drive by MIME type.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM google.main.google_drive(query := "mimeType='application/pdf'", count := 100)

example_queries.description: Search YouTube for 'duckdb' videos and project their view counts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT video_id, title, view_count FROM google.main.google_youtube('duckdb', count := 25)

example_queries.description: Find the Sheets APIs in the directory and their versions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version, title FROM google.main.google_api_directory WHERE name LIKE '%sheets%' ORDER BY name, version

example_queries.description: List the preferred version of every reachable Google API.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version FROM google.main.google_api_directory WHERE preferred ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: List Drive v3 methods reachable via google_call
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, http_method FROM google.main.google_methods('drive', 'v3')

example_queries.description: List the user-created Gmail label names via the generic hatch
example_queries.sql: SELECT result ->> '$.name' AS label FROM google.main.google_call('gmail', 'v1', 'users.labels.list', '{"userId":"me"}') WHERE result ->> '$.type' = 'user' ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: List up to 50 events on the primary calendar
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, summary, start_time FROM google.main.google_calendar(calendar_id := 'primary', count := 50)

example_queries.description: Find the Sheets API and its versions
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version, title FROM google.main.google_apis() WHERE name LIKE '%sheets%'

example_queries.description: Discover which Google Sheets APIs are reachable via the public Discovery Service.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, version, title FROM google.main.google_apis() WHERE name LIKE '%sheets%' ORDER BY name, version LIMIT 5;

## Google API table functions

The `main` schema exposes Google's REST surface as SQL table functions, grouped into three kinds of access.

- **Curated data adapters** give first-class, typed columns for the high-demand surfaces — Sheets ranges, Drive file metadata, Calendar events, and YouTube video statistics.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## google_sheet

Read a rectangular range from a Google Sheet as SQL rows. Pass the **spreadsheet ID** (the long token in the sheet's URL) and an **A1 range** such as `Sheet1!A1:Z`. With `header := true` the first row is treated as column names and surfaced as a JSON `record` per row; otherwise rows come back as a `values` text array.

**When to use:** pull tabular data maintained in Sheets (config, lookups, hand-curated lists) directly into SQL for joins and aggregation. Auth is **service-account-first** (or an API key for a publicly shared sheet) resolved via the VGI secret provider — never inline.

**Inputs:** `spreadsheet_id`, `range`, `header` (default false), `count` (row cap). **Outputs:** `row_number`, `values`, `record`. Empty trailing cells may be omitted by the API, so rows can be ragged; `count` bounds the scan.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# google_sheet

Reads a Google Sheets A1 range into rows. Pass the spreadsheet ID (the long token in the sheet URL) and an A1 range such as `Sheet1!A1:Z`; the attached example queries show the exact call shape.

## Notes

- With the `header` argument true, columns are named from the first row and surfaced in the JSON `record` column; otherwise `record` is NULL and cells live in the `values` array.
- Requires a `google_service_account` secret (or `google_api_key` for a publicly shared sheet); the worker is READ-only.
- The API may omit empty trailing cells, so rows can vary in width.

## google_methods

List the callable methods of a single Google API, one row per method, by reading that API's **discovery document**. Provide the discovery `api` name (e.g. `drive`) and `version` (e.g. `v3`). Each row gives the dotted method path to pass to `google_call`, its HTTP verb, URL path template, description, and the full and required parameter names.

**When to use:** figure out exactly what `method` path and parameters to give `google_call` for an API you discovered via `google_apis()`. This reads Google's **public** discovery documents — no credentials required.

**Inputs:** `api`, `version`. **Outputs:** method path, http_method, path template, description, and parameter / required-parameter lists.

- `required_parameters` lists the parameters `google_call` must receive in `params_json`.

functions.name: google_drive

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## google_drive

List or search Google Drive files and return their metadata as SQL rows. The optional `query` argument uses Drive's native **`q` query syntax** (e.g. `mimeType='application/pdf'`, `name contains 'report'`, `modifiedTime > '2024-01-01'`). Results page automatically; `count` caps the total and `order_by` (e.g. `modifiedTime desc`) sorts them. Pass `drive_id` to search within a Shared Drive.

**When to use:** inventory files, find documents by type/name/date, or join Drive metadata against other tables. This returns **metadata only**, not file contents. Auth is service-account-first via the VGI secret provider.

**Inputs:** `query`, `count`, `page_size`, `order_by`, `drive_id`. **Outputs:** id, name, mime_type, timestamps, size, links, parents, owner, and trashed/starred flags.

functions.name: google_call
functions.comment: Call any Google API method; returns JSON rows (generic escape hatch)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## google_call

The generic escape hatch: invoke **any** Google REST API method (beyond the curated adapters) and get its JSON response as SQL rows. Provide the discovery `api` name (e.g. `gmail`), the `version` (e.g. `v1`), the dotted `method` path (e.g. `users.messages.list`), and a `params_json` JSON object of method parameters.

Row shaping is automatic: if the response has exactly one list-valued field (e.g. `files`, `items`, `messages`), **each element becomes a row**; otherwise the whole response is a single JSON row. `nextPageToken` is followed transparently and `count` caps total rows.

**When to use:** reach a Google surface that has no dedicated adapter here. Discover what to pass with `google_apis()` and `google_methods(api, version)`. Auth is service-account-first via the VGI secret provider; parse the JSON with the DuckDB `json` extension (`result ->> '$.field'`). Parameters are validated at bind time, so malformed `params_json` is a clean error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# google_call

Calls any Google API method and returns JSON rows. The attached example queries show how to project fields out of the JSON `result` column.

## Notes

- A single list field in the response is expanded to one row per element; otherwise the whole response is one row.
- `nextPageToken` is followed automatically; `count` bounds the scan.
- Use `google_apis()` / `google_methods()` to discover api/version/method, and the `json` extension to read the `result` column.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## google_youtube

Search YouTube for videos matching a query and return each hit with its engagement statistics as SQL rows. The first positional argument is the **search query**; `order_by` controls ranking (`relevance`, `date`, `viewCount`, `rating`) and `count` caps the results. Each row carries the video's title, channel, publish time, duration, and view/like/comment counts.

**When to use:** analyze video reach, find recent uploads on a topic, or rank content by views/likes. Auth is by **API key** (`google_api_key`) via the VGI secret provider — YouTube Data API is public. Statistics columns can be NULL when a video hides them.

**Inputs:** `query`, `count`, `page_size`, `order_by`. **Outputs:** video_id, title, description, channel, published_at, view/like/comment counts, duration, and the watch URL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## google_calendar

List events from a Google Calendar as SQL rows. Defaults to the `primary` calendar; pass `calendar_id` (an address or ID) to target another. Bound the window with `time_min` / `time_max` (a date or RFC-3339 timestamp) and free-text filter with `query`. With `single_events := true` (the default) recurring events are expanded into individual instances; set it false to see the recurring master.

**When to use:** pull schedule data into SQL to count meetings, find events in a date range, or join calendar activity with other data. All-day events have NULL `start_time`/`end_time` and `all_day = true`. Auth is service-account-first via the VGI secret provider.

**Inputs:** `calendar_id`, `time_min`, `time_max`, `query`, `count`, `page_size`, `single_events`. **Outputs:** id, summary, description, location, status, start/end timestamps, all_day, organizer, creator, and an HTML link.

workers.title: Grammar Checker
workers.tagline: Grammar/style/spell check & auto-correct for DuckDB (Java, LanguageTool)
workers.summary: Grammar, style, and spelling checking + auto-correction (LanguageTool)
workers.doc_md:
# Grammar, Style & Spelling Checking in SQL

![LanguageTool logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/LanguageTool_Logo.svg/250px-LanguageTool_Logo.svg.png)

**Proofread, spell-check, and auto-correct natural-language text directly in DuckDB SQL** — grammar checking, style suggestions, typo detection, and one-call rewriting, powered by [LanguageTool](https://languagetool.org) and served to DuckDB over Apache Arrow.

This VGI worker turns the open-source LanguageTool proofreading engine into a set of SQL functions, so you can clean up and quality-check text without leaving your database or calling an external API. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and anyone running text-heavy pipelines: validating user-generated content, normalizing product descriptions and support tickets, flagging typos in scraped or imported data, scoring writing quality, or batch-correcting columns of free text. Everything runs locally in the worker process — your text is never sent to a third-party service.

Under the hood the worker embeds [LanguageTool](https://languagetool.org), the same multilingual grammar and style checker used by millions of writers. Each query runs against a cached `JLanguageTool` engine that applies LanguageTool's rule set (grammar, punctuation, style, and spelling rules) to your text and returns structured results. The English language pack (`en-US`, `en-GB`, `en-CA`, and other English variants) is shipped in the JAR; every function accepts an optional `language` argument that defaults to `en-US`. For implementation details and the rule catalog, see the [LanguageTool developer documentation](https://dev.languagetool.org) and the [LanguageTool source on GitHub](https://github.com/languagetool-org/languagetool).

**Key concepts.** An *issue* is a single problem LanguageTool flags — a grammar, punctuation, style, or spelling rule that fired over a span of your text — carrying the rule that matched, a human-readable category and message, the offending span, and an ordered list of suggested replacements (best first). A *language* is a dialect/locale code (this worker ships the English family: `en-US`, `en-GB`, `en-CA`, ...) that decides which spellings and rules apply; it defaults to `en-US`.

**When to reach for it.** Use this worker whenever a SQL pipeline needs to find, quantify, gate on, or repair writing problems in a text column without leaving the database or shipping data to an external proofreading API: validating user-generated content, scoring writing quality, flagging typos in scraped data, or batch-cleaning free-text columns. The functions group into checking (surface or count issues, or test whether text is clean), correction (rewrite text by applying the top suggested fix), and reference (discover the supported language codes).

example_queries.description: Surface each grammar/spelling issue in a sentence with its rule, category, and suggested fixes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message, suggestions FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.') ORDER BY "offset"

example_queries.description: Count the writing issues in a piece of text (default en-US).
example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.grammar_count('I has two dog.') AS issue_count

example_queries.description: Test whether text is free of writing issues.
example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.is_grammatical('The quick brown fox jumps.') AS clean

example_queries.description: Auto-correct text by applying the top suggested fix for each issue.
example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.correct('She go to school evry day.') AS corrected

example_queries.description: List the supported English language codes to pass as the language argument.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, name FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages WHERE code LIKE 'en-%' ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: List every supported language code with its human-readable name, alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, name FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Filter to the English variants accepted by the language argument.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages WHERE code LIKE 'en-%' ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Count how many language codes this worker accepts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS supported_languages FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages

example_queries.description: List every supported language code with its human-readable name, alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, name FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages() ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Filter to the English variants accepted by the language argument.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages() WHERE code LIKE 'en-%' ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Count how many language codes this worker accepts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS supported_languages FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages()

example_queries.description: List each grammar/spelling issue in a sentence with its rule, category, flagged text, and suggested fixes, in reading order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message, bad_text, suggestions FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.') ORDER BY "offset"

example_queries.description: Show the single best suggested replacement for every fixable issue, checking a specific language variant.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, message, suggestions[1] AS top_fix FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('I has a apple.', language := 'en-US') WHERE length(suggestions) > 0

example_queries.description: Aggregate how many issues fall into each LanguageTool category for a passage.
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS issues FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('Their going too the store, its there problem.') GROUP BY category ORDER BY issues DESC

example_queries.description: List every grammar/spelling issue in a sentence, one row each.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.');

example_queries.description: Count the grammar/spelling issues in a sentence (default en-US).

## grammar.main

The single schema for this worker: grammar, style, and spelling checking plus auto-correction over Apache Arrow, powered by LanguageTool. Its functions fall into three groups — checking (surface or quantify writing issues, or test whether text is clean), correction (rewrite text by applying the top suggested fix), and reference (discover the supported language codes).

Every text-checking function takes an optional `language` argument that defaults to `en-US` and controls which dialect's spellings and rules apply. This worker ships the English family (`en-US`, `en-GB`, `en-CA`, ...); query the reference function to enumerate the exact codes before passing one.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message, suggestions FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.') ORDER BY "offset"
vgi.example_queries.description: Surface each grammar/spelling issue in a sentence with its rule, category, and suggested fixes.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.grammar_count('I has two dog.') AS issue_count
vgi.example_queries.description: Count the writing issues in a piece of text (default en-US).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.is_grammatical('The quick brown fox jumps.') AS clean
vgi.example_queries.description: Test whether text is free of writing issues.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT grammar.main.correct('She go to school evry day.') AS corrected
vgi.example_queries.description: Auto-correct text by applying the top suggested fix for each issue.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT code, name FROM grammar.main.grammar_languages WHERE code LIKE 'en-%' ORDER BY code
vgi.example_queries.description: List the supported English language codes to pass as the language argument.

functions.name: grammar_check
functions.comment: Check grammar, style, and spelling of a piece of text with LanguageTool; returns one row per issue with suggested replacements. Accepts an optional language argument (default en-US).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run LanguageTool over a piece of text and return one row per grammar, style, or spelling issue it finds, each with the rule that fired, its category, an explanatory message, the character offset/length of the flagged span, the flagged substring, and an ordered list of suggested replacements (best first). Accepts an optional `language` argument (default `en-US`). Use it to surface and explain every writing problem in detail; for a simple count use `grammar_count`, for a boolean clean test use `is_grammatical`, and to apply fixes use `correct`. `NULL` or empty text yields no rows; an unknown language fails the query.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## grammar_check(text [, language])

Returns one row per grammar/style/spelling issue LanguageTool reports for `text`, with suggested replacements. Each row carries the rule that fired, its category, an explanatory message, the `offset`/`length` of the flagged span, the flagged `bad_text`, and an ordered `suggestions` array (best first). Accepts an optional `language` (default `en-US`).

`NULL` or empty text returns no rows; an unknown language fails the query.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message, bad_text, suggestions FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.') ORDER BY "offset"
vgi.example_queries.description: List each grammar/spelling issue in a sentence with its rule, category, flagged text, and suggested fixes, in reading order.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_id, message, suggestions[1] AS top_fix FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('I has a apple.', language := 'en-US') WHERE length(suggestions) > 0
vgi.example_queries.description: Show the single best suggested replacement for every fixable issue, checking a specific language variant.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS issues FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('Their going too the store, its there problem.') GROUP BY category ORDER BY issues DESC
vgi.example_queries.description: Aggregate how many issues fall into each LanguageTool category for a passage.

vgi.executable_examples.description: List every grammar/spelling issue in a sentence, one row each.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT rule_id, category, message FROM grammar.main.grammar_check('She go to school every day.')

workers.title: Hacker News API
workers.tagline: Hacker News as DuckDB tables — front page, stories, comment threads and users. A read-only VGI worker by Query.Farm
workers.summary: Hacker News front page, stories, comment threads and user profiles, read live from the official API
workers.doc_md:
[Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com) is a link-sharing and discussion site run by Y Combinator. Members submit stories — links, Ask HN questions, Show HN launches, job ads — and discuss them in threaded comments; votes decide what reaches the front page.

### How the data is shaped

Everything posted is an *item* with a numeric id: stories, comments, polls, poll options and jobs share one id sequence and one set of columns. Items point at each other by id — a comment names its `parent`, a story lists its replies in `kids` — so reading a discussion means following ids, which the thread function does for you.

### Freshness and cost

This is the live site through its official API, not an archive: every query reads the current state, and nothing is cached unless you ask. The API has no search and no batch endpoint, so each item costs one request; requests run 32 at a time and rows stream in pages, so a `LIMIT` stops early. A whole ranking reads in a second or two, a large thread in a few seconds.

### Access

The API is public and unauthenticated, and this worker only reads. Content belongs to its authors.

example_queries.title: an_old_item_is_stable
example_queries.description: Item 8863 is Dropbox's 2007 launch post; its title and author never change.
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, author, type FROM hackernews.main.item(8863);

example_queries.title: an_unassigned_id_is_no_row
example_queries.description: An id with no item behind it returns nothing rather than an error.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM hackernews.main.item(999999999999);

example_queries.title: unix_time_becomes_a_timestamp
example_queries.description: created_at is a real instant: pg's account dates from 1160418092 in Unix time.
example_queries.sql: SELECT username, CAST(epoch(created_at) AS BIGINT) FROM hackernews.main.user('pg');

example_queries.title: a_poll_lists_its_options
example_queries.description: A poll carries the ids of its options in parts.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, len(parts) FROM hackernews.main.item(126809);

example_queries.title: a_thread_is_rooted_and_nested
example_queries.description: Every comment in a thread names its root, and the walk starts at depth 1.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(root_id = 8863), min(depth), bool_and(len(path) = depth) FROM hackernews.main.comments(8863);

example_queries.title: a_depth_cap_stops_the_walk
example_queries.description: max_depth => 1 returns exactly the story's direct replies.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM hackernews.main.comments(8863, max_depth => 1)) = (SELECT len(kids) FROM hackernews.main.item(8863));

example_queries.title: a_limit_stops_a_ranking_early
example_queries.description: A ranking streams in pages, so a LIMIT yields its rows without reading the rest.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT id FROM hackernews.main.top_stories LIMIT 30);

example_queries.title: ranks_are_dense_from_one
example_queries.description: A list's ranks run 1..n with no gaps or repeats.
example_queries.sql: SELECT min(rank) = 1 AND max(rank) = count(*) AND count(DISTINCT rank) = count(*) FROM hackernews.main.job_stories;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The whole read-only Hacker News API in one schema. The ranking tables need no arguments and are the way in: each row is a story with its id, author and score. From there an item id opens the discussion under it or any single item, and an author opens that person's profile and history. Item, user and thread lookups accept a subquery or a correlated LATERAL column; a user's full history and the newest items stream in pages and take a literal argument.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One schema holding everything the Hacker News API offers.

### Finding your way in

Start from a ranking: they are ordinary tables, one per page of the site, each row a story in rank order. A story's `id` leads into its discussion, and its `author` to the poster's profile.

### Two shapes of function

Lookups by key — one item, one user, one comment thread — are *blended*: pass a literal or a scalar subquery, or join them to a column with `LATERAL`, and every key in the batch is fetched concurrently. That is how to follow a list of ids such as a story's `kids` or a poll's `parts`, and how to read the thread under a story another query found.

Walks with no useful bound — a user's whole posting history, the newest items on the site — are *streaming scans*: they emit a page at a time so a `LIMIT` stops them. DuckDB does not allow a subquery or a column as an ordinary table function's argument, so these take a literal.

### HTML and time

Comment bodies and profile text are HTML with every special character escaped, so an apostrophe is stored as `'`. Decode with `html_to_text()` before searching them. Times arrive from the API as Unix seconds and are returned as UTC instants.

### A sample, not a directory

The API cannot list users; this feed and item authors are the only ways to discover usernames. It lists a few dozen recently changed profiles, turning over within minutes.

### Payload

Each row carries the user's whole `submitted` list, which for a long-standing account is thousands of ids.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row holding the newest item id on Hacker News. Because every story and comment takes the next id in sequence, it doubles as a running count of everything ever posted, and the difference between two readings is how much was posted in between.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
A single row, a single column.

### Uses

Ids are assigned in one sequence across all item types, so this is both the newest item and the size of the site. `recent_items()` walks back from it, which is usually the easier way to read what it points at.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The job ads currently on the site's jobs page, posted by Y Combinator companies. Each is a job item: the role is in `title`, the details in `url` or `text`. Jobs cannot be voted on or discussed, so `score` carries no signal and `descendants` is NULL. Monthly 'Who is hiring?' threads are ordinary stories, not these.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Up to 200 job ads, as the jobs page ranks them; usually a few dozen.

### Not the hiring threads

The monthly 'Ask HN: Who is hiring?' threads, where any company can post, are stories with the ads in their comments. This list is only the ads YC companies place directly.

### Cost

Rows stream in rank order, 100 per batch and one request per story, so a `LIMIT` reads only what it returns; an `ORDER BY` reads the whole list first.

columns.name: id
columns.comment: Unique item id, assigned in increasing order across every kind of item; the key item() and comments() take, and the value kids, parent, poll and parts refer to.

columns.comment: What the item is: 'story', 'comment', 'job', 'poll' or 'pollopt' (one option of a poll). Ask HN and Show HN posts are stories.

columns.name: author
columns.comment: Username of whoever posted it (the API's `by` field); the key user() takes. NULL on deleted items.

columns.name: created_at

columns.name: title
columns.comment: Headline of a story, poll or job, as plain text. NULL for comments and poll options.

columns.name: url
columns.comment: Address a link story points to. NULL for text posts such as Ask HN, and for comments.

columns.name: text
columns.comment:
Body of a comment, text post, job or poll option, as HTML: entity-escaped, with

paragraph breaks and links. html_to_text() turns it into plain text. NULL when the item has no body.

columns.name: score
columns.comment: Points (net upvotes) on a story, poll or job, or the number of votes cast for a poll option. NULL for comments, whose scores Hacker News does not publish.

columns.name: descendants
columns.comment: Number of live comments in the whole thread under a story or poll, at every depth (deleted and dead comments are not counted). NULL for other item types.

columns.name: parent
columns.comment: Id of the item a comment replies to (another comment, or the story at the top of the thread). NULL for anything that is not a comment.

columns.name: poll
columns.comment: For a poll option, the item id of the poll (its parent). NULL otherwise.

columns.name: kids
columns.comment: Ids of the direct replies, in the ranked order Hacker News displays them. Empty when there are none.

columns.name: parts
columns.comment: For a poll, the ids of its options in display order. NULL for other item types.

columns.name: deleted
columns.comment: Whether the item was deleted. A deleted item keeps its id, type and place in its thread but loses its author and body. Never NULL.

columns.name: dead
columns.comment: Whether the item is dead: killed by moderators or flags, and hidden from readers who have not opted in to seeing it. Never NULL.

The feed says only that an item changed, not how: a reply adds to `kids`, a vote moves `score`, an edit rewrites `text`. To see motion, read twice and compare on `id`.

tables.name: top_stories
tables.comment: The Hacker News front page ranking: up to 500 stories and job ads, in the order the site shows them

tags.vgi.doc_llm: What is on the Hacker News front page right now, in ranked order — the place to start for 'what is the tech world talking about today'. Rank 1 is the top slot and ranks 1-30 are the site's first page. Job ads are ranked here too; filter `type = 'story'` to drop them. Each `id` opens the story's discussion via `comments()`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The ranking behind the site's home page, up to 500 deep.

### What decides the order

Hacker News ranks by votes, decayed by age, and adjusted by moderators and flags — so a lower-scored new story can sit above a higher-scored old one. `rank` is the site's order; `score` is only one input to it.

### Cost

Rows stream in rank order, 100 per batch and one request per story, so a `LIMIT` reads only what it returns; an `ORDER BY` reads the whole list first.

tables.name: ask_stories
tables.comment: Ask HN questions currently listed, as the Ask HN page ranks them

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The Ask HN questions the site's 'ask' page lists right now: members asking the community for advice, opinions or experiences. These are text posts — the question is in `text` (HTML) and `url` is NULL — and the answers are the discussion, which `comments()` returns.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Up to 200 Ask HN posts, in the ranking of the site's 'ask' page; usually far fewer.

### Reading a question

An Ask HN post has no link: its body is in `text`, as HTML. Decode it with `html_to_text()`. Its answers are the thread under its `id`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The highest-voted stories of the last few days, as the site's 'best' page ranks them. Reach for it for 'what did people like most this week', where the front page answers 'what is hot this hour'. Scores here run far higher than on the front page.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Hacker News' 'best' ranking — highest-voted recent links — typically 200 stories deep.

### Versus the front page

The front page decays by age hour to hour; this list holds on to the strongest stories for days. Join the two on `id` to see which of today's front-page stories are also among the week's best.

vgi.example_queries.description: The ten highest-scoring stories of the last few days

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The latest submissions to Hacker News, newest first, before voting has sorted them — what the site's 'new' page shows. Use it to catch a story the moment it is posted, or to see what is being submitted rather than what is popular. Most rows have a score of one or two; that is the point of the list.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Up to 500 of the most recent submissions, in the order the 'new' page lists them.

New stories arrive every minute or so and the list holds roughly the last ten hours of them, so two reads a few minutes apart overlap only partly. Poll it, keyed on `id`, to follow everything submitted.

functions.name: user
functions.comment: Look up a Hacker News user's public profile and karma by username

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A Hacker News user's public profile — account age, karma, the about text and the ids of everything they have posted — by username. Usernames are case-sensitive. Feed it the `author` column of any item-returning object under a correlated LATERAL to put a profile beside each post. Only users with public activity exist in the API; an unknown name returns no row.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per username.

### Case matters

`pg` and `PG` are different names. Matching is exact, as the site does it, so a name in the wrong case finds nothing rather than the account you meant.

### Posts

`submitted` is every id the user has posted, newest first, and can hold tens of thousands of them. To read the posts themselves a page at a time, use `submissions()`.

### Caching

Every call refetches unless `cache_ttl => N` is passed, which caches each profile for N seconds and memoizes repeated names within a `LATERAL`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Paul Graham's account
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT username, created_at, karma, len(submitted) AS posts FROM hackernews.main.user('pg')

vgi.example_queries.description: Karma of the people who posted today's front page
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.rank, s.author, u.karma, u.created_at AS joined FROM (SELECT rank, author FROM hackernews.main.top_stories WHERE rank <= 30) s, LATERAL hackernews.main.user(s.author, cache_ttl => 300) u ORDER BY s.rank

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A user's posting history, newest first: their stories, comments, polls and job ads as full item rows. Reach for this to see what someone writes about, how their stories scored, or when they are active. The username is case-sensitive. tags.vgi.doc_md:
The items behind a user's `submitted` list, hydrated in the order the profile lists them, which is newest first.

### Size

An active account has thousands of posts and an early one tens of thousands, every one a request. Rows arrive 100 per batch, so a `LIMIT` stops the walk: a user's last 50 comments cost about 50 requests whatever their history holds. Filter on `type` to separate stories from comments — the filter runs after the fetch, so it narrows the result, not the cost.

An unknown username, or one in the wrong case, returns no rows.

functions.name: item
functions.comment: Look up any Hacker News story, comment, job or poll by its numeric id

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Any Hacker News item — story, comment, job, poll or poll option — by its numeric id. This is the building block for following the site's links: a story's `kids` are the ids of its top-level comments, a comment's `parent` points back up, and a poll's `parts` are its options, and each of them is one `item()` call. It composes under a correlated LATERAL, so a whole list of ids is looked up in one query. An id with no item behind it returns no row rather than an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per id, in the same shape every other item-returning object uses.

### Following links

The API stores relationships as bare ids, so moving through the site is a chain of lookups. Unnest a list of ids and join this function to it with `LATERAL`, and the ids in each input batch are fetched concurrently rather than one by one. For a whole comment tree at every depth, `comments()` does the walking for you.

### Missing and deleted items

An id that was never assigned yields no row. A deleted item still yields its row, with `deleted` set and `author` and `text` gone, because its replies may still be there.

### Caching

Hacker News marks every response uncacheable, so each call refetches. Pass `cache_ttl => N` to cache each item for N seconds, which also turns on per-value memoization for a `LATERAL` that looks the same id up repeatedly.

vgi.example_queries.description: The Dropbox launch post, from 2007
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT title, author, created_at, url FROM hackernews.main.item(8863)

vgi.example_queries.description: The top-level comments on the current number one story, in display order
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT k.position, c.author, hackernews.main.html_to_text(c.text) AS comment FROM (SELECT unnest(kids) AS kid, generate_subscripts(kids, 1) AS position FROM hackernews.main.top_stories WHERE rank = 1) k, LATERAL hackernews.main.item(k.kid) c ORDER BY k.position

vgi.example_queries.description: How a poll's votes split across its options
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT o.text AS option, o.score AS votes FROM (SELECT unnest(parts) AS part FROM hackernews.main.item(126809)) p, LATERAL hackernews.main.item(p.part) o ORDER BY votes DESC

functions.name: stories
functions.comment: The stories on one Hacker News list, chosen by name, in the order the site ranks them

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Hacker News' ranked story lists, hydrated into full rows with their position. Each list is also a table (`top_stories`, `new_stories`, ...) that reads as plain SQL; reach for this function when the list is chosen by a parameter or you want to compare lists in one query. `top` is the front page, `new` the latest submissions, `best` the highest-voted recent links, and `ask`, `show` and `job` the Ask HN, Show HN and jobs pages.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per story, in the order Hacker News ranks the list, with the whole item attached.

### Rank is a snapshot

The list of ids is read once, when the scan starts, and frozen for the rest of it, so each `rank` appears exactly once. The stories themselves are fetched just after, so a `score` can be a few seconds newer than the ranking it sits in.

### What each request costs

The API has no batch endpoint: reading the list is one request, and every row is one more. Rows are fetched 32 at a time and emitted 100 per batch, in rank order, so a query that stops early — a bare `LIMIT` — stops fetching too. An `ORDER BY` has to see every row first, so it reads the whole list.

### Composing

This is a streaming scan, which means it cannot be the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL`. Drive joins from it: its `id` and `author` columns feed `comments()`, `item()` and `user()`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Stories on both the front page and the best list

functions.name: recent_items
functions.comment: The latest items posted anywhere on Hacker News, comments and stories alike

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Everything posted to Hacker News most recently, across the whole site: the newest comments and stories, newest first. The argument is how many item ids to walk back through from the newest one. Reach for it for site-wide 'right now' questions — what is being discussed, who is commenting, how fast posts arrive — which the ranked lists cannot answer because they hold only stories.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Walks backwards from the newest item id, one id at a time, and returns every item it finds.

### Comments dominate

Ids are shared by every kind of item and most of what is posted is comments, so a window of recent ids is mostly comments with a few stories among them. Filter on `type`.

### Sizing the window

The site takes in tens of thousands of items a day, so a few hundred ids reach back minutes, not hours. Every id is a request, fetched 32 at a time and emitted 100 per batch, newest first; a `LIMIT` stops the walk. The window is fixed when the call starts, so posts that arrive during a long walk are not included.

functions.name: comments
functions.comment: The whole discussion under a Hacker News story or comment, one row per reply

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The complete comment tree under a story (or under any comment), flattened to one row per reply with its depth and its position in the thread. This is the answer to 'what are people saying about X': the API itself only returns each item's direct reply ids, and this walks all of them. Order by `path` to read the thread as the site shows it. The id can come from a subquery or, under LATERAL, from another table's column, so finding the story and reading its thread is one query.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Walks the reply tree under an item and returns every descendant — the item itself is not included.

### Reading the thread in order

`path` is the comment's position among its siblings at each level, so sorting by it reproduces the site's nesting exactly: `[1]`, then `[1, 1]` (the first reply to the first comment), then `[1, 1, 1]`, then `[1, 2]`, then `[2]`. `depth` is the length of the path.

### Deleted and dead comments

They are kept, flagged by `deleted` and `dead`, because replies hang beneath them. Filter them out when counting what was said; keep them when rebuilding the tree. A story's `descendants` counts only live comments, so it matches the row count here once both flags are filtered out.

### Cost

One request per comment, fetched a level at a time with 32 in flight; a thread of a thousand comments takes a few seconds. The whole tree is walked before any row is returned, so a `LIMIT` does not make it cheaper — `max_depth` does: `max_depth => 1` fetches only the direct replies.

### Many threads at once

Under `LATERAL`, every story in an input batch is walked together, so the threads of ten stories cost little more wall-clock time than the largest of them. Keep the driving side small — the front page's top ten, not all 500 — since every comment under every story is a request.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT depth, author, hackernews.main.html_to_text(text) AS comment FROM hackernews.main.comments(8863) WHERE NOT deleted AND NOT dead ORDER BY path

vgi.example_queries.description: Who talked most in the discussion of the current top story
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT author, count(*) AS comments FROM hackernews.main.comments((SELECT id FROM hackernews.main.top_stories WHERE rank = 1)) WHERE author IS NOT NULL GROUP BY author ORDER BY comments DESC, author LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: How many direct replies each of the top five stories has drawn
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.rank, s.title, count(c.id) AS replies FROM (SELECT rank, id, title FROM hackernews.main.top_stories WHERE rank <= 5) s, LATERAL hackernews.main.comments(s.id, max_depth => 1) c GROUP BY s.rank, s.title ORDER BY s.rank

functions.name: html_to_text
functions.comment: Turn Hacker News' HTML (comment bodies, text posts, profiles) into plain text

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Converts the HTML Hacker News stores in `text` and `about` into plain text you can search, count words in, or show a reader. Use it before any `LIKE`, `regexp_matches` or full-text work on comment bodies — in the raw column an apostrophe is `'` and a slash is `/`, so a plain-text pattern silently misses.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Decodes entities, turns `

` into blank lines, replaces each link with its full address, and drops the remaining tags. ### Why the raw column needs this Every special character in a comment is entity-escaped, so the word *don't* is stored as `don't` and a URL's slashes as `/`. Searching the raw column for either finds nothing, without an error to say why. ### Links The site shortens long URLs in the visible link text but keeps the whole address in the link itself, so the full address is what this returns.

vgi.example_queries.description: Decode a snippet of comment HTML
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hackernews.main.html_to_text('Don't panic & carry on') AS plain

vgi.example_queries.description: Search comment text on a thread without tripping over HTML entities
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, author FROM hackernews.main.comments(8863) WHERE hackernews.main.html_to_text(text) ILIKE '%don''t%' ORDER BY path

arguments.name: value
arguments.description: HTML from an item's text or a user's about

examples: SELECT hackernews.main.html_to_text('Don't panic & carry on') AS plain

workers.tagline: Parse HL7 v2 clinical messages for DuckDB (Java)
workers.summary: HL7 v2.x clinical message parsing (pure-Java, no HAPI)
workers.doc_md:
# HL7 v2.x Clinical Message Parsing in SQL

![HL7 International logo](https://brandguide.hl7.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2025/07/HL7-V2Primary-Logo600px.png)

Parse, validate, and query **HL7 v2.x** pipe-delimited clinical messages directly in DuckDB SQL — turn raw ADT, ORU, and ORM feeds into queryable rows over Apache Arrow, with no ETL pipeline and no heavyweight HL7 library to install.

This extension is built for healthcare data engineers, interoperability and integration teams, and anyone who needs to ingest HL7 v2 messages from EHR/EMR systems, interface engines, or message archives and analyze them with plain SQL. HL7 v2 is the most widely deployed healthcare messaging standard in the world, and its segment/field/component/subcomponent layout is notoriously fiddly to parse by hand. Reach for it whenever a clinical feed arrives as raw pipe-delimited text and you want to JOIN, filter, and aggregate its fields the same way you would any other table — rather than pre-processing the messages in an external language first.

The core concepts mirror the HL7 v2 grammar. A **message** is a sequence of carriage-return–separated **segments** (MSH, EVN, PID, PV1, OBX, ...), each of which is a list of **fields**; a field can carry repetitions and decomposes further into **components** and **subcomponents**. Individual elements are addressed by an **HL7 location** path such as `PID-5.1` (component 1 of field 5 of the PID segment) or `MSH-9`, optionally with a segment repetition like `DG1[2]-3`. Indices are 1-based per HL7 convention.

Under the hood the parser is a compact, pure-Java (pure-JDK) implementation — there is **no HAPI dependency**, keeping the worker MIT-licensed and dependency-light. It is fully **MSH-driven**: the field separator (MSH-1) and encoding characters (MSH-2: component, repetition, escape, and subcomponent delimiters) are read from each message rather than assumed, so non-standard delimiters are handled correctly. Malformed input never crashes the worker — it simply parses as invalid and yields no rows, so the functions are safe to run across dirty, mixed-quality feeds.

The format and message grammar follow the official **HL7 v2** standard published by [Health Level Seven International](https://www.hl7.org); see the [HL7 v2 product brief and documentation](https://www.hl7.org/implement/standards/product_brief.cfm?product_id=185) for the canonical segment, field, and message-type definitions. Source code, examples, and issues live in the [Query-farm/vgi-hl7 repository](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-hl7).

example_queries.description: Split an admit message into its segments, in message order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, segment, field_count FROM hl7.main.hl7_segments(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: Explode the PID segment into long-format field rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT segment, field, repetition, value FROM hl7.main.hl7_fields(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') WHERE segment = 'PID' ORDER BY field, repetition

example_queries.description: Extract the patient family name (component 1 of PID-5) by location.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I', 'PID-5.1') AS family_name

example_queries.description: Read the message type (MSH-9) for routing a mixed feed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_message_type(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') AS message_type

example_queries.description: Read the HL7 version id (MSH-12) the message claims to conform to.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_version(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') AS version

example_queries.description: Read the message control id (MSH-10) used for ACK correlation and dedupe.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_message_control_id(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') AS control_id

example_queries.description: Validate that a well-formed HL7 v2 message parses.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.is_valid_hl7(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') AS ok

example_queries.description: List the built-in sample messages, richest first, showing their type, trigger event, and segment count.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, message_type, trigger_event, segment_count FROM hl7.main.example_messages ORDER BY segment_count DESC, name;

example_queries.description: List every segment of an admit message in order (MSH, EVN, PID, PV1) with its field count.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, segment, field_count FROM hl7.main.hl7_segments(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');

example_queries.description: Split an admit message into its segments in order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, segment, field_count FROM hl7.main.hl7_segments(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') ORDER BY seq;

example_queries.description: Explode the PID segment into long-format field rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT field, repetition, value FROM hl7.main.hl7_fields(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') WHERE segment = 'PID' ORDER BY field;

example_queries.description: Extract the patient family name (component 1 of PID-5).
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I', 'PID-5.1') AS family_name;

example_queries.description: Read the message type, version, and control id from MSH.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_message_type(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') AS type, hl7.main.hl7_version(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') AS version, hl7.main.hl7_message_control_id(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') AS control_id;

example_queries.description: Validate that a well-formed message parses.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.is_valid_hl7(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') AS ok;

example_queries.description: List every field of the PID (patient identification) segment as long-format rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT field, value FROM hl7.main.hl7_fields(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') WHERE segment = 'PID';

example_queries.description: Read the HL7 version (MSH-12) from a message.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_version(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');

example_queries.description: Extract the patient's family name (component 1 of PID-5).
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I', 'PID-5.1');

example_queries.description: Extract the message type field (MSH-9) by location.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I', 'MSH-9');

example_queries.description: Address a repeated segment: read the value (OBX-5) of the second OBX result via the 1-based repetition `OBX[2]`.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|LAB|HOSP|EHR|HOSP|20240101123000||ORU^R01|MSG00002|P|2.5\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rOBR|1||ORD123|CBC^Complete Blood Count\rOBX|1|NM|WBC^White Blood Cell Count||7.2|10*3/uL|4.0-11.0|N\rOBX|2|NM|HGB^Hemoglobin||14.1|g/dL|13.5-17.5|N', 'OBX[2]-5');

example_queries.description: Read the message control ID (MSH-10) used for acknowledgements.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_message_control_id(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');

example_queries.description: Read the message type (MSH-9) from an admit message.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_message_type(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');

example_queries.description: Check that a well-formed ADT^A01 message validates.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.is_valid_hl7(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');

example_queries.description: Malformed text validates as false (never errors).
example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.is_valid_hl7('not an hl7 message');

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## HL7 v2.x parsing functions

Clinical-message parsing over Apache Arrow. The functions in this schema fall into three capability areas that mirror how you work with an HL7 v2 feed.

**Parsing** turns a raw message into rows: one row per segment, or a long-format explosion with one row per field value (repetitions expanded), so you can query a message set-wise instead of by hand.

**Extraction** pulls out individual values addressed by an HL7 location path (such as `PID-5.1` or `MSH-9`), including the common MSH header accessors for message type, version, and control id.

**Validation** tests whether text is a well-formed HL7 v2 message, which is handy for filtering dirty feeds before parsing. The parser is pure-JDK and MSH-driven — the field separator and encoding characters are read from each message rather than assumed.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A curated, browsable registry of ready-to-use example HL7 v2 messages, one per row. Query it first to discover what message types this worker handles and to obtain a well-formed sample you can study or copy. Columns: `name` (a short slug id), `message_type` (the HL7 message type such as `ADT^A01` or `ORU^R01`), `trigger_event` (the HL7 trigger-event code such as `A01`), `segment_count` (how many segments the sample has), `description` (a one-line summary), and `message` (the raw, carriage-return-delimited HL7 text). Note: VGI table functions accept only literal arguments, so paste the `message` text inline into `hl7_segments`, `hl7_fields`, or `hl7_get` rather than passing this column as a subquery.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## example_messages

A small, built-in catalog of sample **HL7 v2** messages you can query without supplying any input. It exists so you can see a well-formed message and the message types this worker understands before calling the parsing functions, which all require a message argument.

Each row describes one sample: a slug `name`, the HL7 `message_type` (e.g. `ADT^A01`, `ORU^R01`), the `trigger_event` code, a precomputed `segment_count`, a short `description`, and the raw CR-delimited `message` text itself. Browse it, sort by `segment_count`, or copy a `message` literal into `hl7_segments`, `hl7_fields`, or `hl7_get` to experiment.

The view is defined over an inline `VALUES` list, so it scans instantly with no network access and no credentials.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, message_type, trigger_event, segment_count FROM hl7.main.example_messages ORDER BY segment_count DESC, name;
vgi.example_queries.description: List the built-in sample messages, richest first, showing their type, trigger event, and segment count.

functions.name: hl7_segments
functions.comment: Split an HL7 v2.x message into its segments: one row per segment with its 3-letter id, field count, and raw text.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Splits an HL7 v2.x message into its constituent segments, returning one row per segment in message order. Each row carries the 1-based ordinal (`seq`), the 3-letter segment id (`segment`, e.g. `MSH`, `PID`, `PV1`), the number of fields in the segment (`field_count`, using HL7 numbering so `MSH-1` counts), and the raw segment text (`raw`).

Use it as the first step when ingesting a feed: enumerate what segments a message contains before drilling into fields with `hl7_fields` or `hl7_get`. The `message` argument is polymorphic — a `VARCHAR` carrying the message text or a `BLOB` carrying its bytes. NULL or malformed input (no leading MSH) yields no rows; the worker never throws.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_segments

Returns one row per segment of an HL7 v2.x message, in order. Handy for discovering a message's structure before extracting fields.

Pass the message inline as a `VARCHAR`/`BLOB`. Malformed or NULL input simply produces no rows. The returned columns are listed in this function's result schema.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, segment, field_count FROM hl7.main.hl7_segments(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');
vgi.example_queries.description: List every segment of an admit message in order (MSH, EVN, PID, PV1) with its field count.

vgi.executable_examples.description: Split an admit message into its segments in order.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT seq, segment, field_count FROM hl7.main.hl7_segments(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') ORDER BY seq

vgi.executable_examples.description: Explode the PID segment into long-format field rows.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT field, repetition, value FROM hl7.main.hl7_fields(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') WHERE segment = 'PID' ORDER BY field

vgi.executable_examples.description: Extract the patient family name (component 1 of PID-5).
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I', 'PID-5.1') AS family_name

vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_message_type(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') AS type, hl7.main.hl7_version(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') AS version, hl7.main.hl7_message_control_id(E'MSH|^~\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5EVN|A01|20240101120000PID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|MPV1|1|I') AS control_id

functions.name: hl7_fields
functions.comment: Explode an HL7 v2.x message into long format: one row per field value (repetitions expanded), keyed by segment, segment occurrence, field, and repetition. Component structure is preserved in the raw value text.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Explodes an HL7 v2.x message into long (tidy) format: one row per field value, with repeating fields expanded into separate rows. Each row is keyed by `segment` (3-letter id), `segment_rep` (0-based occurrence of that segment within the message, to disambiguate repeated OBX/DG1/etc.), `field` (1-based HL7 field number), and `repetition` (0-based index of the repeated value); `value` holds the raw field text with its component/subcomponent structure preserved.

Use it to unpivot an entire message for set-based SQL (filtering, grouping, joining) instead of addressing one location at a time with `hl7_get`. Note the MSH quirk: MSH-1 (the field separator) and MSH-2 (the encoding characters, which literally contain `~`) are emitted as single verbatim values and are not re-split on the repetition separator. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or `BLOB` bytes; NULL or malformed input yields no rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_fields

Unpivots a whole HL7 v2.x message into long format — one row per field value with repetitions expanded — so you can query it with ordinary SQL.

Component/subcomponent structure stays intact in `value`; decompose it further with `hl7_get` or by splitting on the encoding characters. MSH-1/MSH-2 are kept verbatim. The returned columns are listed in this function's result schema.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT field, value FROM hl7.main.hl7_fields(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I') WHERE segment = 'PID';
vgi.example_queries.description: List every field of the PID (patient identification) segment as long-format rows.
