functions.name: hl7_version
functions.comment: The HL7 version ID from MSH-12 (e.g. '2.5').

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Reads the HL7 version ID from field MSH-12, e.g. `2.3`, `2.5`, or `2.7`. This tells you which release of the HL7 v2.x standard the message claims to conform to, which affects field semantics across versions.

Use it to branch parsing logic or to audit which versions a feed is sending. Returns the raw MSH-12 text, or NULL when the message is malformed or the field is absent; NULL input yields NULL. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or `BLOB` bytes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_version

Returns MSH-12, the HL7 v2.x version id (e.g. `2.5`).

Useful for version-aware handling and feed audits. Malformed or absent input maps to NULL rather than erroring.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_version(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');
vgi.example_queries.description: Read the HL7 version (MSH-12) from a message.

functions.name: hl7_get
functions.comment: Extract a value from an HL7 v2.x message by location (e.g. 'PID-5', 'PID-5.1', 'MSH-9.1', 'DG1[2]-3'); 1-based field/component/subcomponent indices.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Extracts a single value from an HL7 v2.x message addressed by an HL7 location string. Supports `'PID-5'` (a whole field), `'PID-5.1'` (component 1 of field 5), `'MSH-9.1.2'` (component.subcomponent), and a segment repetition such as `'DG1[2]-3'` or `'DG1(2)-3'`. Field, component, and subcomponent indices are 1-based per HL7 convention; the first repetition of a repeating field is addressed. A segment repetition in brackets is also 1-based, so `'OBX[2]-5'` reads the second OBX — this is the 1-based counterpart of the 0-based `segment_rep` column emitted by `hl7_fields` (`segment_rep = 1` there is `[2]` here).

Use it to pull individual data points (patient name, message type, ordering provider, etc.) out of a feed without exploding the whole message. Returns NULL when the message is malformed, the location syntax is invalid, or the addressed element is absent; a NULL message yields NULL. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or a `BLOB` of bytes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_get

Reads one value from an HL7 v2.x message by location — e.g. `hl7_get(msg, 'PID-5.1')` for a patient's family name.

Location grammar: `SEG-field[.component[.subcomponent]]` with an optional segment repetition `SEG[n]-field`. Indices are 1-based. Missing/invalid locations return NULL rather than erroring, so it is safe to run across dirty data.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I', 'PID-5.1');
vgi.example_queries.description: Extract the patient's family name (component 1 of PID-5).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I', 'MSH-9');
vgi.example_queries.description: Extract the message type field (MSH-9) by location.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|LAB|HOSP|EHR|HOSP|20240101123000||ORU^R01|MSG00002|P|2.5\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rOBR|1||ORD123|CBC^Complete Blood Count\rOBX|1|NM|WBC^White Blood Cell Count||7.2|10*3/uL|4.0-11.0|N\rOBX|2|NM|HGB^Hemoglobin||14.1|g/dL|13.5-17.5|N', 'OBX[2]-5');
vgi.example_queries.description: Address a repeated segment: read the value (OBX-5) of the second OBX result via the 1-based repetition `OBX[2]`.

tags.vgi.title: Extract HL7 Value By Location

arguments.name: message
arguments.description: The HL7 v2.x message to read from, supplied inline as the message itself (either its text or its raw bytes), never a file path. Evaluated per row; NULL or malformed input yields NULL.

arguments.name: location
arguments.description: The HL7 location path identifying the value to extract, supplied as a constant string. A path addresses a value by naming a segment and a field number within it, and may optionally drill deeper into a component and then a subcomponent of that field, as well as pick which repeated occurrence of the segment to read. Indices are numbered from one per HL7 convention. The path is an open-ended grammar spanning arbitrary HL7 segments, not a short fixed vocabulary; the function documentation gives the full syntax and worked examples. An unparseable or absent path yields NULL.

examples: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I', 'PID-5.1');

SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I', 'MSH-9');

SELECT hl7.main.hl7_get(E'MSH|^~\\&|LAB|HOSP|EHR|HOSP|20240101123000||ORU^R01|MSG00002|P|2.5\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rOBR|1||ORD123|CBC^Complete Blood Count\rOBX|1|NM|WBC^White Blood Cell Count||7.2|10*3/uL|4.0-11.0|N\rOBX|2|NM|HGB^Hemoglobin||14.1|g/dL|13.5-17.5|N', 'OBX[2]-5');

functions.name: hl7_message_control_id
functions.comment: The message control ID from MSH-10.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Reads the message control ID from field MSH-10, the sender-assigned unique identifier for this message. It is echoed back in the acknowledgement (ACK MSA-2) and is the key for de-duplication and message tracking.

Use it to correlate a message with its ACK, to dedupe a feed, or to trace a single message end to end. Returns the raw MSH-10 text, or NULL when the message is malformed or the field is absent; NULL input yields NULL. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or `BLOB` bytes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_message_control_id

Returns MSH-10, the message control id — the sender's unique id for the message, echoed in the ACK (MSA-2).

Use it for de-duplication, ACK correlation, and message tracing. Malformed or absent input maps to NULL rather than erroring.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_message_control_id(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');
vgi.example_queries.description: Read the message control ID (MSH-10) used for acknowledgements.

functions.name: hl7_message_type
functions.comment: The HL7 message type from MSH-9 (e.g. 'ADT^A01' or 'ADT^A01^ADT_A01').

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Reads the HL7 message type from field MSH-9, e.g. `ADT^A01` (event) or `ADT^A01^ADT_A01` (with the message structure). This identifies what kind of message it is — an admit (ADT), observation result (ORU), order (ORM), etc.

Use it to route or filter a mixed feed by message type. Returns the raw MSH-9 text, or NULL when the message is malformed or the field is absent; NULL input yields NULL. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or `BLOB` bytes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## hl7_message_type

Returns MSH-9, the HL7 message type/trigger event (e.g. `ADT^A01`).

The most common dispatch key in an HL7 v2 feed — use it to split or route messages by type. Malformed/absent input maps to NULL rather than erroring.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.hl7_message_type(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');
vgi.example_queries.description: Read the message type (MSH-9) from an admit message.

functions.name: is_valid_hl7
functions.comment: True when the input parses as a well-formed HL7 v2.x message (begins with an MSH segment defining the field separator and encoding characters).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Tests whether text parses as a well-formed HL7 v2.x message: it must begin with an `MSH` segment that defines the field separator (MSH-1) and the encoding characters (MSH-2). Returns true for a valid message, false for malformed text (never an error), and NULL for a NULL input.

Use it as a cheap gate before parsing — e.g. filter a staging table to rows that are actually HL7 v2 before calling `hl7_segments`, `hl7_fields`, or `hl7_get`. The `message` argument is a `VARCHAR` text or a `BLOB` of bytes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## is_valid_hl7

Boolean predicate: does this text look like an HL7 v2.x message (leading MSH with separators and encoding chars)?

Designed to be safe on dirty input — malformed text returns `false` rather than raising, and NULL maps to NULL. Pair it with a `WHERE` clause to skip non-HL7 rows before parsing.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.is_valid_hl7(E'MSH|^~\\&|SENDING_APP|SENDING_FAC|RECV_APP|RECV_FAC|20240101120000||ADT^A01|MSG00001|P|2.5\rEVN|A01|20240101120000\rPID|1||10001^^^HOSP^MR||Doe^John||19800101|M\rPV1|1|I');
vgi.example_queries.description: Check that a well-formed ADT^A01 message validates.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hl7.main.is_valid_hl7('not an hl7 message');
vgi.example_queries.description: Malformed text validates as false (never errors).

tags.vgi.title: Validate HL7 v2 Message

workers.doc_md:
# iCalendar (.ics) Parsing in SQL

![iCal4j logo](https://www.ical4j.org/images/logo-48.png)

**Query iCalendar feeds directly in DuckDB SQL** — turn `.ics` calendar files into queryable rows of events, to-dos, and calendar metadata, powered by the battle-tested [iCal4j](https://github.com/ical4j/ical4j) RFC 5545 parser.

This VGI extension brings full iCalendar parsing to your SQL workflow. If you work with calendar exports from Google Calendar, Microsoft Outlook, Apple Calendar, or any RFC 5545-compliant feed, you can load and analyze that data without a separate ETL step. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and developers who want to ingest calendar feeds, run scheduling analytics, deduplicate events, audit recurrence rules, or validate `.ics` files entirely in SQL.

Under the hood the worker wraps [iCal4j](https://www.ical4j.org/), the mature open-source Java library implementing the iCalendar specification ([RFC 5545](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5545)). Parsing runs with relaxed, Outlook-compatible compatibility hints so messy real-world feeds load cleanly, and every timestamp is normalised to UTC and surfaced as `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`. Results stream back to DuckDB over Apache Arrow, so large feeds are processed efficiently and bad or unparsable input never crashes a query — it simply yields no rows, `NULL`, or `false`.

## What you can do

The worker exposes both **table functions**, which expand a feed into one row per calendar entry (surfacing fields such as uid, summary, description, start/end or due timestamps, all-day flag, location, status, organizer, attendees, recurrence rule, priority, and percent-complete), and **scalar functions** for quick, row-level answers such as reading a calendar's display name, tallying entries, or validating a feed.

Every function takes the same polymorphic argument: a `VARCHAR` file path (the worker opens and reads the file) or a `BLOB` of raw `.ics` bytes (parsed in place), making it easy to query files on disk or calendar data already stored in a column. Recurrence rules are surfaced as their raw RRULE strings rather than expanded into individual occurrences.

## Learn more

- [iCal4j source repository](https://github.com/ical4j/ical4j)
- [iCal4j documentation](https://www.ical4j.org/)
- [RFC 5545 (iCalendar specification)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5545)

# iCalendar functions

Parse iCalendar (`.ics`) feeds directly in SQL over Apache Arrow, powered by [iCal4j](https://www.ical4j.org/) ([RFC 5545](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5545)).

The functions in this schema cover three areas:

- **Events** — expand a feed into event rows, or tally them.
- **To-dos** — expand a feed into task rows.
- **Calendar metadata** — read calendar-level properties and validate feed health.

Every function accepts the same polymorphic argument: a `VARCHAR` file path (the worker reads the file) or a `BLOB` of raw `.ics` bytes (parsed in place). Timestamps are normalised to UTC and surfaced as `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`, and bad or NULL input never crashes a query.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A curated, browsable registry of ready-to-use example iCalendar (`.ics`) feeds, one per row. Query it first to discover what a well-formed feed looks like and to obtain a sample you can study or copy. Columns: `name` (a short slug id), `calendar_name` (the feed's X-WR-CALNAME display name), `event_count` (how many VEVENTs the sample has), `todo_count` (how many VTODOs it has), `description` (a one-line summary), and `feed` (the raw iCalendar text). Note: VGI table functions accept only literal arguments, so paste the `feed` text inline into `ical_events`, `ical_todos`, `ical_event_count`, `ical_calendar_name`, or `is_valid_ical` rather than passing this column as a subquery.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## example_calendars

A small, built-in catalog of sample **iCalendar** (`.ics`) feeds you can query without supplying any input. It exists so you can see a well-formed feed and the kinds of calendar this worker understands before calling the parsing functions, which all require a feed argument.

Each row describes one sample: a slug `name`, the `calendar_name` display name (X-WR-CALNAME), a precomputed `event_count` and `todo_count`, a short `description`, and the raw `feed` text itself. Browse it, sort by `event_count`, or copy a `feed` literal into `ical_events`, `ical_todos`, or the scalar helpers to experiment.

The view is defined over an inline `VALUES` list, so it scans instantly with no network access and no credentials.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, calendar_name, event_count, todo_count FROM ical.main.example_calendars ORDER BY event_count DESC, name;

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# ical_todos

Parse an iCalendar (`.ics`) feed into **one row per VTODO** (task). Use it to pull outstanding to-dos out of a shared calendar for task tracking or reporting.

**Input** (positional, polymorphic): a `VARCHAR` file path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of `.ics` bytes.

**Output**: uid, summary, UTC-normalised `due` (`TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`), status (`NEEDS-ACTION` / `IN-PROCESS` / `COMPLETED` / `CANCELLED`), priority (0-9), and percent complete (0-100).

**Edge cases**: a NULL argument or an unparsable feed yields *no rows* (never an error). A feed with only events (no VTODOs) yields no rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Parses an iCalendar (`.ics`) feed into one row per VTODO (task), backed by iCal4j (RFC 5545).

Accepts a `VARCHAR` file path or a `BLOB` of `.ics` bytes. The `due` column is normalised to UTC and surfaced as `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`. Filter on `status` to separate open from completed tasks. Bad or NULL input yields no rows rather than an error.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT summary, status, percent_complete FROM ical.main.ical_todos(array_to_string(['BEGIN:VCALENDAR','VERSION:2.0','PRODID:-//Query Farm//vgi-ical//EN','X-WR-CALNAME:Team Calendar','BEGIN:VEVENT','UID:event-1@query.farm','SUMMARY:Sprint Planning','DESCRIPTION:Plan the next two-week sprint.','DTSTART:20240115T093000Z','DTEND:20240115T103000Z','LOCATION:Conference Room A','STATUS:CONFIRMED','ORGANIZER:mailto:alice@query.farm','ATTENDEE:mailto:bob@query.farm','ATTENDEE:mailto:carol@query.farm','RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO','SEQUENCE:3','END:VEVENT','BEGIN:VTODO','UID:todo-1@query.farm','SUMMARY:Write release notes','DUE:20240120T170000Z','STATUS:NEEDS-ACTION','PRIORITY:2','PERCENT-COMPLETE:40','END:VTODO','END:VCALENDAR'], chr(10))::BLOB) WHERE status <> 'COMPLETED' ORDER BY due;

functions.name: ical_events
functions.comment: Parse an iCalendar (.ics) feed into one row per VEVENT: uid, summary, UTC-normalised start/end, all-day flag, location, status, organizer, attendees array, recurrence rule, sequence, category tags, url, and created/last-modified timestamps (iCal4j).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# ical_events

Parse an iCalendar (`.ics`) feed into **one row per VEVENT**. Use it to ingest a calendar feed for scheduling analytics, reporting, or joining events against other tables.

**Input** (positional, polymorphic): a `VARCHAR` file path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of `.ics` bytes.

**Output**: uid, summary, description, UTC-normalised `dtstart`/`dtend` (`TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`), an `all_day` flag, location, status, organizer, an `attendees VARCHAR[]` array, the recurrence `rrule`, `sequence`, a `categories VARCHAR[]` tag array, `url`, and the UTC-normalised `created` / `last_modified` audit timestamps.

**Edge cases**: a NULL argument or a feed that fails to parse yields *no rows* (never an error). `DATE`-valued starts set `all_day = true`; recurrences are surfaced as the raw RRULE string, not expanded.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Parses an iCalendar (`.ics`) feed into one row per VEVENT, backed by iCal4j (RFC 5545).

Accepts a `VARCHAR` file path or a `BLOB` of `.ics` bytes. Timestamps are normalised to UTC and surfaced as `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`. Bad or NULL input yields no rows rather than an error. Recurrence rules appear as the raw RRULE string in the `rrule` column.

functions.name: ical_event_count
functions.comment: Count the VEVENTs in an .ics feed (0 when the feed is empty or unparsable).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# ical_event_count

Return the **number of VEVENTs** in an iCalendar (`.ics`) feed without materialising the rows. Use it as a cheap probe — e.g. to skip empty feeds or rank feeds by activity.

**Input** (positional, polymorphic): a `VARCHAR` file path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of `.ics` bytes.

**Output**: an `INTEGER` count. NULL input yields NULL; an empty or unparsable feed yields `0` (never an error).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Counts the VEVENTs in an iCalendar (`.ics`) feed.

Accepts a `VARCHAR` file path or a `BLOB` of `.ics` bytes and returns an `INTEGER`. A NULL argument returns NULL; an empty or unparsable feed returns `0`. Cheaper than materialising and counting rows from the event table function when you only need the tally.

functions.name: is_valid_ical
functions.comment: True when the input parses as a well-formed iCalendar (.ics) feed (iCal4j, relaxed).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# is_valid_ical

Test whether the input parses as a **well-formed iCalendar (`.ics`) feed** under iCal4j's compatibility-relaxed rules. Use it to guard a pipeline before calling `ical_events` / `ical_todos`, or to filter dirty data.

**Input** (positional, polymorphic): a `VARCHAR` file path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of `.ics` bytes.

**Output**: a `BOOLEAN`. NULL input yields NULL; malformed bytes yield `false` (never an error). Validation is relaxed, so minor RFC violations still count as valid.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Returns true when the input parses as a well-formed iCalendar (`.ics`) feed (iCal4j, compatibility-relaxed).

Accepts a `VARCHAR` file path or a `BLOB` of `.ics` bytes. A NULL argument returns NULL; malformed input returns `false` rather than raising an error, so it is safe to call across a column of mixed-quality data.

workers.doc_md:
# image — Image Inspection, EXIF/GPS, Perceptual Hashing & Thumbnails in SQL

![image logo](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/49300799?s=240&v=4)

Decode images, read EXIF and GPS metadata, compute perceptual hashes for near-duplicate detection, and generate thumbnails directly in DuckDB SQL — no external tooling or file wrangling required. The `image` worker brings a full image-processing toolbox to the `img` catalog, turning ordinary `BLOB` columns of PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, TIFF and WebP bytes into queryable, structured data.

This extension is for anyone cataloguing, deduplicating, or auditing image collections from SQL: data engineers building media pipelines, analysts hunting near-duplicate or geotagged photos, and teams that want EXIF and perceptual-hash features right next to their existing DuckDB tables. Everything runs in-process over Apache Arrow, so image-derived columns join against the rest of your data without ever leaving the database.

## How it works

The worker is powered by the pure-Rust [`image`](https://github.com/image-rs/image) crate ([docs](https://docs.rs/image)) for decoding, resizing and format conversion; [`kamadak-exif`](https://github.com/kamadak/exif-rs) ([docs](https://docs.rs/kamadak-exif)) for parsing EXIF tags and GPS coordinates; and [`image_hasher`](https://github.com/abonander/img_hash) ([docs](https://docs.rs/image_hasher)) for 64-bit perceptual hashes. Image bytes are passed as DuckDB `BLOB` values and `NULL` inputs flow through to `NULL` results, so the capabilities compose cleanly inside larger queries.

## When to reach for it

Reach for this worker to catalogue a folder of images by their format and dimensions, to read capture metadata and geotags for auditing or mapping, to find near-duplicate or reposted photos by perceptual similarity, and to normalize or preview a mixed set of images — all without leaving SQL or standing up an external image-processing service. Malformed or truncated bytes yield a graceful `NULL` or a clear error, so it is safe to run across messy data at scale.

# img.main

The primary schema of the image worker. It groups its capabilities into a few areas: **inspection** of an image's header (format, dimensions, color model), reading embedded **metadata** (EXIF tags and decimal GPS), perceptual **hashing** for near-duplicate detection, and image **transformation** (thumbnailing and format conversion).

Every function takes a single image `BLOB` (PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, or WebP); a NULL input flows through to a NULL result, and undecodable bytes surface a clear error. Everything runs in-process over Apache Arrow, so image-derived columns join cleanly against the rest of your data.

workers.title: IOC Extraction & Defang/Refang
workers.tagline: Extract & defang/refang IOCs from text for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.summary: Defensive CTI tooling: extract and defang/refang indicators of compromise (IOCs) from free text.
workers.doc_md:
# IOC Extraction & Defang/Refang for DuckDB

Pull indicators of compromise (IOCs) out of cyber-threat-intelligence (CTI) reports and defang or refang them with plain SQL — no Python notebook, regex cheat-sheet, or external service required. The `ioc` extension turns DuckDB into an IOC parser that recognizes IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, domains, URLs, e-mail addresses, file hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512) and CVE identifiers, and converts between live indicators (`http://evil.com`) and the *defanged* form (`hxxp[://]evil[.]com`) that analysts use to share malware artifacts safely. It is built for threat hunters, incident responders, SOC analysts and data engineers who already keep logs, alerts and reports in DuckDB and want indicator extraction to be just another column expression.

This is a purely **defensive** tool: it reads and rewrites indicators that already exist in your text — it never generates attacks, resolves names, or touches the network. Extraction is powered by the Rust [`regex`](https://github.com/rust-lang/regex) crate ([documentation](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)), whose linear-time, backtracking-free engine matches large reports without catastrophic blowup. The worker is a standalone binary that DuckDB attaches over Apache Arrow IPC, so results stream back as native Arrow columns. A key design choice is *refang-before-extract*: every extractor (and `is_ioc` / `extract_iocs`) first refangs a copy of its input, so indicators that were defanged in a report — `10[.]0[.]0[.]5`, `bad[at]evil[.]com`, `hxxp://evil[.]com` — are still found. Only defanging and refanging themselves skip that step.

Reach for it whenever indicators live inside free text rather than tidy columns: enriching an alerts or tickets table, building a watchlist from an incident report, sanitizing artifacts before sharing them, or joining extracted indicators against a threat feed. Functions are grouped into extraction, defang/refang and classification, and each carries its own worked examples.
workers.readme_sql:
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'ioc' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-ioc@v0.2.0');
SET search_path = 'ioc.main';

-- Make an indicator safe to paste into a report.
SELECT defang('http://evil.com/x');          -- → 'hxxp[://]evil[.]com/x'

-- Turn a defanged indicator back into live form.
SELECT refang('hxxp://evil[.]com');          -- → 'http://evil.com'

-- Pull indicators out of a (defanged) report. Extractors refang internally.
SELECT UNNEST(extract_ipv4('beacon from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5'));   -- → '10.0.0.5'
SELECT UNNEST(extract_cves('exploiting CVE-2024-1234'));     -- → 'CVE-2024-1234'

-- Classify a hash by length.
SELECT hash_type('d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e');        -- → 'md5'

-- Does this text contain any IOC?
SELECT is_ioc('CVE-2021-44228 in the logs');                 -- → true

-- Every distinct IOC as typed rows (table function).
SELECT type, value
FROM extract_iocs('beacon to hxxp://evil[.]com from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5')
ORDER BY type, value;
-- type | value
-- ipv4 | 10.0.0.5
-- url  | http://evil.com

example_queries.description: Extract every distinct indicator from a defanged report as (type, value) rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, value FROM ioc.main.extract_iocs('beacon to hxxp://evil[.]com from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5') ORDER BY type, value

example_queries.description: Count the indicators in a report, grouped by type.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS n FROM ioc.main.extract_iocs('c2 hxxp://evil[.]com from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5 and bad[at]evil[.]com') GROUP BY type ORDER BY type

example_queries.description: Defang a live URL so it is safe to paste into a report.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ioc.main.defang('http://evil.com/x') AS safe

example_queries.description: Pull the defanged IPv4 addresses out of a report, one per row.
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_ipv4('beacon from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5')) AS ip

example_queries.description: Classify a hex digest by algorithm.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ioc.main.hash_type('d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e') AS algorithm

example_queries.description: List the network-layer indicator types and the function that extracts each.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, extractor FROM ioc.main.ioc_types WHERE kind = 'network' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Count how many indicator types fall into each coarse group.
example_queries.sql: SELECT kind, count(*) AS n_types FROM ioc.main.ioc_types GROUP BY kind ORDER BY kind

example_queries.description: Count the distinct indicators found in a report, grouped by indicator type.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS n FROM ioc.main.extract_iocs('beacon to hxxp://evil[.]com from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5 and bad[at]evil[.]com') GROUP BY type ORDER BY type

example_queries.description: Keep only the network-layer indicators (IPs, domains, URLs) from a report.
example_queries.sql: SELECT value FROM ioc.main.extract_iocs('c2 hxxp://evil[.]com from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5') WHERE type IN ('ipv4', 'ipv6', 'url', 'domain') ORDER BY value

example_queries.description: Pull a defanged URL out of a report (returns 'http://evil.com/x').
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_urls('payload from hxxp://evil[.]com/x'));

example_queries.description: Pull a bare defanged domain out of a report (returns 'evil.example.com').
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_domains('callback to evil[.]example[.]com'));

example_queries.description: Pull a CVE identifier out of a report (returns 'CVE-2024-1234').
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_cves('exploiting CVE-2024-1234 in the wild'));

example_queries.description: Defang a live URL so it is safe to paste into a report (returns 'hxxp[://]evil[.]com/x').
example_queries.sql: SELECT ioc.main.defang('http://evil.com/x');

example_queries.description: Classify a 32-character hex string as an MD5 hash (returns 'md5').
example_queries.sql: SELECT ioc.main.hash_type('d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e');

example_queries.description: Pull a defanged e-mail address out of a report (returns 'bad@evil.com').
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_emails('phish from bad[at]evil[.]com'));

example_queries.description: Pull a file hash out of a report (returns 'd41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e').
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_hashes('sample md5 d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e'));

example_queries.description: Refang a defanged URL back to live form (returns 'http://evil.com').
example_queries.sql: SELECT ioc.main.refang('hxxp://evil[.]com');

example_queries.description: Pull the defanged IPv4 address out of a report (returns '10.0.0.5').
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_ipv4('beacon from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5'));

example_queries.description: Pull an IPv6 address out of free text (returns '2001:db8::1').
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_ipv6('C2 at 2001:db8::1 observed'));

## IOC extraction & defang/refang

Indicator-of-compromise tooling for cyber-threat intelligence, served over Apache Arrow. Pull IPv4/IPv6 addresses, domains, URLs, e-mails, file hashes and CVE identifiers out of free-text reports with plain SQL, and convert between live and *defanged* indicator forms.

### Key concepts

- **Refang-before-extract** — every extractor refangs a copy of its input first, so indicators defanged in a report (`hxxp://evil[.]com`, `10[.]0[.]0[.]5`, `bad[at]evil[.]com`) are still found.
- **Defang / refang** — neutralize live indicators so they are safe to paste into a ticket or chat, or restore them to live form.
- **Deduplicated, typed output** — the all-in-one extractor returns one `(type, value)` row per distinct indicator.

### When to use it

Reach for this schema when indicators live inside free text rather than tidy columns — enriching an alerts table, building a watchlist from an incident report, or sanitizing artifacts before sharing them. Browse the functions below, grouped by category, each with its own worked examples.

vgi.example_queries.description: Extract every distinct indicator from a defanged report as (type, value) rows.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type, value FROM ioc.main.extract_iocs('beacon to hxxp://evil[.]com from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5') ORDER BY type, value

vgi.example_queries.description: Count the indicators in a report, grouped by type.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS n FROM ioc.main.extract_iocs('c2 hxxp://evil[.]com from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5 and bad[at]evil[.]com') GROUP BY type ORDER BY type

vgi.example_queries.description: Defang a live URL so it is safe to paste into a report.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ioc.main.defang('http://evil.com/x') AS safe

vgi.example_queries.description: Pull the defanged IPv4 addresses out of a report, one per row.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(ioc.main.extract_ipv4('beacon from 10[.]0[.]0[.]5')) AS ip

vgi.example_queries.description: Classify a hex digest by algorithm.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ioc.main.hash_type('d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e') AS algorithm

tables.comment: Registry of the indicator-of-compromise types this worker recognizes: for each type, the group it belongs to, the function that extracts it, a defanged example, and a one-line description.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A browsable reference table listing every indicator-of-compromise type this worker can recognize. Columns: `name` (the type, e.g. ipv4, sha256, cve), `kind` (a coarse group: network, email, hash, or vulnerability), `extractor` (the scalar function that pulls this type out of text, e.g. extract_ipv4), `example` (a short defanged sample value), and `description`. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `ioc_types` — indicator type registry

A small, static reference table you can browse to see exactly which indicator-of-compromise types this worker recognizes and which function extracts each. Handy as a first stop before calling a specific extractor.

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | the indicator type — `ipv4`, `ipv6`, `domain`, `url`, `email`, `md5`, `sha1`, `sha256`, `sha512`, `cve` |
| `kind` | coarse group: `network`, `email`, `hash`, or `vulnerability` |
| `extractor` | the scalar function that pulls this type out of text |
| `example` | a short defanged sample value |
| `description` | one-line notes on how the type is matched |

Ten rows, one per type. It is backed by an inline literal list, so scanning it needs no network or credentials. To pull every type out of a report at once, use the `extract_iocs` table function instead.

vgi.example_queries.description: List the network-layer indicator types and the function that extracts each.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, extractor FROM ioc.main.ioc_types WHERE kind = 'network' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Count how many indicator types fall into each coarse group.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT kind, count(*) AS n_types FROM ioc.main.ioc_types GROUP BY kind ORDER BY kind

workers.title: ISO 20022 Payments
workers.tagline: Parse ISO 20022 (pacs/camt/pain) and SWIFT MT payment messages in DuckDB with SQL — no egress. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Parse SWIFT MT and ISO 20022 MX payment messages into typed, queryable rows. Local-only, no network, no egress.
workers.doc_md:
# iso20022 — SWIFT MT & ISO 20022 MX Payment Parsing in SQL

**Turn SWIFT MT and ISO 20022 MX payment messages into typed, queryable rows directly in DuckDB.** ATTACH the worker over Apache Arrow and parse FIN/MT files and MX XML documents locally — one typed row per message, transaction, or statement entry — so payments become plain relational data instead of something you feed to a bespoke parser.

It is built for **bank / fintech / payment-processor** data teams doing reconciliation, ISO 20022 migration dual-running QA (MT vs MX equivalence), and sanctions/feature extraction. Money is parsed with exact decimals (no float drift) so amount-equality joins hold; dates use the SWIFT century pivot and ISO 8601. **Data residency:** the worker makes zero outbound calls and parses every message locally — debtor/creditor names, IBANs, and amounts never leave the host.

Reach for it whenever you have MT statements or transfers, or camt/pacs/pain XML, on disk (or inline) and want them as rows. It provides file-glob **readers** (one row per message, transaction, or statement), per-message **exploders** that unnest statement entries and lines, and **inspection scalars** that sniff the MT type, read a field, return the exact settled amount, and validate a message. Money is parsed as exact decimals so amount-equality joins hold, and dates use the SWIFT century pivot plus ISO 8601. The parsers are built on permissive open-source components and the open, freely published ISO 20022 message standard (iso20022.org); the [source repository](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-iso20022) carries the full catalog and examples.

example_queries.description: Sniff the SWIFT MT message type of an inline FIN message.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT iso20022.main.iso20022_mt_type('{1:F01X}{2:I103X}{4:
:20:R
-}') AS mt

example_queries.description: Read the exact :32A: interbank settled amount of an inline MT103 as a fixed-scale decimal.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT iso20022.main.iso20022_mt103_amount('{1:F01X}{2:I103X}{4:
:20:R
:32A:260101EUR1234,56
-}') AS amount

example_queries.description: Validate an inline pacs.008 message and read the ok flag.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (iso20022.main.iso20022_validate('<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pacs.008.001.08"><FIToFICstmrCdtTrf><GrpHdr><MsgId>M</MsgId></GrpHdr></FIToFICstmrCdtTrf></Document>')).ok AS ok

example_queries.description: List the message types that have a dedicated entry/line exploder function, with their reader.
example_queries.sql: SELECT message_type, reader_function, exploder_function FROM iso20022.main.supported_messages WHERE exploder_function IS NOT NULL ORDER BY message_type

example_queries.description: Parse an inline MT103 credit transfer and read its exact settled amount, currency, and parties.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT senders_ref, value_date, ccy, amount, beneficiary FROM iso20022.main.mt103_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:I103DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{3:{121:e3bf1c2a-1111-4aaa-8bbb-1234567890ab}}{4:
:20:TXN-REF-1
:23B:CRED
:32A:260101EUR1234,56
:50K:/DE89370400440532013000
ACME CORP
:59:/FR1420041010050500013M02606
WIDGETS SARL
:70:INVOICE 998877
:71A:SHA
:72:/EToE/E2E-REF-001
-}') WHERE amount > 1000;

example_queries.description: Parse an inline MT942 interim (intra-day) statement header: account, currency, and the credit/debit turnover counts.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT transaction_ref, account, ccy, credit_count, credit_sum, debit_count FROM iso20022.main.mt942_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:O942DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{4:
:20:INTERIM-1
:25:DE89370400440532013000
:28C:99/1
:34F:EURD0,00
:34F:EURC1000,00
:13D:2601021430+0100
:61:2601020102C500,00NTRFNONREF//BANK-A
:86:INCOMING
:90D:5EUR2500,00
:90C:3EUR1500,00
-}') WHERE account IS NOT NULL;

example_queries.description: Read an MT942 interim report inline, then explode its :61: lines.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT value_date, credit_debit, amount FROM iso20022.main.mt942_lines((SELECT raw FROM iso20022.main.mt942_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:O942DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{4:
:20:INTERIM-1
:25:DE89370400440532013000
:28C:99/1
:34F:EURD0,00
:34F:EURC1000,00
:61:2601020102C500,00NTRFNONREF//BANK-A
:86:INCOMING
-}')));

example_queries.description: Parse an inline MT940 end-of-day statement header: account, currency, closing balance, and the number of statement lines.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT transaction_ref, account, ccy, closing_balance, line_count FROM iso20022.main.mt940_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:O940DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{4:
:20:STMT-1
:25:DE89370400440532013000
:28C:12345/1
:60F:C260101EUR1000,00

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Functions to parse SWIFT MT and ISO 20022 MX payment messages: file-glob readers (mt103_read … camt054_read), per-message entry/line exploders, and scalars for type sniffing, field access, exact amount, and validation.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## The `iso20022` worker schema

This is the single schema for the worker. Everything it exposes turns SWIFT MT and ISO 20022 MX payment messages into typed, relational rows you can query directly in SQL, with **no network access and no egress** — messages are parsed on the host.

The objects fall into three groups:

- **Message readers** scan a glob of message files on disk and return one typed row per message, transaction, or statement.
- **Statement exploders** take an already-selected statement or notification and unnest it into its individual entries or lines, carrying every input column through so children correlate back to the parent.
- **Message inspection** scalars sniff the message type, pull individual fields and the exact settled amount out of a single inline message, validate it against structural and CBPR+ rules, and report the worker version.

Money is parsed with exact decimals so amount-equality joins hold, and dates use the SWIFT century pivot plus ISO 8601. Each function documents its result columns and carries a runnable example.

tables.comment: Registry of the SWIFT MT and ISO 20022 MX message types this worker parses, with the reader and exploder function for each.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A browsable registry of every SWIFT MT and ISO 20022 MX message type this worker parses. One row per message type carries its family (SWIFT MT / ISO 20022 MX), the reader function that turns the message (inline text, a file path, or a glob) into rows, the optional exploder function that unnests its entries or lines, and a one-line description. Query it to discover what the worker supports before guessing reader arguments.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## supported_messages

A browsable registry of the message types this worker parses — one row per type with its `family`, `reader_function`, optional `exploder_function`, and a short `description`. Filter it (for example on `exploder_function IS NOT NULL`) to find which messages have an entry/line exploder. Local-only, no network.

vgi.example_queries.description: List the message types that have a dedicated entry/line exploder function, with their reader.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read MT103 Credit Transfers

Scan a glob of SWIFT MT103 (single customer credit transfer) text files into one row per message: ordering customer and beneficiary (name/account/BIC), the exact :32A: settled amount and currency, instructed amount, charges, remittance info, the derived end-to-end id, and the block-3 UETR. Use it for payment ingestion and MT103<->pacs.008 migration-QA joins.

The argument may be the **message text supplied inline** (handy for a single message or an example), a file path, or a glob that scans many files. All reads are local on the worker host — no network, no egress; payment data never leaves the machine. See the result columns for the full schema.

vgi.executable_examples.description: Parse an inline MT103 credit transfer and read its exact settled amount, currency, and parties.
vgi.executable_examples.sql:
SELECT senders_ref, value_date, ccy, amount, beneficiary FROM iso20022.main.mt103_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:I103DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{3:{121:e3bf1c2a-1111-4aaa-8bbb-1234567890ab}}{4:
:20:TXN-REF-1
:23B:CRED
:32A:260101EUR1234,56
:50K:/DE89370400440532013000
ACME CORP
:59:/FR1420041010050500013M02606
WIDGETS SARL
:70:INVOICE 998877
:71A:SHA
:72:/EToE/E2E-REF-001
-}') WHERE amount > 1000

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read MT942 Interim Reports

Scan a glob of SWIFT MT942 (interim transaction report) text files into one row per report: floor limits, the datetime indication, debit/credit count and sum summaries, and the line count. Use the raw column with mt942_lines(raw) to explode the :61: lines — identical in shape to mt940_lines.

The argument may be the **message text supplied inline** (handy for a single message or an example), a file path, or a glob that scans many files. All reads are local on the worker host — no network, no egress; payment data never leaves the machine. See the result columns for the full schema.

:25:DE89370400440532013000

:34F:EURD0,00
:34F:EURC1000,00

:61:2601020102C500,00NTRFNONREF//BANK-A
:86:INCOMING
:90D:5EUR2500,00
:90C:3EUR1500,00
-}') WHERE account IS NOT NULL

functions.name: mt942_lines
functions.comment: Explode MT942 :61: report lines (one per line, joined to :86:; input columns passthrough).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Explode the :61: lines of one or more MT942 interim (intra-day) reports — each :61: line joined to its following :86: narrative — into one row per line. Identical column shape to mt940_lines (`line_idx`, `value_date`/`entry_date`, `credit_debit`, positive `amount` `DECIMAL(38,9)`, `transaction_type_id`, references, flattened `narrative`, and `narrative_struct` `MAP`), with every input column passed through so lines correlate back to their parent report. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg :=`) holds each report: for example the output of `mt942_read('…')`, or an inline report.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Explode MT942 Report Lines

Explode the :61: lines of one or more MT942 interim (intra-day) reports — each :61: line joined to its following :86: narrative — into one row per line. Identical column shape to mt940_lines (`line_idx`, `value_date`/`entry_date`, `credit_debit`, positive `amount` `DECIMAL(38,9)`, `transaction_type_id`, references, flattened `narrative`, and `narrative_struct` `MAP`), with every input column passed through so lines correlate back to their parent report. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg :=`) holds each report: for example the output of `mt942_read('…')`, or an inline report.

## Calling it

This is a table-in-out function: pass the relation to explode as a subquery, e.g. `mt942_lines((SELECT raw FROM <reader>('…')))`, or feed it any relation that exposes a `raw` message column (rename it with `msg := 'col'`). Every input column is passed through unchanged, repeated once per child row, so results correlate back to the parent.

## Result schema

The passthrough input columns come first, followed by the fixed child columns — their names, types, and meanings are documented in `vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md`, and a runnable call is in `vgi.executable_examples`. Local-only — no network, no egress.

vgi.executable_examples.description: Read an MT942 interim report inline, then explode its :61: lines.
vgi.executable_examples.sql:
SELECT value_date, credit_debit, amount FROM iso20022.main.mt942_lines((SELECT raw FROM iso20022.main.mt942_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:O942DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{4:
:20:INTERIM-1
:25:DE89370400440532013000
:28C:99/1
:34F:EURD0,00
:34F:EURC1000,00
:61:2601020102C500,00NTRFNONREF//BANK-A
:86:INCOMING
-}')))

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result schema is **dynamic**: every column of the input relation you pass is returned first, unchanged and repeated once per child row, followed by the fixed child columns below. When the input is the output of a `*_read` function (or any relation that exposes a `raw` message column), that `raw` column is passed through too.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| raw | VARCHAR | Passthrough: the parent message text carried from the input relation (present whenever the input exposes a `raw` column). |
| line_idx | INTEGER | Ordinal within the statement. |
| value_date | DATE | :61: subfield 1 (YYMMDD). |
| entry_date | DATE | :61: subfield 2 (MMDD; year from value_date). |
| credit_debit | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 3 mark: C/D/RC/RD. |
| funds_code | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 3 funds code. |
| amount | DECIMAL(38,9) | :61: subfield 4 (positive; sign via credit_debit). |
| transaction_type_id | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 5 (e.g. NTRF, NMSC). |
| customer_ref | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 6 up to //. |
| bank_ref | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 6 after //. |
| supplementary | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 7. |
| narrative | VARCHAR | :86: flattened (continuations joined). |
| narrative_struct | MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR) | :86: structured ?NN/>NN subfields. |

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read pain.001 Credit Initiations

Scan a glob of ISO 20022 pain.001 (CstmrCdtTrfInitn) XML files into one row per CdtTrfTxInf, with the PmtInf debtor block carried down: control sum, requested execution date, debtor/creditor names + IBANs + BICs, amount and currency, end-to-end id, UETR, and remittance info. # Read MT202 / MT202 COV FI Transfers

Scan a glob of SWIFT MT202 / MT202 COV (general financial-institution transfer) text files into one row per message: references, value date, amount and currency, the institution chain, and — for cover messages — the underlying customer block (is_cover, cov_ordering_customer, cov_beneficiary, cov_remittance_info).

The argument may be the **message text supplied inline** (handy for a single message or an example), a file path, or a glob that scans many files. All reads are local on the worker host — no network, no egress; payment data never leaves the machine. See the result columns for the full schema.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read camt.054 Debit/Credit Notifications

Scan a glob of ISO 20022 camt.054 (BkToCstmrDbtCdtNtfctn) XML files into one row per notification, sharing the camt.053 statement column layout (account, period, balances when present, entry count). Pair with camt054_entries(raw) to explode the individual Ntry advice lines — identical in shape to camt053_entries.

The argument may be the **message text supplied inline** (handy for a single message or an example), a file path, or a glob that scans many files. All reads are local on the worker host — no network, no egress; payment data never leaves the machine. See the result columns for the full schema.

functions.name: camt054_entries

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Explode the Ntry rows of camt.054 debit/credit notifications into one row per entry — identical column shape to camt053_entries, so reconciliation queries are portable. tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Explode camt.054 Entries

Explode the Ntry rows of camt.054 debit/credit notifications into one row per entry — identical column shape to camt053_entries, so reconciliation queries are portable. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg`) holds each notification, typically the output of camt054_read.

## Calling it

This is a table-in-out function: pass the relation to explode as a subquery, e.g. `camt054_entries((SELECT raw FROM <reader>('…')))`, or feed it any relation that exposes a `raw` message column (rename it with `msg := 'col'`). Every input column is passed through unchanged, repeated once per child row, so results correlate back to the parent.

## Result schema

The passthrough input columns come first, followed by the fixed child columns — their names, types, and meanings are documented in `vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md`, and a runnable call is in `vgi.executable_examples`. Local-only — no network, no egress.

vgi.executable_examples.description: Explode the entries of an inline camt.054 notification.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT amount, credit_debit, end_to_end_id FROM iso20022.main.camt054_entries((SELECT '<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:camt.054.001.08"><BkToCstmrDbtCdtNtfctn><Ntfctn><Id>N</Id><Ntry><Amt Ccy="EUR">250.50</Amt><CdtDbtInd>DBIT</CdtDbtInd><NtryDtls><TxDtls><Refs><EndToEndId>E2E</EndToEndId></Refs></TxDtls></NtryDtls></Ntry></Ntfctn></BkToCstmrDbtCdtNtfctn></Document>' AS raw))

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result schema is **dynamic**: every column of the input relation you pass is returned first, unchanged and repeated once per child row, followed by the fixed child columns below. When the input is the output of a `*_read` function (or any relation that exposes a `raw` message column), that `raw` column is passed through too.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| raw | VARCHAR | Passthrough: the parent message text carried from the input relation (present whenever the input exposes a `raw` column). |
| entry_idx | INTEGER | Ordinal of the Ntry within the statement. |
| tx_idx | INTEGER | Ordinal of the TxDtls within the entry. |
| amount | DECIMAL(38,9) | Ntry/Amt. |
| ccy | VARCHAR | Ntry/Amt/@Ccy. |
| credit_debit | VARCHAR | Ntry/CdtDbtInd (CRDT/DBIT). |
| reversal | BOOLEAN | Ntry/RvslInd. |
| status | VARCHAR | Ntry/Sts (BOOK/PDNG/INFO). |
| booking_date | DATE | Ntry/BookgDt/Dt (or DtTm). |

| account_servicer_ref | VARCHAR | Ntry/AcctSvcrRef. |
| bank_tx_domain | VARCHAR | Ntry/BkTxCd/Domn/Cd. |
| bank_tx_family | VARCHAR | Ntry/BkTxCd/Domn/Fmly/Cd. |
| bank_tx_subfamily | VARCHAR | Ntry/BkTxCd/Domn/Fmly/SubFmlyCd. |
| bank_tx_proprietary | VARCHAR | Ntry/BkTxCd/Prtry/Cd. |
| end_to_end_id | VARCHAR | TxDtls/Refs/EndToEndId. |
| tx_id | VARCHAR | TxDtls/Refs/TxId. |
| uetr | VARCHAR | TxDtls/Refs/UETR. |
| instr_id | VARCHAR | TxDtls/Refs/InstrId. |
| mandate_id | VARCHAR | TxDtls/Refs/MndtId. |
| counterparty_name | VARCHAR | Debtor (CRDT) / creditor (DBIT) name. |
| counterparty_iban | VARCHAR | Counterparty account IBAN. |
| counterparty_agent_bic | VARCHAR | Counterparty agent BICFI. |
| remittance_unstructured | VARCHAR[] | TxDtls/RmtInf/Ustrd (repeatable). |
| remittance_struct_ref | VARCHAR | TxDtls/RmtInf/Strd/CdtrRefInf/Ref. |
| addtl_entry_info | VARCHAR | Ntry/AddtlNtryInf. |

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Explode the :61: statement lines of one or more MT940 end-of-day statements — each :61: line joined to its following :86: narrative — into one row per line. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg :=`) holds each statement: for example the output of `mt940_read('…')`, or any relation exposing a `raw` message column, or an inline statement. Each output line carries `line_idx`, `value_date` and `entry_date` (`DATE`), the `credit_debit` mark (C/D/RC/RD), positive `amount` `DECIMAL(38,9)`, `transaction_type_id` (e.g. NTRF/NMSC), `customer_ref`/`bank_ref`, the flattened `narrative`, and `narrative_struct` `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` for structured `?NN`/`>NN` narratives.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Explode MT940 Statement Lines

Explode the :61: statement lines of one or more MT940 end-of-day statements — each :61: line joined to its following :86: narrative — into one row per line. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg :=`) holds each statement: for example the output of `mt940_read('…')`, or any relation exposing a `raw` message column, or an inline statement. Every input column is passed through, repeated once per child line, so lines correlate back to their parent statement. Each output line carries `line_idx`, `value_date` and `entry_date` (`DATE`), the `credit_debit` mark (C/D/RC/RD), positive `amount` `DECIMAL(38,9)`, `transaction_type_id` (e.g. NTRF/NMSC), `customer_ref`/`bank_ref`, the flattened `narrative`, and `narrative_struct` `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` for structured `?NN`/`>NN` narratives.

## Calling it

This is a table-in-out function: pass the relation to explode as a subquery, e.g. `mt940_lines((SELECT raw FROM <reader>('…')))`, or feed it any relation that exposes a `raw` message column (rename it with `msg := 'col'`). Every input column is passed through unchanged, repeated once per child row, so results correlate back to the parent.

## Result schema

The passthrough input columns come first, followed by the fixed child columns — their names, types, and meanings are documented in `vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md`, and a runnable call is in `vgi.executable_examples`. Local-only — no network, no egress.

vgi.executable_examples.description: Read an MT940 statement inline, then explode its :61: lines (one row per line, joined to its :86: narrative).
vgi.executable_examples.sql:
SELECT value_date, credit_debit, amount, transaction_type_id FROM iso20022.main.mt940_lines((SELECT raw FROM iso20022.main.mt940_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:O940DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{4:
:20:STMT-1
:25:DE89370400440532013000
:28C:12345/1
:60F:C260101EUR1000,00
:61:2601020102C500,00NTRFNONREF//BANK-A
:86:GROCERY STORE PAYMENT
:61:2601030103D250,50NMSCCUST-REF//BANK-B
:86:RENT
:62F:C260103EUR1249,50
-}')))

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result schema is **dynamic**: every column of the input relation you pass is returned first, unchanged and repeated once per child row, followed by the fixed child columns below. When the input is the output of a `*_read` function (or any relation that exposes a `raw` message column), that `raw` column is passed through too.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| raw | VARCHAR | Passthrough: the parent message text carried from the input relation (present whenever the input exposes a `raw` column). |
| line_idx | INTEGER | Ordinal within the statement. |
| value_date | DATE | :61: subfield 1 (YYMMDD). |
| entry_date | DATE | :61: subfield 2 (MMDD; year from value_date). |
| credit_debit | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 3 mark: C/D/RC/RD. |
| funds_code | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 3 funds code. |
| amount | DECIMAL(38,9) | :61: subfield 4 (positive; sign via credit_debit). |
| transaction_type_id | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 5 (e.g. NTRF, NMSC). |
| customer_ref | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 6 up to //. |
| bank_ref | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 6 after //. |
| supplementary | VARCHAR | :61: subfield 7. |
| narrative | VARCHAR | :86: flattened (continuations joined). |
| narrative_struct | MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR) | :86: structured ?NN/>NN subfields. |

# Explode camt.053 Entries

Explode the Ntry rows of camt.053 statements (or any camt.053/054 documents) into one row per entry, with multi-TxDtls split by tx_idx and every input column passed through. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg`) holds each statement — typically the output of camt053_read — to get amount, credit/debit, dates, references, counterparty, and remittance for reconciliation.

functions.name: iso20022_mt103_field
functions.comment: Return the raw text of an MT field by tag (newline-joined if repeatable)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the raw text of any SWIFT MT field by its tag (e.g. '50K', '59', '71F', '32A') from a message's block 4. Repeatable tags (e.g. '71F') are joined with a newline. workers.doc_md:
# Jolt JSON Transformation for DuckDB

**Reshape, rename, and restructure JSON directly in SQL** with declarative JSON-to-JSON transformations powered by [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt) — no imperative parsing code, no external ETL step, just a Jolt spec and a SQL query.

This extension brings Jolt's battle-tested declarative JSON transformation engine to DuckDB so data engineers, analysts, and API integrators can normalize, remap, flatten, and enrich JSON documents where the data already lives. Instead of writing language-specific code to walk and rebuild nested objects, you describe the *target shape* with a Jolt spec and let the engine do the structural work. It is ideal for cleaning up messy API responses, conforming event-stream payloads to a canonical schema, and reshaping nested records for downstream analytics — entirely inside your DuckDB pipeline.

Under the hood the worker embeds [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt) (Apache-2.0), the widely used JVM library for specification-driven JSON transformation. A Jolt **chainr** spec is a JSON array of ordered operations — `shift` (path-based copy/move of values into a new tree), `default` (supply missing keys), `remove`, `cardinality` (single↔list coercion), `sort`, and the `modify-*-beta` function operators — applied in sequence to transform an input document into an output document. The worker compiles each spec once per Arrow batch and reuses it across rows for efficient columnar execution. To learn the spec language hands-on, try the [interactive Jolt demo](https://jolt-demo.appspot.com/) and read the [Jolt documentation](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt/blob/master/README.md).

## When to reach for it

Reach for this worker whenever a JSON document arrives in the wrong shape for what comes next: keys need renaming, values need lifting out of (or nesting into) deep structures, arrays need flattening or grouping, missing fields need sensible defaults, or a heterogeneous feed needs conforming to one canonical schema. Because the transformation is a declarative spec rather than procedural code, the same query adapts to new shapes by editing the spec — not by rewriting logic.

## Key concepts

- **Spec-driven.** You describe the *target* shape; Jolt does the structural walking. A full **chainr** spec is an ordered JSON array of operations, applied in sequence.
- **Operation vocabulary.** `shift` (path-based copy/move), `default` (supply absent keys), `remove`, `cardinality` (single↔list coercion), `sort`, and the `modify-*-beta` function operators.
- **Validation first.** Companion predicates let a pipeline check that a spec compiles and that a payload is well-formed JSON before attempting a transform, so bad rows can be filtered rather than fault the query.
- **Columnar & batched.** Each spec is compiled once per Arrow batch and reused across rows, and the document column is the data vector while the spec is a query constant.

A worked example — lift a deeply nested value up to a top-level key with a full chainr spec:

```sql
SELECT jolt.jolt_transform(
  '{"rating":{"primary":{"value":3}}}',
  '[{"operation":"shift","spec":{"rating":{"primary":{"value":"Rating"}}}}]');
```

Built and maintained by [Query.Farm](https://query.farm) for the [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) ecosystem.

# Jolt transformation & validation

Declarative JSON→JSON transformation and validation over Apache Arrow, powered by [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt). This schema groups the worker's SQL functions for reshaping JSON documents and for guarding those transforms against malformed input.

## What lives here

- **Transformation** — reshape, rename, nest, flatten, and default JSON fields by describing the target shape as a Jolt spec instead of writing imperative traversal code.
- **Validation** — cheap, never-throwing predicates that check a spec compiles and a payload is well-formed JSON, so a pipeline can filter bad rows before transforming.

## When to use it

Use it to normalize messy API responses, conform event-stream payloads to a canonical schema, and restructure nested records for downstream analytics — all inside DuckDB, with no external ETL step. Transforms raise on malformed input, while the validation predicates never throw — pair them to guard a pipeline and filter bad rows before reshaping.

# jolt_default

Apply one Jolt **default** operation — supply values for keys absent from the input document.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT jolt.main.jolt_default(
  '{"name":"widget"}',
  '{"inStock":true,"currency":"USD"}');

```

Keys already present in the input win; the spec only fills gaps. The spec is the **bare** default spec object, not the chainr operation envelope.

## Notes

- Returns `VARCHAR` JSON; output key order is not guaranteed.
- NULL input row maps to a NULL result.
- Malformed input JSON or default spec raises an error.

Apply one Jolt **shift** operation — path-based copy/move of input values into an output tree.

Apply a full [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt) **chainr** spec to a JSON document and return the transformed JSON string.

A chainr spec is a JSON **array** of operation entries, each `{"operation": <name>, "spec": <op-spec>}`, applied in order. Supported operations include `shift` (path-based copy/move), `default` (fill absent keys), `remove` (delete keys), `cardinality` (single↔list), `sort`, and the `modify-*-beta` function operations.

workers.title: Kalshi Prediction Markets
workers.tagline: Kalshi prediction-market data as ordinary DuckDB tables — a read-only VGI worker. Markets, order books, candlesticks, trades, events and the series catalog, over SQL.
workers.summary: Read-only Kalshi prediction-market data: markets, order books, candlesticks, trades, events, series
workers.doc_md:
Kalshi is a CFTC-regulated exchange for event contracts. A contract pays $1 if its question resolves YES and $0 if it resolves NO, so its price is the market's implied probability of that outcome.

### How the data is shaped

Kalshi nests in three levels, and nearly every question starts by picking one at the top:

- **Series** — a recurring question, such as KXBTCD for the Bitcoin daily price. This is the level the `series` table lists, and its ticker is the key almost everything else requires.
- **Event** — one occurrence of a series, with a single resolution date.
- **Market** — one strike within an event. This is what actually trades, and its ticker is what the per-market lookups take.

### Reading prices

Every `*_dollars` column is dollars per contract between 0 and 1, so a best bid of 0.62 is a 62% implied probability. They are `DECIMAL`, never `DOUBLE`: Kalshi sends exact fixed-point strings, and rounding them through a float would throw that away silently. Contract counts (`*_fp`) are decimals for the same reason.

### Access

No credentials are needed. Kalshi's whole market-data surface is public; only portfolio and order endpoints require an API key, and this worker exposes none of them. It is read-only by construction, not by configuration.

### Rate limits

Unauthenticated traffic is limited tightly enough that a handful of back-to-back requests draws an HTTP 429. A correlated `LATERAL` issues one request per input row, so a join across a whole series is hundreds of calls. Requests are retried with exponential backoff, and the per-market functions take a `cache_ttl` argument that turns repeated lookups of the same ticker into cache hits when a few seconds of staleness is acceptable.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The whole read-only Kalshi surface, in one schema. Work top-down: the `series` table lists every recurring question on the exchange and needs no arguments, so start there and take a series ticker. That ticker unlocks the tradeable contracts under it, and each contract's ticker in turn unlocks resting order-book depth, OHLC price history and the raw trade tape. Every function is keyed — none of them will scan the whole exchange for you — and every one composes under a correlated LATERAL, so a per-row lookup becomes a set-based query without a second registration.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One schema holding the whole read-only Kalshi surface.

### Finding your way in

Almost everything here is keyed, so the unkeyed `series` table is the way in: it lists every recurring question on the exchange, filterable by category. From a series ticker you reach the tradeable contracts, and from a contract ticker you reach depth, history and the trade tape.

Contracts carry a `series_ticker` column that Kalshi's own payload does not include — it is stamped on by the function that fetched them, so their output can feed the price-history lookup, which needs a series ticker as well as a contract ticker, without you repeating it by hand.

### Everything composes under LATERAL

Every function here is blended: one registration serves both a literal call and a correlated `LATERAL`, so a per-row lookup composes into a set-based query. That is also what makes it easy to issue hundreds of requests by accident — see the catalog notes on rate limits and the `cache_ttl` argument.

### The one real trap

Kalshi filters and reports contract status in two different vocabularies. The `status` **argument** accepts `unopened`, `open`, `closed` and `settled`; the `status` **column** reports `initialized`, `active`, `closed`, `determined`, `settled` and `finalized`. They are not interchangeable — filter with `status => 'open'`, but match the column against `'active'`. A wrong argument is a hard error from Kalshi; a wrong predicate silently matches nothing.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row saying where Kalshi's live endpoints stop and its archive begins. Read it before querying a date range: the live functions return no rows — not an error — for anything older, so an empty result is otherwise indistinguishable from a market that never traded. Compare a date against `market_settled_ts` for markets and candles, or `trades_created_ts` for the tape, and pick the live or the historical function accordingly.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row, four timestamps, because Kalshi archives each kind of data on its own schedule.

### Why this is a table and not a note in the docs

The boundary moves. Hardcoding a date works until it quietly does not, and the failure mode is an empty result rather than an error — which reads like an answer.

### Which column governs what

`market_settled_ts` covers markets and their candles; `trades_created_ts` covers the trade tape. The remaining two describe order and position archives, which this read-only worker does not expose; they are reported because Kalshi reports them.

tables.name: exchange_status
tables.comment: Whether the exchange, and each venue within it, is open for trading

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Whether Kalshi is open for trading right now, one row per venue. Check this before concluding that an empty order book or an unmoving price means anything — outside trading hours it means the venue is closed. Kalshi runs several venues that open and close independently, so the exchange-wide flag alone is not the answer.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per trading venue, with the exchange-wide flags repeated on each.

### Read the venue, not just the exchange

Crypto trades around the clock while sports venues follow their seasons, so `exchange_active` does not tell you whether the contract you care about is tradeable. Match on `description`, or use the `*_overall` columns to ignore the distinction deliberately.

### Freshness

The most volatile thing Kalshi publishes, and it says so: `max-age=1`, the shortest TTL in the API. That directive is forwarded to the result cache rather than invented.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The catalog of every recurring question on the exchange — around 13,600 rows, small and slow-changing. This is the discovery entry point: nearly every other object needs a series ticker, and this is where you find one. Filter by `category` to narrow to a topic such as Crypto, Politics or Economics.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Every series Kalshi lists, as an ordinary table — no argument required.

### Why this is a table and everything else is a function

It has no required key, it is small enough to return whole in one response, and it changes slowly. The market-data functions are none of those things, which is why they take a key.

### Where to go next

Take a `ticker` and pass it to `markets()` for the tradeable contracts, `events()` for resolution dates, or `candlesticks()` for price history.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Markets that have settled and been archived out of `markets()`. Reach for this for anything resolved — how a past question turned out, what it paid, how it was priced before it closed. Same columns as the live `markets()` plus `settlement_value_dollars`, so a query moves across the boundary by changing only the function name. Check `historical_cutoff` if you are unsure which side a date falls on; the live functions return nothing rather than erroring for anything older.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The archive of settled markets.

### Why this is a separate function

Kalshi archives settled markets out of the live endpoints entirely. Asking `markets()` for something that settled last month returns no rows — not an error — so the split has to be visible rather than inferred.

### What it adds

`settlement_value_dollars` is what one contract actually paid: 1 for the winning side and 0 for the losing one, or a value in between for a scalar market. Every other column matches the live shape.

### Finding the boundary

`historical_cutoff` reports the timestamp where the archive begins. It moves, so read it rather than hardcoding a date.

functions.name: trades
functions.comment: Executed trades for a Kalshi market (the public tape)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Individual executed trades on one market — the public tape, newest first. Reach for this when you need actual prints rather than quotes or aggregated bars: trade-by-trade flow, taker direction, or a precise volume-weighted price. Use `candlesticks()` instead when bars are enough; the tape is far more rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per execution, with the trade quoted from both sides of the contract.

### Polling, and why there is no WebSocket

Kalshi's WebSocket `trade` channel pushes these, but a dropped connection is a gap you cannot recover. Polling with `min_ts` is lossless instead: the cursor is replayable, so a failed poll costs a retry rather than lost prints. Track the highest `created_time` you have seen and pass it as the next `min_ts`.

### Reading the price columns

`yes_price_dollars` and `no_price_dollars` are the same execution seen from each side and always sum to 1. `taker_side` tells you which side the aggressor bought, which is the direction signal.

### Volume

An active market can have a very long tape, so cap it with `max_rows` unless you genuinely want the whole history.

vgi.example_queries.description: The most recent trades on the busiest open market in a series
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.created_time, t.taker_side, t.yes_price_dollars, t.count_fp FROM (SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL kalshi.main.trades(m.ticker, max_rows => 100) t ORDER BY t.created_time DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Volume-weighted average price from the tape
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(t.yes_price_dollars * t.count_fp) / sum(t.count_fp) AS vwap_dollars FROM (SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL kalshi.main.trades(m.ticker, max_rows => 500) t

functions.name: events
functions.comment: Events under a Kalshi series (series_ticker required)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The layer between a series and its markets: one row per resolution date, with the strike date, settlement sources and whether its markets are mutually exclusive. Reach for this to find a specific `event_ticker` — which `markets()` accepts as a filter — without scanning every market in the series.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
A Kalshi series recurs; each occurrence is an event; each event carries many markets, one per strike. `KXBTCD` (Bitcoin daily) opens one event per day, and each event holds a market for every strike price.

### Narrowing from here

Take an `event_ticker` from this and pass it to `markets()` as its `event_ticker` argument to get just that day's strikes rather than the whole series. Note that has to be a literal or a scalar subquery: `event_ticker` is a named argument, and DuckDB does not allow a correlated column to be passed as one.

### Settlement sources

`settlement_sources` stays a nested list of `{name, url}` structs — flattening it would fan every event out into one row per source. Apply DuckDB's `unnest` to the column when you do want one row per source; the example queries show it. For the images as well, use `event_metadata()`.

### Paging

`/events` caps its page size at 200 rather than the usual 1000 and rejects anything larger outright. Rows stream a page at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_ticker, title, strike_date FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD') ORDER BY strike_date

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_ticker, unnest(settlement_sources).name AS source FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD') ORDER BY event_ticker, source

functions.name: event_metadata

tags.vgi.doc_llm: What an event settles against, flattened to one row per source, plus the images Kalshi displays for it. Reach for this to answer 'how is this decided?' — the named source is the thing that determines the outcome. Distinct from the `settlement_sources` column on `events()`, which is the summary inlined into the listing; the images only exist here.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per settlement source for one event.

### Why one row per source

An event can settle against more than one source. Flattening them means they join and aggregate like ordinary rows, at the cost of repeating the image columns — the same trade-off `orderbook()` makes with price levels. An event with no declared sources still returns one row, so a lookup always answers with its images rather than with nothing.

### Versus the events() column

`events()` carries a nested `settlement_sources` list, which is the right shape when you are already scanning events. This endpoint is the one that also has the images, and it is a point lookup rather than a scan.

functions.name: orderbook
functions.comment: Kalshi order book flattened to one row per side and price level

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Resting order-book depth for one market, flattened to one row per side and price level so it aggregates and joins like an ordinary table. Reach for this to see liquidity behind the best quote — spread, depth at a price, or the shape of one side. For just the top of book, `markets()` already carries the best bid and ask without a second request.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Kalshi returns the book as a nested object of `[price, count]` pairs; this flattens it to one row per (side, price level).

### Reading the two sides

A binary contract has two books that mirror each other: a YES bid at 0.40 is economically a NO ask at 0.60. Both sides are returned, labelled in `side`.

### An empty result is not an error

An unknown ticker is answered with HTTP 200 and two empty sides rather than a 404, so zero rows means 'no resting orders' *or* 'no such market' — check the ticker against `markets()` if that distinction matters.

### Cost under LATERAL

One request per input row. Over a whole series that is hundreds of calls into a rate-limited API, so pass `cache_ttl => N` to enable per-value memoization when a few seconds of staleness is acceptable.

vgi.example_queries.description: Full depth on both sides of one market's book

functions.name: markets
functions.comment: Markets under a Kalshi series (series_ticker required)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The entry point to Kalshi's market data: one row per tradeable contract under a series, with its current quotes, volume and lifecycle state. Reach for this when you know the series (from the `series` table) and want the individual strikes. The series ticker is required, so start from `series` if you do not have one. Every deeper function keys off the `ticker` this returns, and the `series_ticker` it stamps on is what lets its output drive `candlesticks()` directly.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Markets are the tradeable contracts under one Kalshi series — a series like `KXBTCD` (Bitcoin daily) opens a new event each day, and each event carries many markets, one per strike price.

### Why the series ticker is required

An unfiltered market scan pages past 400,000 rows, roughly 398,000 of which are zero-volume `KXMVECROSSCATEGORY` parlay combinations, and takes minutes. Requiring the series keeps a naive unfiltered scan honest.

### The two status vocabularies

The `status` **argument** filters on `unopened`, `open`, `closed` or `settled`. The `status` **column** reports `initialized`, `active`, `closed`, `determined`, `settled` or `finalized`. They are not interchangeable: `status => 'open'` returns rows whose column reads `active`, and passing `active` as the filter is an error from Kalshi.

### Streaming

Rows arrive one API page at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early instead of paying for the whole series. The cost of that is this cannot be used as the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL` — drive a join from it, not into it.

### Prices

All `*_dollars` columns are dollars per contract between 0 and 1, carried as `DECIMAL(18,4)` — Kalshi sends them as exact fixed-point strings and rounding them through a float would lose that.

### Reading a strike ladder

A series like `KXWTI` lists one market per threshold. `strike_type` says how to read the bounds — `greater` sets `floor_strike`, `less` sets `cap_strike`, `between` sets both — and the units are the series' own: dollars for a price market, thousands of barrels for an inventory one. Do not parse the threshold out of the ticker or the subtitle; `subtitle` is not always populated, and a ticker is not a contract.

Each row is `P(settles above floor_strike)`, so a ladder read in strike order is a survival curve and the implied median is where it crosses 0.5.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, status FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') ORDER BY ticker

vgi.example_queries.description: Which series carry the most open interest, across the whole exchange
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT regexp_extract(event_ticker, '^([A-Z0-9]+)', 1) AS series, count(*) AS markets, sum(open_interest_fp) AS open_interest FROM kalshi.main.markets('', status => 'open') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY open_interest DESC LIMIT 20

vgi.example_queries.description: The implied probability curve for a price ladder, in strike order
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT floor_strike, (yes_bid_dollars + yes_ask_dollars) / 2 AS implied_probability FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXWTI', status => 'open') WHERE strike_type = 'greater' AND floor_strike IS NOT NULL ORDER BY floor_strike
