functions.name: historical_candlesticks
functions.comment: Archived OHLC candlesticks for a settled Kalshi market

tags.vgi.doc_llm: OHLC bars for a market that has settled and been archived. The columns match the live `candlesticks()` exactly, but the signature does not: this takes only the market ticker, because the archive is not scoped by series. Reach for it to chart or backtest a resolved question.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Archived price history for one settled market.

### One ticker, not two

The live candlestick endpoint lives under a series and needs both tickers; the archive is keyed on the market alone. That is the only difference in how you call it — the returned columns are identical.

### No batched form

There is no archive equivalent of the batched live endpoint, so a LATERAL over many markets issues one request per market against a rate-limited API. Drive it from a narrow set of tickers.

### Immutable, so cached

Nothing in the archive can change, so results are cached for a day regardless of what the window looks like — the live function's forming-candle problem cannot arise here.

functions.name: event
functions.comment: One Kalshi event by ticker

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A single event by its exact ticker, with the same columns `events()` returns. Use this when you already have an `event_ticker` — from a market row, say — and want its resolution date or settlement sources without scanning the series it belongs to. `events()` is the browse path; this is the lookup.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row for one event.

### When to use this instead of `events()`

`events()` needs a series ticker and returns every event under it. If you already hold an `event_ticker` — every market row carries one — this fetches just that event, and composes under a LATERAL driven by markets.

### What it does not return

Kalshi's response also carries the event's markets. They are not returned here: `markets(series, event_ticker => ...)` is the way to ask for those, and it paginates properly where the inlined copy does not.

functions.name: all_series
functions.comment: Every Kalshi series (the scan backing the `series` table)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every series on the exchange, as a function. Prefer the `series` table, which scans this and reads as plain SQL; this form exists for the rare case you want the scan itself. Either way it is the discovery starting point: a series ticker from here is the required key for `markets()`, `events()` and `candlesticks()`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The whole Kalshi series catalog — roughly 13,600 rows, returned in a single unpaginated response.

### Prefer the table

The `series` catalog table is backed by this function, so it can be selected from directly, without parentheses. This function returns exactly the same rows; it is named `all_series` only so that the function and the table it backs can coexist in one schema.

### Where to go next

A series is the top of Kalshi's hierarchy: series → events → markets. Take a `ticker` from here and pass it to `markets()` or `events()`.

functions.name: candlesticks
functions.comment: Kalshi OHLC candlesticks for a market (series and market ticker)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Historical OHLC price and quote bars for one market, at 1-minute, hourly or daily resolution. This is the time-series view — reach for it to chart or backtest how a contract's price moved, rather than where it stands now. It needs BOTH the series ticker and the market ticker, so drive it from `markets()`, whose `series_ticker` column exists precisely to feed this.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
OHLC bars for one market. Three nested Kalshi structs — traded `price`, `yes_bid` and `yes_ask` — are flattened into `price_*`, `yes_bid_*` and `yes_ask_*` column families.

### Both tickers are required

The endpoint lives under the series (`/series/{series}/markets/{ticker}/candlesticks`), not under the market, so the series ticker is not redundant. `markets()` stamps a `series_ticker` column on its output for exactly this.

### Periods with no trades

The `price_*` columns are NULL for any period that saw no trades — Kalshi sends an empty struct. The `yes_bid_*` and `yes_ask_*` columns still carry quotes, so prefer them when you need an unbroken series.

### Window and caching

`period_interval` is the bar width in minutes: 1, 60 or 1440. The window defaults to the last 24 hours. A window that ends in the past contains only closed bars, which can never change and are cached for a day; a window running up to now contains a still-forming bar and is never cached.

vgi.example_queries.description: Hourly closing prices for one market over the last day
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.end_period_ts, c.price_close_dollars FROM (SELECT series_ticker, ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 AND open_time < now() - INTERVAL 3 HOUR LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL kalshi.main.candlesticks(m.series_ticker, m.ticker, period_interval => 60) c ORDER BY c.end_period_ts

vgi.example_queries.description: Hourly candles for every market in a series, driven by markets()
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.ticker, c.end_period_ts, c.price_close_dollars FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') m, LATERAL kalshi.main.candlesticks(m.series_ticker, m.ticker, period_interval => 60) c ORDER BY m.ticker, c.end_period_ts

functions.name: historical_trades
functions.comment: Archived executed trades for a Kalshi market

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Executed trades from before the archive cutoff — the same tape as `trades()`, for markets old enough to have been moved out of it. Identical columns, so the two can be combined with UNION ALL to span the boundary. `trades()` answers with no rows, not an error, for anything this old, which is the mistake this function exists to prevent.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The archived half of the public trade tape.

### Same shape as the live tape

Every column matches `trades()`, deliberately: a query spanning the cutoff can `UNION ALL` the two without reshaping either side.

### Where the boundary is

`historical_cutoff.trades_created_ts` is the moment the archive takes over. It advances, so read it rather than assuming a fixed date.

### Volume

An archived market's whole life is in here, so cap it with `max_rows` or a `min_ts`/`max_ts` window unless you want all of it.

vgi.example_queries.description: The last hundred archived trades on a settled market
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT created_time, taker_side, yes_price_dollars, count_fp FROM kalshi.main.historical_trades('KXBTCD-26JUL0119-T68299.99', max_rows => 100) ORDER BY created_time DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Archived volume by taker side for one market
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT taker_side, sum(count_fp) AS contracts FROM kalshi.main.historical_trades('KXBTCD-26JUL0119-T68299.99') GROUP BY taker_side ORDER BY taker_side

functions.name: all_historical_cutoff
functions.comment: The live/archive boundary (the scan backing `historical_cutoff`)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The single row that says where Kalshi's live endpoints stop and its archive begins. Read it before querying a date range: the live functions return no rows, rather than an error, for anything older than this, so an empty result is otherwise indistinguishable from 'nothing happened'. Prefer the `historical_cutoff` table, which scans this.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row, four timestamps — Kalshi archives each kind of data on its own schedule.

### Why it matters

Asking a live function for something older than its cutoff is not an error. It returns nothing, which reads exactly like a market that never traded. Comparing against this row is the only way to tell those apart.

### Which column

`market_settled_ts` governs markets and their candles; `trades_created_ts` governs the tape. The other two describe order and position archives, which this worker does not expose — they are here because Kalshi reports them and omitting them would misrepresent the response.

vgi.example_queries.description: Where does the archive begin?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT market_settled_ts, trades_created_ts FROM kalshi.main.all_historical_cutoff()

vgi.example_queries.description: Is a date served by the live functions or the archive?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT DATE '2026-08-01' >= market_settled_ts AS use_live_functions FROM kalshi.main.all_historical_cutoff()

functions.name: all_exchange_status
functions.comment: Exchange and per-venue trading status (the scan backing `exchange_status`)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Whether Kalshi is open for trading right now, per venue. Prefer the `exchange_status` table, which scans this. Worth checking before concluding that an empty order book or a stale quote means something — outside trading hours it means the venue is closed. Kalshi runs several venues (Default, Combos, Crypto, sports) that open and close independently, so this returns one row per venue plus the exchange-wide flags repeated on each.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per trading venue, plus the exchange-wide flags on every row.

### Why this is per-venue

Kalshi is not one market. Crypto trades around the clock while sports venues follow their seasons, so `exchange_active` on its own does not tell you whether the contract you care about is tradeable. Match the venue by its `description`, or read the `*_overall` columns to ignore the distinction.

### Freshness

This is the most volatile thing Kalshi publishes and it says so: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=1`, the shortest TTL anywhere in the API. That one second is forwarded to the result cache rather than invented here.

vgi.example_queries.description: Every venue and whether it is currently trading

vgi.example_queries.description: Every venue's status, newest venue ids last

functions.name: market
functions.comment: One Kalshi market by ticker

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A single market's current snapshot, by exact ticker. Use this when you already have a ticker and want one fresh row; use `markets()` when you want to browse or filter a series. Same columns as `markets()`, so the two are interchangeable downstream. Quotes are live and uncached unless you pass `cache_ttl`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row for one market, refetched on every call.

### When to use this instead of `markets()`

`markets()` is the browse path and returns a whole series; this is the point lookup. It is also the cheaper way to re-check a single contract's quote, since it fetches one market rather than paging a series.

### Caching

Kalshi declares no freshness at all on this endpoint, so nothing is cached by default. Pass `cache_ttl => N` to cache for N seconds and enable per-value memoization — worth it when a `LATERAL` repeats the same ticker, at the cost of a quote up to N seconds stale.

vgi.example_queries.description: Current quote for one market by ticker
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, status, yes_bid_dollars, yes_ask_dollars FROM kalshi.main.market((SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1))

workers.summary: Parse + normalize international postal addresses (libpostal) for SQL
workers.doc_md:
# International Address Parsing & Normalization in SQL

**Parse, standardize, and normalize free-form postal addresses from anywhere in the world directly in DuckDB SQL** — turn a messy one-line address string into clean, structured components (house number, road, unit, city, state, postcode, country) without leaving your query.

The `postal` catalog brings [libpostal](https://github.com/openvenues/libpostal) — the open-source statistical address parser trained on OpenStreetMap and open address data — to SQL. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and anyone doing geocoding pre-processing, address standardization, record linkage, entity resolution, or deduplication over customer, shipping, or location data. Because libpostal is trained on real addresses from [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org) across hundreds of countries and languages, it handles international formats, transliteration, and local abbreviations far better than hand-written regular expressions or fixed format rules.

Under the hood this worker wraps libpostal's C library through its official Python binding, [pypostal](https://github.com/openvenues/pypostal), and exposes it over DuckDB's VGI interface. libpostal does two core things: it *parses* an address — using a sequence model to tag each token with a component label — and it *expands/normalizes* abbreviations into canonical forms (for example `St` → `street`, `E` → `east`, `Rd` → `road`), which is what makes two differently written versions of the same address comparable. All output is lower-cased; an empty string yields an empty result and `NULL` yields `NULL`, so the functions compose cleanly inside larger queries.

## Key concepts

- **Parsing** turns a one-line address into labeled components (house number, road, unit, city, state, postcode, country, and more). Labels are statistical and best-effort — a borough can come back as a city district rather than a city — so treat them as a strong signal, not a strict schema.
- **Normalization / expansion** rewrites abbreviations into canonical, fully-spelled-out forms and can return several valid variants for an ambiguous token; two addresses match when their expansion sets overlap.

## When to reach for it

Use this catalog for geocoding pre-processing, address standardization, record linkage, entity resolution, and deduplication over customer, shipping, or location data — anywhere you need messy free-form addresses made comparable directly in SQL, without shipping data to an external service.

Learn more from the [libpostal source repository](https://github.com/openvenues/libpostal) and its [installation and usage documentation](https://github.com/openvenues/libpostal#installation).

# address_labels

Discovery table of every component label libpostal can emit, exposed as a regular table so you can query it as a plain table (no trailing parentheses).

## Columns

- `label` (`VARCHAR`, primary key) -- a component label libpostal can emit (`road`, `city`, `state`, `postcode`, `country`, `house_number`, `unit`, ...).

## Usage

Query it like any table: order the `label` column to browse the full vocabulary, filter it to validate that a candidate key is one libpostal recognizes, or count the rows to size the label set. Ready-to-run examples are carried in this relation's example-query metadata.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## parse_address_components

Table function: parse a single address string and emit one `(label, value)` **row per libpostal component**, in libpostal's order. This is the long-format complement to the `parse_address` `MAP` scalar.

**Use it when** you want to filter, join, or aggregate over address components in set-based SQL (e.g. `... WHERE label = 'city'`) rather than indexing a map.

**Argument:** `text` (`VARCHAR`) -- the address to parse. **Returns:** rows of `(label VARCHAR, value VARCHAR)`.

**Behaviors / edge cases:** values are lower-cased; labels are statistical and best-effort (see `address_labels()` for the full set). An empty / whitespace input yields **no rows** (not an error).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# parse_address_components

Parse an address into one `(label, value)` row per libpostal component -- the long-format complement to the `parse_address` `MAP` scalar.

## Result

Each returned row pairs a libpostal component `label` (such as `house_number`, `road`, `city`, `state`, or `postcode`) with its lower-cased `value`, in libpostal's own token order. Because it is a table function, you consume it in the `FROM` clause and can freely filter, join, or aggregate the component rows -- for example keeping only the `city` label, or counting how many components libpostal recovered. Runnable examples are carried in this object's example-query metadata.

## Notes

Values are lower-cased; empty/whitespace input yields no rows. See the `address_labels` discovery relation for the full label set.

functions.comment: Parse an address into a MAP of libpostal components (road, city, state, postcode, country, house_number, unit, ...). Values are lower-cased; empty string -> empty map; NULL -> NULL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## parse_address

Parse a single free-form postal address string into a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` of libpostal components, keyed by the component label libpostal assigns (`house_number`, `road`, `unit`, `city`, `state`, `postcode`, `country`, and more).

**Use it when** you have unstructured address text and need it broken into addressable fields for geocoding pre-processing, standardization, deduplication, or record linkage -- all inline in SQL.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` address per row. **Output:** a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`. Index a single field with `parse_address(addr)['city']`.

**Behaviors / edge cases:** libpostal is a statistical (OSM-trained) parser, so labels are best-effort and occasionally surprising (a borough may come back as `city_district`, not `city`). All values are **lower-cased**. An empty string parses to an empty map (not an error); a `NULL` input yields `NULL`. For the long-format `(label, value)` row shape, use the `parse_address_components` table function instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# parse_address

Parse a free-form postal address into a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` of libpostal components.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT postal.main.parse_address('1600 Pennsylvania Ave NW, Washington, DC 20500');
SELECT postal.main.parse_address('10 Downing St, London SW1A 2AA, UK')['postcode'];
```

## Notes

- Keys are libpostal labels (`house_number`, `road`, `unit`, `city`, `state`, `postcode`, `country`, ...).
- Values are lower-cased; an empty string yields an empty map and `NULL` yields `NULL`.
- Labels are statistical and may vary across address styles; see `address_labels()` for the full label set.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## expand_address

Normalize a single address string into a `VARCHAR[]` of libpostal **expansions** -- canonical, fully-spelled-out forms where abbreviations and tokens are rewritten (`St` -> `street`, `E` -> `east`, `Ave` -> `avenue`).

**Use it when** you need to compare or deduplicate addresses that are written inconsistently. libpostal may return several equally valid normalizations (e.g. `st` could mean `street` or `saint`), so the result is a *list*; match two addresses if their expansion lists intersect.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` address per row. **Output:** a `VARCHAR[]` of normalized strings. Use `UNNEST(...)` to get one expansion per row.

**Behaviors / edge cases:** output is lower-cased. An empty string yields an empty list (not an error); a `NULL` input yields `NULL`. This is normalization for matching -- it does not split the address into fields; use `parse_address` for that.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# expand_address

Normalize an address into a `VARCHAR[]` of libpostal expansions, rewriting abbreviations into canonical forms for matching and deduplication.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT postal.main.expand_address('120 E 96th St');
SELECT UNNEST(postal.main.expand_address('120 E 96th St'));
```

## Notes

- Multiple expansions can be returned for an ambiguous token.
- Output is lower-cased; an empty string yields an empty list and `NULL` yields `NULL`.
- For field extraction (not normalization), use `parse_address`.

workers.doc_md:
# AI SQL for DuckDB

**Call LLMs and embed text directly in DuckDB SQL.** `vgi-llm` brings Snowflake Cortex AISQL-style functions -- completion, classification, filtering, extraction, sentiment, summarization, and group-level map-reduce -- to DuckDB over a pluggable provider (Anthropic, OpenRouter, OpenAI, or a local Ollama), plus **keyless** local embeddings and cosine similarity.

## Keyless first

```sql
-- No API key required: local ONNX embeddings + similarity
SELECT ai_similarity(ai_embed('cat'), ai_embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

Add one OpenRouter key (or run Ollama locally) to unlock cloud/local completions:

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE llm, openrouter_api_key 'sk-or-...');
SELECT ai_complete('Write a haiku about DuckDB', 'openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-5');
```

## Notes

- The model argument routes by prefix (`anthropic/…`, `openrouter/…`, `openai/…`, `ollama/…`).
- Empty/NULL input maps to NULL; a provider error or missing key raises a DuckDB error.
- Embeddings run locally (fastembed/ONNX); pair with the DuckDB VSS extension.

## llm.main schema

The single schema of the AI SQL worker. It groups the surface into a few concepts: free-form completion and summarization, structured outputs (classification, boolean filtering, extraction, sentiment), keyless local embeddings and cosine similarity for semantic search / RAG, group-level LLM map-reduce aggregates, and pure utilities (prompt templating and local token estimation). Completions route to a pluggable provider by a model-prefix string; embeddings and similarity run in-process with no key. Reach for the keyless embedding/similarity pair first (semantic search works with no setup), add a provider key only when you need generative completion or structured extraction.

# llm.main

AI functions over Apache Arrow for DuckDB: completion, structured output, embeddings, aggregates, and utilities.

## Overview

Completions call a pluggable LLM provider (Anthropic / OpenRouter / OpenAI / Ollama) chosen by a model-prefix string. Embeddings and `ai_similarity` run locally (fastembed/ONNX) with no key. The aggregates reduce a whole group to one answer via chunked map-reduce.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT ai_similarity(ai_embed('cat'), ai_embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

## Notes

- Empty/NULL input maps to NULL; a provider error or missing key raises a DuckDB error.
- Embeddings are keyless; completions need a key (or keyless Ollama).

functions.name: prompt
functions.comment: Safely substitute positional args into a template ({} / {n}); pure, no model call.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## prompt(template, args...)

Build a prompt string from a `template` and one or more positional `args` by **safe** positional substitution: `{}` (sequential) and `{n}` (explicit index), with `{{`/`}}` escapes. This is **pure** -- it calls **no** model -- so it is the cheap building block for assembling prompts from columns before feeding them to `ai_complete` / `ai_classify` / etc. Unlike Python `str.format`, it rejects format specs and attribute/index access, so a template can never traverse object attributes or trigger a giant-width allocation.

**Input/output.** Inputs: a `VARCHAR` `template` and >= 1 further column values (any type). Output: one `VARCHAR` per row. A NULL template, a malformed placeholder, or an out-of-range index -> NULL row.
tags.vgi.doc_md:

functions.name: ai_similarity
functions.comment: Cosine similarity of two FLOAT[] vectors, in [-1, 1] (pure arithmetic); NULL on mismatch.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_similarity(a, b)

Cosine similarity of two `FLOAT[]` vectors (typically from `ai_embed`), a `DOUBLE` in `[-1, 1]` where 1 means identical direction. Pure arithmetic -- **no model, no key, no I/O** -- so it is cheap over large joins.

**When to use.** Rank or threshold embedding pairs: `ORDER BY ai_similarity(ai_embed(q), ai_embed(doc)) DESC` for retrieval, or `WHERE ai_similarity(...) > 0.8` for near-duplicate detection.

**Input/output.** Inputs: two `FLOAT[]` vectors. Output: `DOUBLE`. NULL, empty, or length-mismatched pairs -> NULL (never an error).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# ai_similarity

Cosine similarity of two `FLOAT[]` vectors, in `[-1, 1]` (pure arithmetic, keyless).

## Notes

- 1.0 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal, -1 = opposite.
- NULL / empty / length-mismatch returns NULL.

functions.comment: Embed text into a 384-dim FLOAT[] with the local default model (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5); keyless. NULL/empty -> NULL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_embed(input[, model])

Embed each `input` text into a fixed-length `FLOAT[]` vector using a local ONNX model (fastembed) -- **no API key, no network** after the one-time model download. The default model (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`) produces 384-dim vectors; pass a second argument to pick another supported model.

**When to use.** Semantic search, RAG, clustering, and dedup inside SQL: embed a corpus once, embed a query, and rank rows by `ai_similarity`. Pairs naturally with the DuckDB VSS extension.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` per row (+ optional model). Output: one `FLOAT[]` per row; NULL/empty text -> NULL vector.

functions.name: ai_count_tokens
functions.comment: Count tokens per text with a local tiktoken tokenizer (no network); BIGINT.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_count_tokens(input[, model])

Count the number of tokens in each `input` text with a **local tiktoken** tokenizer and return a `BIGINT` -- **no** network/provider call, so it is fast, deterministic, and free. The optional `model` argument selects the tokenizer: OpenAI/GPT-family models are counted **exactly**; other models (Anthropic, Ollama, ...) use `o200k_base`, a strong cross-model estimate. Use it to budget prompts, chunk long text, or estimate cost before calling a model.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` per row. Output: `BIGINT` token count (>= 1 for non-empty text). NULL/empty input -> NULL. For exact Anthropic counts use the provider's own token-count API.

functions.name: ai_complete_image
functions.comment: Multimodal LLM completion over a text prompt + an image BLOB (default model).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_complete_image(prompt, image[, model])

Multimodal completion: send a text `prompt` together with an `image` (a `BLOB` of PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP bytes) to a vision-capable model and return the text reply as `VARCHAR`. Use it to caption, describe, OCR, or answer questions about images stored in a column.

**Input/output.** Inputs: `VARCHAR` prompt, `BLOB` image, optional model. Output: one `VARCHAR` per row. NULL/empty prompt or NULL image -> NULL (no model call); a provider failure (including a non-vision model or a missing key) **raises** a DuckDB error. The media type is sniffed from the image's magic bytes.

functions.name: ai_filter
functions.comment: Evaluate a natural-language predicate over text; BOOLEAN, NULL on empty/unclear, errors raise.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_filter(predicate, input[, model])

Evaluate a natural-language `predicate` against each `input` text and return a `BOOLEAN` -- true when the predicate holds, false when it does not. Designed for `WHERE` and `CASE`: keep only the rows an LLM judges to match a condition you phrase in plain English.

**When to use.** Semantic filtering that a `LIKE`/regex can't express ("is this review angry?", "does this mention a refund?"). For the matched labels use `ai_classify`; for extracted fields use `ai_extract`.

**Input/output.** Inputs: `VARCHAR` predicate, `VARCHAR` text, optional model. Output: `BOOLEAN`. NULL/empty input, or an answer with no clear yes/no, -> NULL (excluded by a `WHERE`); a provider failure or missing key **raises** a DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# ai_filter

LLM boolean predicate over text, for semantic `WHERE` filtering.

## Notes

- Returns TRUE/FALSE; NULL/empty input or an unparseable reply -> NULL.
- A NULL is treated as not-matching by a `WHERE` clause.

vgi.example_queries.description: Boolean predicate over text
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_filter('the text is a question', 'How do I reset my password?')

vgi.example_queries.description: Boolean predicate with an explicit provider/model
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_filter('mentions a refund', body, 'ollama/llama3.2') FROM (VALUES ('Please refund my order')) AS x(body)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_extract(input, response_format[, model])

Extract structured data from each `input` text according to a `response_format` -- a JSON Schema string describing the fields you want -- and return the model's JSON result as a `VARCHAR`. Parse it with DuckDB's JSON functions (`->`, `json_extract`, `from_json(..., schema)`).

**When to use.** Pull typed fields (names, dates, amounts, nested objects) out of unstructured text. For a fixed label set use `ai_classify`; for a boolean use `ai_filter`.

**Input/output.** Inputs: `VARCHAR` text, a constant JSON-Schema string, optional model. Output: a JSON `VARCHAR`. NULL/empty input -> NULL (no model call); a provider failure, or a reply that is not a JSON object, **raises** a DuckDB error. The schema is sent to the provider as a structured-output constraint when supported.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# ai_extract

Schema-driven extraction from text to a JSON `VARCHAR`.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT ai_extract(
  'Invoice 42 for $9.99 due 2026-01-01',
  '{"type":"object","properties":{"amount":{"type":"number"}}}'
)::JSON->>'amount';
```

## Notes

- `response_format` is a JSON-Schema string (a positional constant).
- Output is a JSON string; NULL/empty input -> NULL, an unparseable reply raises.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_complete(prompt[, model])

Send each row's `prompt` to a large language model and return its text reply as a `VARCHAR`. The optional second argument selects the provider/model (`anthropic/…`, `openrouter/…`, `openai/…`, `ollama/…`, or a bare model id for the default provider); omit it to use the configured default.

**When to use.** Free-form generation, rewriting, or answering over a column of prompts. For a structured result use `ai_classify` / `ai_extract` / `ai_sentiment`; for a yes/no filter use `ai_filter`.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` prompt per row. Output: one `VARCHAR` per row. NULL/empty prompt -> NULL (no model call); a provider error or a missing key **raises** a DuckDB error -- it is not swallowed to NULL. Calls are fanned across a bounded thread pool, so a wide column completes concurrently.

functions.comment: Aggregate a group's text rows by applying a task via chunked LLM map-reduce; VARCHAR per group.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_agg(input, task)

Aggregate a whole column of text within each `GROUP BY` group by applying a natural-language `task` to all the rows at once, returning one `VARCHAR` answer per group. It is a hierarchical **chunked map-reduce**: rows are buffered, split into context-sized chunks, each chunk mapped to a partial answer, then the partials reduced with your task -- so a group larger than the model's context window still produces a single answer.

**When to use.** One summary, theme, or answer per category over all its rows -- grouping a text column and applying a task such as listing the top complaints to each group. For a per-row answer use `ai_complete`; for a plain summary-per-group use `ai_summarize_agg`.

**Input/output.** Inputs: a `VARCHAR` column and a constant `task` string. Output: one `VARCHAR` per group. A group with no rows yields NULL; a provider failure is raised as a DuckDB error. Keys come from a CREATE SECRET (TYPE llm) or provider env vars (or keyless Ollama).

workers.title: Data Masking & De-identification
workers.tagline: FF1 format-preserving encryption, HMAC tokenization & redaction for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.summary: Reversible format-preserving encryption, deterministic tokenization, and irreversible partial redaction of sensitive values.
workers.doc_md:
# Mask: Data Masking, Format-Preserving Encryption & PII De-identification in SQL

![RustCrypto logo](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/22351541?s=240)

**Mask** brings production-grade data masking to DuckDB — reversible format-preserving encryption (FPE), deterministic tokenization, and irreversible redaction of sensitive values, all callable as plain SQL scalar functions over Apache Arrow. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and privacy teams who need to de-identify PII such as credit card numbers, Social Security numbers, email addresses, and account IDs directly in their queries, views, and pipelines, with no external service or pre-processing step.

Under the hood, Mask uses real, vetted, permissively-licensed cryptography — never hand-rolled ciphers. Format-preserving encryption is implemented with the NIST [SP 800-38G](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-38g/final) **FF1** algorithm from the [`fpe`](https://github.com/str4d/fpe) crate ([docs](https://docs.rs/fpe)), keyed with AES-256 from the [RustCrypto `aes`](https://github.com/RustCrypto/block-ciphers) crate ([docs](https://docs.rs/aes)). Deterministic tokenization uses HMAC-SHA-256, and keys are derived with SHA-256, both from the [RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto) hashing and MAC crates ([`hmac`](https://docs.rs/hmac), [`sha2`](https://docs.rs/sha2)). FPE preserves a value's *shape*: a 16-digit card stays a Luhn-valid 16-digit card, an SSN stays SSN-shaped, and an email keeps its `@domain` — so masked data still passes format validation and flows through schemas unchanged.

Mask offers three complementary de-identification strategies, and you choose between them based on whether the original value must be recoverable later. **Reversible format-preserving encryption** protects a value under a secret key while keeping its shape, so authorized holders of the key can recover it and downstream format checks still pass — ideal for masked views, reversible data sharing, and generating referentially-consistent synthetic test data that mirrors production shape. **Deterministic tokenization** replaces an identifier with a stable, non-reversible HMAC-SHA-256 pseudonym so equal inputs always map to equal tokens and masked columns stay joinable across tables for analytics without ever exposing the real value. **Irreversible redaction** stars out the sensitive portion of a value for human-facing display, keeping only a small non-secret hint such as the last four digits. Mask supports GDPR- and HIPAA-driven anonymization and pseudonymization workflows; note that key management (KMS/HSM, rotation) is intentionally out of scope — the worker simply takes a key. Learn more about [format-preserving encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Format-preserving_encryption) and the [RustCrypto](https://www.rustcrypto.org/) project that powers Mask.

# mask.main

Data-masking scalar functions over Apache Arrow, grouped into three complementary strategies:

- **Format-preserving encryption** — reversibly protect a value under a key while keeping its shape (a card stays a Luhn-valid 16-digit card).
- **Tokenization** — replace an identifier with a stable, non-reversible HMAC-SHA-256 pseudonym that stays joinable across tables.
- **Redaction** — irreversibly star out the sensitive portion of a value for display.

Only format-preserving encryption is reversible (under the same key); tokenization and redaction are one-way, and tokenization keeps equal inputs equal so masked columns stay joinable.

## `mask_redact(value, mode)`

Irreversibly **partially masks** a value for display, replacing the sensitive portion with `*` characters while keeping a small, non-secret hint visible. No key is involved and the original value cannot be recovered.

### When to use
Use this for human-facing display masking — showing the last four digits of a card on a receipt, the first character of an email in a UI, or fully starring a column in an export. It is the simplest masking strategy; choose `mask_token` instead when you need joinable pseudonyms, or `mask_fpe` when you need to reverse the transform later.

### Inputs
- `value` — the string to redact (`VARCHAR`). NULL passes through to NULL.
- `mode` — redaction strategy (see below).

### Modes
| mode | keeps | example |
|---|---|---|
| `last4` | last four characters | `4012888888881881` → `************1881` |
| `first4` | first four characters | `4012888888881881` → `4012************` |
| `email` | first local char + `@domain` | `alice@example.com` → `a****@example.com` |
| `all` | nothing | `secret` → `******` |

### Behavior & edge cases
- Irreversible: the starred characters are discarded, not encrypted.
- NULL input → NULL; an unknown `mode` raises an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Irreversible Partial Redaction

`mask_redact(value, mode)` partially masks a value for display by starring out the sensitive portion. It is one-way — the original cannot be recovered.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT mask.main.mask_redact('4012888888881881', 'last4'); -- ************1881
SELECT mask.main.mask_redact('alice@example.com', 'email'); -- a****@example.com
```

## Modes

- `last4` — keep only the last four characters.
- `first4` — keep only the first four characters.
- `email` — keep the first local character plus the `@domain`.
- `all` — star out everything.

## Notes

- For joinable pseudonyms use `mask_token`; for reversible masking use `mask_fpe`.
- NULL in → NULL out; an unknown mode is an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `mask_fpe(value, format, key)`

Reversibly encrypts a sensitive string under a secret `key` using **FF1 format-preserving encryption** (FF1 over AES-256), so the ciphertext keeps the *shape* of the input and can be substituted wherever the original was used.

### When to use
Reach for this when you need to de-identify PII but downstream consumers still expect the original format — masked views over cards/SSNs/emails, generating referentially-consistent test data, or sharing data while keeping it reversible for authorized holders of the key. If you never need to recover the value, prefer `mask_token` (one-way pseudonym) or `mask_redact` (display masking).

### Inputs
- `value` — the string to encrypt (`VARCHAR`). NULL passes through to NULL.
- `format` — shape profile: `card`, `ssn`, `digits`, `alnum`, or `email`.
- `key` — secret key string; the AES key is derived from it via SHA-256.

### Output
A `VARCHAR` ciphertext with the same shape as the input. `card` stays a Luhn-valid 16-digit number, `ssn` keeps its dashes, `email` keeps `@domain` and FPEs only the local part, `digits`/`alnum` keep their length and character class.

### Behavior & edge cases
- Reverse with `mask_unfpe` under the **same** `format` and `key`.
- **Small-domain pass-through:** FF1 refuses domains below 1,000,000 (radix 10 ⇒ fewer than 6 digits; radix 62 ⇒ fewer than 4 chars), so very short values are returned unchanged — they still round-trip.
- NULL input → NULL; an unknown `format` or an empty `key` raises an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Format-Preserving Encrypt

`mask_fpe(value, format, key)` reversibly encrypts a value while preserving its shape, using FF1 format-preserving encryption over AES-256.

## Usage

```sql
-- card stays a Luhn-valid 16-digit number
SELECT mask.main.mask_fpe('4012888888881881', 'card', 'my-secret-key');
-- SSN keeps its dashes
SELECT mask.main.mask_fpe('123-45-6789', 'ssn', 'my-secret-key');
```

The `format` profile selects the shape to preserve: `card`, `ssn`, `digits`, `alnum`, or `email`.

## Notes

- Reverse the transform with `mask_unfpe` under the same `format` and `key`.
- Values too short for FF1's minimum domain are passed through unchanged but still round-trip.
- NULL in → NULL out; an unknown format or empty key is an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `mask_token(value, key)`

Produces a stable, **one-way pseudonym** for a value using **HMAC-SHA-256** under a secret `key`, returned as a hex string. The mapping is deterministic: the same `value` and `key` always yield the same token.

### When to use
Choose tokenization when you need to de-identify an identifier *and* keep it joinable. Because identical inputs map to identical tokens, you can replace an account ID or email with its token in two different tables and still join on it — referential integrity is preserved without ever exposing the original. Unlike `mask_fpe`, this is **not reversible**; unlike `mask_redact`, it does not preserve the input's shape.

### Inputs
- `value` — the identifier to tokenize (`VARCHAR`). NULL passes through to NULL.
- `key` — secret key string; the HMAC key is domain-separated from the FPE key.

### Output
A hexadecimal HMAC-SHA-256 token (`VARCHAR`). The original value cannot be recovered from it.

### Behavior & edge cases
- Deterministic and collision-resistant; same input+key ⇒ same token across runs and tables, so it is safe for joins.
- **Caution:** deterministic tokens are frequency-analyzable on low-cardinality columns — equal inputs always produce equal tokens.
- NULL input → NULL; an empty `key` raises an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Deterministic Tokenize

`mask_token(value, key)` returns a stable, non-reversible HMAC-SHA-256 pseudonym for a value, as a hex string.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT mask.main.mask_token('customer-42', 'my-secret-key');
```

The same input and key always produce the same token, so tokens stay joinable across tables.

## Notes

- Tokens are one-way: the original value cannot be recovered (use `mask_fpe` if you need reversibility).
- Deterministic output is frequency-analyzable on low-cardinality data.
- NULL in → NULL out; an empty key is an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `mask_unfpe(value, format, key)`

The **inverse of `mask_fpe`**: recovers the original plaintext from a format-preserving ciphertext using FF1 decryption over AES-256.

### When to use
Use this on the authorized side of a masking pipeline to recover a value that was protected with `mask_fpe`. It only succeeds when you supply the **same** `format` profile and the **same** `key` that produced the ciphertext — a different key yields different (wrong) output, which is the point of keyed encryption.

### Inputs
- `value` — the format-preserving ciphertext to reverse (`VARCHAR`).
- `format` — the profile used to encrypt: `card`, `ssn`, `digits`, `alnum`, or `email`.
- `key` — the same secret key that was used with `mask_fpe`.

### Output
The recovered original `VARCHAR` value.

### Behavior & edge cases
- For `card`, decryption re-derives the Luhn check digit, so the original 16-digit number is reproduced exactly.
- Values that were passed through unchanged by `mask_fpe` (small-domain rule) decrypt to themselves.
- NULL input → NULL; an unknown `format` or an empty `key` raises an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Format-Preserving Decrypt

`mask_unfpe(value, format, key)` reverses `mask_fpe`, recovering the original value from a format-preserving ciphertext.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT mask.main.mask_unfpe(
  mask.main.mask_fpe('123-45-6789', 'ssn', 'k'), 'ssn', 'k');
-- => '123-45-6789'
```

## Notes

- You must pass the same `format` and `key` used to encrypt; a different key produces incorrect output.
- `card` decryption re-derives the Luhn check digit so the round-trip is exact.
- NULL in → NULL out; an unknown format or empty key is an error.

workers.doc_md:
# Match: Probabilistic Entity Resolution & Record Linkage in SQL

![Splink logo](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7570107/85285114-3969ac00-b488-11ea-88ff-5fca1b34af1f.png)

**Match brings fuzzy entity resolution, record linkage, and deduplication directly into DuckDB SQL** -- point it at a messy relation, name the columns to compare, and get back clusters of rows that refer to the same real-world person, customer, contact, or product.

## What it does and who it's for

Real-world data is full of duplicates that exact `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` can never catch: `John Smith` vs `Jon Smith`, `j.smith@x.com` vs `J.Smith@x.com`, typos, nicknames, and transpositions. Match solves this *probabilistic matching* problem in plain SQL. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and data-quality teams who need to deduplicate customer master data, consolidate CRM contacts, link records across systems, or clean a product catalog -- without exporting to a separate Python pipeline. You stay in DuckDB; Match does the fuzzy matching and clustering and hands you back the same rows plus an entity label.

## How it works and the engine behind it

Match is powered by [Splink](https://github.com/moj-analytical-services/splink), the open-source probabilistic record-linkage library from the UK Ministry of Justice. Under the hood it uses the **Fellegi-Sunter** statistical model with fuzzy string comparisons (Jaro-Winkler for name-like columns, Levenshtein edit distance for the rest) to estimate, for every candidate pair of records, the probability that they describe the same entity. Pairs scoring above a threshold are linked, and connected components of linked records collapse into entity clusters. The default model is deterministic and robust on relations of any size, while `train := true` opts into Splink's unsupervised EM estimation for larger datasets. See the [Splink documentation](https://moj-analytical-services.github.io/splink/) and this [introduction to probabilistic linkage](https://www.robinlinacre.com/intro_to_probabilistic_linkage/) for the theory.

## SQL use cases and the function surface

Match exposes a single, focused table function, `match_resolve(relation, columns := '...', threshold := 0.5, train := false)`. Pass a relation as a subquery and the comparison columns; it returns every input row unchanged plus two appended columns: `cluster_id` (rows sharing it are the same entity) and `match_probability` (confidence per row). Use it to deduplicate a customer or contact list, link records that refer to the same organization, or detect duplicate products before a migration.

A typical call passes your rows as a parenthesised subquery and names the comparison columns -- `match_resolve(relation, columns := 'first_name,last_name,email')` -- then orders or groups the result by `cluster_id` to inspect each resolved entity or to count how many records collapsed into it. Fully runnable, coverage-checked queries live in the function's own example set (see `match.main.match_resolve`) and in the `main` schema examples.

## Notes

- The default model is deterministic and robust on relations of any size; `train := true` opts into Splink's unsupervised EM (weak on tiny inputs).
- This is a buffer-all-then-compute operator (entity resolution is an all-pairs problem), so block tightly for very large inputs.

example_queries.description: Resolve three records on name + email and inspect the entity each row was assigned to, grouped by cluster.
example_queries.sql: SELECT first_name, last_name, email, cluster_id FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','j@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','j@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') ORDER BY cluster_id, first_name

example_queries.description: Count how many records collapsed into each resolved entity, largest duplicate group first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cluster_id, count(*) AS n FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('Ann','Lee'),('Anne','Lee'),('Bob','Ng')) AS t(first_name,last_name)), columns := 'first_name,last_name') GROUP BY cluster_id ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: Count the sample records that belong to each ground-truth entity -- the planted duplicate groups match_resolve should reproduce.
example_queries.sql: SELECT expected_entity, count(*) AS records FROM match.main.sample_customers GROUP BY expected_entity ORDER BY records DESC, expected_entity

example_queries.description: Inspect just the messy Smith records (three spelling variants of one real person) to see the kind of duplication entity resolution targets.
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_id, first_name, last_name, email FROM match.main.sample_customers WHERE last_name = 'Smith' ORDER BY record_id

example_queries.description: Dedup on name + email; the John/Jon Smith rows share a cluster_id, Jane Doe is separate.
example_queries.sql: SELECT first_name, last_name, email, cluster_id, match_probability FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') ORDER BY cluster_id, first_name

example_queries.description: Surface only duplicate groups by clustering and keeping entities with more than one record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cluster_id, count(*) AS rows_in_entity FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com'),('Jayne','Doe','jane@y.com'),('Bob','Ng','bob@z.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') GROUP BY cluster_id HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY rows_in_entity DESC

example_queries.description: Stricter resolution: raise the link threshold and keep only the more-confident matches.
example_queries.sql: SELECT first_name, last_name, cluster_id, match_probability FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email', threshold := 0.9) WHERE match_probability >= 0.5 ORDER BY cluster_id, first_name

example_queries.description: Deduplicate three records on name + email; the two John/Jon Smith rows resolve to one cluster, Jane Doe to another.

# match.main

The `main` schema holds the probabilistic **entity-resolution / record-linkage / deduplication** functions, operating over Apache Arrow relations.

## Overview

One table function, `match_resolve`, takes a whole input relation plus the comparison columns and returns the input rows unchanged with an appended `cluster_id` and `match_probability`.

## Usage

Call `match_resolve(relation, columns := 'first_name,last_name')`, passing your rows as a parenthesised subquery, then group by `cluster_id` to count records per resolved entity. Runnable, coverage-checked queries are attached to the `match.main.match_resolve` function and to this schema's example set.

## Notes

Comparison columns are passed through to the output too; every non-comparison column rides along unchanged.

# sample_customers

A small, **browsable demo relation** of seven customer records with planted duplicates, so you can try entity resolution without supplying your own data.

## The planted story

- **Smith, John** -- rows 1-3 (`John` / `Jon` / `Johnny`, same email) are one real person with spelling variants.
- **Doe, Jane** -- rows 4-5 (`Jane` / `Janet`, same email) are one real person.
- **Jones** -- rows 6-7 (`Robert`, `Alice`) are *different* people who only share a surname -- the over-merge trap.

## Columns

`record_id`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `email`, `city`, and `expected_entity` (the ground-truth grouping label). Compare `expected_entity` against the `cluster_id` a resolver assigns to gauge quality.

## Notes

The relation is static and credential-free (VALUES-backed), so it scans instantly and is safe to use in docs, demos, and tests.

functions.comment: Probabilistic entity resolution / record linkage / dedup (Splink, MIT). Buffers the whole input relation, runs Splink's Fellegi-Sunter model with fuzzy (Jaro-Winkler / Levenshtein) comparisons over the chosen columns, links record pairs above a match-probability threshold, and returns the input rows unchanged plus an appended cluster_id (rows sharing one are the same real-world entity) and match_probability. Use it to deduplicate or link customer, contact, or product records that exact GROUP BY / JOIN miss.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Probabilistic entity resolution over a whole SQL relation. Pass a relation of records as the first positional argument (a `(SELECT ...)` subquery) and name the comparison columns with `columns := 'col1,col2,...'`. The function buffers every input row, runs Splink's Fellegi-Sunter model with fuzzy comparisons (Jaro-Winkler on name-like columns, Levenshtein elsewhere), links candidate pairs above `threshold` (default 0.5), and assigns each row a `cluster_id` (rows sharing one are the same real-world entity) plus a `match_probability`. Every input column is returned unchanged. Use it to deduplicate customer/contact/product lists or to link records that refer to the same entity. Inputs: the relation, `columns`, optional `threshold` and `train` (opt-in unsupervised EM, weak on tiny inputs). Edge cases: an empty relation raises an error; singletons get their own cluster_id and a match_probability of 1.0; an input column already named `cluster_id` or `match_probability` is replaced by the produced one.

# match_resolve

Cluster the rows of a relation into **resolved entities** (deduplication / record linkage) using probabilistic matching.

## What it does

Buffers the whole input relation, scores every candidate record pair with [Splink](https://github.com/moj-analytical-services/splink)'s Fellegi-Sunter model (fuzzy Jaro-Winkler / Levenshtein comparisons), links pairs above the threshold, and groups linked records into clusters.

## Calling it

Signature: `match_resolve(relation, columns := '...', threshold := 0.5, train := false)`. The first positional argument is the relation to resolve, passed as a parenthesised subquery over your source rows; the runnable, coverage-checked examples are attached to this function's example set.

- `columns` — comma-separated comparison columns to match on (required).
- `threshold` — match-probability cutoff in `[0,1]` for linking pairs (default `0.5`).
- `train` — opt into Splink's unsupervised EM refinement (default `false`; weak on tiny inputs).

## Returns

Every input column unchanged, plus `cluster_id` (`VARCHAR`) and `match_probability` (`DOUBLE`).

## Notes

- Singletons get their own `cluster_id` and `match_probability = 1.0`.
- An empty input relation raises an error.
- This is a buffer-all-then-compute operator; block tightly for very large inputs.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT first_name, last_name, email, cluster_id, match_probability FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') ORDER BY cluster_id, first_name

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result schema is **dynamic**: it is the input relation's own columns, passed through unchanged, followed by two appended columns. The passthrough columns therefore vary with whatever relation you pass as the first argument; the two appended columns are always present. If the input already has a `cluster_id` or `match_probability` column, it is replaced by the produced one.

### Appended columns (always present)

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| cluster_id | VARCHAR | Resolved-entity id; rows sharing a cluster_id are the same entity (a singleton entity gets its own id). |
| match_probability | DOUBLE | Strongest pairwise match probability linking the row into its cluster, in [0, 1] (1.0 for a singleton). |

### Passthrough columns (vary by input) — shown for the (first_name, last_name, email) demo relation

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| first_name | VARCHAR | Echo of the like-named input column (a comparison column in this demo). |
| last_name | VARCHAR | Echo of the like-named input column (a comparison column in this demo). |
| email | VARCHAR | Echo of the like-named input column (a comparison column in this demo). |

workers.doc_md:
# Media Metadata Extraction in SQL with ffprobe

![FFmpeg logo](https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-logo.png)

Inspect video, audio, and container files directly from DuckDB SQL: read codec, resolution, duration, bitrate, frame rate, and embedded metadata tags from MP4, MKV, MOV, WAV, MP3, WebM, and every other format that [FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org) can open — no manual transcoding, no external scripts.

This extension is for data engineers, media pipelines, and anyone who needs to take inventory of a media library, triage transcoding jobs, or run quality and conformance checks at scale. Instead of shelling out to a command-line tool and parsing JSON by hand, you query your media the same way you query any other table, and join the results against the rest of your warehouse.

## How it works

Under the hood the worker runs [ffprobe](https://ffmpeg.org/ffprobe.html), the media analyzer that ships with the [FFmpeg](https://github.com/FFmpeg/FFmpeg) project, in a sandboxed subprocess with bounded probe size and timeouts so that truncated or untrusted bytes can never hang a query. Every function accepts either a filesystem path (`VARCHAR`) or the raw media bytes (`BLOB`), so you can probe files on disk or `BLOB` columns already loaded into DuckDB. ffprobe's findings are surfaced over Apache Arrow as native SQL columns; missing or unparseable fields return NULL rather than erroring.

## What you can read

The worker groups its surface into a few kinds of reading:

- **Container-level facts** — one value per file, such as the format name, playback duration, overall bit rate, byte size, and how many elementary streams the file holds.
- **Video attributes** — for the first video track: its codec, pixel width and height, a combined resolution string, and the average frame rate.
- **Audio attributes** — for the first audio track, such as its codec.
- **Full enumeration** — table functions that return one row per elementary stream, and one row per format-level metadata tag, when you need every detail rather than a single summary value.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker whenever media files are part of your data and you want their technical metadata available in SQL: cataloguing an asset library, validating that uploads meet a resolution or codec policy, or driving transcoding decisions from a query rather than a bespoke script.

See the official [ffprobe documentation](https://ffmpeg.org/ffprobe.html) and the broader [FFmpeg documentation](https://ffmpeg.org/documentation.html) for details on the underlying analyzer.

## Media function registry

A browsable, argument-free view that catalogues every media metadata function in this worker. Because every other object is a function that needs a media path or `BLOB` before it returns anything, this view is the entry point for discovery: read it to see the full surface and each function's return type, then call the function you need.

Columns:

- `name` — function name as called in SQL.
- `kind` — `scalar` or `table`.
- `category` — `container`, `video`, `audio`, or `enumeration`.
- `result_type` — the SQL type a scalar returns, or `TABLE` for a table function.
- `description` — a one-line summary.

For example, list only the video functions and their return types, or count how many functions fall into each category.

vgi.example_queries.description: List every video-category function and its return type, alphabetically.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, result_type FROM media.main.media_functions WHERE category = 'video' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Count how many functions fall into each navigation category.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS n FROM media.main.media_functions GROUP BY category ORDER BY category

workers.title: NTFS $MFT Forensic Timeline
workers.tagline: Forensic NTFS \$MFT timelines in DuckDB with SQL — file records, MACB timestamps, ADS, deleted entries and timestomp detection. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Parse the NTFS $MFT into a forensic filesystem timeline: path reconstruction, the SI/FN MACB timestamp pair, timestomp detection, deleted-record recovery, and alternate data streams — straight into SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# mft — NTFS $MFT Forensic Timeline in SQL

Parse a collected NTFS **`$MFT`** (Master File Table) into a full forensic filesystem timeline — one row per FILE record — without a per-host CLI run and with **zero egress**. Built for DFIR / incident-response / threat-hunt teams who want to timeline thousands of collected `$MFT`s and join the result to known-bad paths, hashes, and rules in one query.

**Key concepts.** The `$MFT` is NTFS's index of every file and directory. Each FILE record carries the metadata this worker turns into columns: the full path reconstructed by walking parent references, logical and physical sizes, allocated / deleted and file / directory flags, alternate data streams, and inline resident content. Deleted-but-resident records are recovered by default.

**The timestomp engine.** `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` is user-writable (the Win32 `SetFileTime` API and anti-forensic tools rewrite it) while `$FILE_NAME` is kernel-only, so a standard-information timestamp that predates its file-name counterpart — naturally impossible — and whole-second values are strong anti-forensic tells. Both MACB timestamp quads are first-class columns.

Built on the permissively-licensed `mft` crate (omerbenamram); the NTFS on-disk layout is documented openly by Microsoft and the forensics community.

example_queries.description: The headline forensic timeline: one row per FILE record with its reconstructed path and deleted flag.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT entry, full_path, is_deleted FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample'))

example_queries.description: Hunt for timestomped records — the SI-vs-FN heuristic exposed as a plain WHERE clause.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) WHERE is_timestomp_suspect

example_queries.description: Surface every alternate data stream (a classic malware hiding spot) via streams mode.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path, ads_name FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample'), mode := 'streams') WHERE ads_name IS NOT NULL

example_queries.description: Browse the whole NTFS attribute-type registry, lowest code first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type_id, type_name, purpose FROM mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types ORDER BY type_id

example_queries.description: Look up the name and purpose of attribute type 128 (the $DATA attribute).
example_queries.sql: SELECT type_name, purpose FROM mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types WHERE type_id = 128

example_queries.description: List the $DATA streams (primary + each ADS) of one sample $MFT record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entry, name, logical_size, resident FROM mft.main.streams((FROM (SELECT content AS blob, 22::UBIGINT AS entry FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'))))

example_queries.description: List the $DATA streams of one sample $MFT record, surfacing the hidden ADS by name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, logical_size, resident FROM mft.main.streams((FROM (SELECT content AS blob, 22::UBIGINT AS entry FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')))) ORDER BY name NULLS FIRST;

example_queries.description: The headline timeline: one row per FILE record with its reconstructed path and deleted flag.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT entry, full_path, is_deleted FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) ORDER BY entry;

example_queries.description: Hunt the sample $MFT for timestomped records — the SI-vs-FN mismatch is a plain WHERE clause.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) WHERE is_timestomp_suspect ORDER BY full_path;

example_queries.description: Surface every alternate data stream by switching to streams mode.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path, ads_name FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample'), mode := 'streams') WHERE ads_name IS NOT NULL ORDER BY full_path;

example_queries.description: List every attribute (type, residency, ADS name, size) of one sample $MFT record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entry, type_name, resident, name, logical_size FROM mft.main.attributes((FROM (SELECT content AS blob, 22::UBIGINT AS entry FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'))))

example_queries.description: List every attribute (type, residency, ADS name, size) of one sample $MFT record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type_name, resident, name, logical_size FROM mft.main.attributes((FROM (SELECT content AS blob, 22::UBIGINT AS entry FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')))) ORDER BY attribute_id;

example_queries.description: Flag a record whose $STANDARD_INFORMATION quad predates its $FILE_NAME quad — the naturally-impossible ordering timestomping produces.
example_queries.sql: SELECT mft.main.timestomp({'created': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'modified': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'accessed': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'mft_modified': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01'}, {'created': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'modified': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'accessed': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'mft_modified': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01'}).suspect AS suspect

example_queries.description: Reconstruct the full filesystem path of one record (entry 20) in the sample $MFT.
example_queries.sql: SELECT mft.main.full_path((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')), 20) AS full_path

example_queries.description: Fully decode one sample $MFT record, exposing its primary name and how many alternate data streams it carries.
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.fn[1].name AS primary_name, len(r.ads) AS ads_count FROM (SELECT mft.main.mft_record((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')), 22) AS r)

example_queries.description: Probe just the FILE-record header of one sample record (entry 12): signature, directory flag, and sequence number.
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.signature, h.is_dir, h.sequence FROM (SELECT mft.main.record_header((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')), 12) AS h)

example_queries.description: Validate one sample record (entry 20) — a clean record reports ok = true with kind 'ok'.
example_queries.sql: SELECT w.ok, w.kind FROM (SELECT mft.main.well_formed((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')), 20) AS w)

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## The `mft` worker

Turns a collected NTFS `$MFT` into a forensic filesystem timeline you can query with SQL. Point it at a captured `$MFT` — a path, a glob across many hosts, or an in-memory `BLOB` — and it reconstructs what the filesystem looked like, and what was tampered with. Qualify calls as `mft.main.<fn>(...)`.

**Key concepts**

- *Path reconstruction* — parent-reference walking rebuilds absolute paths, flagging orphans and reference cycles.
- *MACB timelines* — the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and `$FILE_NAME` timestamp quads surfaced side by side.
- *Timestomp heuristic* — the user-writable-SI vs kernel-only-FN comparison that flags manipulated timestamps.
- *Recovery & robustness* — deleted-record recovery and never-panic decode over hostile or truncated input, plus attribute and `$DATA` / alternate-data-stream fan-out.

**When to use it** — DFIR triage, threat hunting, and incident response over Windows hosts.

SELECT entry, full_path, is_deleted FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample'))

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A browsable reference table (no arguments, no $MFT needed) listing the fifteen standard NTFS attribute type codes with their canonical `$`-prefixed name and a one-line purpose. Columns: `type_id` (`UINTEGER`, e.g. 128), `type_name` (`VARCHAR`, e.g. `$DATA`), `purpose` (`VARCHAR`). It is the vocabulary behind the `type_id` and `type_name` columns of the attributes() function — join or filter it to explain a record's attributes without parsing bytes. tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `ntfs_attribute_types`

A static, browsable reference of the fifteen standard NTFS attribute type codes — the vocabulary behind the `type_id` / `type_name` columns of the `attributes()` function. No arguments, no `$MFT`, no network.

## Columns

- `type_id` (`UINTEGER`) -- the on-disk NTFS attribute type code, e.g. `128` (`0x80`).
- `type_name` (`VARCHAR`) -- the canonical `$`-prefixed name, e.g. `$DATA`.
- `purpose` (`VARCHAR`) -- a one-line description of what the attribute stores.

Join it to the `attributes()` output on `type_id` to label each attribute, or browse it on its own.

vgi.example_queries.description: Browse the whole NTFS attribute-type registry, lowest code first.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type_id, type_name, purpose FROM mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types ORDER BY type_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Look up the name and purpose of attribute type 128 (the $DATA attribute).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type_name, purpose FROM mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types WHERE type_id = 128

functions.name: read_mft
functions.comment: Parse a collected NTFS $MFT into a forensic filesystem timeline

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Parse a collected NTFS $MFT (Master File Table) into a full forensic filesystem timeline — one row per FILE record, with the path reconstructed from parent references, both the $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME MACB timestamp quads (so the SI-vs-FN timestomp mismatch is a plain WHERE clause), logical/physical sizes, allocated/deleted and file/dir flags, alternate data streams, and resident file content. The first argument is a `VARCHAR` path or glob ('/cases/*/$MFT', 's3://…') or a `BLOB` of $MFT bytes. `host :=` scopes a collection (defaults to the source filename); `mode :=` is 'files' (one row per record, the default), 'streams' (one row per $DATA stream — primary + each ADS), or 'allocated' (live files only). Deleted but still-resident records are included by default — filter with WHERE is_allocated for live files only.

functions.name: timestomp
functions.comment: Score the SI-vs-FN timestomp heuristic over two MACB quads

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Score the anti-forensic SI-vs-FN timestamp heuristic over a $STANDARD_INFORMATION MACB quad `si` and a $FILE_NAME MACB quad `fn` (each a `STRUCT(created, modified, accessed, mft_modified)` of `TIMESTAMP`). Returns `STRUCT(suspect BOOLEAN, reasons LIST<VARCHAR>)`; reasons ⊆ {si-before-fn, si-creation-before-fn-creation, zero-subsecond, fn-newer-than-si, all-four-equal}. SI is user-writable (tools like timestomp edit it) while FN is kernel-only, so SI earlier than FN — naturally impossible — and whole-second SI values are strong tells. Composable over the read_mft si_* / fn_* columns.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Score the SI-vs-FN timestomp heuristic: `timestomp(si, fn)` → `STRUCT(suspect, reasons)`. reasons ⊆ {si-before-fn, si-creation-before-fn-creation, zero-subsecond, fn-newer-than-si, all-four-equal}.

vgi.example_queries.description: Flag a record whose $STANDARD_INFORMATION quad predates its $FILE_NAME quad — the naturally-impossible ordering timestomping produces.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT mft.main.timestomp({'created': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'modified': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'accessed': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'mft_modified': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01'}, {'created': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'modified': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'accessed': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'mft_modified': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01'}).suspect AS suspect

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Reconstruct the full filesystem path of MFT entry `entry` in a $MFT `blob` by walking parent references up to the volume root. Returns `\$Orphan\…` when a parent is missing or its slot was reused, and `\$Cycle\…` when a corrupt parent loop is detected (the walk is depth- and cycle-bounded, never spins). NULL when the entry has no name record.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Fully decode MFT entry `entry` in a $MFT `blob` into a `STRUCT` carrying the header (entry, sequence, in_use, is_dir, base_ref, lsn, hard_links), the $STANDARD_INFORMATION MACB + DOS attrs + USN (`si`), the full `LIST` of every $FILE_NAME (`fn` — including the 8.3 DOS short name, with namespace and parent reference), the primary $DATA (`data` — resident bytes when small), the alternate data streams (`ads`), and every attribute (`attributes`). The raw, lossless per-record view, NULL for an empty slot.

functions.comment: Validate one $MFT record; never panics on corrupt input

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Validate MFT entry `entry` in a $MFT `blob`, returning a `STRUCT(ok BOOLEAN, error VARCHAR, kind VARCHAR)`. `kind` is one of ok, baad, fixup-mismatch, bad-signature, attr-overrun, truncated, not-an-mft. workers.summary: Read-only Major League Baseball standings and player statistics from MLB's Stats API
workers.doc_md:
# MLB standings and player statistics

Query current and historical Major League Baseball data directly from SQL. The catalog contains team standings and complete batting, pitching, and fielding season lines, plus advanced metrics, career totals, team splits, and per-game logs.

## Data model

Current tables are the quickest entry point. Parameterized functions select seasons, leagues, game types, qualified pools, or individual players. Multi-team season totals never claim to belong to one club: use the team-split functions when attribution matters.

All access is read-only and requires no credential. Rate statistics are exact decimals; baseball innings remain display strings alongside exact integer outs.

example_queries.title: current_standings_are_populated
example_queries.description: MLB regular-season standings contain team rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS populated FROM mlb.main.current_standings;

example_queries.title: current_batting_has_players
example_queries.description: The complete current batting pool has stable player identifiers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AND count(player_id) = count(*) AS populated FROM mlb.main.current_batting;

example_queries.title: baseball_innings_are_exact
example_queries.description: Every displayed pitching inning count agrees with the exact outs count.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(outs >= 0) AS valid_outs FROM mlb.main.current_pitching WHERE innings_pitched IS NOT NULL;

example_queries.description: Current division tables in official rank order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division_name, division_rank, team_name, wins, losses, games_back FROM mlb.main.current_standings ORDER BY division_name, division_rank

example_queries.description: Teams with the best run differential.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, wins, losses, run_differential FROM mlb.main.current_standings ORDER BY run_differential DESC

example_queries.description: Current MLB home-run leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, home_runs, ops FROM mlb.main.current_batting ORDER BY home_runs DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Current shortstops with substantial defensive playing time.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, outs, errors, fielding_percentage FROM mlb.main.current_fielding WHERE position_abbreviation = 'SS' AND outs >= 600 ORDER BY fielding_percentage DESC

example_queries.description: Current qualified ERA leaders with at least 300 outs.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, innings_pitched, strikeouts, era FROM mlb.main.current_pitching WHERE outs >= 300 ORDER BY era LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Jhoan Duran's 2025 pitching totals separated by team.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, games_pitched, innings_pitched, strikeouts, era FROM mlb.main.pitching_team_splits(661395, 2025) ORDER BY team_name

example_queries.description: Qualified 2025 pitchers ordered by ERA.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, innings_pitched, strikeouts, era FROM mlb.main.pitching_stats(season := 2025, qualified_only := true) ORDER BY era LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: 2025 shortstops with at least 900 defensive outs.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, outs, errors, fielding_percentage FROM mlb.main.fielding_stats(season := 2025) WHERE position_abbreviation = 'SS' AND outs >= 900 ORDER BY fielding_percentage DESC

example_queries.description: Shohei Ohtani's June 2025 batting game log.
example_queries.sql: SELECT game_date, opponent_abbreviation, summary FROM mlb.main.batting_game_log(660271, season := 2025, start_date := DATE '2025-06-01', end_date := DATE '2025-06-30') ORDER BY game_date

example_queries.description: Josh Naylor's 2025 batting totals separated by team.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, games_played, hits, home_runs, ops FROM mlb.main.batting_team_splits(647304, 2025) ORDER BY team_name

example_queries.description: The 2025 final division standings.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division_name, division_rank, team_name, wins, losses FROM mlb.main.standings(season := 2025) ORDER BY division_name, division_rank

example_queries.description: The current American League wild-card race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT wild_card_rank, team_name, wild_card_games_back FROM mlb.main.standings(league := 'AL', standings_type := 'wildCard') ORDER BY wild_card_rank

example_queries.description: Qualified 2025 pitchers by K-minus-BB percentage.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, strikeouts_minus_walks_percentage, whiff_percentage FROM mlb.main.advanced_pitching_stats(season := 2025, qualified_only := true) ORDER BY strikeouts_minus_walks_percentage DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Shohei Ohtani's regular-season career batting totals.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, games_played, hits, home_runs, batting_average, ops FROM mlb.main.batting_career(660271)

example_queries.description: Qualified 2025 MLB OPS leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, home_runs, ops FROM mlb.main.batting_stats(season := 2025, qualified_only := true) ORDER BY ops DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Shohei Ohtani's regular-season career pitching totals.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, games_started, innings_pitched, strikeouts, era, whip FROM mlb.main.pitching_career(660271)

example_queries.description: Qualified 2025 isolated-power leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, plate_appearances, isolated_power, strikeouts_per_plate_appearance FROM mlb.main.advanced_batting_stats(season := 2025, qualified_only := true) ORDER BY isolated_power DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Current shortstop fielding lines from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, outs, errors FROM mlb.main.all_current_fielding() WHERE position_abbreviation = 'SS' ORDER BY outs DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Current home-run leaders from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, home_runs FROM mlb.main.all_current_batting() ORDER BY home_runs DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Current strikeout leaders from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, strikeouts FROM mlb.main.all_current_pitching() ORDER BY strikeouts DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Read the table's backing scan directly.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division_name, team_name, wins, losses FROM mlb.main.all_current_standings() WHERE division_rank = 1 ORDER BY division_name

example_queries.description: Shohei Ohtani's 2025 pitching game log.
example_queries.sql: SELECT game_date, opponent_abbreviation, innings_pitched, strikeouts, summary FROM mlb.main.pitching_game_log(660271, season := 2025) ORDER BY game_date
