tags.vgi.doc_llm: Season pitching lines at player grain: appearances, starts, wins, saves, innings, outs, strikeouts, walks, ERA, WHIP, opponent slash line, K/BB and per-nine rates. Defaults to all players in MLB's current season. Set qualified_only => true for qualified leaders, or pass a season and AL/NL league. Use outs—not the display innings_pitched string—for exact innings arithmetic.
tags.vgi.doc_md: One aggregate season pitching line per player. `innings_pitched` preserves baseball notation, where .1 and .2 mean one and two outs; divide `outs` by three for arithmetic. Rate statistics are exact `DECIMAL` columns.

vgi.example_queries.description: Qualified 2025 pitchers ordered by ERA.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, innings_pitched, strikeouts, era FROM mlb.main.pitching_stats(season := 2025, qualified_only := true) ORDER BY era LIMIT 20

functions.name: fielding_stats
functions.comment: MLB player fielding statistics by season, league, and game type

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Season fielding lines at player-position grain, including defensive innings, putouts, assists, errors, chances, double plays, fielding percentage and range factors. A player can have several rows when he appeared at several positions.
tags.vgi.doc_md: One row per player and position. `innings` preserves baseball notation; use the derived integer `outs` for exact defensive-inning arithmetic.

vgi.example_queries.description: 2025 shortstops with at least 900 defensive outs.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, outs, errors, fielding_percentage FROM mlb.main.fielding_stats(season := 2025) WHERE position_abbreviation = 'SS' AND outs >= 900 ORDER BY fielding_percentage DESC

functions.name: standings
functions.comment: MLB standings by season, league, and standings view

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per MLB team with rankings, wins and losses, games back, run differential, streak, home/away and last-ten records, and clinching state. Use season for historical standings, league => 'AL' or 'NL' to narrow, and standings_type => 'wildCard' for the wild-card race. With no arguments it returns the current regular-season standings for both leagues.
tags.vgi.doc_md: MLB standings flattened to one row per team. All arguments are named and optional. `games_back` is numeric for sorting and arithmetic; the original MLB marker remains in `games_back_display`. The same applies to wild-card games back. Percentages use exact `DECIMAL` values rather than binary floats.

vgi.example_queries.description: The 2025 final division standings.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT division_name, division_rank, team_name, wins, losses FROM mlb.main.standings(season := 2025) ORDER BY division_name, division_rank

vgi.example_queries.description: The current American League wild-card race.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT wild_card_rank, team_name, wild_card_games_back FROM mlb.main.standings(league := 'AL', standings_type := 'wildCard') ORDER BY wild_card_rank

functions.name: batting_stats
functions.comment: MLB player batting statistics by season and league

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Season batting lines at player grain: games, plate appearances, hits, extra-base hits, home runs, RBI, steals, walks, strikeouts, AVG, OBP, SLG, OPS and BABIP. Defaults to all players in MLB's current season. Set qualified_only => true for the official rate-stat leaderboard pool, or pass a season and AL/NL league.
tags.vgi.doc_md: One aggregate season batting line per player. Rate statistics are exact `DECIMAL` columns. The full player pool is returned and completely paged by default; `qualified_only := true` narrows to official qualifiers.

vgi.example_queries.description: Qualified 2025 MLB OPS leaders.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, last_team_abbreviation, home_runs, ops FROM mlb.main.batting_stats(season := 2025, qualified_only := true) ORDER BY ops DESC LIMIT 20

workers.title: Mapbox Vector Tile Reader
workers.tagline: Read Mapbox Vector Tiles, PMTiles & MBTiles as tables with geometry in DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary:
# Read Mapbox Vector Tiles in DuckDB

**Turn vector tiles back into data.** Decode Mapbox Vector Tiles into rows with a DuckDB `GEOMETRY` column and the features' attributes, from PMTiles (file or URL), MBTiles, `{z}/{x}/{y}` tile servers, single `.mvt` / `.pbf` tiles or tile blobs in a query.

Coordinates come back as WGS84 longitude/latitude by default; Web Mercator metres and raw tile pixels are available too. Vector tiles are a lossy, display-oriented format: coordinates snap to a grid of usually 4096 per tile, and features are clipped at tile edges and simplified at low zoom, so read the highest zoom for the most faithful geometry.
workers.doc_md:
# Read Mapbox Vector Tiles in DuckDB

**Turn vector tiles back into data.** Decode Mapbox Vector Tiles into rows with a DuckDB `GEOMETRY` column and the features' attributes, from PMTiles (file or URL), MBTiles, `{z}/{x}/{y}` tile servers, single `.mvt` / `.pbf` tiles or tile blobs in a query.

Coordinates come back as WGS84 longitude/latitude by default; Web Mercator metres and raw tile pixels are available too. Vector tiles are a lossy, display-oriented format: coordinates snap to a grid of usually 4096 per tile, and features are clipped at tile edges and simplified at low zoom, so read the highest zoom for the most faithful geometry.

attach_options.name: tileset
attach_options.description: PMTiles file or http(s) URL, or local MBTiles file, to expose as tables (one per layer). Empty attaches only the reader functions.

attach_options.name: zoom
attach_options.description: Zoom level the layer tables read; -1 (default) uses the tileset's maxzoom.

attach_options.name: bbox
attach_options.description: Limit every layer table to the tiles covering 'west,south,east,north' (degrees); empty reads all.

attach_options.name: coordinates
attach_options.description: Geometry coordinates of the layer tables: 'wgs84' (default), 'web_mercator' or 'tile'.

attach_options.name: max_tiles
attach_options.description: A layer table scan fails rather than read more than this many tiles.

attach_options.name: tile_edges
attach_options.description: Features reaching a tile edge: 'merge' (default, one row per feature), 'clip' (one non-overlapping piece per tile) or 'raw' (as stored, tile buffers included).

example_queries.description: Features per layer of the fixture tileset: one row each, joined across tile edges
example_queries.sql: SELECT layer, geometry_type, count(*) AS features, round(sum(ST_Area(geometry)), 1) AS area FROM mvt.main.read_tiles('test/fixtures/edges.pmtiles', zoom := 3) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: A spatial filter on the geometry also chooses which tiles are read
example_queries.sql: SELECT layer, count(*) AS features FROM mvt.main.read_tiles('test/fixtures/sample.pmtiles') WHERE ST_Intersects(geometry, ST_MakeEnvelope(8, 44, 18, 54)) GROUP BY layer ORDER BY layer

example_queries.description: Road kinds in the Protomaps Florence sample, read over HTTP range requests
example_queries.sql: SELECT properties->>'pmap:kind' AS kind, count(*) AS n FROM mvt.main.read_tiles('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/protomaps/PMTiles/main/spec/v3/protomaps(vector)ODbL_firenze.pmtiles', zoom := 14) WHERE layer = 'roads' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC

## main

Read vector tiles as tables: whole tilesets at one zoom, single tiles, or tile blobs already in DuckDB, plus the layer and metadata catalogues that describe a tileset.

Feature rows always carry `layer`, `z`, `x`, `y`, `feature_id`, `geometry_type`, `geometry` and `properties`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Vector tile readers. Every feature-reading function returns the same leading columns: layer, z, x, y, feature_id, geometry_type, geometry (`GEOMETRY`), properties (`JSON`). Tile addresses use the XYZ scheme (row 0 at the north); MBTiles stores TMS rows and is flipped for you. Whole tilesets are read one zoom at a time, limited by an optional WGS84 bbox (west, south, east, north) that selects tiles, not features: filter features afterwards with `ST_Intersects`. A `max_tiles` guard (default 10000) stops accidental planet-sized reads. Use DuckDB spatial (ST_*) on the geometry column; old (MVT v1) tilesets can contain self-intersecting polygons, which `ST_MakeValid` repairs.

functions.name: read_tiles
functions.comment: Read the features of a PMTiles, MBTiles or XYZ vector tileset as rows with a GEOMETRY column

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a Mapbox Vector Tile tileset back into rows, one per feature. `source` is a PMTiles archive (local path or http(s) URL, read with range requests), a local MBTiles file, or a tile URL template with `{z}/{x}/{y}`. Named arguments: `zoom` (defaults to the tileset maxzoom), `layer` (read one layer and add a typed column per attribute), `west`/`south`/`east`/`north` (WGS84 bbox; all four or none; required for URL templates), `coordinates` ('wgs84' default, 'web_mercator' or 'tile') and `max_tiles` (default 10000; the call fails rather than read more). A constant `WHERE ST_Intersects(geometry, <geometry>)` (or ST_Within/ST_Contains/...) also narrows the tiles read, so it can replace the bbox arguments. Columns: layer, z, x, y, feature_id, geometry_type, geometry (GEOMETRY), properties (JSON) and, with `layer`, one typed column per layer attribute. `tile_edges` ('merge' default, 'clip', 'raw') controls features that cross tile edges: 'merge' returns one row per feature, joining the per-tile pieces that share a feature_id (features without an id may come back as several non-overlapping pieces); 'raw' returns each tile's copy, buffer included. A feature extending past the tiles read is cut at their edge. Use `tileset_layers` first to discover layer and attribute names.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## read_tiles(source, zoom := maxzoom, layer := NULL, west/south/east/north := NULL, coordinates := 'wgs84', max_tiles := 10000, tile_edges := 'merge')

One row per vector-tile feature, with a `GEOMETRY` column and a JSON `properties` column. Sources: PMTiles (file or URL), MBTiles (file) or an `{z}/{x}/{y}` URL template.

Pass `layer` to also get each attribute of that layer as its own typed column. Features crossing tile edges come back once (`tile_edges := 'merge'`); use `'raw'` for each tile's stored copy.

**Without `layer`** (every layer):

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| layer | VARCHAR | Vector tile layer name. |
| z | INTEGER | Tile zoom level. |
| x | INTEGER | Tile column (XYZ scheme). |
| y | INTEGER | Tile row (XYZ scheme, 0 at the north). |
| feature_id | UBIGINT | Feature id from the tile; NULL if absent. |
| geometry_type | VARCHAR | OGC geometry type of the feature. |
| geometry | GEOMETRY | Feature geometry (WGS84 lon/lat by default). |
| properties | JSON | All feature attributes as a JSON object. |

**With `layer := '<name>'`**: the columns above, then one column per attribute of that layer. Number becomes `DOUBLE`, Boolean `BOOLEAN`, String and anything else `VARCHAR`; names that clash case-insensitively with another column are skipped (they stay in `properties`).

|---|---|---|

arguments.description: Output coordinate system: 'wgs84' (longitude/latitude degrees, the default), 'web_mercator' (EPSG:3857 metres) or 'tile' (raw tile pixels, 0..extent from the tile's top-left corner).

arguments.description: East edge of the area to read, degrees longitude.

arguments.description: Read only this layer. Also adds one typed column per attribute of the layer (from the tileset's vector_layers metadata, or inferred from the tile). NULL reads every layer.

arguments.name: max_tiles
arguments.description: Fail instead of reading more than this many tiles (a guard for huge archives).

arguments.name: north
arguments.description: North edge of the area to read, degrees latitude.

arguments.name: south
arguments.description: South edge of the area to read, degrees latitude.

arguments.name: tile_edges
arguments.description: How features that reach a tile edge come back: 'merge' (the default: one row per feature; points only in the tile that owns them, lines and polygons clipped to their tile and the pieces sharing a feature id joined into one geometry), 'clip' (clipped to each tile, not joined: pieces never overlap) or 'raw' (exactly as stored in the tiles, including the buffer each tile repeats from its neighbours).

arguments.description: West edge of the area to read, degrees longitude.

arguments.name: zoom
arguments.description: Zoom level to read; defaults to the tileset's maxzoom.

functions.name: mvt_decode
functions.comment: Decode vector tile BLOBs from a query (tile, z, x, y) into one row per feature

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table in-out function: pass a subquery whose rows hold vector tiles and get one row per feature back. The input needs a `BLOB` column `tile` (or `tile_data`; gzip is detected) and whole-number columns `z`, `x`, `y` in the XYZ scheme (row 0 at the north). MBTiles rows are TMS: convert with `(1 << zoom_level) - 1 - tile_row AS y`. Named arguments `layer` and `coordinates` work as in `read_tiles`. Output columns: layer, z, x, y, feature_id, geometry_type, geometry (GEOMETRY), properties (JSON). Use `read_tiles` instead when the tileset is a file or URL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## mvt_decode(data, layer := NULL, coordinates := 'wgs84')

Explode vector-tile blobs that are already in DuckDB into features. Input rows need `tile` (`BLOB`) and XYZ `z`, `x`, `y`. MBTiles rows are TMS: flip them with `(1 << zoom_level) - 1 - tile_row`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Decode MBTiles rows read with DuckDB's sqlite extension
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT layer, count(*) AS n FROM mvt.main.mvt_decode((SELECT tile_data AS tile, zoom_level AS z, tile_column AS x, (1 << zoom_level) - 1 - tile_row AS y FROM sqlite_scan('test/fixtures/sample.mbtiles', 'tiles') WHERE zoom_level = 2)) GROUP BY layer ORDER BY n DESC

vgi.executable_examples.description: Decode a hand-made tile holding one point at the centre of tile 0/0/0
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT layer, feature_id, ST_AsText(geometry) AS wkt FROM mvt.main.mvt_decode((SELECT from_hex('1a2e78020a06706f696e7473120f0807120200001801220509802080201a046e616d6522080a066f726967696e288020') AS tile, 0 AS z, 0 AS x, 0 AS y)) ORDER BY layer

workers.title: NASCAR Racing Data
workers.tagline: NASCAR Cup, Xfinity & Truck schedules, results, standings & lap data in DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Read-only NASCAR schedules, results, standings, lap times and pit stops from NASCAR's feeds
workers.doc_md:
# NASCAR schedules, results and lap data

Query NASCAR's three national series directly from SQL: schedules and race summaries since 2015, official results, stage and session results, cautions, lead changes, lap-by-lap times (2020 onwards), pit stops, commentary, loop-data driver ratings and current points standings.

## Data model

Races are identified by `race_id`; drivers by `driver_id`. Find a race in `current_schedule` or `schedule()`, then pass its `race_id` (and `season` to skip the lookup) to the per-race functions. Missing upstream files yield empty results, not errors.

Data is fetched on demand and cached in-process; nothing is rehosted. Not affiliated with NASCAR.

example_queries.title: current_schedule_is_populated
example_queries.description: The current season's schedule covers all three national series.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT series_id) = 3 AS populated FROM nascar.main.current_schedule;

example_queries.title: current_standings_have_drivers
example_queries.description: Every current standings row has a driver and a non-negative points total.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AND bool_and(points >= 0) AND count(driver_id) = count(*) AS valid FROM nascar.main.current_standings;

example_queries.title: championship_race_2026_winner
example_queries.description: Ryan Blaney won the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race (race 5601).
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name FROM nascar.main.race_results(5601, season := 2026) WHERE finishing_position = 1;

example_queries.title: lead_stints_match_laps_led
example_queries.description: Lead stints in race 5601 add up to the 267 laps run.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(laps_led)::INTEGER AS laps FROM nascar.main.race_leaders(5601, season := 2026);

example_queries.description: Current Cup Series top ten.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, points, points_behind_leader, wins, top_5 FROM nascar.main.current_standings WHERE series_id = 1 ORDER BY position LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Points leader of each series.
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_name, driver_name, points FROM nascar.main.current_standings WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY series_id

example_queries.description: Whether a session is on track, with its lap and flag.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS sessions_on_track, max(run_name) AS session, max(lap_number) AS lap, max(flag) AS flag FROM nascar.main.live_race

example_queries.description: Top five of the latest Cup Series race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT race_name, finishing_position, driver_name, team_name, laps_led FROM nascar.main.last_race_results WHERE series_id = 1 AND finishing_position <= 5 ORDER BY finishing_position

example_queries.description: Cup Series winners so far this season.
example_queries.sql: SELECT race_date, race_name, track_name, winner_name FROM nascar.main.current_schedule WHERE series_id = 1 AND is_completed ORDER BY race_date

example_queries.description: The 2025 Cup Series points races and their winners.
example_queries.sql: SELECT race_date, race_name, track_name, winner_name FROM nascar.main.schedule(season := 2025, series := 'cup') WHERE is_points_race ORDER BY race_date

example_queries.description: Tracks visited by every national series in 2024.
example_queries.sql: SELECT track_name, count(DISTINCT series_id) AS series FROM nascar.main.schedule(season := 2024) GROUP BY track_name HAVING series = 3

example_queries.description: Laps led by driver in the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name, sum(laps_led) AS laps_led, count(*) AS stints FROM nascar.main.race_leaders(5601, season := 2026) GROUP BY driver_name ORDER BY laps_led DESC

example_queries.description: 2025 Cup Series wins and top-fives by driver, points races only.
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.driver_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.finishing_position = 1) AS wins, count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.finishing_position <= 5) AS top_5 FROM nascar.main.season_results(season := 2025) r JOIN nascar.main.schedule(season := 2025, series := 'cup') USING (race_id) WHERE is_points_race GROUP BY r.driver_name ORDER BY wins DESC, top_5 DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Laps led by team in the 2025 Truck Series.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, sum(laps_led) AS laps_led FROM nascar.main.season_results(season := 2025, series := 'truck') GROUP BY team_name ORDER BY laps_led DESC

example_queries.description: Finishing order of the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT finishing_position, car_number, driver_name, team_name, laps_led, finishing_status FROM nascar.main.race_results(5601, season := 2026) ORDER BY finishing_position

example_queries.description: Read the table's backing scan directly: the Cup Series top ten.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, points, wins FROM nascar.main.all_current_standings() WHERE series_id = 1 ORDER BY position LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Fastest four-tire green-flag stops in the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name, lap, stop_seconds, pit_road_seconds FROM nascar.main.pit_stops(5601, season := 2026) WHERE stop_type = 'FOUR_WHEEL_CHANGE' AND pit_in_flag_state = 1 ORDER BY stop_seconds LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Published Cup Series driver profiles with hometowns.
example_queries.sql: SELECT full_name, team, hometown_city, hometown_state, birth_date FROM nascar.main.drivers(series := 'cup') WHERE profile_published ORDER BY last_name

example_queries.description: Read the table's backing scan directly: is anything on track right now?
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS sessions_on_track, max(lap_number) AS lap, max(flag) AS flag FROM nascar.main.all_live_race()

example_queries.description: Qualifying order for the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, best_lap_time_seconds, best_lap_speed FROM nascar.main.session_results(5601, season := 2026) WHERE run_type = 'qualifying' ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Races scheduled and already run in each series this season.
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_name, count(*) AS races, count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_completed) AS completed FROM nascar.main.all_current_schedule() GROUP BY series_name ORDER BY series_name

example_queries.description: Read the table's backing scan directly: each series' latest winner.
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_id, race_name, driver_name FROM nascar.main.all_last_race_results() WHERE finishing_position = 1 ORDER BY series_id

example_queries.description: Highest driver ratings in the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name, driver_rating, green_flag_passes, quality_passes, average_position FROM nascar.main.loop_stats(5601, season := 2026) ORDER BY driver_rating DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Commentary for the final ten laps of the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT lap, note FROM nascar.main.lap_notes(5601, season := 2026) WHERE lap >= 258 ORDER BY lap, note_id

example_queries.description: Cautions in the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT caution_number, start_lap, end_lap, laps, reason, comment FROM nascar.main.race_cautions(5601, season := 2026) ORDER BY caution_number

example_queries.description: Each driver's fastest lap in the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name, min(lap_time_seconds) AS best_lap, max(lap_speed) AS best_speed FROM nascar.main.lap_times(5601, season := 2026) GROUP BY driver_name ORDER BY best_lap LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Stage winners of the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT stage_number, driver_name, stage_points FROM nascar.main.stage_results(5601, season := 2026) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY stage_number

## NASCAR analytical data

Rows are race-, car-in-race-, stage-, caution-, lap- or pit-stop-grain, keyed by `race_id` and `driver_id`. Times and speeds are exact decimals.

Start with the current tables. For history, find a `race_id` with `schedule()` and pass it to the per-race functions; aggregate `season_results()` for season, team and manufacturer statistics.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Current-season race calendar for Cup, O'Reilly Auto Parts (Xfinity) and Truck: one row per race with race_id, date (US Eastern wall clock), track, laps, stage lengths, pole winner, winner, lead changes and cautions. is_completed separates results from upcoming races. tables.name: current_standings
tables.comment: Current-season driver points standings, one row per driver per series

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Current-season driver championship standings for all three national series, one row per driver per series (series_id 1 Cup, 2 O'Reilly Auto Parts/Xfinity, 3 Truck). Start here for points, position, wins, top 5s, top 10s, laps led, stage wins, DNFs and playoff status. Always filter series_id. For past seasons aggregate season_results() instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md: NASCAR's current points feed for each national series as a read-only table. Historical points feeds are not exposed because NASCAR's season paths for them do not reliably match their contents; use `season_results()` for past-season aggregates.

vgi.example_queries.description: Current Cup Series top ten.

vgi.example_queries.description: Points leader of each series.

functions.name: schedule
functions.comment: NASCAR race schedule and race summaries by season and series

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per race (points races and exhibitions) with date, track, laps, distance, stage lengths, pole and race winner, lead changes, cautions and broadcaster. Seasons 2015 onwards (NASCAR's 2017 list holds 2018 races, so 2017 is empty); series cup, oreilly (xfinity) or truck, NULL for all. Use race_id from here with race_results(), lap_times(), pit_stops() and the other per-race functions.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Season race lists from NASCAR's own feeds. `race_date` is the published wall-clock start time: US Eastern for most races, track-local for some 2019-2023 races in the Pacific and Mountain zones. Before a race runs, `winner_driver_id` is NULL and `is_completed` is false. Where a race list omits the winner (2018-2019, parts of 2022) it is read from the official results; 2015-2016 winners stay NULL.

vgi.example_queries.description: The 2025 Cup Series points races and their winners.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT race_date, race_name, track_name, winner_name FROM nascar.main.schedule(season := 2025, series := 'cup') WHERE is_points_race ORDER BY race_date

vgi.example_queries.description: Tracks visited by every national series in 2024.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT track_name, count(DISTINCT series_id) AS series FROM nascar.main.schedule(season := 2024) GROUP BY track_name HAVING series = 3

functions.name: race_leaders
functions.comment: Lap-by-lap lead stints of one NASCAR race

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per lead stint (start lap, end lap, laps led) with the leading car and driver. Summing laps_led per driver reproduces race_results laps_led.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Lead stints from the race's weekend feed, with drivers matched by car number.

vgi.example_queries.description: Laps led by driver in the 2026 Cup Series Championship Race.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name, sum(laps_led) AS laps_led, count(*) AS stints FROM nascar.main.race_leaders(5601, season := 2026) GROUP BY driver_name ORDER BY laps_led DESC

functions.name: season_results
functions.comment: Official results of every completed race in one NASCAR series season

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per car per completed race of a season (points races and exhibitions; join schedule() on race_id and filter is_points_race when that matters). Aggregate it for season driver, team, owner or manufacturer statistics: wins, top 5s, laps led, average finish, DNFs (finishing_status <> 'Running'). Defaults to the current Cup season.
tags.vgi.doc_md: The per-race official results for a whole season, fetched with bounded concurrency and cached. This is the source for season and career aggregates in SQL; NASCAR's points feeds are only reliable for the current season.

vgi.example_queries.description: 2025 Cup Series wins and top-fives by driver, points races only.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT r.driver_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.finishing_position = 1) AS wins, count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.finishing_position <= 5) AS top_5 FROM nascar.main.season_results(season := 2025) r JOIN nascar.main.schedule(season := 2025, series := 'cup') USING (race_id) WHERE is_points_race GROUP BY r.driver_name ORDER BY wins DESC, top_5 DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Laps led by team in the 2025 Truck Series.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, sum(laps_led) AS laps_led FROM nascar.main.season_results(season := 2025, series := 'truck') GROUP BY team_name ORDER BY laps_led DESC

workers.title: NBA Basketball Data
workers.tagline: NBA, WNBA & G League standings, scores, box scores & player stats in DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Read-only NBA, WNBA, and NBA G League standings, scores, and statistics from the NBA Stats API
workers.doc_md:
# NBA, WNBA, and G League basketball data

Query current and historical basketball data from SQL. Each league is its own schema (`nba`, `wnba`, `gleague`) with the same surface: standings, scores, schedules, teams, rosters, player and team statistics, leaderboards, game logs, careers, box scores, and play-by-play.

## Data source

Data is fetched on demand from the NBA's public Stats API and content CDN; nothing is stored or rehosted. NBA data is for personal, non-commercial use under the NBA.com Terms of Use. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by the NBA, WNBA, or NBA G League.

example_queries.title: nba_teams_are_populated
example_queries.description: The NBA has thirty active teams with stable identifiers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) = 30 AS thirty_teams FROM nba.nba.current_teams;

example_queries.title: wnba_franchises_include_summaries
example_queries.description: Every active WNBA team has an all-time franchise summary row.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) >= 13 AS populated FROM nba.wnba.franchise_history WHERE row_kind = 'franchise';

example_queries.title: historical_standings_balance
example_queries.description: Final 2025-26 NBA standings: 30 teams whose wins equal their losses in total.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) = 30 AND sum(wins) = sum(losses) AS balanced FROM nba.nba.standings(season := 2025);

example_queries.title: box_score_points_match_scoreboard
example_queries.description: A completed game's player points sum to the published final score.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (SELECT sum(points) FROM nba.nba.box_score('0022600201')) = (SELECT home_score + away_score FROM nba.nba.scoreboard(DATE '2026-11-08') WHERE game_id = '0022600201') AS consistent;

example_queries.description: Current conference standings in seeding order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conference, playoff_rank, team_name, wins, losses, conference_games_back FROM nba.gleague.current_standings ORDER BY conference, playoff_rank

example_queries.description: Franchises with the most league titles.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_city, team_name, start_year, league_titles FROM nba.gleague.franchise_history WHERE row_kind = 'franchise' ORDER BY league_titles DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Rostered players per team.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## NBA G League

Same tables and functions as the nba schema for the NBA G League, except there is no published season-schedule feed (current_schedule is absent; use scoreboard() by date). season => 2025 is 2025-26. Game IDs start with 20.

Every object is read-only and fetched on demand from the NBA Stats API or the league CDN. Game IDs are ten-digit text; keep the leading zeros when filtering.

functions.name: play_by_play

Parameterized functions cover historical seasons, playoffs, advanced ratings, leaderboards, game logs, careers, box scores, and play-by-play. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## National Basketball Association

Use current_standings, current_scoreboard, current_schedule, current_teams, current_players, current_player_stats, and current_team_stats for the live season. Parameterized functions cover historical seasons, playoffs, advanced ratings, leaderboards, game logs, careers, box scores, and play-by-play. Seasons are passed as their start year: season => 2025 is 2025-26.

Every object is read-only and fetched on demand from the NBA Stats API or the league CDN. Game IDs are ten-digit text; keep the leading zeros when filtering.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Same tables and functions as the nba schema for the WNBA (no divisions). Seasons are single calendar years: season => 2025 is the 2025 season. Game IDs start with 10.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Women's National Basketball Association

Same tables and functions as the nba schema for the WNBA (no divisions). Seasons are single calendar years: season => 2025 is the 2025 season. Game IDs start with 10.

Every object is read-only and fetched on demand from the NBA Stats API or the league CDN. Game IDs are ten-digit text; keep the leading zeros when filtering.

workers.title: NCAA Division I Basketball
workers.tagline: NCAA men's & women's college basketball scores, standings, rankings & stats in DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Read-only NCAA Division I men's and women's basketball data from ESPN and ncaa-api
workers.doc_md:
# NCAA Division I basketball

Men's (`mens`) and women's (`womens`) college basketball from ESPN's public endpoints, plus the official NCAA NET rankings, statistical leaderboards and tournament brackets through the ncaa-api proxy of ncaa.com.

## Data model

Current tables are the quickest entry point. Parameterized functions select seasons, weeks, dates, teams and games. ESPN `team_id` and `event_id` link standings, scoreboards, schedules, rosters and box scores. Seasons are labelled by their ending year.

Data is fetched on demand and cached briefly in process; nothing is rehosted.

example_queries.title: mens_standings_cover_division_i
example_queries.description: Current men's standings cover more than 300 Division I teams.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 300 AS populated FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.current_standings;

example_queries.title: womens_standings_cover_division_i
example_queries.description: Current women's standings cover more than 300 Division I teams.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 300 AS populated FROM ncaa_basketball.womens.current_standings;

example_queries.title: mens_2026_champion
example_queries.description: Michigan won the 2026 men's national championship game.
example_queries.sql: SELECT winner FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.bracket(2026) WHERE round_number = 7;

example_queries.title: pinned_box_score_totals
example_queries.description: UConn's player points sum to its 83-point team total against Wagner.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(points) AS points FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.box_score(401920686) WHERE team_id = 41;

example_queries.description: The current AP Top 25.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_location, record FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.current_rankings WHERE poll_id = 1 AND rank IS NOT NULL ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Teams with the best current conference record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, conference_name, conference_wins, conference_losses FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.current_standings ORDER BY conference_win_percentage DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: The NET top ten with Quadrant 1 records.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, school, conference, record, quad1_record FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.net_rankings WHERE rank <= 10 ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Find the points-per-game leaderboard id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, stat_id, name FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.stat_categories WHERE name ILIKE '%per game%' ORDER BY category, name

example_queries.description: Largest conferences.
example_queries.sql: SELECT short_name, abbreviation, team_count FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.conferences ORDER BY team_count DESC

example_queries.description: Today's games involving ranked teams.
example_queries.sql: SELECT short_name, status_detail, away_rank, away_score, home_rank, home_score FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.current_scoreboard WHERE away_rank IS NOT NULL OR home_rank IS NOT NULL ORDER BY start_time

example_queries.description: Current rebounding leaders with at least three games.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, team_abbreviation, games_played, rebounds_per_game FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.current_player_stats WHERE games_played >= 3 ORDER BY rebounds_per_game DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: The current AP Top 25.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_location, record, points, first_place_votes FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.current_rankings WHERE poll_id = 1 AND rank IS NOT NULL ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Current Big Ten table in conference order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conference_seed, team_name, conference_wins, conference_losses, wins, losses FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.current_standings WHERE conference_abbreviation = 'big10' ORDER BY conference_seed

example_queries.description: Find a team id by name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_id, display_name, conference_name FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.teams WHERE display_name ILIKE '%duke%'

example_queries.description: Duke's current roster.
example_queries.sql: SELECT jersey, full_name, position, display_height, class_year FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.team_roster(150) ORDER BY full_name

example_queries.description: Top scorers in {game} on 9 November 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_abbreviation, player_name, minutes, points FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.box_score(401920686) ORDER BY points DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Teams in the Big Ten from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_id, display_name FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.all_teams() WHERE conference_abbreviation = 'big10' ORDER BY display_name

example_queries.description: Final 2025-26 Big Ten standings.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conference_seed, team_name, conference_wins, conference_losses, wins, losses FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.standings(season := 2026, conference := 'Big Ten') ORDER BY conference_seed

example_queries.description: Results from 9 November 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT away_team_name, away_score, home_team_name, home_score, status FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.scoreboard(DATE '2026-11-09') ORDER BY start_time

example_queries.description: The 2026 Final Four and championship game.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: NCAA Men's Basketball, Division I. Start with current_rankings, current_standings, current_scoreboard, current_player_stats, teams or conferences. Parameterized functions cover past polls (rankings), past standings, any date's scoreboard, team schedules and rosters, past player seasons, box scores and play-by-play by ESPN event_id, and the official NCAA NET, stat leaders and tournament bracket. Seasons are labelled by the year they end: 2025-26 is 2026.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## NCAA Men's Basketball

Polls, standings, scores, schedules, rosters, player statistics, box scores and play-by-play from ESPN, plus the official NCAA NET, statistical leaderboards and tournament bracket via ncaa-api.

ESPN `team_id` and `event_id` join the tables and functions. Seasons are labelled by the year they end, so the 2025-26 season is `2026`.

Use the ordinary tables for what is happening now and the parameterized functions for earlier seasons, other dates, a single team or a single game.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Current men's Division I standings, one row per team, with overall and conference records, conference_seed (ESPN's order within the conference), games behind, home/road splits, points for and against and streak. For a past season or one conference call standings().

vgi.example_queries.description: Current Big Ten table in conference order.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT conference_seed, team_name, conference_wins, conference_losses, wins, losses FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.current_standings WHERE conference_abbreviation = 'big10' ORDER BY conference_seed

functions.name: scoreboard
functions.comment: Every NCAA men's basketball Division I game on one date

tags.vgi.doc_llm: NCAA Men's Basketball. One row per Division I game on game_date (US Eastern calendar day): teams, AP ranks, scores, status, venue and attendance. Pass conference to narrow to one conference's games. event_id feeds box_score, team_box_score and play_by_play.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Full Division I scoreboard for a date (ESPN `groups=50`, so not just featured games).

vgi.example_queries.description: Results from 9 November 2026.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT away_team_name, away_score, home_team_name, home_score, status FROM ncaa_basketball.mens.scoreboard(DATE '2026-11-09') ORDER BY start_time

tags.vgi.doc_llm: NCAA Women's Basketball, Division I. Start with current_rankings, current_standings, current_scoreboard, current_player_stats, teams or conferences. Parameterized functions cover past polls (rankings), past standings, any date's scoreboard, team schedules and rosters, past player seasons, box scores and play-by-play by ESPN event_id, and the official NCAA NET, stat leaders and tournament bracket. Seasons are labelled by the year they end: 2025-26 is 2026.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## NCAA Women's Basketball

Polls, standings, scores, schedules, rosters, player statistics, box scores and play-by-play from ESPN, plus the official NCAA NET, statistical leaderboards and tournament bracket via ncaa-api.

ESPN `team_id` and `event_id` join the tables and functions. Seasons are labelled by the year they end, so the 2025-26 season is `2026`.

Use the ordinary tables for what is happening now and the parameterized functions for earlier seasons, other dates, a single team or a single game.

vgi.example_queries.description: The current AP Top 25.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_location, record FROM ncaa_basketball.womens.current_rankings WHERE poll_id = 1 AND rank IS NOT NULL ORDER BY rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Teams with the best current conference record.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, conference_name, conference_wins, conference_losses FROM ncaa_basketball.womens.current_standings ORDER BY conference_win_percentage DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 10

functions.name: player_stats

One row per Division I player for a season: games, minutes, points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, shooting splits and percentages (0-100 scale), double-doubles and triple-doubles. workers.title: NCAA College Football Data
workers.tagline: NCAA FBS & FCS college football scores, standings, AP polls & stats in DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Read-only NCAA FBS and FCS college football scores, standings, rankings and statistics
workers.doc_md:
# NCAA college football

Query FBS and FCS college football from SQL: weekly scoreboards, bowls and the College Football Playoff, conference standings, AP/Coaches/CFP polls, team and player box scores, drives, play-by-play, team season statistics, national leaders and player game logs.

## Data model

The `current_*` tables are the quickest entry point. Parameterized functions select seasons, weeks, divisions, conferences, teams, games or players by ESPN id. Statistics are long format (one row per statistic) because ESPN's stat sets differ by position and game.

## Source

Data is fetched on demand from ESPN's undocumented public endpoints, cached briefly in process and never stored or redistributed by the worker. ESPN's terms apply; this worker is not affiliated with ESPN, The Walt Disney Company or the NCAA.

example_queries.title: current_standings_are_populated
example_queries.description: Current Division I standings contain FBS teams with stable ids.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 100 AND count(team_id) = count(*) AS populated FROM ncaa_football.main.current_standings WHERE division = 'FBS';

example_queries.title: current_rankings_have_an_ap_top_25
example_queries.description: The latest AP poll ranks 25 teams.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) = 25 AS ranked FROM ncaa_football.main.current_rankings WHERE poll_id = 1 AND rank IS NOT NULL;

example_queries.title: national_title_game_2025
example_queries.description: Indiana beat Miami 27-21 in the 2025 national championship game.
example_queries.sql: SELECT home_team_name, home_score, away_team_name, away_score FROM ncaa_football.main.game_summary(401769076);

example_queries.title: cfp_week15_number_one
example_queries.description: Ohio State topped the 2025 week-15 CFP committee ranking.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name FROM ncaa_football.main.rankings(season := 2025, week := 15, poll := 'cfp') WHERE rank = 1;

example_queries.description: This week's ranked matchups.
example_queries.sql: SELECT start_time, away_rank, away_team_name, home_rank, home_team_name, status_detail FROM ncaa_football.main.current_scoreboard WHERE home_rank IS NOT NULL OR away_rank IS NOT NULL ORDER BY start_time

example_queries.description: This week's games grouped by state (scheduled, live, final).
example_queries.sql: SELECT status_state, count(*) AS games FROM ncaa_football.main.current_scoreboard GROUP BY status_state ORDER BY status_state

example_queries.description: Current rushing-yards leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, player_name, team_abbreviation, value FROM ncaa_football.main.current_stat_leaders WHERE category = 'rushingYards' ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Current SEC standings in order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT conference_rank, team_name, overall_record, conference_record FROM ncaa_football.main.current_standings WHERE conference_abbreviation = 'sec' ORDER BY conference_rank

example_queries.description: Unbeaten FBS teams.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, conference_name, overall_record FROM ncaa_football.main.current_standings WHERE division = 'FBS' AND losses = 0 ORDER BY wins DESC

example_queries.description: The current AP top ten.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_name, record, first_place_votes FROM ncaa_football.main.current_rankings WHERE poll_id = 1 AND rank <= 10 ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Where the AP and CFP rankings disagree.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ap.team_name, ap.rank AS ap_rank, cfp.rank AS cfp_rank FROM ncaa_football.main.current_rankings ap JOIN ncaa_football.main.current_rankings cfp USING (team_id) WHERE ap.poll_id = 1 AND cfp.poll_id = 21 AND ap.rank <> cfp.rank ORDER BY cfp.rank

example_queries.description: Indiana's 2025 offense versus its opponents.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## College football analytical data

Game-, team-, poll-, drive-, play- and statistic-grain tables. Use the current tables for the live season and the parameterized functions for history and detail.

## Identifiers

Every row carries ESPN ids: look teams up with `teams()`, conferences with `conferences()`, and pass `game_id` values from `scoreboard()` or `team_schedule()` to the per-game functions.

functions.name: standings
functions.comment: Conference standings by season and division (FBS or FCS)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per team with conference, conference_rank (ESPN's standings order), overall and conference wins/losses, win percentages, home/away and vs-AP-Top-25 records, points for and against, and streak. season and division ('fbs', 'fcs' or 'all') are named and optional; the default is the current FBS season.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Conference standings flattened to one row per team. `win_percentage` is computed exactly from overall wins and losses; `conference_win_percentage` is ESPN's conference figure. Split conferences carry their division in `subdivision_name`.

vgi.example_queries.description: The final 2025 Big Ten standings.

functions.name: scoreboard
functions.comment: College football games for one week: matchups, kickoff, status, and scores

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per game for a season week with kickoff time, status, venue, rankings and home/away scores. Use season and week for a regular-season week, season_type := 'postseason' for bowls and the College Football Playoff, division := 'fcs' for FCS, or conference_id for one conference. All arguments are named and optional.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Weekly college-football scoreboard, one row per game. Scores are NULL before kickoff; `notes` names bowls and playoff rounds. Games between an FBS and an FCS team appear in both divisions; `division := 'all'` returns each game once.

workers.title: NetFlow Decoder
workers.tagline: Decode NetFlow v5/v9, IPFIX and sFlow in DuckDB with SQL — template-aware flow records joinable on INET. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Decode captured NetFlow v5/v9, IPFIX, and sFlow v5 flow-export datagrams into normalized flow rows — template-stateful, in-engine, no collector stack.
workers.doc_md:
# netflow

Decode captured **flow-export datagrams** — NetFlow **v5** (fixed), NetFlow **v9** (RFC 3954, template-based), **IPFIX** (RFC 7011, template-based, enterprise + variable-length IEs), and **sFlow v5** (packet sampling) — from a `BLOB` column of captured exporter datagrams (or UDP payloads carved out of pcap) into one **normalized** wide flow row per record.

The moat is correct **template-stateful** v9/IPFIX decode at lake scale: a Data Set carries no field descriptors, only a template id, and the Template Set that defines the layout arrives out-of-band — so the worker keeps a **template cache keyed by (exporter, observation domain, template id)** as serializable VGI scan state that survives scan-batch boundaries and HTTP worker rehydration (a template seen in datagram 1 decodes data in datagram 10,000). A data record that arrives before its template is buffered and retried, or emitted with `diagnostics = 'missing-template:…'` — never dropped.

Addresses are emitted as DuckDB **INET** (`LOAD inet;`), so `src_addr::INET <<= '10.0.0.0/8'::INET` containment joins to geoip / threat-intel work directly. The worker decodes captured bytes only — it opens no UDP socket and makes no egress (collector mode is roadmap).

example_queries.description: Route a mixed column of captured datagrams: label each by its flow-export version before decoding.

example_queries.sql: SELECT f.src_addr::INET AS src, f.dst_port, f.bytes FROM netflow.main.flows((FROM (SELECT content AS datagram, filename AS exporter FROM read_blob('caps/*.dat')))) f WHERE f.diagnostics IS NULL AND f.src_addr::INET <<= '10.0.0.0/8'::INET

It groups flow-export decoders (turn a captured datagram column into normalized flow rows), template-cache introspection, and lightweight probe/validation scalars. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## The `netflow` schema

Everything the worker exposes lives in this one schema — qualify every call as `netflow.main.<name>(...)`. Its job is to turn a column of raw captured flow-export datagrams into normalized, typed flow rows, entirely in-engine and with no collector stack.

The capabilities fall into a few groups:

- **Decoders** take a relation with a `datagram` `BLOB` column and return the wide normalized flow schema, auto-detecting NetFlow v5/v9, IPFIX, and sFlow v5 (or restricting to a single family).
- **Template-cache introspection** projects the per-exporter, per-observation-domain templates the stateful v9/IPFIX decoders have learned so far in the session.
- **Probe / validation scalars** identify or structurally validate a single datagram cheaply, without running a full decode.

A small **reference** table lists the flow-export formats the worker understands and which decoder handles each, so an agent can orient before calling anything. Browse that first, then reach for the matching decoder.

# news

Global news search as a DuckDB/SQL VGI worker.

Query worldwide news coverage with a single unified schema regardless of provider.

**Table functions**

- `news_search(query, provider := ..., count := ..., timespan := ..., country := ..., language := ..., page_size := ...)` — search news articles.
- `news_providers()` — list available providers and their API-key requirements.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# news_search

Search worldwide news coverage by free-text query and return a **unified article schema** regardless of which upstream provider served the rows. This is the worker's primary surface: use it whenever you need to find, filter, or analyze recent news articles directly from SQL.

## When to use

- Find which outlets/domains are covering a topic right now.
- Pull recent headlines with their URLs and publish times for a feed or digest.
- Measure coverage volume or sentiment (`tone`) over a look-back window.
- Filter coverage by source country or language.

## Inputs

- `query` (positional, required): the free-text search string.
- `provider :=` (default `'gdelt'`): `'gdelt'` (free, no key, worldwide, includes sentiment `tone`) or `'newsapi'` (requires a `TYPE newsapi` DuckDB secret).
- `count :=` (default 25): total maximum rows across all internally-paged requests.
- `timespan :=` (default `'1d'`): look-back window such as `'6h'`, `'1d'`, `'2w'`.
- `country :=` / `language :=`: optional provider-mapped filters (empty = no filter).
- `page_size :=` (default 50): rows fetched per upstream request / per scan tick.

## Outputs

One row per article over `title, url, domain, language, seendate, country, tone, source, extra`. `seendate` is a real `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`; `tone` is a `DOUBLE` sentiment score (GDELT only, NULL otherwise); `extra` carries provider-specific fields as a JSON string.

## Behavior & edge cases

- Results are paginated transparently across `process()` ticks: GDELT pages by time window (carrying the oldest `seendate` as the next window edge — a window-edge approximation, since GDELT has no deep cursor), NewsAPI pages by page number.
- An empty/blank `query` raises a clean error; an unknown `provider` lists the known ones. Upstream HTTP failures (rate limits, 5xx) surface as a clean DuckDB error.
- Missing provider fields map to `NULL`. GDELT is rate-limited (~1 request / 5s).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# News Article Search

`news_search(query, provider := ..., count := ..., timespan := ..., country := ..., language := ..., page_size := ...)` searches global news coverage and returns a single unified column set for every provider.

## Overview

Pass a free-text `query` and get back recent articles with their headline, URL, publisher domain, language, publish time, source country, sentiment tone, the originating provider, and a JSON `extra` blob of provider-specific fields. Runnable queries are attached as this function's example queries.

## Notes

- Default provider is **GDELT** (free, no API key, includes `tone`).
- **NewsAPI** requires a `TYPE newsapi` DuckDB secret holding an `api_key`; never inline a key in SQL.
- `count` caps total rows; `page_size` controls the per-request fetch size.
- GDELT enforces a ~1 request / 5 seconds rate limit and has no deep cursor, so very large look-backs are approximated at window edges.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT title, url, seendate FROM news.main.news_search('election', count := 10, timespan := '1w')

vgi.example_queries.description: Count how many domains are covering 'elections' over the last two days.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT domain, count(*) AS articles FROM news.main.news_search('elections', timespan := '2d', count := 50) GROUP BY domain ORDER BY articles DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: NewsAPI search (requires a TYPE newsapi secret with an api_key).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT title, source FROM news.main.news_search('elections', provider := 'newsapi', count := 20, timespan := '2d')

workers.doc_md:
# NFL scores, standings, and statistics

Query live and historical National Football League data from SQL.

## Data model

* **Live (ESPN):** scoreboards, standings, injuries, rosters, depth charts, and per-game box scores, drives, scoring plays, and play-by-play.
* **Analytics (nflverse, CC-BY 4.0):** schedules with lines and weather, play-by-play with EPA/WP, weekly and season player stats, team stats, snap counts, draft, combine, and Next Gen Stats.
* **Calendar (Sleeper):** the current season and week.

Data is fetched on demand, cached briefly in memory, and never rehosted. This worker is not affiliated with the NFL, ESPN, Disney, nflverse, or Sleeper.

example_queries.description: Fastest 40-yard dashes at the 2025 combine.

example_queries.description: Patrick Mahomes's 2025 passing yards by week.

example_queries.description: Kansas City's offensive starters.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, athlete_name FROM nfl.main.depth_chart('KC') WHERE depth = 1 AND formation NOT IN ('Special Teams') ORDER BY formation, position

example_queries.description: 2025 season leaders in completion percentage above expectation.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_display_name, team, attempts, completion_percentage_above_expectation FROM nfl.main.ngs_passing(season := 2025, week := 0) WHERE season_type = 'REG' ORDER BY completion_percentage_above_expectation DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Kansas City's 2025 regular season.
example_queries.sql: SELECT week, short_name, away_score, home_score, winner_abbreviation FROM nfl.main.team_schedule('KC', season := 2025) ORDER BY week

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## NFL data

Current tables answer live questions about this week's games, standings, injuries, the current week, teams, and players.

Parameterized ESPN functions take a season and week, a team abbreviation, or a game id. nflverse functions take a season with optional week and team filters and download one cached release file per call.

functions.name: play_by_play
functions.comment: Season play-by-play with EPA, win probability, and player ids (nflverse)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per play for an NFL season from nflverse (1999 onward), including expected points (ep, epa), win probability (wp, wpa), completion probability over expected (cpoe), success, down and distance, formation flags, and passer/rusher/receiver GSIS ids and names. Always pass season; add week and team (either side of the game) to limit the download-backed scan. Use play_by_play_game() for a live ESPN feed.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Curated nflverse play-by-play. The season file is downloaded once and cached in memory; filters apply before rows reach SQL. `posteam` is the offense. Join players to `players` on GSIS id.

vgi.example_queries.description: Passing EPA per dropback leaders for 2025 week 1.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT passer_player_name, count(*) AS dropbacks, round(avg(epa), 3) AS epa_per_play FROM nfl.main.play_by_play(season := 2025, week := 1) WHERE qb_dropback AND passer_player_name IS NOT NULL GROUP BY passer_player_name HAVING count(*) >= 20 ORDER BY epa_per_play DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Fourth-down attempts by Philadelphia in 2025.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT week, quarter, yards_to_go, play_type, first_down FROM nfl.main.play_by_play(season := 2025, team := 'PHI') WHERE down = 4 AND posteam = 'PHI' AND play_type IN ('run', 'pass') ORDER BY week

workers.title: National Hockey League Data
workers.tagline: NHL standings, schedules, box scores, play-by-play & player stats in DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Read-only National Hockey League standings, schedules, scores, game detail, and player and team statistics from the NHL's public web and stats APIs
workers.doc_md:
# NHL standings, games, and statistics

Query current and historical National Hockey League data directly from SQL: standings, schedules and scores, season reports for every skater, goalie, and team, official leaderboards, rosters and player careers, and per-game box scores, play-by-play, and shift charts.

## Identifiers

Seasons are 8-digit ids (`20252026` is 2025-26). `game_type` is 2 for the regular season, 3 for the playoffs, and 1 for the preseason. Game ids are 10 digits (`2025020001`) and player ids 7 digits (`8478402`); `player_search()` finds them.

## Source

All access is read-only, keyless, and on demand from NHL.com's own backends; nothing is stored or rehosted. This project is not affiliated with the NHL.

example_queries.title: opener_final_score
example_queries.description: The 2025-26 opener (game 2025020001) ended Florida 3, Chicago 2.
example_queries.sql: SELECT home_team_abbrev, home_score, away_team_abbrev, away_score FROM nhl.main.scores(date := DATE '2025-10-07') WHERE game_id = 2025020001;

example_queries.title: opener_goal_events
example_queries.description: The opener's play-by-play contains its five goals.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS goals FROM nhl.main.play_by_play(2025020001) WHERE event_type = 'goal';

example_queries.title: current_standings_have_teams
example_queries.description: Today's standings list every NHL team with a team code.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) >= 32 AND count(team_abbrev) = count(*) AS populated FROM nhl.main.current_standings;

example_queries.description: Current division tables in official order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division_name, division_rank, team_abbrev, points, games_played FROM nhl.main.current_standings ORDER BY division_name, division_rank

example_queries.description: Eastern Conference wild-card race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT wildcard_rank, team_abbrev, points, games_played FROM nhl.main.current_standings WHERE conference_name = 'Eastern' AND wildcard_rank > 0 ORDER BY wildcard_rank

example_queries.description: All NHL franchises alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT franchise_id, full_name FROM nhl.main.franchises ORDER BY full_name

example_queries.description: Every team that has played for the Avalanche/Nordiques franchise.
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.team_id, t.full_name, t.tricode FROM nhl.main.teams t JOIN nhl.main.franchises f USING (franchise_id) WHERE f.common_name = 'Avalanche'

example_queries.description: Seasons whose standings used the wild card, newest first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT season, standings_start, standings_end FROM nhl.main.standings_seasons WHERE wildcard_in_use ORDER BY season DESC

example_queries.description: Current save-percentage leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, player_name, team_abbrev, value AS save_pct FROM nhl.main.current_goalie_leaders WHERE category = 'savePctg' ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Today's scoreboard.
example_queries.sql: SELECT away_team_abbrev, away_score, home_team_abbrev, home_score, game_state, period FROM nhl.main.current_scores ORDER BY start_time_utc

example_queries.description: This week's games in start order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT game_date, start_time_utc, away_team_abbrev, home_team_abbrev, venue FROM nhl.main.current_schedule ORDER BY start_time_utc

example_queries.description: Current scoring race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, player_name, team_abbrev, value AS points FROM nhl.main.current_skater_leaders WHERE category = 'points' ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Final 2023-24 Atlantic Division table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division_rank, team_name, wins, losses, ot_losses, points FROM nhl.main.standings(date := DATE '2024-04-18') WHERE division_name = 'Atlantic' ORDER BY division_rank

example_queries.description: Toronto's 2025-26 regular-season home results.
example_queries.sql: SELECT game_date, away_team_abbrev, away_score, home_score FROM nhl.main.team_schedule('TOR', season := 20252026) WHERE game_type = 2 AND home_team_abbrev = 'TOR' ORDER BY game_date

example_queries.description: The 2025-26 regular-season scoring leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, team_abbrevs, games_played, goals, assists, points FROM nhl.main.skater_stats(season := 20252026) ORDER BY points DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: 2025-26 playoff goal leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, team_abbrevs, goals FROM nhl.main.skater_stats(season := 20252026, game_type := 3) ORDER BY goals DESC LIMIT 10

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## NHL analytical data

Rows are explicitly team-, game-, player-, player-season-, player-game-, event-, or shift-grain. Current tables reflect today; functions take seasons, dates, team codes, player ids, or game ids.

Reference tables (`teams`, `franchises`, `standings_seasons`) supply the identifiers the functions accept. Percentages are 0-1 fractions and times on ice come both as MM:SS text and as integer seconds.

arguments.description: Stable 7-digit NHL player id, such as 8478402 (find one with player_search()).

arguments.name: game_type
arguments.description: NHL game type: 2 regular season (default), 3 playoffs, or 1 preseason.

arguments.name: season
arguments.description: 8-digit NHL season id such as 20252026 for 2025-26. NULL selects the current season.

examples: SELECT game_date, opponent_abbrev, goals, assists, points, toi FROM nhl.main.player_game_log(8478402, season := 20252026) WHERE points >= 2 ORDER BY game_date

workers.title: Classical NLP
workers.tagline: Classical NLP — NER, sentiment, language detection & lemmatization for DuckDB (Python, spaCy)
workers.summary: Classical NLP (spaCy + fastText + VADER): language ID, sentiment, NER, tokenization for SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# Classical NLP for DuckDB SQL

![spaCy logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/88/SpaCy_logo.svg)

Run **classical natural language processing in SQL** -- language detection, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition (NER), lemmatization, and tokenization -- directly over your text columns in DuckDB, with no LLM and no API key required. This worker turns the proven open-source NLP stack of [spaCy](https://spacy.io), [fastText](https://fasttext.cc/), and [VADER](https://github.com/cjhutto/vaderSentiment) into fast, deterministic SQL functions for bulk, cheap, per-row text enrichment.

## Who it is for

Data engineers and analysts who want to enrich large text tables -- product reviews, support tickets, articles, social posts -- without leaving SQL or paying per token. Because the underlying models are rule- and statistics-based rather than generative, output is reproducible and runs at column scale -- ideal *upstream* of, not as a replacement for, LLM workers.

## Key concepts

- **Models load once per worker process and are cached**, so the one-time model-load cost is amortized across every row of every query.
- **Language identification** uses Facebook's [fastText lid.176](https://fasttext.cc/docs/en/language-identification.html) model (176 languages). When you do not pin a language, each row is routed to the matching language pipeline automatically.
- **Sentiment** uses the lexicon-and-rule-based VADER scorer, tuned for English and social media text; it understands negation, intensifiers, and emoji.
- **Linguistic analysis** -- structured span extraction, part-of-speech tagging, sentence boundaries, noun-phrase mining, lemmatization, and Unicode normalization -- uses spaCy's small English pipeline (`en_core_web_sm`) by default; pin a language or name a specific model to override it.

## When to reach for it

Use it whenever you need to enrich or filter free text at scale in SQL: detect and segment multilingual corpora, score or bucket opinion, clean and canonicalize text so free-text keys join and group reliably, or split documents into structured rows you can aggregate and join back to their source. Attach the worker, then call the functions directly from SQL -- `nlp.main.detect_lang(body)`, `nlp.main.sentiment(body)`, or `nlp.main.entities((SELECT id, body FROM docs), id := 'id')`:

```sql
INSTALL vgi FROM community;
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'nlp' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run nlp_worker.py');
```

Powered by spaCy ([source](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy) - [docs](https://spacy.io/usage)), fastText ([source](https://github.com/facebookresearch/fastText) - [docs](https://fasttext.cc/docs/en/language-identification.html)), and VADER ([source & docs](https://github.com/cjhutto/vaderSentiment)). Source for this worker: [Query-farm/vgi-nlp](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-nlp).

example_queries.description: Detect the language of a French string.
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang('Bonjour tout le monde') AS lang

example_queries.description: Score the sentiment of a positive English review.
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.sentiment('I absolutely love this product!') AS score

example_queries.description: Bucket a review into a neg/neu/pos sentiment label.
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.sentiment_label('This was a terrible experience') AS mood

example_queries.description: Lemmatize an English string with the language pinned.
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.lemmatize('The cats were running', 'en') AS lemmas

example_queries.description: Canonicalize a messy string for dedup/matching.
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.normalize('  Café   DELUXE  ') AS canonical

example_queries.description: Extract named entities from a literal document, keyed back to its id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, ent_text, label FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Apple is based in California.' AS body), id := 'id', lang := 'en')

example_queries.description: Count the languages that have a default spaCy pipeline.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n_languages FROM nlp.main.supported_languages

example_queries.description: Look up the default spaCy model for English.
example_queries.sql: SELECT spacy_model FROM nlp.main.supported_languages WHERE lang_code = 'en'

example_queries.description: Count the languages that have a default spaCy pipeline
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n_languages FROM nlp.main.supported_languages()

example_queries.description: Look up the default spaCy model for English
example_queries.sql: SELECT spacy_model FROM nlp.main.supported_languages() WHERE lang_code = 'en'

example_queries.description: Explode a literal English document into tokens, projecting its key columns
example_queries.sql: SELECT token, pos FROM nlp.main.tokens((SELECT 'The quick brown fox jumps.' AS body), lang := 'en')

example_queries.description: Explode a literal English document into sentences, projecting its key columns
example_queries.sql: SELECT sent_index, sentence FROM nlp.main.sentences((SELECT 'First sentence here. Second one follows.' AS body), lang := 'en')

example_queries.description: Explode a literal English document into noun_chunks, projecting its key columns
example_queries.sql: SELECT chunk, root FROM nlp.main.noun_chunks((SELECT 'The big red car drove down the long road.' AS body), lang := 'en')

example_queries.description: Explode a literal English document into entities, projecting its key columns
example_queries.sql: SELECT ent_text, label FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT 'Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in California.' AS body), lang := 'en')

example_queries.description: Extract named entities from a literal document, keyed back to its id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, ent_text, label FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in California.' AS body), id := 'id', lang := 'en');

example_queries.description: Tokenize a literal document with part-of-speech tags, keyed back to its id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, token, pos FROM nlp.main.tokens((SELECT 1 AS id, 'The quick brown fox jumps.' AS body), id := 'id', lang := 'en');

example_queries.description: Split a literal document into sentences, keyed back to its id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, sent_index, sentence FROM nlp.main.sentences((SELECT 1 AS id, 'First sentence here. Second one follows.' AS body), id := 'id', lang := 'en');

example_queries.description: Extract noun chunks from a literal document, keyed back to its id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, chunk, root FROM nlp.main.noun_chunks((SELECT 1 AS id, 'The big red car drove down the long road.' AS body), id := 'id', lang := 'en');

example_queries.description: Score the sentiment of a literal English string
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.sentiment('I absolutely love this, it is fantastic!') AS score

example_queries.description: Identify the language of a literal string
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog') AS lang

example_queries.description: Confidence of the top language guess for a literal string
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang_conf('The quick brown fox') AS conf

example_queries.description: Drop stop-words from a literal string with per-row auto-detect
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.strip_stopwords('this is a really great movie') AS kept

example_queries.description: Drop English stop-words from a literal string
example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.strip_stopwords('this is a really great movie', 'en') AS kept

example_queries.description: Drop stop-words from a literal string with an explicit spaCy model

agent_tasks: Identify the language of the text 'Bonjour tout le monde, comment allez-vous aujourd''hui?' and return its two-letter ISO-639 language code in a column named lang.

Decide whether the language detector is highly confident (more than 90%) that the text 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' is English. Return a single boolean column named confident_english that is true only when the detected ISO-639 code is 'en' and the detection confidence exceeds 0.9.

Decide whether the sentence 'I absolutely love this product, it works wonderfully!' expresses positive sentiment. Using the compound sentiment score, return a single boolean column named is_positive that is true when the score is above the standard positive threshold of 0.05.
Classify the sentiment of the sentence 'This is the worst experience I have ever had' into a coarse label of negative, neutral, or positive, and return the label in a column named mood.
Produce a canonical, comparable form of the string '  Cafe   DELUXE  ' by applying Unicode normalization, lowercasing, and collapsing runs of whitespace. Return it in a column named canonical.

Lemmatize the English sentence 'The cats were running quickly', reducing each word to its dictionary base form. Decide whether the lemmatized result contains the base form 'run'. Return a single boolean column named has_run. Treat the text as English.

Remove English stop-words and punctuation from the sentence 'this is a really great movie'. Decide whether the content word 'great' survives the stop-word removal. Return a single boolean column named keeps_great. Treat the text as English.
Decide whether the sentence 'Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in California.' contains at least two named entities. Treat the text as English. Return a single boolean column named has_entities.

Tokenize the English sentence 'The quick brown fox jumps.' into individual tokens with part-of-speech tags. Decide whether it yields more than three tokens. Treat the text as English. Return a single boolean column named many_tokens.

Split the text 'First sentence here. Second one follows.' into sentences and decide whether it contains exactly two sentences. Treat the text as English. Return a single boolean column named two_sentences.

Extract the base noun phrases (noun chunks) from the English sentence 'The big red car drove down the long road.' and decide whether it yields at least two noun chunks. Treat the text as English. Return a single boolean column named has_chunks.

Determine whether this worker has a default spaCy pipeline for English (ISO-639 code 'en'), i.e. whether English text can be lemmatized and run through NER without naming a custom model. Return a single boolean column named supported.

# main

Classical NLP functions exposed to SQL.

- **Scalars:** language ID/confidence, sentiment score/label, lemmatize, strip stop-words, normalize.
- **Table functions:** entities, tokens, sentences, noun_chunks (one text row in, N rows out, with an optional `id :=` passthrough).

tables.name: supported_languages
tables.comment: Languages with a default spaCy pipeline: (lang_code, spacy_model) -- discovery table.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `supported_languages` (table)

One row per language that has a default spaCy pipeline, so the extraction table functions and the `lemmatize` / `strip_stopwords` scalars can process it without naming a model. Columns:

- `lang_code` (`VARCHAR`, primary key) -- the ISO-639 code you pass as the `lang` argument (or that per-row auto-detect must resolve to).
- `spacy_model` (`VARCHAR`) -- the default small spaCy pipeline that backs it.

Read this table directly to discover which languages can be lemmatized, tokenized, or run through NER. Note `detect_lang` recognizes far more languages (fastText covers 176) than have a spaCy pipeline installed -- this table lists only the latter. Backed by the identically-named table function, so the rows are identical.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `supported_languages`

Discovery table of every language the worker has a default spaCy pipeline for, exposed as a regular table you can read without parentheses.

## Columns

- `lang_code` (`VARCHAR`, primary key) -- ISO-639 code accepted by the `lang` argument.
- `spacy_model` (`VARCHAR`) -- the default small spaCy model backing it.

Language detection (`detect_lang`) spans 176 languages via fastText, but only the languages listed here can be lemmatized, tokenized, or run through NER without naming a custom model.

vgi.example_queries.description: Count the languages that have a default spaCy pipeline.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n_languages FROM nlp.main.supported_languages

vgi.example_queries.description: Look up the default spaCy model for English.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT spacy_model FROM nlp.main.supported_languages WHERE lang_code = 'en'

functions.name: tokens
functions.comment: Tokens per text row: (id, token, lemma, pos, tag, is_stop, dep)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Tokenization plus linguistic annotation as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per token**, each carrying its lemma, part-of-speech, fine-grained tag, stop-word flag, and dependency relation from the spaCy pipeline.

**When to use:** linguistic analysis, building token-level features, counting parts of speech, or filtering to content words -- anything that needs the words of a document as queryable rows.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key; `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(token, lemma, pos, tag, is_stop, dep)` plus the optional id. Output order is not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY` for determinism.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# tokens

Tokenizes a text column with spaCy and emits one row per token with rich annotations. Pass the input relation positionally; `id :=` names the join key copied onto every token row, and `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each row gives the token text, its lemma, coarse and fine POS tags, a stop-word flag, and its dependency label. Filter on `is_stop` or `pos` to isolate content words; use `id :=` to join tokens back to their source document.

vgi.example_queries.description: Explode a literal English document into tokens, projecting its key columns
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT token, pos FROM nlp.main.tokens((SELECT 'The quick brown fox jumps.' AS body), lang := 'en')

functions.name: sentences
functions.comment: Sentences per text row: (id, sent_index, sentence) -- chunking for embeddings

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Sentence segmentation as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per sentence**, in document order, with a 0-based index.

**When to use:** chunk long documents into sentence-sized units before embedding/retrieval, sentence-level sentiment, or any per-sentence analysis.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key copied onto every sentence row; `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(sent_index, sentence)` plus the optional id. The `sent_index` preserves order; output row order across documents is otherwise not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY id, sent_index` for determinism.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# sentences

Splits a text column into sentences with spaCy, emitting one indexed row per sentence. Pass the input relation positionally; `id :=` names the join key copied onto every sentence row, and `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each row carries the 0-based `sent_index` and the trimmed sentence text. This is the standard first step for sentence-level embeddings or retrieval chunking; use `id :=` to keep sentences tied to their source document, and order by `id, sent_index` for determinism.
