functions.name: elevation
functions.comment: Terrain elevation (90m DEM) for a coordinate (Open-Meteo elevation).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Terrain elevation for a coordinate, from Open-Meteo's 90 m digital elevation model. Supply latitude/longitude in WGS84 degrees; it returns a single row echoing the requested coordinate plus its `elevation` in metres above sea level. Use it for altitude lookups or to enrich a coordinate before charting weather against terrain height. If you have a place name rather than a coordinate, join `geocoding(...)` in front of it — both arguments take column references, so name → elevation is one query.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## elevation

Terrain elevation (metres above sea level) for a coordinate, sampled from a 90 m digital elevation model (Copernicus DEM).

Returns exactly one row per coordinate: the requested `latitude` and `longitude` echoed back, plus `elevation`. `elevation` is null where the model has no value for the point (open ocean, for instance). Coordinates may come from a column, and the endpoint takes them in batches of 100, so resolving a whole table of points costs one request per 100 rows rather than one per row.

Place names go through `geocoding(...)` first; because its output columns can feed these arguments directly, that is still a single query — one request resolves the name, one resolves the height.

vgi.example_queries.description: Terrain elevation at Berlin (metres).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT elevation FROM open_meteo.main.elevation(52.52, 13.41)

vgi.example_queries.description: Near the summit of Everest.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT latitude, longitude, elevation FROM open_meteo.main.elevation(27.99, 86.93)

vgi.example_queries.description: Elevation for a whole table of coordinates in one correlated join.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.name, e.elevation FROM (VALUES ('Berlin', 52.52, 13.41), ('Everest', 27.99, 86.93)) AS c(name, lat, lon), LATERAL open_meteo.main.elevation(c.lat, c.lon) AS e

vgi.example_queries.description: Elevation for a place looked up by name rather than by coordinate.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, e.elevation FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Denver', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.elevation(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS e

vgi.example_queries.description: Rank a column of place names by terrain height, geocoding each one.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.city, e.elevation FROM (VALUES ('Denver'), ('La Paz'), ('Amsterdam')) AS p(city), LATERAL open_meteo.main.geocoding(p.city, count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.elevation(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS e ORDER BY e.elevation DESC

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Point weather query returning daily values from the Open-Meteo API. Daily ensemble maximum temperature: control run plus up to 30 perturbed members. Supply latitude and longitude in WGS84 degrees; it returns one row per day, with the `time` column always emitted in UTC. Notes: the window is set with forecast_days / past_days; units are configurable (temperature_unit, wind_speed_unit, precipitation_unit); specific models can be selected with the models argument; timezone only shifts where the window starts and how daily buckets are aligned — instants stay UTC; use timezone := 'auto' to resolve the zone from each row's coordinates; the provider holds one UTC offset across a response. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## ensemble_daily

Daily ensemble maximum temperature: control run plus up to 30 perturbed members.

Pass `latitude` and `longitude` in WGS84 degrees. The function returns one row per day; every timestamp is emitted in UTC. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## forecast_current

Current weather conditions for a coordinate.

Pass `latitude` and `longitude` in WGS84 degrees. The function returns a single row with the most recent values; every timestamp is emitted in UTC. Notes: units are configurable (temperature_unit, wind_speed_unit, precipitation_unit); select one model with model; model_selection records that request, while retrieved_at records response retrieval, not forecast issuance; timezone changes response context; weather instants remain UTC.

If you have a place name rather than a coordinate, resolve it with `geocoding(...)` and join its `latitude`/`longitude` straight in — the positional arguments take column references, so name → weather stays one query.

Returned columns are `time` plus `temperature_2m`, `relative_humidity_2m`, `apparent_temperature` and more — see the result schema for the full set with types. Decode the `weather_code` column with the `weather_code_text` / `weather_code_emoji` macros. Runnable queries live in this function's example queries rather than inline here.

vgi.example_queries.description: Current weather conditions for a coordinate (Berlin).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, temperature_2m, relative_humidity_2m FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

vgi.example_queries.description: Imperial units (°F, mph).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, temperature_2m, relative_humidity_2m FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41, temperature_unit := 'fahrenheit', wind_speed_unit := 'mph')

vgi.example_queries.description: Select a model explicitly and inspect the response provenance. Retrieval time does not identify the forecast run.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, temperature_2m, relative_humidity_2m, model_selection, grid_latitude, grid_longitude, retrieved_at FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41, model := 'gfs_global')

vgi.example_queries.description: Many locations in one query — coordinates supplied by a column.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.city, w.time, w.temperature_2m FROM (VALUES ('Berlin', 52.52, 13.41), ('Tokyo', 35.69, 139.69)) AS c(city, lat, lon), LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(c.lat, c.lon) AS w

vgi.example_queries.description: Current weather conditions for a coordinate, starting from the place name 'Berlin' instead of a coordinate.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, w.time, w.temperature_2m FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Berlin', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w

vgi.semantic_entity.description: Latest modeled conditions, normally based on 15-minute data which may be interpolated. The provider supplies the current aggregation duration. Select snapshot values directly; there are no period aggregates.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Invocation row key
vgi.semantic_members.description: Row identity within one coordinate invocation. Driving location identifiers remain part of correlated query grain.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Requested latitude
vgi.semantic_members.description: Requested WGS84 latitude in degrees north, retained per input location. This is not the provider's grid-cell coordinate.

vgi.semantic_members.description: Requested WGS84 longitude in degrees east, retained per input location. Use the driving site's identifier to distinguish sites sharing coordinates.

vgi.semantic_members.description: UTC valid time of the current model estimate. This is not a station observation or a forecast issue time.

vgi.semantic_members.description: Whether the location is in daylight at the current valid time.

vgi.semantic_members.description: Total precipitation water equivalent over the preceding interval_seconds (normally 15 minutes). Bounds come from the provider's current.interval; modeled values may be interpolated.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Current wind speed (10 m)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Current modeled wind speed at 10 metres, distinct from gust speed.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Current wind direction (10 m)

vgi.semantic_members.title: Current modeled gust (10 m)

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## climate_daily

Daily downscaled climate-change projections (1950→2050) for a coordinate.

Pass `latitude` and `longitude` in WGS84 degrees. The function returns one row per day; every timestamp is emitted in UTC. Notes: a start_date/end_date range is required (yyyy-mm-dd); specific models can be selected with the models argument; timezone only shifts where the window starts and how daily buckets are aligned — instants stay UTC; use timezone := 'auto' to resolve the zone from each row's coordinates; the provider holds one UTC offset across a response.

If you have a place name rather than a coordinate, resolve it with `geocoding(...)` and join its `latitude`/`longitude` straight in — the positional arguments take column references, so name → weather stays one query.

Returned columns are `time` and the calendar `date` plus `temperature_2m_max`, `temperature_2m_min`, `temperature_2m_mean` and more — see the result schema for the full set with types. Runnable queries live in this function's example queries rather than inline here.

vgi.example_queries.description: Daily downscaled climate-change projections (1950→2050) for a coordinate over an explicit date range (Berlin).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT date, temperature_2m_max, temperature_2m_min FROM open_meteo.main.climate_daily(52.52, 13.41, '2024-06-01', '2024-06-07') ORDER BY date

vgi.example_queries.description: Pick specific downscaled climate models.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## forecast_daily

Daily weather forecast (up to 16 days) for a coordinate.

Pass `latitude` and `longitude` in WGS84 degrees. The function returns one row per day; every timestamp is emitted in UTC. Notes: the window is set with forecast_days / past_days; units are configurable (temperature_unit, wind_speed_unit, precipitation_unit); select one model with model; model_selection records that request, while retrieved_at records response retrieval, not forecast issuance; timezone only shifts where the window starts and how daily buckets are aligned — instants stay UTC; use timezone := 'auto' to resolve the zone from each row's coordinates; the provider holds one UTC offset across a response.

If you have a place name rather than a coordinate, resolve it with `geocoding(...)` and join its `latitude`/`longitude` straight in — the positional arguments take column references, so name → weather stays one query.

Returned columns are `time` and the calendar `date` plus `weather_code`, `temperature_2m_max`, `temperature_2m_min` and more — see the result schema for the full set with types. Decode the `weather_code` column with the `weather_code_text` / `weather_code_emoji` macros. Runnable queries live in this function's example queries rather than inline here.

vgi.semantic_entity.title: Daily forecast
vgi.semantic_entity.description: All returned daily fields. Dates follow the provider's fixed-offset intervals in the requested zone (auto by default), which may differ from civil days across DST changes. Select date for daily results or omit it for a period summary.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Invocation row key
vgi.semantic_members.description: Row identity within one coordinate invocation. Driving location identifiers remain part of correlated query grain.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Requested latitude
vgi.semantic_members.description: Requested WGS84 latitude in degrees north, retained per input location. This is not the provider's grid-cell coordinate.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Requested longitude
vgi.semantic_members.description: Requested WGS84 longitude in degrees east, retained per input location. Use the driving site's identifier to distinguish sites sharing coordinates.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily interval start (UTC)
vgi.semantic_members.description: UTC start instant of the provider's daily interval. Select date for the provider's calendar label; this instant is not a UTC-day aggregate.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Date in requested zone
vgi.semantic_members.description: Calendar label of the provider's daily interval in the requested zone (auto by default). The API holds one UTC offset across the response; intervals crossing a DST transition may differ from civil calendar days.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily weather condition code
vgi.semantic_members.description: Most severe WMO condition in the provider's daily interval. Follow weather_codes for readable conditions; do not average these codes.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily high temperature (2 m)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Maximum air temperature in the provider's daily interval.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily low temperature (2 m)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Minimum air temperature in the provider's daily interval.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily high feels-like temperature
vgi.semantic_members.description: Maximum apparent temperature in the provider's daily interval.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily low feels-like temperature
vgi.semantic_members.description: Minimum apparent temperature in the provider's daily interval.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Sunrise (UTC)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Sunrise instant for the provider's date, in UTC. May be unavailable during polar day or night.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Sunset (UTC)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Sunset instant for the provider's date, in UTC. May be unavailable during polar day or night.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily precipitation (water equivalent)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Total rain, showers and snowfall water equivalent in the provider's daily interval.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily new snowfall depth
vgi.semantic_members.description: Total new snowfall depth in the provider's daily interval; not water equivalent or final snowpack depth.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Hours with precipitation
vgi.semantic_members.description: Provider count of wet hourly intervals in this day. This is not an exact duration of rainfall, and includes precipitation other than rain.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily maximum wind speed (10 m)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Maximum wind speed at 10 metres in the provider's daily interval.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily strongest gust (10 m)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Maximum wind gust at 10 metres in the provider's daily interval.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily dominant wind direction (10 m)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Provider's dominant wind direction, FROM which wind blows, clockwise from north. Do not compute arithmetic averages of angles.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily solar energy
vgi.semantic_members.description: Global shortwave solar energy on a horizontal surface (direct plus diffuse) in the provider's daily interval. Energy (MJ/m²), not irradiance (W/m²).

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily large-scale rain
vgi.semantic_members.description: Large-scale rain in the provider's daily interval. Convective showers are separate; use precipitation_sum for all precipitation types.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Highest daily high
vgi.semantic_members.description: Highest available daily high in the selected period at each location.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Lowest daily low
vgi.semantic_members.description: Lowest available daily low in the selected period at each location.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Total precipitation
vgi.semantic_members.description: Sum of available daily water-equivalent precipitation amounts at each location. Missing days are excluded, not dry; not a regional total across sites.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Total new snowfall depth
vgi.semantic_members.description: Sum of new snowfall depths over selected days at each location, not final snowpack depth.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Total hours with precipitation
vgi.semantic_members.description: Sum of provider wet-hour counts over selected days at each location, not exact rain duration.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Strongest wind gust
vgi.semantic_members.description: Strongest reported daily gust in the selected period at each location.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Days with any reported precipitation
vgi.semantic_members.description: Count of days with reported precipitation greater than zero. Missing values are excluded. This is not a climatological wet-day index with a fixed millimetre threshold.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Daily precipitation samples available
vgi.semantic_members.description: Count of days with a precipitation amount, including zero. Other variables may have different coverage.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Days with both temperature extremes
vgi.semantic_members.description: Count of days where both high and low temperature are available. This does not establish coverage of other variables.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Requested model selection
vgi.semantic_members.description: Requested model selector, or provider_default where model selection is unavailable. best_match may combine models. Even an explicit selector does not identify the source of every derived field, such as precipitation probability.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Source API product
vgi.semantic_members.description: Public API product URL, without query parameters or credentials. Commercial requests use the corresponding customer host.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Response retrieved at (UTC)
vgi.semantic_members.description: When this worker received the upstream JSON response. Preserved on worker-cache hits. This is not a model run time, issue time or data freshness guarantee.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Returned grid latitude
vgi.semantic_members.description: Provider-returned grid latitude, which may differ from the requested location. It does not identify every component grid in blended or derived data.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Returned grid longitude
vgi.semantic_members.description: Provider-returned grid longitude, which may differ from the requested location.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Downscaling elevation
vgi.semantic_members.description: Provider-returned target elevation used for location selection and downscaling, where supplied. This is not necessarily the raw model-grid elevation.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Resolved response timezone
vgi.semantic_members.description: Timezone identifier returned by the provider. Timestamps remain UTC instants; the response UTC offset labels provider daily intervals.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Response UTC offset
vgi.semantic_members.description: Provider's fixed UTC offset for this response. It is not recomputed for DST transitions within the response.

vgi.semantic_members.title: Aggregation interval start (UTC)
vgi.semantic_members.description: Start of the row's nominal aggregation window. Applies only to fields assigned this window in open_meteo.temporal metadata; instantaneous values use time instead.

vgi.semantic_members.description: End of the row's nominal aggregation window. Hourly/current accumulation windows end at time; daily windows start at time. Source-dependent fields have no asserted common window.

vgi.semantic_members.description: Length of the nominal aggregation window: 3600 seconds hourly, 86400 seconds for a provider day, or the provider's current.interval. Unknown current intervals stay NULL. This is not the native model resolution.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## air_quality_hourly

Hourly air-quality (pollutants + AQI) forecast for a coordinate.

Pass `latitude` and `longitude` in WGS84 degrees. The function returns one row per hour; every timestamp is emitted in UTC. Notes: the window is set with forecast_days / past_days; timezone only shifts where the window starts and how daily buckets are aligned — instants stay UTC; use timezone := 'auto' to resolve the zone from each row's coordinates; the provider holds one UTC offset across a response.

If you have a place name rather than a coordinate, resolve it with `geocoding(...)` and join its `latitude`/`longitude` straight in — the positional arguments take column references, so name → weather stays one query.

Returned columns are `time` plus `pm10`, `pm2_5`, `carbon_monoxide` and more — see the result schema for the full set with types. Runnable queries live in this function's example queries rather than inline here.

## air_quality_current

Current air-quality (pollutants + AQI) for a coordinate.

Pass `latitude` and `longitude` in WGS84 degrees. The function returns a single row with the most recent values; every timestamp is emitted in UTC. Notes: timezone changes response context; weather instants remain UTC.

If you have a place name rather than a coordinate, resolve it with `geocoding(...)` and join its `latitude`/`longitude` straight in — the positional arguments take column references, so name → weather stays one query.

functions.name: european_aqi_category
functions.comment: Bucket a European AQI value into its CAMS band (e.g. 75 → 'Poor').

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Buckets a European Air Quality Index value (the european_aqi column from air_quality_* functions) into its CAMS band: Good, Fair, Moderate, Poor, Very Poor, or Extremely Poor. The European scale differs from the US one, so use the matching macro. NULL in, NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## european_aqi_category

Maps a European AQI number to its CAMS band (distinct from the US scale). Apply it to the `european_aqi` column of an air_quality function; see this macro's example queries for a runnable form.

vgi.example_queries.description: European AQI band for current conditions in Berlin.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT european_aqi, open_meteo.main.european_aqi_category(european_aqi) AS band FROM open_meteo.main.air_quality_current(52.52, 13.41)

vgi.example_queries.description: Rank named European cities by their current AQI band.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.city, a.european_aqi, open_meteo.main.european_aqi_category(a.european_aqi) AS band FROM (VALUES ('Berlin'), ('Milan'), ('Warsaw')) AS p(city), LATERAL open_meteo.main.geocoding(p.city, count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.air_quality_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS a ORDER BY a.european_aqi DESC

arguments.name: aqi
arguments.description: European Air Quality Index value from an air_quality function (european_aqi column).

examples: SELECT european_aqi, open_meteo.main.european_aqi_category(european_aqi) AS band FROM open_meteo.main.air_quality_current(52.52, 13.41)

SELECT p.city, a.european_aqi, open_meteo.main.european_aqi_category(a.european_aqi) AS band FROM (VALUES ('Berlin'), ('Milan'), ('Warsaw')) AS p(city), LATERAL open_meteo.main.geocoding(p.city, count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.air_quality_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS a ORDER BY a.european_aqi DESC
functions.macro_definition: CASE  WHEN ((aqi IS NULL)) THEN (NULL) WHEN ((aqi <= 20)) THEN ('Good') WHEN ((aqi <= 40)) THEN ('Fair') WHEN ((aqi <= 60)) THEN ('Moderate') WHEN ((aqi <= 80)) THEN ('Poor') WHEN ((aqi <= 100)) THEN ('Very Poor') ELSE 'Extremely Poor' END

functions.name: uv_index_category

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## uv_index_category

Maps a UV index number to its WHO exposure-risk category. Apply it to the `uv_index` column of a forecast or air_quality function; see this macro's example queries for a runnable form.

vgi.example_queries.description: UV-index risk category over the next day of hourly forecast.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, uv_index, open_meteo.main.uv_index_category(uv_index) AS risk FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_hourly(52.52, 13.41, forecast_days := 1) ORDER BY time

arguments.name: uv
arguments.description: UV index value from a forecast or air_quality function (uv_index column).

examples: SELECT time, uv_index, open_meteo.main.uv_index_category(uv_index) AS risk FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_hourly(52.52, 13.41, forecast_days := 1) ORDER BY time

SELECT w.time, w.uv_index, open_meteo.main.uv_index_category(w.uv_index) AS risk FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Nairobi', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_hourly(g.latitude, g.longitude, forecast_days := 1) AS w ORDER BY w.uv_index DESC LIMIT 5

functions.name: weather_code_text
functions.comment: Translate a WMO weather_code into an English description (e.g. 61 → 'Slight rain').

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Maps a WMO 4677 weather_code (the raw number returned by forecast_* and historical_* functions) to a short English description such as 'Clear sky', 'Slight rain' or 'Thunderstorm with heavy hail'. Expands inline as SQL — no round-trip. Unknown codes return 'Unknown (<code>)'.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## weather_code_text

Turns the raw WMO `weather_code` (an integer) into an English description. Apply it to the `weather_code` column of any forecast or historical function; see this macro's example queries for a runnable form.

vgi.example_queries.description: Decode the current weather code to text.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT weather_code, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

vgi.example_queries.description: Same, starting from a place name: geocode, then decode.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(w.weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Lisbon', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w

arguments.name: code
arguments.description: WMO weather-interpretation code from a forecast/historical function.

examples: SELECT weather_code, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

SELECT g.name, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(w.weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Lisbon', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w
functions.macro_definition: CASE  WHEN ((code = 0)) THEN ('Clear sky') WHEN ((code = 1)) THEN ('Mainly clear') WHEN ((code = 2)) THEN ('Partly cloudy') WHEN ((code = 3)) THEN ('Overcast') WHEN ((code = 45)) THEN ('Fog') WHEN ((code = 48)) THEN ('Depositing rime fog') WHEN ((code = 51)) THEN ('Light drizzle') WHEN ((code = 53)) THEN ('Moderate drizzle') WHEN ((code = 55)) THEN ('Dense drizzle') WHEN ((code = 56)) THEN ('Light freezing drizzle') WHEN ((code = 57)) THEN ('Dense freezing drizzle') WHEN ((code = 61)) THEN ('Slight rain') WHEN ((code = 63)) THEN ('Moderate rain') WHEN ((code = 65)) THEN ('Heavy rain') WHEN ((code = 66)) THEN ('Light freezing rain') WHEN ((code = 67)) THEN ('Heavy freezing rain') WHEN ((code = 71)) THEN ('Slight snowfall') WHEN ((code = 73)) THEN ('Moderate snowfall') WHEN ((code = 75)) THEN ('Heavy snowfall') WHEN ((code = 77)) THEN ('Snow grains') WHEN ((code = 80)) THEN ('Slight rain showers') WHEN ((code = 81)) THEN ('Moderate rain showers') WHEN ((code = 82)) THEN ('Violent rain showers') WHEN ((code = 85)) THEN ('Slight snow showers') WHEN ((code = 86)) THEN ('Heavy snow showers') WHEN ((code = 95)) THEN ('Thunderstorm') WHEN ((code = 96)) THEN ('Thunderstorm with slight hail') WHEN ((code = 99)) THEN ('Thunderstorm with heavy hail') ELSE (('Unknown (' || code) || ')') END

workers.title: OR-Tools Optimization
workers.tagline: Constraint solving & optimization in DuckDB with SQL — CP-SAT, vehicle routing (VRP/TSP), assignment, scheduling, flows, knapsack and bin-packing via Google OR-Tools. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: Google OR-Tools optimization / constraint solving as SQL functions.
workers.doc_md:
# Optimization & Constraint Solving in SQL (Google OR-Tools)

**Prescriptive compute inside DuckDB: constraint programming, vehicle routing, scheduling, assignment, network flow, and packing as plain SQL functions.**

This catalog turns [Google OR-Tools](https://developers.google.com/optimization) into DuckDB table and scalar functions, so an operations, logistics, or planning team that already lives in DuckDB can solve optimization problems next to their data instead of standing up a separate Python optimization microservice with its own deploy, data copy, and ETL round-trip.

## When to reach for it

Use it when a question is a *decision* problem rather than an aggregation -- matching supply to demand at least cost, sequencing work under precedence and resource limits, routing a fleet under capacity and time windows, maximizing the throughput of a network, or any hand-built constraint model mixing the global constraints (all-different, no-overlap, cumulative, circuit) that LP/MIP solvers such as the community `highs` extension stop short of. It is the decision-making complement to the predictive ML workers.

## How it works

Build the cost, distance, demand, or capacity matrices using ordinary SQL joins and `array_agg`, hand them to a solver as integer list arguments (OR-Tools is an integer engine -- scale fractional data first), and get the optimal or best-found solution back as rows you can join straight back into the warehouse. Every solver returns a `status` column, and a problem with no solution returns exactly one status row rather than an empty result.

## Data residency

The worker makes **no outbound network calls** -- pure local CPU, no API keys, no rate limits, no data egress. Your problem instances never leave the box. OR-Tools is Apache-2.0; the worker is MIT.

example_queries.description: Least-cost assignment of three workers to three tasks (returns each worker's chosen task and its cost).
example_queries.sql: SELECT worker, task, cost FROM ortools.main.solve_assignment(cost := [[0,0,90],[0,1,76],[0,2,75],[1,0,35],[1,1,85],[1,2,55],[2,0,125],[2,1,95],[2,2,90]]::BIGINT[][], maximize := false) ORDER BY worker

example_queries.description: Optimal travelling-salesperson tour over a 5-node distance matrix, in visit order.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Optimization and constraint-solving table and scalar functions backed by Google OR-Tools, organized into constraint programming, routing, assignment, scheduling, network flow, packing, and introspection categories.

Problems are passed as scalar integer list arguments built by `array_agg`, or -- for the general constraint solver -- as a versioned JSON model. Every solver returns a `status` column, and an unsolved problem yields exactly one status row rather than an empty result.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## OR-Tools Solvers

Prescriptive optimization and constraint-solving functions backed by Google OR-Tools, covering:

- **Constraint programming** -- a general CP-SAT model expressed as versioned JSON
- **Routing** -- shortest tours and capacitated, time-windowed vehicle routing
- **Assignment** -- least-cost matching of workers to tasks
- **Scheduling** -- job-shop and resource-constrained project scheduling
- **Network flow** -- minimum-cost and maximum flow
- **Packing** -- knapsack and bin packing
- **Introspection** -- solver versions and last-solve statistics

Every solver takes its problem as scalar integer list arguments (or a JSON model) and returns rows carrying a `status` column; a problem with no solution yields a single status row, never an empty result.

This is per-process, not strictly per-connection -- the authoritative, race-free source is the metadata columns on each solver's own result rows.

## last_solve_stats

A browsable table of the most recent solve's metrics, one row per metric: `status`, `objective`, `best_bound`, `wall_time`, `num_branches`, `num_conflicts`, `num_booleans`, `deterministic_time`. Scan it after a solve; every `value` is NULL until the first solve runs. It reflects the last solve on this worker *process*, so for a race-free per-query value prefer the metadata columns on the solver's own result rows.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_tsp`

Find the **shortest single-vehicle tour** that visits every node once and returns to `start`, over a distance matrix.

**Inputs.** `distance` is either sparse `[from, to, meters]` integer triples (build with `array_agg([f, t, m])`) or a dense `n x n` matrix; `start` is the depot node. **Outputs.** The tour in visit order: `seq`, `node`, `arrival` (cumulative distance), `status`. The tour rotation / direction may vary but the length is optimal.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_rcpsp`

Solve a **resource-constrained project scheduling problem**: schedule tasks (each with a duration and a per-resource demand) subject to finish-to-start **precedences** and renewable **resource capacities**, minimizing the makespan.

**Inputs.** `tasks` = `[task, duration, r0_demand, r1_demand, ...]` (one demand column per resource, in `resources` order); `precedences` = `[pred, succ]`; `resources` = `[resource, capacity]`. **Outputs.** One row per task with `start` / `end`, the optimal `makespan`, and `status`.

Choose a subset of items to **maximize total value** subject to one or more **capacity dimensions** (multi-dimensional 0/1 knapsack).

**Inputs.** `item_values` = `[v0, v1, ...]`; `weights` = `[[w0_d0, w0_d1, ...], ...]` (one row per item, one column per capacity dimension); `capacities` = `[c_d0, c_d1, ...]`. **Outputs.** One row per item with `chosen` (`BOOLEAN`) and `status`.

functions.name: solve_cpsat
functions.comment: Solve an arbitrary CP-SAT constraint-programming model expressed as a versioned JSON document (variables, constraints, objective). Returns one row per variable plus solve metadata. The general escape hatch for constraints highs/LP cannot express.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_cpsat`

Solve an **arbitrary CP-SAT constraint-programming model** handed in as a **versioned JSON document** -- the general escape hatch for everything the per-domain builders and the `highs` LP/MIP extension cannot express (global constraints like `all_different`, `no_overlap`, `cumulative`, `circuit`, reification, intervals).

**The model.** A JSON object with `version` (must be 1), `variables` (each `int` / `bool` / `interval` with a unique `name`), `constraints`, and an optional `objective`. All numeric domains are **integers** -- a fractional bound / coefficient / constant is rejected with a clear error (scale floats to integers first). The full grammar is in the README (section A).

**Outputs.** One row per variable: `var`, `value`, plus the solve metadata (`status`, `objective`, `best_bound`, `wall_time`, `num_branches`) repeated on every row so a single SELECT is self-describing. Interval variables expand to `<name>.start` / `.size` / `.end` (and `.presence` for optional intervals).

**The empty-vs-infeasible contract.** A model with no solution still returns **exactly one row** carrying `status` in {`INFEASIBLE`, `MODEL_INVALID`, `UNKNOWN`} with NULL `var`/`value`; a solve is never an empty result set. Test `WHERE status='INFEASIBLE'`, never `count(*)=0`.

**Determinism.** Single-threaded by default (`num_workers := 0`) with a fixed `random_seed`, so the objective and assignment are reproducible.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# solve_cpsat

Solve a hand-built **CP-SAT** model expressed as a versioned JSON document.

See the README (section A) for the full JSON dialect: `variables` (int / bool / interval), `constraints` (linear, all_different, element, table, no_overlap, cumulative, circuit, reservoir, mult/div/abs/min/max equality, bool_or/and/xor, implication, with optional `enforce` reification), and an optional `objective`.

All numeric domains are integers. A no-solution model returns a single status row.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver)

vgi.example_queries.description: 0/1 knapsack as a CP-SAT model: maximize value within a weight budget (optimum 40).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT var, value, status, objective FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"bool","name":"a"},{"kind":"bool","name":"b"},{"kind":"bool","name":"c"}],"constraints":[{"type":"linear","expr":{"sum":[{"coef":5,"var":"a"},{"coef":10,"var":"b"},{"coef":15,"var":"c"}]},"op":"<=","rhs":20}],"objective":{"sense":"maximize","terms":[{"coef":10,"var":"a"},{"coef":20,"var":"b"},{"coef":30,"var":"c"}]}}') ORDER BY var

vgi.example_queries.description: Single-machine no-overlap schedule minimizing makespan (optimum 10).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT objective, status FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"int","name":"s0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"interval","name":"i0","start":{"var":"s0"},"size":{"const":3},"end":{"var":"e0"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i1","start":{"var":"s1"},"size":{"const":5},"end":{"var":"e1"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i2","start":{"var":"s2"},"size":{"const":2},"end":{"var":"e2"}},{"kind":"int","name":"makespan","lb":0,"ub":20}],"constraints":[{"type":"no_overlap","intervals":["i0","i1","i2"]},{"type":"max_equality","target":{"var":"makespan"},"exprs":[{"var":"e0"},{"var":"e1"},{"var":"e2"}]}],"objective":{"sense":"minimize","terms":[{"coef":1,"var":"makespan"}]}}', time_limit_s := 5.0) LIMIT 1

vgi.executable_examples.description: 0/1 knapsack as a CP-SAT model: maximize value within a weight budget (optimum 40).

functions.name: solve_vrp
functions.comment: Vehicle routing problem: route a fleet from a depot to serve stops at minimum total distance, with optional capacity dimensions, time windows, service/travel time, pickup-delivery pairs, droppable stops, and route balancing. OR-Tools routing library.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_vrp`

Route a **fleet of vehicles** from a depot to serve a set of stops at **minimum total distance**, with the full routing surface: multi-dimension **capacity** (`demand` + `vehicle_capacity`), **time windows** (`time_windows` + `service_time` / `travel_time`), **pickup-delivery** pairs (same vehicle + precedence), droppable stops (`allow_dropping` + `drop_penalty`), route balancing (`span_cost_coefficient`), and the OR-Tools `first_solution_strategy` / `local_search_metaheuristic`.

**Inputs.** `distance` (sparse `[from, to, meters]` or dense `n x n`); `demand` = `[node, d0, d1, ...]` (the number of demand columns sets the number of capacity dimensions and therefore the `load_0` .. `load_k` output columns); `num_vehicles`; `vehicle_capacity`; `depot`. Advanced shapes -- per-vehicle / per-dimension capacities, per-vehicle `[start, end]` depots -- go through `settings_json`.

**Outputs.** One row per stop: `route_id` (vehicle), `seq`, `node`, `arrival`, `departure`, `load_0` .. `load_k`, `is_dropped`, `status`. A dropped node appears as a single row with `is_dropped = true` and NULL `route_id`. An unsolved instance returns one status row.

**Determinism.** Governed by the fixed `first_solution_strategy` / `local_search_metaheuristic`. The output `load_*` column count is fixed at bind time from the `demand` argument, so pass `demand` as a literal or a session VARIABLE that is set before the query binds.

# solve_vrp

Capacitated, time-windowed vehicle routing.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/routing/cvrp)

vgi.executable_examples.description: Capacitated VRP: 1 depot, 3 stops of demand 1, 2 vehicles of capacity 2 (optimal distance 6).

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The number of `load_d` columns is fixed at bind time from the `demand` argument (one per capacity dimension), so the output schema varies by call. For `k+1` capacity dimensions the columns are:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| route_id | INTEGER | Vehicle index (NULL on a dropped-node row). |
| seq | INTEGER | 0-based stop order on the vehicle. |
| node | BIGINT | Node id (depot at seq 0 and last). |
| arrival | BIGINT | Cumulative time/distance at arrival. |
| departure | BIGINT | Arrival + service time. |
| load_0 | BIGINT | Cumulative load for capacity dimension 0. |
| load_k | BIGINT | Cumulative load for capacity dimension k (one load_d column per dimension). |
| is_dropped | BOOLEAN | True on the row emitted for a dropped node. |
| status | VARCHAR | OPTIMAL / FEASIBLE / INFEASIBLE / UNKNOWN / MODEL_INVALID. |
tags.vgi.title: Vehicle Routing (Capacitated / Time-Windowed)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_jobshop`

Schedule the tasks of several **jobs** onto shared **machines** to minimize the **makespan** (the time the last task finishes). Within a job, tasks run in `task` order; each machine runs one task at a time.

**Inputs.** `tasks` = `[job, task, machine, duration]` integer rows. Optional `horizon` (defaults to the sum of durations), `time_limit_s`, `random_seed`.

**Outputs.** One row per task with its `start` / `end`, the optimal `makespan` (repeated on every row), and `status`. An infeasible / unsolved instance returns a single status row.

functions.name: solve_assignment
functions.comment: Linear sum assignment: match workers to tasks over sparse [worker, task, cost] arcs, minimizing (or maximizing) total cost. Backed by OR-Tools SimpleLinearSumAssignment.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_assignment`

Solve a **linear sum assignment**: match each worker to at most one task (and each task to at most one worker) so the **total arc cost is minimized** (or maximized).

**Inputs.** `cost` is a sparse `LIST<LIST<BIGINT>>` of `[worker, task, cost]` integer triples (build it with `array_agg([w, t, c])`); a pair that is absent is a disallowed assignment. `maximize := true` negates costs internally. All costs must be integers.

**Outputs.** One row per matched worker: `worker`, `task`, `cost`, `status`. When no perfect matching of every worker exists the result is **exactly one row** with `status = 'INFEASIBLE'` and NULL `task`/`cost` -- never an empty set.

**Edge cases.** A non-integer cost raises a clear error (scale to integers first).

workers.title: PDF Structure & Rendering
workers.tagline: PDF tables, word boxes, form fields & page render for DuckDB (Python, pdfplumber)
workers.summary: Extract PDF structure (tables, word boxes, geometry, forms, metadata) and render pages to PNG.
workers.doc_md:
# PDF Structure & Rendering for DuckDB

Query the **structure, layout, and coordinates of PDF documents directly in SQL** -- pull tabular data, per-word geometry, page dimensions, form submissions, and document properties, check whether a file is encrypted, and rasterize any page to an image, all streamed to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. Where a plain-text extractor flattens a document to a string, this worker preserves *where* every word, cell, and box sits on the page.

## Who it is for

Built for data engineers, analysts, and document-mining pipelines that need to pull structured data out of reports, invoices, statements, and scanned forms without leaving SQL. Reach for it whenever the *position* of content matters -- reconstructing tabular layouts, locating text by coordinate, auditing filled-in forms, or generating page thumbnails -- and reach for a plain-text extraction worker instead when you only need the raw prose.

## Key concepts

- **Path or bytes.** Inputs are accepted as either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of raw bytes travelling over Arrow -- so a document already living in a DuckDB column works as directly as a file on disk.
- **PDF points.** All geometry is reported in PDF points (1 pt = 1/72 inch) with the origin at the top-left corner of the page.
- **Long-format output.** Set-returning functions expand one document into many tidy rows, ready to pivot, filter, and join with ordinary SQL.

## Backed by permissive libraries only

Table detection and word geometry come from [pdfplumber](https://github.com/jsvine/pdfplumber) ([docs](https://github.com/jsvine/pdfplumber#readme)); high-fidelity page rasterization is powered by [pypdfium2](https://github.com/pypdfium2-team/pypdfium2) ([docs](https://pypdfium2.readthedocs.io/)), Google's Chromium PDFium engine; document properties, encryption detection, and AcroForm reading use [pikepdf](https://github.com/pikepdf/pikepdf) ([docs](https://pikepdf.readthedocs.io/)); and rendered bitmaps are encoded to PNG with [Pillow](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow) ([docs](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/)). Deliberately **never PyMuPDF** -- only permissively licensed dependencies.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# PDF Structure -- `main`

The `main` schema groups every PDF structure, layout, and rendering capability this worker exposes, all served to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. It reads a document's *structure and coordinates* -- not its plain text -- so you always know where content sits on the page.

## What you can do here

- **Structure** -- count pages and read per-page geometry (width, height, rotation).
- **Content** -- pull detected table cells in long format, per-word bounding boxes, and filled-in form-field values.
- **Metadata** -- read the document information dictionary and check encryption status.
- **Rendering** -- rasterize a single page to a PNG image at a chosen resolution.

## Conventions

Inputs are accepted as either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path or a `BLOB` of raw bytes, and all coordinates are expressed in PDF points (1/72 inch) measured from the top-left corner. The set-returning functions take DuckDB `name := value` keyword arguments; the per-row question-answering functions are ordinary scalars used inline in any projection.

# functions

A **browsable discovery view** listing every object this worker exposes, one row per object: `name`, `kind` (`scalar`, `table function`, or `view`), `category` (Structure/Content/Metadata/Rendering/Discovery), and a one-line `summary`. It is a plain view -- read it as `pdf.main.functions` with no arguments.

Use it as the entry point when you do not yet know what the worker offers: read this view first to pick the right object, then call that object with a PDF path or bytes. Filter by `category` to narrow to a capability area, or by `kind` to separate per-row scalars from set-returning table functions.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# List Worker Objects

A static registry view of every object this worker exposes -- the browsable entry point for discovering the surface before calling anything.

## Example

Reading `pdf.main.functions` returns one row per object with its `name`, `kind`, `category`, and `summary`; keep rows whose `category` equals `Content` to see the table-cell, word-box, and form-field extractors. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | Object name (call it as `pdf.main.<name>`). |
| `kind` | VARCHAR | `scalar`, `table function`, or `view`. |
| `category` | VARCHAR | Structure, Content, Metadata, Rendering, or Discovery. |
| `summary` | VARCHAR | One-line description of what the object returns. |

## Notes

The view is static and offline -- it needs no PDF, file, or network access, so it always answers instantly.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# words

Table function returning **one row per word** in a PDF, with each word's text and its bounding box: `page` (1-based), `text`, and the box edges `x0`/`top`/`x1`/`bottom` in PDF points (origin at the top-left). Call by keyword: `words(pdf := '...')`, with the optional `page := N` filter to restrict to one page. `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Use it to locate text by coordinate, reconstruct reading order (`ORDER BY top, x0`), find where a keyword appears on a page, or build a spatial layout index.

**Edge cases:** a scanned/image-only page yields no words; a NULL `pdf` raises a clean argument error; an unreadable PDF raises a clean DuckDB error. Output streams in bounded slices, so pages with thousands of words page safely over every transport.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Extract PDF Word Boxes

Returns every word in a PDF together with its bounding box, one row per word.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.words(pdf := 'invoice.pdf')` returns one row per word -- its `text` and the box edges `x0`, `top`, `x1`, `bottom` (PDF points, origin top-left). Order by `top` then `x0` to recover reading order, or pass `page := 1` to restrict to the first page. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | INTEGER | 1-based page number the word is on. |
| `text` | VARCHAR | The word's text. |
| `x0` | DOUBLE | Left edge, in PDF points from the left. |
| `top` | DOUBLE | Top edge, in PDF points from the top. |
| `x1` | DOUBLE | Right edge, in PDF points from the left. |
| `bottom` | DOUBLE | Bottom edge, in PDF points from the top. |

## Notes

Coordinates are in PDF points with the origin at the top-left. Image-only (scanned) pages produce no words -- this reads the text layer, it does not OCR. Call by keyword (`pdf := ...`, optional `page := N`).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# tables

Table function that detects tables in a PDF and returns them in **long (tidy) format -- one row per cell**: `page` (1-based), `table_index` (0-based ordinal of the table on the page), `row` and `col` (0-based indices within the table), and `value` (the cell text, NULL when empty). Call by keyword: `tables(pdf := '...')`, with the optional `page := N` filter. `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Use it to mine numeric/tabular data out of reports and statements. Pivot back to a grid with conditional aggregation on `row`/`col`, or filter a single table with `table_index`.

**Gotcha:** `row` is a SQL keyword -- quote it as `"row"`. **Edge cases:** a page with no detectable table contributes no rows; a NULL `pdf` raises a clean argument error; an unreadable PDF raises a clean DuckDB error. Output streams in bounded slices.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Extract PDF Table Cells

Detects tables in a PDF and returns their cells in long (one-row-per-cell) format.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.tables(pdf := 'report.pdf')` yields one row per cell, with `page`, `table_index`, `row`, `col`, and `value`. Order by `page, table_index, "row", col` to read cells in layout order, and pivot back to a grid with conditional aggregation over `row`/`col`. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | INTEGER | 1-based page number the cell is on. |
| `table_index` | INTEGER | 0-based table ordinal within the page. |
| `row` | INTEGER | 0-based row index in the table (SQL keyword: quote as `"row"`). |
| `col` | INTEGER | 0-based column index within the table. |
| `value` | VARCHAR | Cell text (NULL for an empty/missing cell). |

## Notes

The `row` column is a SQL keyword -- quote it as `"row"`. Pages without a detectable table produce no rows. Call by keyword (`pdf := ...`, optional `page := N`).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# pages

Table function returning **one row per page** of a PDF with its physical geometry: `page` (1-based), `width` and `height` in PDF points (1 pt = 1/72 inch), and `rotation` in degrees. Call by keyword: `pages(pdf := '...')`, where `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB` of raw bytes.

Use it to learn how many pages a document has and each page's size/orientation -- e.g. to detect landscape vs portrait pages, find oversized pages, or drive per-page rendering.

**Edge cases:** a NULL `pdf` is rejected with a clean argument error; an unreadable/encrypted PDF surfaces a clean DuckDB error (not a crash). Output streams in bounded slices so even very large documents page safely over every transport.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# List PDF Page Geometry

Returns the geometry of every page in a PDF, one row per page: the 1-based page number and each page's width, height, and rotation.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.pages(pdf := 'report.pdf')` yields one row per page; a US-Letter portrait page reports a width of `612` and a height of `792` (points) with a rotation of `0`. Restrict to landscape pages by keeping rows where `width` exceeds `height`. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | INTEGER | 1-based page number. |
| `width` | DOUBLE | Page width in PDF points. |
| `height` | DOUBLE | Page height in PDF points. |
| `rotation` | INTEGER | Page rotation in degrees (0/90/180/270). |

## Notes

Dimensions are in PDF points (1/72 inch). Call the function by keyword (`pdf := ...`). A NULL `pdf` raises an argument error; an unreadable document raises a clean error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# pdf_metadata

Return the PDF's **document information dictionary** as a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` -- keys such as `Title`, `Author`, `Subject`, `Creator`, `Producer`, `CreationDate`, and `ModDate`. The `pdf` argument is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Index a single field with `pdf_metadata(...)['Title']`, or expand the whole map with `UNNEST(map_entries(...))`. Use it to catalog documents, sort by author, or extract titles.

**Edge cases:** keys present depend on the producer (any subset may be missing); a NULL input or an unreadable PDF returns NULL. Never raises.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read PDF Document Metadata

Extracts the document information dictionary (Title, Author, Producer, dates, ...) as a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`.

## Example

Index a single field with `pdf.main.pdf_metadata('report.pdf')['Title']`, or expand the whole map with `map_entries(...)` to list every key/value pair. Typical keys are `Title`, `Author`, `Subject`, `Creator`, `Producer`, `CreationDate`, and `ModDate`. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

Available keys vary by the tool that produced the PDF. Returns `NULL` for a NULL input or an unreadable document.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# pdf_metadata

Return the PDF's **document information dictionary** as a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` -- keys such as `Title`, `Author`, `Subject`, `Creator`, `Producer`, `CreationDate`, and `ModDate`. The `pdf` argument is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Index a single field with `pdf_metadata(...)['Title']`, or expand the whole map with `UNNEST(map_entries(...))`. Use it to catalog documents, sort by author, or extract titles.

**Edge cases:** keys present depend on the producer (any subset may be missing); a NULL input or an unreadable PDF returns NULL. Never raises.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read PDF Document Metadata

Extracts the document information dictionary (Title, Author, Producer, dates, ...) as a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`.

## Example

Index a single field with `pdf.main.pdf_metadata('report.pdf')['Title']`, or expand the whole map with `map_entries(...)` to list every key/value pair. Typical keys are `Title`, `Author`, `Subject`, `Creator`, `Producer`, `CreationDate`, and `ModDate`. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

Available keys vary by the tool that produced the PDF. Returns `NULL` for a NULL input or an unreadable document.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# form_fields

Return the values of an **AcroForm** (fillable PDF form) as a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` mapping each field's fully-qualified name to its current value. The `pdf` argument is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.

Use it to read submitted form data -- applications, invoices, government forms -- straight into SQL, then pivot fields into columns with `['field_name']` lookups.

**Edge cases:** a document with no AcroForm yields an empty map; checkbox/radio values are the export value strings; a NULL input or unreadable PDF returns NULL. Never raises.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Extract PDF Form Fields

Reads filled-in AcroForm field values from a fillable PDF, returning a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` of field name to value.

## Example

Read one field with `pdf.main.form_fields('application.pdf')['applicant_name']`, or read the whole map to pivot every submitted field into columns. Checkbox and radio values come back as their export-value strings. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

A PDF without a form returns an empty map. Returns `NULL` for a NULL input or an unreadable document.

functions.name: is_encrypted
functions.comment: True if the PDF (VARCHAR path) is encrypted, NULL if unreadable

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# is_encrypted

Return `TRUE` if the PDF is **encrypted** (password/permissions protected), `FALSE` if it is plain, or `NULL` if the bytes are not a readable PDF at all. The `pdf` argument is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB` of bytes.

Use it to triage a batch of documents before processing -- encrypted files cannot be parsed for words/tables/metadata without a password.

**Key behavior:** an encrypted file that has no user password still returns `TRUE`. Encryption is a *successful* answer, not an error, so the function never attempts to brute-force a password and never hangs. NULL input yields NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Detect PDF Encryption

Reports whether a PDF is encrypted, returning a `BOOLEAN`.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.is_encrypted('secret.pdf')` returns `true` for a password/permissions protected document and `false` for a plain one. Use it to triage a batch of uploads before parsing, since encrypted files cannot be read for words, tables, or metadata without a password. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

`TRUE` means the document is password/permissions protected. `NULL` means the input was not a readable PDF. Detection is purely structural -- no password guessing is performed.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.is_encrypted((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-pdf/v0.2.0/test/sql/data/form.pdf'))) AS encrypted

vgi.example_queries.description: Whether a PDF held as bytes is encrypted (NULL for non-PDF bytes)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.is_encrypted('not-a-pdf'::BLOB) AS encrypted

functions.name: page_count
functions.comment: Number of pages in a PDF (VARCHAR path), or NULL if unreadable

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# page_count

Return the **number of pages** in a PDF as an `INTEGER`. The `pdf` argument is either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens or a `BLOB` of the raw PDF bytes.

Use it to size a document before paging through `pages`, `words`, or `tables`, to validate an upload, or to drive a `generate_series(1, page_count(...))` loop over `render_page`.

**Edge cases:** a NULL input returns NULL; a malformed, encrypted-beyond-reading, or otherwise unreadable PDF also returns NULL rather than raising -- this scalar never throws and never hangs.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Count PDF Pages

Counts the pages in a PDF document, returning an `INTEGER`.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.page_count('report.pdf')` on a twelve-page report returns `12`. The `pdf` argument is a `VARCHAR` filesystem path or a `BLOB` of raw bytes, so a document already sitting in a table column works exactly like a file on disk. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

Returns `NULL` for a NULL input or a PDF that cannot be read. Useful for sizing a document ahead of the `pages`, `words`, and `tables` table functions.

vgi.example_queries.description: Page count of a sample PDF fetched with read_blob (returns 3)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.page_count((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-pdf/v0.2.0/test/sql/data/multipage.pdf'))) AS pages

vgi.example_queries.description: Page count of a PDF held as bytes (NULL for non-PDF bytes)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.page_count('not-a-pdf'::BLOB) AS pages

functions.name: render_page
functions.comment: Render one (1-based) page of a PDF (VARCHAR path) to a PNG BLOB (default 150 DPI)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# render_page

Rasterize **one (1-based) page** of a PDF to a **PNG image** returned as a `BLOB`. Signature `render_page(pdf, page[, dpi])`: `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`, `page` is the 1-based page number, and the optional `dpi` sets the resolution (default 150, capped at 300).

Use it to thumbnail PDFs, preview a page, or feed a page image to a vision model.

**Bounds & edge cases:** the output bitmap area is capped (an enormous page renders at reduced scale rather than exhausting memory); a NULL input, NULL page, out-of-range page, or unreadable PDF returns NULL. Never raises and never OOMs.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Render PDF Page to Image

Rasterizes a single PDF page to a PNG image, returned as a `BLOB`.

## Example

Calling `pdf.main.render_page('report.pdf', 1)` renders the first page at the default 150 DPI and hands back the raw PNG bytes; pass a third argument to override the resolution, as in `pdf.main.render_page('report.pdf', 1, 72)` for a lighter 72-DPI thumbnail. The `page` argument is 1-based and `dpi` is clamped to 300. The input `pdf` is a `VARCHAR` filesystem path or a `BLOB` of raw bytes. Ready-to-run SQL lives in the example queries.

## Notes

The rendered bitmap area is capped to avoid runaway memory use. Returns `NULL` for a NULL input, an out-of-range page, or an unreadable document.

vgi.example_queries.description: Render page 1 to a PNG and report its byte size
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(pdf.main.render_page((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-pdf/v0.2.0/test/sql/data/multipage.pdf')), 1)) AS png_bytes

vgi.example_queries.description: Render page 1 at 72 DPI and report its byte size
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(pdf.main.render_page((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-pdf/v0.2.0/test/sql/data/multipage.pdf')), 1, 72)) AS png_bytes

vgi.example_queries.description: Rendering non-PDF bytes yields NULL rather than an error
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.render_page('not-a-pdf'::BLOB, 1) IS NULL AS unreadable

vgi.example_queries.description: Rendering non-PDF bytes at 72 DPI yields NULL rather than an error
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pdf.main.render_page('not-a-pdf'::BLOB, 1, 72) IS NULL AS unreadable

workers.doc_md:
# Executable Binary Analysis in SQL (PE / ELF / Mach-O)

![LIEF logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lief-project/LIEF/main/doc/sphinx/_static/logo_blue.png)

**Static, read-only malware triage and binary forensics over Apache Arrow** — parse Windows PE, Linux ELF, and macOS Mach-O executables and query their format, architecture, entropy, imports, exports, sections, and strings directly from DuckDB SQL.

The `pe` catalog turns static binary analysis into ordinary SQL. It is built for malware analysts, incident responders, threat hunters, reverse engineers, and anyone running build-provenance or binary-corpus checks at scale. Instead of shelling out to a pile of command-line tools and stitching their output together, you `ATTACH` this worker and `SELECT` the facts you need — across thousands of samples — with the full power of joins, filters, and aggregation. Every input is treated as untrusted and possibly hostile: the worker only **reads and describes** the bytes. It NEVER executes the sample and never resolves an external reference, and malformed, truncated, or non-binary input degrades cleanly to `NULL` (scalars) or no rows (table functions) rather than crashing or hanging.

Cross-format parsing is powered by [LIEF](https://lief.re) (Library to Instrument Executable Formats), a permissive Apache-2.0 library that reads PE, ELF, and Mach-O through one consistent API. See the [LIEF source on GitHub](https://github.com/lief-project/LIEF) and the [LIEF documentation](https://lief.re/doc/stable/index.html) for format details. The worker wraps LIEF in total, crash-proof extractors and exposes them as Arrow-native DuckDB functions; bounds on input size, string counts, and row counts keep even adversarial "bomb" inputs from exhausting memory.

The catalog exposes two shapes of query. **Per-binary facts** answer a single question about a sample — its container format and CPU architecture, its entry point, whether it is code-signed, its build timestamp and import-hash fingerprint, and its whole-file entropy — so they slot directly into a projection or a filter and scale across an entire corpus. **Set-returning functions** expand one binary into many rows — its per-section layout with entropy, its imported and exported symbols, and its printable strings — for row-level IOC hunting, filtering, and joining. Every function accepts the binary as either a filesystem path it opens or raw bytes passed inline, so you can analyze files on disk or blobs already living in a table, and each pairs its narrative with runnable, tested example queries. Static analysis only — the binary is never executed.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'pe' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-pe@v0.2.0 vgi-pe-worker');

SELECT pe.binary_format('sample.exe');            -- 'PE' | 'ELF' | 'MachO' | NULL
SELECT pe.machine('sample.exe');                  -- 'X86_64', 'ARM64', ...
SELECT pe.is_signed('sample.exe');                -- Authenticode / Mach-O code signature
SELECT pe.imphash('sample.exe');                  -- PE import hash (clustering)
SELECT pe.overall_entropy('sample.exe');          -- 0-8; high => packed/encrypted

SELECT * FROM pe.sections('sample.exe') ORDER BY name;   -- per-section entropy + flags
SELECT * FROM pe.imports('sample.exe');                  -- imported symbols
SELECT * FROM pe.exports('sample.so');                   -- exported symbols
SELECT * FROM pe.strings('sample.exe', min_len := 8);    -- printable strings

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Enumerate the **imported symbols** of a binary, one row per import, as `(library, function)`. For PE the `library` is the DLL (e.g. `KERNEL32.dll`) and `function` the imported API, or `ordinal#N` when imported by ordinal; for ELF/Mach-O `library` is empty and `function` is the symbol. Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; unparseable input yields no rows.

The import table is one of the richest behavioral fingerprints of a binary: which APIs it pulls in (networking, crypto, process injection, registry, file I/O) sketches what it *can* do without running it, and the normalized import set underlies `pe.imphash(...)` clustering. Watch for tiny import tables (a packer that resolves APIs at runtime) and for suspicious API combinations. Static read-only.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## imports

One row per imported symbol, as `(library, function)`.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `library` | VARCHAR | Imported library/DLL name (empty for ELF/Mach-O). |
| `function` | VARCHAR | Imported symbol name, or `ordinal#N` when imported by ordinal. |

### Notes

PE rows carry the DLL in `library` (functions imported by ordinal appear as `ordinal#N`); ELF/Mach-O leave `library` empty. A suspiciously small import table often means runtime API resolution (a packing/evasion signal). Feeds `pe.imphash(...)`.

functions.name: strings

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Extract **printable strings** from a binary, one row per string, as `(seq, value)` in file order. It recovers both ASCII and UTF-16LE runs at least `min_len` characters long (`min_len` defaults to 5 and is passed as the named argument `min_len :=`). Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; output is capped for safety against string-bomb input, and unparseable input yields no rows.

Strings are the fastest way to surface human-readable indicators inside an opaque binary: URLs, IP addresses, file paths, registry keys, command lines, mutex names, embedded error messages, and crypto constants. Filter `value` with SQL `LIKE`/regex to hunt for IOCs across a corpus. Raise `min_len` to cut noise from packed samples. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## strings

One row per printable string (ASCII + UTF-16LE) of length `>= min_len`.

### Arguments

- `binary` — a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.
- `min_len` (named, default 5) — minimum string length to report.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `seq` | BIGINT | 1-based ordinal of the string in file order. |
| `value` | VARCHAR | Printable ASCII/UTF-16 string (length >= `min_len`). |

### Notes

Output is bounded against string-bomb inputs. Use `WHERE value LIKE '%http%'` (and friends) to hunt URLs, paths, registry keys, and other IOCs; raise `min_len` to reduce noise on packed samples.

functions.name: strings

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Extract **printable strings** from a binary, one row per string, as `(seq, value)` in file order. It recovers both ASCII and UTF-16LE runs at least `min_len` characters long (`min_len` defaults to 5 and is passed as the named argument `min_len :=`). Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; output is capped for safety against string-bomb input, and unparseable input yields no rows.

Strings are the fastest way to surface human-readable indicators inside an opaque binary: URLs, IP addresses, file paths, registry keys, command lines, mutex names, embedded error messages, and crypto constants. Filter `value` with SQL `LIKE`/regex to hunt for IOCs across a corpus. Raise `min_len` to cut noise from packed samples. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## strings

One row per printable string (ASCII + UTF-16LE) of length `>= min_len`.

### Arguments

- `binary` — a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`.
- `min_len` (named, default 5) — minimum string length to report.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `seq` | BIGINT | 1-based ordinal of the string in file order. |
| `value` | VARCHAR | Printable ASCII/UTF-16 string (length >= `min_len`). |

### Notes

Output is bounded against string-bomb inputs. Use `WHERE value LIKE '%http%'` (and friends) to hunt URLs, paths, registry keys, and other IOCs; raise `min_len` to reduce noise on packed samples.

functions.name: sections
functions.comment: Per-section (name, virtual_size, raw_size, entropy, flags) of a binary (VARCHAR path)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Enumerate the **sections** of a binary, one row per section, with size and **per-section Shannon entropy** — the workhorse table for layout-level triage. Columns: `name`, `virtual_size`, `raw_size`, `entropy` (0–8), `characteristics` (PE flags; empty for ELF/Mach-O). Accepts a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`; unparseable or non-binary input yields **no rows** (never an error).

Use it to find *where* in a file suspicious data lives: a high-entropy (`> ~7`) `.text`/code section, an executable+writable section, or a section whose raw size dwarfs its virtual size all point to packing, embedded payloads, or self-modifying code. Cross-reference with `pe.entry_point(...)` to confirm the entry point lands in a sane section. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## sections

One row per section of the binary, with sizes and per-section entropy.

### Returns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | Section name (e.g. `.text`, `.data`, `__TEXT`). |
| `virtual_size` | BIGINT | Size in bytes when mapped into memory. |
| `raw_size` | BIGINT | Size in bytes on disk. |
| `entropy` | DOUBLE | Per-section Shannon entropy (0-8); high (>~7) suggests packing/encryption. |
| `characteristics` | VARCHAR | Comma-joined section flags (PE only; empty for ELF/Mach-O). |

### Notes

`characteristics` is populated for PE only. High `entropy` (`> ~7`) localizes packing/encryption to a specific section; a large `raw_size`-vs-`virtual_size` gap or an entry point outside an executable section are further packing signals. Unparseable input returns no rows.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Enumerate the **exported symbols** of a binary, one row per export, as `(name, address)` where `address` is the symbol's address/value (0 when unavailable). functions.name: overall_entropy
functions.comment: Shannon entropy (bits/byte, 0-8) of a binary (VARCHAR path); high => packed/encrypted

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **Shannon entropy** of the entire file as a `DOUBLE` in bits-per-byte on a `0.0`–`8.0` scale. It is computed over the raw file bytes (independent of the section layout), so it works even when LIEF can't fully resolve the structure — but it still returns `NULL` for NULL or non-binary input so a random text blob isn't given a misleading number.

High whole-file entropy (typically `> ~7.0`) is the single strongest cheap signal of **packing, compression, or encryption**: most native code sits around `5.5`–`6.5`, while packed/encrypted payloads push toward `8.0`. Use it as a first-pass triage filter, then drill into per-section entropy via `pe.sections(...)`. Static read-only.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## overall_entropy

Whole-file Shannon entropy as a `DOUBLE`, in bits/byte on a `0`–`8` scale.

### Interpreting the value

| range | typical meaning |
|---|---|
| ~5.5–6.5 | ordinary native code/data |
| > ~7.0 | likely packed, compressed, or encrypted |

Computed over raw bytes (independent of section layout). Returns `NULL` for non-binary input. For where the high entropy lives, see per-section entropy in `pe.sections(...)`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Overall entropy of a binary file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.overall_entropy('test/sql/data/hello.exe')

vgi.example_queries.description: Overall entropy of binary bytes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pe.main.overall_entropy((SELECT content FROM read_blob('test/sql/data/hello.exe')))

functions.name: binary_format
functions.comment: Executable format ('PE'/'ELF'/'MachO') of a binary (VARCHAR path), or NULL

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Detect the **container format** of an executable image and return it as a short string: `PE` (Windows portable executable), `ELF` (Linux/Unix), or `MachO` (macOS). Pass the binary as either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens or a `BLOB` of raw bytes. Returns `NULL` when the input is NULL, empty, truncated, or not a recognizable executable, so it is safe to run across a mixed corpus.

Use this first when triaging an unknown sample: the format decides which downstream signals are meaningful (e.g. `imphash` and `compile_timestamp` are PE-only). The binary is parsed statically and **never executed**.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## binary_format

Call it with a single argument — a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of raw bytes — and it returns the container-format string (for example `PE` for a Windows executable). Returns `NULL` for NULL, empty, or unrecognizable input — never an error. Typically the first step in a triage pipeline because the format gates which other functions apply. Ready-to-run example queries are attached to this function.

functions.name: compile_timestamp
functions.comment: PE build timestamp (TimeDateStamp) of a binary (VARCHAR path); NULL for ELF/Mach-O

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the PE **build timestamp** (the COFF header `TimeDateStamp`) as a `TIMESTAMP`. This is **PE-only**: ELF and Mach-O have no equivalent header field and return `NULL`, as does any unparseable input. The raw field is a Unix epoch in seconds; the worker scales it to microsecond-precision Arrow timestamp.

Use it for build-provenance and timeline analysis — bucketing samples by build date, spotting implausible values (the field is attacker-controllable, so a zero, far-future, or suspiciously round timestamp is itself a signal), and correlating related builds. Treat the value as a *claim*, not ground truth.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## compile_timestamp

The PE COFF `TimeDateStamp` as a `TIMESTAMP` (PE only).

### Usage

```sql
SELECT pe.compile_timestamp('sample.exe');
```

Returns `NULL` for ELF, Mach-O, and unparseable input. The field is stored as a Unix epoch (seconds) and is **attacker-controllable** — implausible values (zero, far future, round numbers) are a triage signal, not an error.

functions.name: imphash
functions.comment: PE import hash (for clustering) of a binary (VARCHAR path); NULL for ELF/Mach-O

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the **imphash** (import hash) of a PE: the MD5 over the normalized, ordered list of imported library/function names. It is **PE-only** — ELF and Mach-O, and any unparseable input, return `NULL`. Two PEs built from the same source/toolchain with the same import table share an imphash even if their bytes differ, which makes it a classic **clustering / family-attribution** key for malware triage.

Use it to `GROUP BY` related samples, to pivot from one known-bad sample to others, or to match against threat-intel imphash blocklists. Caveat: packers and import obfuscation can collapse or mangle the import table, so an imphash is a strong-but-not-definitive link. Static read-only; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## imphash

The PE import hash — MD5 of the normalized import table — as a hex string (PE only).

Call it with one argument (a `VARCHAR` path or a `BLOB`) to get the sample's 32-character hex import hash, or `NULL` for ELF, Mach-O, and unparseable input. Because two PEs built from the same toolchain and import table share an imphash, it is a classic clustering / family-attribution key: group a corpus by this value to bucket related samples. Packing or import obfuscation weakens the signal, so treat a match as a strong hint rather than proof. Ready-to-run example queries are attached to this function.

functions.name: is_signed
functions.comment: True if a binary (VARCHAR path) carries a code signature (PE Authenticode / Mach-O)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return whether a binary carries an embedded **code signature**: `true`/`false`, or `NULL` for unparseable input. The check is format-aware — PE Authenticode signatures, Mach-O embedded code signatures — and ELF, which has no native embedded-signature concept, always reports `false`. A `false` result is a *successful* answer (the file simply isn't signed), not a parse failure.

Use it as a quick trust signal during triage: unsigned system-looking binaries, or binaries that masquerade as signed vendors but report `false`, are worth a closer look. Note: this reports the *presence* of a signature, not whether the signature is valid or trusted. Static read-only check; the binary is never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## is_signed

Boolean: does the binary carry an embedded code signature?

### Behavior by format

| format | meaning |
|---|---|
| PE | has an Authenticode signature |
| Mach-O | has an embedded code signature |
| ELF | always `false` (no native embedded signature) |

Returns `NULL` only for input that cannot be parsed. This reports *presence*, not cryptographic *validity* — verify the chain separately if trust matters.
