workers.doc_md:
# Cross-Encoder Reranking in SQL

![fastembed (Qdrant) logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qdrant/fastembed/main/docs/assets/favicon.png)

**Rerank retrieval results directly in DuckDB with a local cross-encoder reranker (fastembed / ONNX Runtime, no torch) -- the precision second stage that turns a good recall set into a great answer for RAG and semantic search.**

Retrieval-augmented generation and semantic search almost always run in two stages. A fast *recall* stage (DuckDB [VSS](https://duckdb.org) approximate nearest-neighbor search over embeddings, or BM25 full-text search) cheaply pulls a top-K candidate set out of a large corpus, but it ranks each document in isolation, so the truly best passage is often buried at rank 7 instead of rank 1. This worker adds the *precision* second stage: a **cross-encoder** that reads the query and a candidate document *together* in a single transformer forward pass and emits a relevance score that is far more accurate than bi-encoder cosine similarity. It is for anyone building local RAG pipelines, document search, or recommendation ranking who wants higher answer quality without standing up a separate model-serving service -- the reranking happens inside your SQL query.

Scores are computed entirely locally by [fastembed](https://github.com/qdrant/fastembed) (from Qdrant, Apache-2.0), which runs quantized cross-encoder models on [ONNX Runtime](https://onnxruntime.ai/) -- there is **no PyTorch dependency** and no network call at query time. The default model, [`Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`](https://huggingface.co/Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2) (~80 MB, Apache-2.0), is fetched once on first use and cached, and the ONNX session is built a single time per worker process and amortized across every row. Because a cross-encoder scores each (query, document) pair at query time and cannot be precomputed or cached the way an embedding can, you should only ever run it over a recall-produced top-K candidate set -- never over a whole corpus.

The catalog exposes a small, focused surface. `rerank_score(query, document)` returns a `DOUBLE` relevance logit (higher = more relevant, meaningful only relative to other documents for the *same* query), so it drops straight into `ORDER BY rerank.rerank_score(:q, chunk) DESC LIMIT k`; a three-argument overload `rerank_score(query, document, model)` lets you pick a specific reranker such as `BAAI/bge-reranker-base`. The `supported_models()` table function (also available as the `supported_models` table) lists every reranker the worker can run together with the license of its weights. A NULL or empty query or document always yields a NULL score, so odd input never crashes a query.

## Getting started

Install and load the `vgi` community extension, then `ATTACH` this worker as a catalog (for example named `rerank`) pointed at `uv run rerank_worker.py`. Once attached, order any recall-produced candidate set by `rerank.main.rerank_score(:query, document) DESC` and keep the top *k* rows. Ready-to-run SQL for every function lives in each object's own examples and in the schema's example queries.

## Learn more

- fastembed source: <https://github.com/qdrant/fastembed>
- fastembed documentation: <https://qdrant.github.io/fastembed/>
- ONNX Runtime: <https://onnxruntime.ai/>

## main

The single schema of the `rerank` catalog: local cross-encoder relevance scoring exposed as SQL over Apache Arrow. Everything runs on-device via fastembed / ONNX Runtime (no torch, no network at query time once a model is cached), so second-stage RAG reranking becomes ordinary SQL.

**What you can do here**

- Score a `(query, document)` pair to a relevance logit and reorder a candidate set with `ORDER BY rerank_score(:q, doc) DESC LIMIT k`.
- Pick a specific reranker via the three-argument overload `rerank_score(query, document, model)`.
- Discover the available reranker models and their licenses.

**When to use it**

Apply reranking as the precision second stage over a recall-produced top-K candidate set (from DuckDB VSS ANN or BM25) -- never over a whole corpus, since a cross-encoder scores every pair at query time and cannot be precomputed. See each object's own documentation for arguments, worked examples, and output columns.

# supported_models

A discovery table of every cross-encoder reranker the worker can run -- one row per model. Backed by the `supported_models()` table function, it is queried without parentheses -- project the `model` and `license` columns and order by `model`; see the examples below for ready-to-run SQL.

## Columns

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | VARCHAR | Name to pass as the optional third argument to `rerank_score(query, document, model)` (primary key). |
| `license` | VARCHAR | SPDX-style license of the model weights. |

## Notes

Every advertised model is permissive / commercially usable. Reading this table loads no model, so it is always cheap.

# rerank_score(query, document, model)

Score a `(query, document)` pair with an **explicit** cross-encoder model (the three-argument arity overload of `rerank_score`).

## Arguments

- `query`, `document` -- the pair to score.
- `model` -- a model name from `supported_models()` (e.g. `Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`, `BAAI/bge-reranker-base`). Heavier models trade speed for quality and download on first use.

## Returns

`DOUBLE` -- the same relevance logit as the two-argument form.

## Notes

- Scalars are positional; this is an arity overload, not a named arg.
- NULL/empty query or document -> NULL score.

workers.doc_md:
# Rugby union data

Analyse rugby union from SQL: official world rankings and a match feed covering every sanctioned competition, plus league tables, fixtures, results and box scores for the major club and international competitions (Six Nations, Rugby Championship, Gallagher Prem, URC, Top 14, the European cups, Super Rugby and the Rugby World Cup).

## Two sources, two id spaces

- **World Rugby** (the governing body) supplies rankings, the cross-competition match feed and per-match team statistics, team sheets and timelines, keyed by World Rugby's 36-character `match_id`.
- **ESPN** supplies league tables with bonus points, season fixtures and results, and team and player box scores, keyed by a league key (such as `six_nations`) and ESPN's integer `event_id`.

Join the two sources on team names and dates, never on ids. Split seasons are labelled by their end year, so the 2026-27 Premiership is season 2027.

Access is read-only and keyless. The worker is not affiliated with World Rugby, ESPN or any league; data is fetched on demand and never rehosted.

example_queries.title: both_rankings_are_populated
example_queries.description: The current rankings table carries both the men's and women's tables.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT gender) = 2 AND count(*) > 100 AS populated FROM rugby.main.current_world_rankings;

example_queries.title: six_nations_2026_champion
example_queries.description: France won the 2026 Six Nations with 21 table points.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, table_points FROM rugby.main.standings(league := 'six_nations', season := 2026) WHERE rank = 1;

example_queries.title: six_nations_2026_has_fifteen_results
example_queries.description: A Six Nations championship is fifteen matches.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS matches FROM rugby.main.results(league := 'six_nations', season := 2026);

example_queries.title: rankings_after_2023_world_cup
example_queries.description: South Africa led the men's rankings after winning the 2023 Rugby World Cup.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name FROM rugby.main.world_rankings(as_of := DATE '2023-10-30') WHERE position = 1;

example_queries.description: The current Gallagher Prem table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_name, games_played, table_points FROM rugby.main.current_standings WHERE league = 'premiership' ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Champions Cup pool leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT group_name, team_name, table_points FROM rugby.main.current_standings WHERE league = 'champions_cup' AND rank = 1 ORDER BY group_name

example_queries.description: International competitions and their current season.
example_queries.sql: SELECT league, name, current_season FROM rugby.main.competitions WHERE level = 'international' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Recent results in men's international rugby.
example_queries.sql: SELECT local_date, competition, home_team_name, home_score, away_score, away_team_name FROM rugby.main.current_matches WHERE is_complete AND gender = 'men' AND (competition ILIKE '%Nations%' OR competition ILIKE '%International%') ORDER BY kickoff

example_queries.description: Upcoming matches in the next week.
example_queries.sql: SELECT kickoff, competition, home_team_name, away_team_name FROM rugby.main.current_matches WHERE NOT is_complete AND kickoff > now() ORDER BY kickoff LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Current men's top ten.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, team_name, points, points_change FROM rugby.main.current_world_rankings WHERE gender = 'men' AND position <= 10 ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Biggest risers in the latest women's update.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, previous_position, position FROM rugby.main.current_world_rankings WHERE gender = 'women' ORDER BY previous_position - position DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: The final 2026 Six Nations table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_name, wins, losses, points_difference, bonus_points, table_points FROM rugby.main.standings(league := 'six_nations', season := 2026) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: The 2025-26 Gallagher Prem table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_name, table_points FROM rugby.main.standings(league := 'premiership', season := 2026) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Super Saturday, 14 March 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT kickoff, home_team_name, home_score, away_score, away_team_name, status_detail FROM rugby.main.scoreboard(league := 'six_nations', dates := '20260314') ORDER BY kickoff

example_queries.description: Side-by-side key statistics for England v Australia, 8 November 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT stat, max(value) FILTER (WHERE team_index = 0) AS home, max(value) FILTER (WHERE team_index = 1) AS away FROM rugby.main.match_stats('d21f7bed-f2f9-45bd-be33-3a0fc9beec42') WHERE stat IN ('carries_metres', 'clean_breaks', 'tackles', 'possession') GROUP BY stat

example_queries.description: Metres carried by each side in England v Australia, 8 November 2026
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, value AS metres FROM rugby.main.match_stats('d21f7bed-f2f9-45bd-be33-3a0fc9beec42') WHERE stat = 'carries_metres' ORDER BY team_index

example_queries.description: Scoring sequence of England v Australia, 8 November 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT clock_label, team_name, event_type, player_name, home_score, away_score FROM rugby.main.match_timeline('d21f7bed-f2f9-45bd-be33-3a0fc9beec42') WHERE points > 0 ORDER BY sequence

example_queries.description: Top tacklers in England v Australia, 8 November 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, player_name, tackles, missed_tackles FROM rugby.main.match_squads('d21f7bed-f2f9-45bd-be33-3a0fc9beec42') ORDER BY tackles DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Starting fifteens for England v Australia, 8 November 2026
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, jersey_number, player_name, position FROM rugby.main.match_squads('d21f7bed-f2f9-45bd-be33-3a0fc9beec42') WHERE is_starter ORDER BY team_index, jersey_number

example_queries.description: Every 2026 Six Nations result.
example_queries.sql: SELECT kickoff::DATE AS day, home_team_name, home_score, away_score, away_team_name FROM rugby.main.results(league := 'six_nations', season := 2026) ORDER BY kickoff

example_queries.description: Leading tacklers in Ireland v Scotland, 14 March 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, player_name, tackles, missed_tackles FROM rugby.main.match_player_stats('six_nations', 602514) ORDER BY tackles DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Point scorers in Ireland v Scotland, 14 March 2026
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, player_name, points, tries FROM rugby.main.match_player_stats('six_nations', 602514) WHERE points > 0 ORDER BY points DESC

example_queries.description: Current leaders of every headline competition.
example_queries.sql: SELECT league_name, group_name, team_name, table_points FROM rugby.main.all_current_standings() WHERE rank = 1 ORDER BY league_name, group_name

example_queries.description: Test results from the 2026 autumn window.
example_queries.sql: SELECT local_date, home_team_name, home_score, away_score, away_team_name FROM rugby.main.matches(start_date := DATE '2026-11-01', end_date := DATE '2026-11-10') WHERE competition ILIKE 'Nations Championship%' ORDER BY kickoff

example_queries.description: Upcoming 2026-27 Gallagher Prem fixtures.
example_queries.sql: SELECT kickoff, home_team_name, away_team_name, venue_name FROM rugby.main.fixtures(league := 'premiership', season := 2027) ORDER BY kickoff LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Opening fixtures of the 2027 Rugby World Cup
example_queries.sql: SELECT kickoff, home_team_name, away_team_name FROM rugby.main.fixtures(league := 'rugby_world_cup', season := 2027) ORDER BY kickoff LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Read both current number-one teams from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT gender, team_name, points FROM rugby.main.all_current_world_rankings() WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY gender

example_queries.description: Ireland v Scotland, 14 March 2026: tackles and metres.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, stat, value FROM rugby.main.match_team_stats('six_nations', 602514) WHERE stat IN ('tackles', 'metres') ORDER BY stat, home_away

example_queries.description: Teams in the United Rugby Championship.

Parameterized functions cover historical rankings, any date range of World Rugby matches, match statistics/squads/timelines by match_id, and per-league standings, fixtures, results, scoreboards, box scores, lineups and teams by league key and event_id.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Rugby union analytical data

Rows are explicitly team-, match-, team-statistic-, player- or event-grain. Current tables give today's view; parameterized functions select dates, seasons, leagues and individual matches.

World Rugby identifiers (`match_id`, `wr_team_id`, `wr_player_id`) and ESPN identifiers (`event_id`, `team_id`, `player_id`) are separate id spaces; join across the two sources on team names, not ids.

vgi.example_queries.description: Champions Cup pool leaders.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT group_name, team_name, table_points FROM rugby.main.current_standings WHERE league = 'champions_cup' AND rank = 1 ORDER BY group_name

tables.name: current_matches
tables.comment: World Rugby matches from seven days ago to seven days ahead, one row per match

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every match World Rugby records across all sanctioned competitions from seven days ago to seven days ahead: kick-off, competition, teams, score, outcome and venue. Start here for 'this weekend's results' or 'upcoming tests'. Use matches(start_date, end_date) for other windows and match_id with match_stats(), match_squads() and match_timeline().
tags.vgi.doc_md: A rolling two-week window of World Rugby's match feed. `is_complete` separates results from fixtures; filter `competition` with ILIKE.

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent results in men's international rugby.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT local_date, competition, home_team_name, home_score, away_score, away_team_name FROM rugby.main.current_matches WHERE is_complete AND gender = 'men' AND (competition ILIKE '%Nations%' OR competition ILIKE '%International%') ORDER BY kickoff

vgi.example_queries.description: Upcoming matches in the next week.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT kickoff, competition, home_team_name, away_team_name FROM rugby.main.current_matches WHERE NOT is_complete AND kickoff > now() ORDER BY kickoff LIMIT 20

tags.vgi.subtitle: Every World Rugby-recorded match from a week ago to a week ahead.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Current official World Rugby rankings for both men (gender = 'men') and women (gender = 'women'), one row per national team with position, points and movement since the previous update. Use world_rankings(as_of := ...) for a past day.

vgi.example_queries.description: Current men's top ten.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT position, team_name, points, points_change FROM rugby.main.current_world_rankings WHERE gender = 'men' AND position <= 10 ORDER BY position

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, previous_position, position FROM rugby.main.current_world_rankings WHERE gender = 'women' ORDER BY previous_position - position DESC LIMIT 5

functions.name: standings
functions.comment: Rugby league table for one competition and season

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Rugby league table for one competition and season, one row per team with rank, played, won, drawn, lost, points for/against/difference, tries for/against, try and losing bonus points and table points. Pool competitions (Champions Cup, Rugby World Cup) return one row per team per pool in group_name. season NULL returns the season in progress or, before it starts, the last completed one.

functions.name: match_stats
functions.comment: Team statistics for one World Rugby match, one row per team and statistic

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Over 100 team statistics for one World Rugby match in long form (team, stat, value): carries, metres, clean_breaks, tackles, missed_tackles, possession and territory (0-1 ratios), lineouts, scrums, rucks, penalties_conceded, kicks and more. Pivot with FILTER or PIVOT to compare the two teams side by side. Detailed stats exist mainly for top-tier matches; lower-tier matches can return no rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Long-form team statistics; `stat` is snake_case and `source_stat` keeps World Rugby's name.

vgi.example_queries.description: Side-by-side key statistics for England v Australia, 8 November 2026.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT stat, max(value) FILTER (WHERE team_index = 0) AS home, max(value) FILTER (WHERE team_index = 1) AS away FROM rugby.main.match_stats('d21f7bed-f2f9-45bd-be33-3a0fc9beec42') WHERE stat IN ('carries_metres', 'clean_breaks', 'tackles', 'possession') GROUP BY stat

vgi.example_queries.description: Metres carried by each side in England v Australia, 8 November 2026
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, value AS metres FROM rugby.main.match_stats('d21f7bed-f2f9-45bd-be33-3a0fc9beec42') WHERE stat = 'carries_metres' ORDER BY team_index

functions.name: matches
functions.comment: World Rugby's cross-competition match feed for a date range

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every match World Rugby records across all sanctioned competitions (tests, Six Nations, Premiership, Top 14, URC, Super Rugby, Sevens, women's rugby and dozens of second-tier competitions), one row per match with kick-off, competition, teams, score, outcome and venue. Filter by competition name with ILIKE, for example competition ILIKE 'Six Nations%'. match_id feeds match_stats(), match_squads() and match_timeline(). Ranges are limited to 366 days per query.
tags.vgi.doc_md: World Rugby's match feed flattened to one row per match. `home_*` is the first-listed team and `away_*` the second, which World Rugby uses for the home side. Scores of matches that are not `is_complete` may be provisional or zero.

vgi.example_queries.description: Test results from the 2026 autumn window.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT local_date, home_team_name, home_score, away_score, away_team_name FROM rugby.main.matches(start_date := DATE '2026-11-01', end_date := DATE '2026-11-10') WHERE competition ILIKE 'Nations Championship%' ORDER BY kickoff

workers.title: SAML Forensics
workers.tagline: Parse and verify SAML in DuckDB with SQL — XML-DSig / C14N signature validation and golden-SAML / XML-signature-wrapping detection. A VGI worker.
workers.summary: SAML 2.0 decode + XML-DSig / exclusive-C14N signature verification + XSW / Golden-SAML detection, in SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# SAML — Decode, Signature Verification & Attack Detection in SQL

**Shred and security-check SAML 2.0 single-sign-on messages directly in DuckDB.** The `saml` worker base64-decodes (and, for the HTTP-Redirect binding, raw-DEFLATE inflates) a column of `SAMLResponse` blobs, decodes them into typed rows — subject, issuer, audience, the `Conditions` validity window, `AuthnContext`, and attribute statements — and, more importantly, runs the **XML-DSig** structural check the one-off tools only do one message at a time: exclusive XML canonicalization (`xml-exc-c14n#`), per-`Reference` digest verification, and signature math (RSA / ECDSA / EdDSA) against the **embedded** certificate.

The defensible value is **bulk security compute**: running **XML Signature Wrapping (XSW)** and **Golden-SAML** detection across millions of historical SAML messages in a forensic lake — in SQL, joinable against your IdP cert inventory and login telemetry. The worker flags the structural invariants every XSW1-XSW8 attack violates (multiple assertions, a signature that covers a different element than the consumer reads, duplicate/dangling reference IDs, an unsigned assertion inside a signed response, comment-splitting NameIDs, digest mismatches), and surfaces the signer certificate SHA-256 fingerprint so a left join against your known-good IdP certs surfaces the Golden-SAML smoking gun (a cryptographically perfect signature from a key you do not trust).

**Trust stays with you.** `sig_valid = true` means the embedded cert signed these bytes — never that the cert is authorized. The worker holds no private keys, no trust store, makes no network calls, and decrypts nothing; an `EncryptedAssertion` is counted and flagged, not opened. All decode and canonicalization is local CPU on bytes you already hold, so it is safe for air-gapped / regulated forensic data.

**Hardened against hostile input.** Every blob is attacker-controlled, so the XML loader rejects DTDs and entities unparsed (defeating XXE and billion-laughs/exponential-entity-expansion), bounds document size and inflate ratio (DEFLATE-bomb guard), and never panics — a hostile message returns an error verdict, it does not crash the scan. A well-formedness triage verdict reports the reason, and its dtd-present / entity-blocked kinds double as XXE and billion-laughs signals.

**When to reach for it.** Use it whenever you already hold a column of raw or encoded SAML messages and need to shred, verify, or threat-hunt over them at warehouse scale rather than one message at a time in a browser plugin. The signer certificate SHA-256 fingerprint left-joins against your IdP cert inventory, and decoded NameIDs can be scrubbed before sharing extracts when the source data is sensitive.

example_queries.sql: SELECT saml.main.message_type('<samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol"/>') AS kind

tags.vgi.doc_llm: SAML decode and XML-DSig verification functions: decode a message to a struct, explode attribute statements, read the Conditions window and AuthnContext, verify the signature (exclusive C14N + embedded-cert math), enumerate signatures and assertions, flag XSW / Golden-SAML anomalies, triage well-formedness, and decode the base64/DEFLATE/URL transport.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
SAML 2.0 forensic decoding and XML-DSig verification, in-database.

## What it does

Turns an opaque SAML message — a base64 / DEFLATE / URL-encoded blob or raw XML — into typed, queryable rows, and independently re-verifies its cryptographic signature so you can trust (or distrust) what an identity provider asserted, without leaving SQL. Each capability is a separate function that takes one content-sniffed message argument (raw XML, base64, base64+DEFLATE, or a URL-encoded wrapper).

## Key concepts

- **Signature verification is real, not implied.** The outermost XML-DSig signature is re-checked here — SignedInfo is re-canonicalized with exclusive C14N, per-Reference digests are recomputed, and SignatureValue is verified (RSA / ECDSA / EdDSA) against the certificate embedded in the message itself. A validity result reports whether that embedded key signed these exact bytes; it never asserts the key is trusted, so Golden-SAML detection is a downstream JOIN of the signer certificate SHA-256 fingerprint against your own IdP cert inventory. No key store, no network egress.
- **Attack detection.** Structural red flags for XML Signature Wrapping (XSW) and Golden-SAML — multiple assertions, a signature that covers a different element than the consumer reads, duplicate/dangling reference IDs, digest mismatches, comment-splitting NameIDs — surface tampering a naive parser misses.
- **Hostile-input safety.** Every entry point is total and panic-free, with DTD / entity expansion disabled (defeating XXE and billion-laughs) and decompression bomb-bounded.

## When to use

Reach for this schema to audit or bulk-scan SAML responses and assertions offline: confirming who signed a message, reading its subject / issuer / audience / validity window / AuthnContext / attribute statements, checking whether its signature holds, and flagging attack fingerprints — over millions of historical messages, joinable against your cert inventory and login telemetry.

functions.name: well_formed
functions.comment: Triage a SAML blob into STRUCT(ok BOOL, kind VARCHAR, detail VARCHAR); kind is one of ok / not-xml / not-saml / bad-base64 / bad-deflate / dtd-present / entity-blocked / truncated / encoding-error. Never panics.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Classify an attacker-controlled blob into a (ok, kind, detail) triage verdict without ever panicking. `kind` is one of ok, not-xml, not-saml, bad-base64, bad-deflate, dtd-present, entity-blocked, truncated, or encoding-error. The dtd-present and entity-blocked kinds double as XXE / billion-laughs signals: the hardened loader rejects any DOCTYPE/entity before it can be expanded, so their presence is reported rather than processed.

functions.name: signature
functions.comment: Verify the outermost XML-DSig signature: STRUCT(signed, c14n_ok, digest_ok, sig_valid, algo, c14n_method, digest_method, signer_cert BLOB, signer_cert_sha256, signer_subject, signer_issuer, references LIST<STRUCT>). sig_valid is math against the EMBEDDED cert — trust is your JOIN.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run the XML-DSig structural check on a SAML message's outermost signature using exclusive XML canonicalization, and return a struct: signed (is there a signature), digest_ok (do the per-Reference digests match the referenced nodes — i.e. does the signature cover the bytes you think it does), c14n_ok (does SignedInfo canonicalize under a recognized exclusive-C14N method), sig_valid (does SignatureValue verify against the EMBEDDED KeyInfo cert — RSA/ECDSA/EdDSA math), algo (RS256/ES256/EdDSA/…), the c14n/digest method URIs, the signer_cert (DER `BLOB`), signer_cert_sha256 (the join key to your IdP trust table), signer_subject / signer_issuer, and the references list. Crucially, sig_valid=true means only that the embedded cert signed these bytes — NOT that the key is trusted. Detecting Golden SAML (a forgery with a stolen-but-valid IdP key) is a downstream LEFT JOIN of signer_cert_sha256 against your known-good cert inventory.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Structurally verify a SAML signature (exclusive C14N + digest + embedded-cert math) → `(signed, c14n_ok, digest_ok, sig_valid, algo, signer_cert_sha256, …)`. Trust is your JOIN.

functions.comment: Decode a SAML message (raw XML / base64 / base64+DEFLATE / URL-encoded) to a STRUCT of core fields: subject, issuer, audience, conditions window, authn_context, status, ids, counts, and signed. Never errors on bad input — returns null fields + signed=false (see well_formed).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a SAML 2.0 Response or Assertion to a struct of its core fields — response_id / assertion_id, issuer, subject (+ NameID format and SP qualifier), SubjectConfirmation recipient / in_response_to, the Conditions NotBefore / NotOnOrAfter window, audience(s), AuthnInstant / SessionIndex / AuthnContext class, Status, Destination, IssueInstant, Version, the assertion/encrypted counts, and whether a top-level Signature is present. The input is content-sniffed: it accepts raw XML, base64 (HTTP-POST binding), base64+raw-DEFLATE (HTTP-Redirect binding), or a URL-encoded wrapper. It never errors on malformed input — a bad blob yields a struct with null fields and signed=false (call well_formed for the reason). Timestamps are `TIMESTAMPTZ` (UTC); the worker surfaces the window but does not decide 'expired'.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the structural anomaly flags for a SAML message as a `LIST(VARCHAR)`. These are the invariants every XML Signature Wrapping (XSW1-XSW8) attack violates plus the XXE-class text-extraction tells: multiple-assertions, signature-covers-other-element, reference-uri-id-mismatch, unsigned-assertion-in-signed-response, signature-placement-anomaly, detached-signature, nameid-comment-splitting, digest-mismatch, c14n-inclusive-on-moved-assertion, and encrypted-assertion-present. An EMPTY list is not a safety guarantee — Golden SAML (a forgery with a stolen but valid IdP key) leaves no structural trace, so combine this with a trust-table JOIN on signer_cert_sha256.

workers.tagline: Scholarly search across OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref for DuckDB (Python)
workers.summary: Scholarly-literature search across OpenAlex, arXiv, and Crossref, unified for SQL and RAG
workers.doc_md:
# Scholarly Literature Search in SQL

**Search academic papers, preprints, and citations directly from DuckDB/SQL** across [OpenAlex](https://docs.openalex.org), [arXiv](https://arxiv.org), and [Crossref](https://www.crossref.org) — three free, ToS-clean scholarly APIs unified behind one pluggable query surface, with no API key required.

The `scholar` catalog turns the world's open scholarly-metadata graph into ordinary SQL tables. It is built for researchers, data engineers, librarians, and anyone wiring up retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines who would rather write a query than glue together three different REST clients. Every search returns the **same unified result schema** — `title`, `authors`, `abstract`, `doi`, `year`, `published`, `venue`, `citations_count`, `url`, `source`, and a JSON `extra` column — so a query never has to know or care which provider produced a given row. Switch providers with a single named argument and the rest of your SQL stays identical.

Under the hood the worker talks plain HTTP to each provider's public API: the [OpenAlex API](https://docs.openalex.org) (the open catalog of ~250M scholarly works, used by default), the [arXiv API](https://info.arxiv.org/help/api/index.html) for physics, math, and CS preprints, and the [Crossref REST API](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/rest-api/) for DOI-registered publications. Results are fetched page by page and streamed back to DuckDB as Arrow, so large result sets never have to be buffered in full. Pagination cursors round-trip through the worker, retries back off on rate limits, and a provider error surfaces as a clean SQL error rather than crashing the attach.

## Table functions

- `scholar_search(query, provider := 'openalex', count := 10, page_size := 0)` — full-text search scholarly works and stream up to `count` rows in the unified schema. Pass `provider := 'arxiv'` or `provider := 'crossref'` to target a different source.
- `scholar_providers()` — list every provider `scholar_search` can target (also queryable as the table `scholar.main.scholar_providers`), with its keyless and default flags.

## Getting started

Install and load the signed `vgi` community extension, `ATTACH` this worker at a `LOCATION` such as `uv run scholar_worker.py`, and then call the two table functions directly. Ready-to-run, copy-paste queries live in this schema's example queries and in each function's own examples, so they are executed and coverage-checked rather than duplicated inline here.

Typical uses: find papers by topic, resolve and enrich DOIs, gather citation counts, assemble a literature-review corpus, or feed a RAG index — all without leaving SQL. **No API key is required** for any provider; set `VGI_SCHOLAR_MAILTO` to your contact e-mail to join OpenAlex's and Crossref's faster "polite pool".

Powered by [OpenAlex](https://docs.openalex.org) ([source](https://github.com/ourresearch/openalex-guts)), [arXiv](https://arxiv.org) ([API docs](https://info.arxiv.org/help/api/index.html)), and [Crossref](https://www.crossref.org) ([REST API docs](https://github.com/CrossRef/rest-api-doc)).

# scholar.main

Scholarly-literature search over **OpenAlex**, **arXiv**, and **Crossref**, normalized into a single unified schema.

## Functions

- `scholar_search(query, provider := 'openalex', count := 10)` — search works and stream unified-schema rows.
- `scholar_providers()` — list the providers `scholar_search` can target.

## Notes

No API key is required for any provider. Set `VGI_SCHOLAR_MAILTO` to join the OpenAlex / Crossref polite pool. `scholar_search` requires outbound network access; `scholar_providers` is pure metadata and always runs offline.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## scholar_providers (table)

The fixed set of scholarly-search providers that `scholar_search` can target, one row per provider. This is the table form of the `scholar_providers()` function: because it takes no arguments and always returns the same rows, you can read it as a plain table — `scholar.main.scholar_providers`, no parentheses — rather than calling it as a function. Use it to discover the valid values for `scholar_search`'s `provider :=` argument, to find the default provider, or to confirm a provider is keyless before running a search.

Columns: `provider` (the name to pass as `provider := '...'`; unique per row and the table's primary key), `requires_key` (true if the provider needs an API key — all current providers are keyless, so false), and `default` (true for the single provider used when `scholar_search` omits `provider`). Reading this table makes no network calls.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# scholar_providers (table)

Every scholarly-search provider available to `scholar_search`, one row each. This is the table form of the parameterless `scholar_providers()` function.

Read it with no parentheses, e.g. `scholar.main.scholar_providers`, to enumerate the valid `provider :=` values, filter on the `"default"` flag to see which provider is used when a search omits `provider`, or count the `requires_key` column to confirm a provider is keyless. Runnable examples are attached as this table's example queries.

## Columns

- `provider` (`VARCHAR`, primary key) — name to pass as `provider := '...'`.
- `requires_key` (`BOOLEAN`) — whether the provider needs an API key (all v1 providers are keyless).
- `default` (`BOOLEAN`) — whether this is the default provider; exactly one row is true.

## Notes

Reading this table needs no network access, so it is a reliable capability/health probe.

functions.name: scholar_search
functions.comment: Search academic literature (OpenAlex / arXiv / Crossref) into a unified schema

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## scholar_search

Search scholarly / academic literature and stream up to `count` matching works as rows in a single **unified schema**, regardless of which provider answered. Use this whenever an agent needs to find papers by topic, resolve DOIs, gather citation counts, assemble a literature review, or build a corpus for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

### Inputs
- `query` (positional, `VARCHAR`) — free-text search string, e.g. `'retrieval augmented generation'`.
- `provider :=` (`VARCHAR`, default `'openalex'`) — one of `'openalex'`, `'arxiv'`, `'crossref'`. Call `scholar_providers()` to enumerate the valid values.
- `count :=` (`INTEGER`, default 10, 1–1000) — maximum rows to return; the function pages the provider until this budget is met or results are exhausted.
- `page_size :=` (`INTEGER`, default 0, 0–200) — rows fetched per provider request; 0 picks an automatic page size.

### Output
One row per work in the unified schema (`title`, `authors`, `abstract`, `doi`, `year`, `published`, `venue`, `citations_count`, `url`, `source`, `extra`). `authors` is a `LIST<VARCHAR>`, `published` is a UTC `TIMESTAMPTZ`, and `extra` is provider-specific JSON.

### Behavior & edge cases
- No API key is required for any provider; set `VGI_SCHOLAR_MAILTO` to join the OpenAlex / Crossref polite pool.
- An unknown `provider` is rejected at bind time with a clean DuckDB error.
- Provider/network failures surface as a DuckDB error rather than crashing the worker.
- Fields a provider does not supply (e.g. missing `doi` or `abstract`) come back as NULL.
- Requires outbound network access to the provider's public API to return rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# scholar_search

Search scholarly literature across **OpenAlex** (default), **arXiv**, and **Crossref**, returning matches in one normalized schema so SQL never has to branch on the provider.

## Usage

Call it as a table function, passing the free-text query positionally and refining with the named arguments: `provider :=` to pick a source, `count :=` to cap the rows, and `page_size :=` to tune paging. Project the unified columns you need (`title`, `authors`, `year`, `published`, `doi`, `citations_count`, …) and order or filter as usual. Ready-to-run queries are attached as this function's example queries.

## Notes

- `provider` accepts `openalex`, `arxiv`, or `crossref`; `scholar_providers()` lists them.
- `count` (1–1000) caps the rows returned; the function pages the provider transparently.
- No API key is needed. Set `VGI_SCHOLAR_MAILTO` for the polite pool.
- Network access to the provider API is required; provider errors become DuckDB errors.
- Every row uses the unified result schema: `title`, `authors` (`VARCHAR[]`), `abstract`, `doi`, `year`, `published` (`TIMESTAMPTZ`), `venue`, `citations_count`, `url`, `source`, and a JSON `extra` column.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT title, published FROM scholar.main.scholar_search('large language models', provider := 'arxiv', count := 20) ORDER BY published DESC
