workers.title: scikit-bio
workers.tagline: scikit-bio for DuckDB/SQL — sequence analysis, pairwise alignment, community diversity, ordination, and phylogenetics, exposed as a VGI worker
workers.summary: scikit-bio for SQL: sequence analysis, community diversity, ordination, and phylogenetics in DuckDB
workers.doc_md:
# scikit-bio for SQL

Exposes [scikit-bio](https://scikit.bio) to DuckDB/SQL as VGI functions:

- **Sequence** — GC content, reverse complement, translation (incl. six-frame), composition, validation, sequence distances
- **Alignment** — global/local pairwise alignment (scores and aligned strings)
- **Diversity** — the full alpha-diversity metric family (aggregates), beta-diversity matrices, phylogenetic Faith's PD & UniFrac, and rarefaction
- **Stats** — PCA/CA/PCoA ordination, PERMANOVA / ANOSIM / Mantel tests, CLR/ILR/ALR transforms, ANCOM & Dirichlet-multinomial differential abundance
- **Tree** — neighbour joining / UPGMA / minimum evolution, Newick inspection, and tree comparison

example_queries.description: GC content of a DNA sequence.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.gc_content('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS gc;

example_queries.description: Reverse complement of a DNA sequence.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.reverse_complement('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS rc;

example_queries.description: 3-mer composition of two reads (long format).
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM skbio.sequence.kmer_frequencies((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 'ATGCGGATTACAGG'), (2, 'TTGCACGT')) AS reads(id, seq)), id := 'id', k := 3);

example_queries.description: Optimal global alignment score between two DNA sequences.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.alignment.align_score_nucleotide('ACTGGT', 'ACTGT') AS score;

example_queries.description: Faith's phylogenetic diversity per sample given a tree.
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM skbio.diversity.faith_pd((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','f1',1),('s1','f2',1),('s2','f3',1),('s2','f4',1)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), tree := '((f1:0.1,f2:0.2):0.3,(f3:0.15,f4:0.25):0.35);');

example_queries.description: Shannon alpha diversity per sample over a long feature table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.shannon(count) AS shannon FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id;

example_queries.description: Bray-Curtis distance matrix, then a 2-axis PCoA embedding.
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM skbio.stats.pcoa((SELECT * FROM skbio.diversity.beta_diversity((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',1),('s2','a',3),('s2','b',2),('s3','a',0),('s3','b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)))), n_components := 2);

example_queries.description: Global alignment score of two DNA sequences
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.alignment.align_score_nucleotide('ACTGGT', 'ACTGT')

example_queries.description: Align candidate protein sequences against their references and inspect the gapped alignment beside the score. Comparing an imperfect pair with an identical one shows what a 'good' score looks like for this substitution matrix, which a bare score column cannot tell you.
example_queries.sql: SELECT read_id, aligned_1, aligned_2, score, length FROM skbio.alignment.pairwise_align_protein((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('p1', 'MRITMK', 'MRIMK'), ('p2', 'MKVLAA', 'MKVLAA')) AS p(read_id, ref, read)), id := 'read_id', seq1 := 'ref', seq2 := 'read') ORDER BY read_id

example_queries.description: Align each read against its reference and rank the reads by how well they match: the aligned strings show where the gaps ('-') fell, so you can see the indel that the score alone only hints at. Carrying read_id through (id := 'read_id') is what lets the alignment be joined back to the source rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT read_id, aligned_1, aligned_2, score, length FROM skbio.alignment.pairwise_align_nucleotide((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('r1', 'ACTGGT', 'ACTGT'), ('r2', 'GATTACA', 'GATACA')) AS p(read_id, ref, read)), id := 'read_id', seq1 := 'ref', seq2 := 'read') ORDER BY score DESC

example_queries.description: Score two protein sequences under a substitution matrix, so chemically similar amino acids cost less than unrelated ones -- the reason protein similarity cannot be measured by counting identities. Use pairwise_align_protein when the alignment itself matters.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.alignment.align_score_protein('MRITMK', 'MRIMK') AS score

example_queries.description: Shannon diversity per sample
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.shannon(count) FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Order sample pairs by how much evolutionary history they fail to share. Unlike Bray-Curtis, two samples holding different-but-closely-related features come out close together here, which is why UniFrac is the default beta metric for 16S data. Keep the full matrix (drop the filter) to feed pcoa or permanova.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id_1, id_2, round(distance, 4) AS distance FROM skbio.diversity.unifrac((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','f1',1),('s1','f2',1),('s2','f3',1),('s2','f4',1),('s3','f1',1),('s3','f3',1)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), tree := '((f1:0.1,f2:0.2):0.3,(f3:0.15,f4:0.25):0.35);') WHERE id_1 < id_2 ORDER BY distance

example_queries.description: Level two samples sequenced to different depths (12 and 20 counts) down to a common 8, so a later richness or diversity comparison measures biology rather than sequencing effort. Every sample's counts now sum to 8; run this before the alpha metrics, which are all depth-sensitive.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM skbio.diversity.subsample_counts((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',6),('s2','a',10),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',5)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), depth := 8) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

example_queries.description: Rank samples by how much evolutionary history they contain, not just how many features they have. s3 holds one feature from each clade and so spans more of the tree than s1 or s2, whose two features are siblings -- the distinction plain richness cannot make and the reason to pass a tree at all.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, round(faith_pd, 4) AS faith_pd FROM skbio.diversity.faith_pd((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','f1',1),('s1','f2',1),('s2','f3',1),('s2','f4',1),('s3','f1',1),('s3','f3',1)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), tree := '((f1:0.1,f2:0.2):0.3,(f3:0.15,f4:0.25):0.35);') ORDER BY faith_pd DESC

example_queries.description: Rank the sample pairs from most to least similar under Bray-Curtis. The id_1 < id_2 filter keeps one row per unordered pair (the function emits the full square matrix, diagonal included) — drop the filter when feeding pcoa, permanova, or a tree builder, all of which want the whole matrix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id_1, id_2, round(distance, 4) AS distance FROM skbio.diversity.beta_diversity((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9),(3,'a',0),(3,'b',5)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), metric := 'braycurtis') WHERE id_1 < id_2 ORDER BY distance

example_queries.description: Score two communities with brillouin_d in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Brillouin's index, an entropy diversity for a fully-censused (not sampled) community. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.brillouin_d(count) AS brillouin_d FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with simpson_e in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Simpson's evenness, the inverse-Simpson diversity divided by richness, in [0, 1]. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.simpson_e(count) AS simpson_e FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with singles in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the number of features observed exactly once (singletons). Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.singles(count) AS singles FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with simpson_d in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Simpson's dominance index D, the probability that two individuals share a feature. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.simpson_d(count) AS simpson_d FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with simpson in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the chance two random individuals belong to different features (1 minus dominance), in [0, 1]. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.simpson(count) AS simpson FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with osd in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the (observed richness, singletons, doubletons) triple used by richness estimators. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.osd(count) AS osd FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with tsallis in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the Tsallis entropy of order q, a non-extensive generalisation of Shannon entropy. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table. The diversity order `q` (2nd positional arg) is what tunes the metric: q = 0 counts features equally, higher q weights the abundant ones more.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.tsallis(count, 1) AS tsallis FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with chao1 in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It corrects observed richness with the singleton and doubleton counts to estimate unseen features. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.chao1(count) AS chao1 FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with heip_evenness in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Heip's evenness index, a richness-corrected evenness in [0, 1]. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.heip_evenness(count) AS heip_evenness FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with observed_features in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is plain richness: the number of features with a non-zero abundance. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.observed_features(count) AS observed_features FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with menhinick in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Menhinick's richness index: richness divided by the square root of the total count. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.menhinick(count) AS menhinick FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with inv_simpson in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the reciprocal of Simpson's dominance — the effective number of equally-abundant features. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.inv_simpson(count) AS inv_simpson FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with margalef in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Margalef's richness index: richness scaled by the natural log of the total count. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.margalef(count) AS margalef FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with kempton_taylor_q in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the Kempton-Taylor Q index, the slope of the ranked log-abundance curve between its quartiles. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.kempton_taylor_q(count) AS kempton_taylor_q FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with hill in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the Hill number of order q (effective feature count): q=0 richness, q~1 exp(Shannon), q=2 inv-Simpson. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table. The diversity order `q` (2nd positional arg) is what tunes the metric: q = 0 counts features equally, higher q weights the abundant ones more.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.hill(count, 1) AS hill FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with gini_index in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the Gini coefficient of the abundance distribution — the inequality of abundances, in [0, 1]. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.gini_index(count) AS gini_index FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with goods_coverage in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Good's coverage estimate: the estimated proportion of the community that has actually been observed. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.goods_coverage(count) AS goods_coverage FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with robbins in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the Robbins estimator of the probability that the next individual sampled belongs to an unseen feature. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.robbins(count) AS robbins FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with mcintosh_d in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is McIntosh's dominance index, based on the Euclidean norm of the abundance vector. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.mcintosh_d(count) AS mcintosh_d FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with esty_ci in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Esty's confidence interval for the community coverage, as [lower, upper]. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.esty_ci(count) AS esty_ci FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with strong in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Strong's dominance index (DW): the peak departure of the cumulative-abundance curve from evenness. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.strong(count) AS strong FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with mcintosh_e in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is McIntosh's evenness index, in [0, 1]. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.mcintosh_e(count) AS mcintosh_e FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with enspie in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the effective species count from the probability of interspecific encounter (= inverse Simpson). Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.enspie(count) AS enspie FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with dominance in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the chance two random individuals share a feature (Simpson's D); higher means a few dominate. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.dominance(count) AS dominance FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with renyi in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the Renyi entropy of order q, a family of diversity indices generalising richness/Shannon/Simpson. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table. The diversity order `q` (2nd positional arg) is what tunes the metric: q = 0 counts features equally, higher q weights the abundant ones more.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.renyi(count, 1) AS renyi FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with berger_parker_d in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the proportional abundance of the single most abundant feature (Berger-Parker dominance). Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.berger_parker_d(count) AS berger_parker_d FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with pielou_evenness in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Shannon diversity over its maximum, measuring how evenly abundance spreads, in [0, 1]. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.pielou_evenness(count) AS pielou_evenness FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with chao1_ci in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the confidence interval around the Chao1 richness estimate, as [lower, upper]. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.chao1_ci(count) AS chao1_ci FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with ace in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the abundance-based coverage estimator of total richness, weighting the contribution of rare features. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.ace(count) AS ace FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with fisher_alpha in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Fisher's alpha, the parameter of the log-series model fitted to the abundance distribution. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.fisher_alpha(count) AS fisher_alpha FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: Score two communities with doubles in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the number of features observed exactly twice (doubletons). Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.doubles(count) AS doubles FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

example_queries.description: GC content of a DNA sequence
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.gc_content('ATGCGGATTACAGG')

example_queries.description: Break each read down into its per-base counts, in alphabetical order so the two reads line up column-for-column. Reading the A/C/G/T counts side by side is how you spot a skewed or low-complexity read before it distorts a downstream analysis.
example_queries.sql: SELECT read_id, residue, count FROM skbio.sequence.residue_frequencies((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('r1', 'ATGCGGATTACAGG'), ('r2', 'TTGCACGT')) AS reads(read_id, seq)), id := 'read_id') ORDER BY read_id, residue

example_queries.description: Translate a read in all six reading frames and surface the stop-codon-free ones first — the practical way to find the open reading frame when the coding strand and offset are unknown. The residue count shows how long each candidate peptide is.
example_queries.sql: SELECT read_id, frame, protein, length(protein) AS residues FROM skbio.sequence.translate_six_frames((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('r1', 'ATGCGGATTACAGG')) AS reads(read_id, seq)), id := 'read_id') ORDER BY protein NOT LIKE '%*%' DESC, frame

example_queries.description: Profile the 3-mer composition of each read, most frequent k-mer first. This is the building block of alignment-free comparison: the long (read, kmer, count) output PIVOTs straight into a feature matrix for clustering or taxonomic classification.
example_queries.sql: SELECT read_id, kmer, count FROM skbio.sequence.kmer_frequencies((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('r1', 'ATGCGGATTACAGG'), ('r2', 'TTGCACGT')) AS reads(read_id, seq)), id := 'read_id', k := 3) ORDER BY read_id, count DESC, kmer

example_queries.description: Turn a coding sequence into its amino-acid sequence, reading codons from base 0 with the standard genetic code. Note the trailing base that does not complete a codon is simply dropped -- if the frame is unknown, use translate_six_frames instead of guessing this one.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.translate('ATGCGGATTACAGGT') AS protein

example_queries.description: Bring RNA-alphabet sequences (U instead of T) back into DNA space so they can be compared against a DNA reference or run through the DNA-only functions. It is the exact inverse of transcribe.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.reverse_transcribe('AUGCGGAUUACAGG') AS dna

example_queries.description: Count agreeing positions between two equal-length sequences — the complement of mismatch_count (the two always sum to the length). Divide by the length for percent identity, the number most similarity thresholds are quoted in.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.match_count('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS matches

example_queries.description: Screen a text column before running the DNA transforms over it. Contrasting a degenerate-but-valid read (N is a legal IUPAC code) with free text shows where the line is: use it in a WHERE clause so junk rows are filtered rather than silently turning into NULLs downstream.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_valid_dna('ATGCN') AS looks_like_dna, skbio.sequence.is_valid_dna('HELLO') AS looks_like_dna_too

example_queries.description: Count how often a motif occurs in a sequence — here the ATG start codon, three times. This is the cheap way to screen a table of reads for a restriction site, primer binding site, or repeat before spending an alignment on them.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.count_subsequence('ATGCGATGCATG', 'ATG') AS start_codons

example_queries.description: Recover the original sequence from an aligned one by dropping the gap characters an alignment inserted. Run it before length, composition, or k-mer calculations, all of which would otherwise count '-' as if it were a residue.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.degap('AC-GT--A') AS ungapped

example_queries.description: Decide whether two reads are the same sequence seen from opposite strands, in one predicate rather than reverse-complementing one side and comparing. Use it to collapse strand-duplicate reads or to check a primer pair points the right way.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_reverse_complement('ATGC', 'GCAT') AS same_locus

example_queries.description: Flag reads containing ambiguity codes (N, R, Y, ...), i.e. positions the basecaller could not resolve. Filtering these out is a standard quality step before variant calling or exact-match lookups, where an N would otherwise silently fail to match.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.has_degenerates('ACGTN') AS ambiguous_read, skbio.sequence.has_degenerates('ACGT') AS clean_read

example_queries.description: Count G and C bases outright rather than as a fraction. The raw count is what you want when summing across reads or weighting by length; gc_content gives the same information already divided by the sequence length.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.gc_frequency('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS gc_bases

example_queries.description: Produce the RNA transcript of a DNA template (every T becomes U). Use it when a downstream tool or reference is written in RNA alphabet, or as the explicit middle step of the DNA -> RNA -> protein chain that translate otherwise does in one hop.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.transcribe('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS rna

example_queries.description: Count differing positions between a read and its reference as a whole number, which is what edit-distance thresholds are usually expressed in ('accept up to 2 mismatches'). hamming_distance gives the same comparison as a length-normalised fraction.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.mismatch_count('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS mismatches

example_queries.description: Score how far a read has drifted from its reference as a length-normalised fraction, so reads of different lengths stay comparable. One substitution in eight bases gives 0.125; multiply by the length to recover the raw mismatch count. Requires equal lengths -- align first if there are indels.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.hamming_distance('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS distance

example_queries.description: Tell aligned sequences apart from raw ones in a mixed column — the gapped row is the one that came out of an alignment. Use it to decide which rows need degap before a length or composition calculation.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.has_gaps('AC-GT') AS aligned_row, skbio.sequence.has_gaps('ACGT') AS raw_row

example_queries.description: Check a column really holds amino-acid sequences before feeding the protein aligners. Beware the asymmetry this example hints at: a pure A/C/G/T string is *also* valid protein, so pair this with is_valid_dna when you need to tell the two alphabets apart.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_valid_protein('MRIT') AS looks_like_protein, skbio.sequence.is_valid_protein('ATGC1') AS looks_like_protein_too

example_queries.description: Complement each base while keeping 5'->3' order — deliberately *not* the opposite strand. Compare it with reverse_complement on the same input to see the difference that trips people up: only the reversed form is what actually pairs with the original.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.complement('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS comp

example_queries.description: PCoA of a distance matrix

Take log-ratios of a feature table without inventing a pseudocount: rclr excludes zeros from each sample's geometric mean instead of offsetting them. Reach for this rather than clr whenever the table is sparse, as microbiome count tables almost always are.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(rclr, 4) AS rclr FROM skbio.stats.rclr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

example_queries.description: Sharpen a composition by squaring every part and re-closing it: the dominant features gain share and the rare ones lose it, while the result still sums to 1. An exponent below 1 does the opposite (flattens), which is how compositional data is up- or down-weighted without leaving the simplex.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(value, 4) AS value FROM skbio.stats.power((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value)), power := 2.0) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

example_queries.description: Test whether two groups of samples really are separated in community space, end to end: build the Bray-Curtis matrix, join each sample's group label onto id_1, and read off pseudo-F with its permutation p-value. The join is the pattern worth copying — a table function takes one input relation, so the grouping has to ride in as a fourth column rather than a second argument.
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, round(test_statistic, 4) AS pseudo_f, p_value, number_of_groups FROM skbio.stats.permanova((SELECT b.id_1, b.id_2, b.distance, g.grp FROM skbio.diversity.beta_diversity((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',1),('s2','a',3),('s2','b',2),('s3','a',1),('s3','b',8),('s4','a',0),('s4','b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count))) AS b JOIN (VALUES ('s1','x'),('s2','x'),('s3','y'),('s4','y')) AS g(sample, grp) ON b.id_1 = g.sample))

example_queries.description: Collapse a 3-sample distance matrix into two plottable coordinates and order the samples along the leading axis. Rounding keeps the output readable; sorting by pc_1 reads off the dominant gradient — which samples sit at the extremes of the largest source of variation.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, round(pc_1, 4) AS pc_1, round(pc_2, 4) AS pc_2 FROM skbio.stats.pcoa((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','a',0.0),('a','b',0.5),('a','c',0.7),('b','a',0.5),('b','b',0.0),('b','c',0.6),('c','a',0.7),('c','b',0.6),('c','c',0.0)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance)), n_components := 2) ORDER BY pc_1

example_queries.description: Score three samples on the two leading principal components straight from a long feature table — no distance matrix needed, unlike pcoa. Ordering by pc_1 shows which samples the dominant feature gradient separates.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, round(pc_1, 4) AS pc_1, round(pc_2, 4) AS pc_2 FROM skbio.stats.pca((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',2),('s2','a',1),('s2','b',9),('s3','a',0),('s3','b',5)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value)), n_components := 2) ORDER BY pc_1

example_queries.description: Fill in zeros with small positive values while holding every non-zero ratio fixed — the principled alternative to adding an arbitrary pseudocount. Run this before clr, ilr, or alr, all of which are undefined at zero.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(value, 4) AS value FROM skbio.stats.multi_replace((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

example_queries.description: Test whether two dissimilarities measured over the same samples covary — community distance against geographic distance, say. Both matrices ride in as two aligned distance columns over the same id pairs, which is exactly what joining two beta_diversity results on (id_1, id_2) produces.
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, round(correlation, 4) AS correlation, p_value, n FROM skbio.stats.mantel((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','b',0.5,0.4),('a','c',0.7,0.9),('b','c',0.6,0.5)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance_x, distance_y)))

example_queries.description: Rebuild a full composition from its D-1 isometric coordinates — note that 2 input coordinates come back as 3 parts. Pair it with ilr to round-trip: transform, model or perturb in real space, then invert to get proportions again.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature, round(value, 6) AS value FROM skbio.stats.ilr_inv((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1',1,0.1),('s1',2,-0.2),('s2',1,0.3),('s2',2,-0.1)) AS t(sample_id, coordinate, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature

example_queries.description: Report an effect size and a multiple-testing-corrected q-value per feature, most significant first. Prefer this over ancom when you need a direction and magnitude (the log2 fold change) rather than just a ranked W statistic; the seed is fixed, so the numbers are reproducible.
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_id, round(log2_fold_change, 4) AS log2_fold_change, round(qvalue, 4) AS qvalue, significant FROM skbio.stats.dirmult_ttest((SELECT s.sample_id, s.feature_id, s.count, g.grp FROM (VALUES ('s1','b1',12),('s1','b2',11),('s2','b1',9),('s2','b2',11),('s3','b1',1),('s3','b2',11),('s4','b1',22),('s4','b2',21),('s5','b1',20),('s5','b2',22),('s6','b1',23),('s6','b2',21)) AS s(sample_id, feature_id, count) JOIN (VALUES ('s1','x'),('s2','x'),('s3','x'),('s4','y'),('s5','y'),('s6','y')) AS g(sample, grp) ON s.sample_id = g.sample)) ORDER BY qvalue

example_queries.description: Express every part as a log-ratio against one chosen reference feature (here the first by sorted order, via the default ref_idx := 0). Use alr rather than clr or ilr when a genuine reference exists — a spike-in, a housekeeping gene — because then the coordinates stay directly interpretable.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, component, round(value, 4) AS value FROM skbio.stats.alr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, component

example_queries.description: Normalise two samples with different totals (6 and 15 counts) onto a common scale, so their proportions can be compared directly. Closure is the first step of essentially every compositional workflow, and running it alone shows what the later transforms silently assume about their input.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(proportion, 4) AS proportion FROM skbio.stats.closure((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

example_queries.description: Map log-ratio coordinates back to readable proportions that sum to 1 per sample. This is the step that makes a model fitted in clr space reportable: predictions come out as log-ratios, and stakeholders want percentages.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature, round(value, 6) AS value FROM skbio.stats.clr_inv((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1',1,0.1),('s1',2,-0.2),('s2',1,0.3),('s2',2,-0.1)) AS t(sample_id, coordinate, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature

example_queries.description: Move a feature table out of the simplex and into real space, where ordinary statistics (correlation, regression, distance) are meaningful again. A negative clr value means the feature is below its sample's geometric mean, positive above — the sign, not the raw count, is what carries the signal.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(clr, 4) AS clr FROM skbio.stats.clr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

example_queries.description: Rank feature pairs by how tightly they track each other across samples, smallest variance first — the pair at the top moves proportionally and is a candidate for co-occurring taxa. Filtering to feature_1 < feature_2 drops the zero diagonal and the mirrored half of the symmetric matrix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_1, feature_2, round(vlr, 4) AS vlr FROM skbio.stats.pairwise_vlr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6),('s3','a',2),('s3','b',1),('s3','c',7)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) WHERE feature_1 < feature_2 ORDER BY vlr

example_queries.description: Find which features differ between two groups of samples, strongest evidence first. The join is the part worth copying: a table function gets one input relation, so the per-sample group label has to ride in as a fourth column rather than a second argument.
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_id, w, significant FROM skbio.stats.ancom((SELECT s.sample_id, s.feature_id, s.count, g.grp FROM (VALUES ('s1','b1',12),('s1','b2',11),('s2','b1',9),('s2','b2',11),('s3','b1',1),('s3','b2',11),('s4','b1',22),('s4','b2',21),('s5','b1',20),('s5','b2',22),('s6','b1',23),('s6','b2',21)) AS s(sample_id, feature_id, count) JOIN (VALUES ('s1','x'),('s2','x'),('s3','x'),('s4','y'),('s5','y'),('s6','y')) AS g(sample, grp) ON s.sample_id = g.sample)) ORDER BY w DESC

example_queries.description: Ask the same question as permanova but on ranked distances, which makes ANOSIM the more robust choice when the distances are skewed or the groups differ in spread. Its R statistic is directly interpretable on its own scale: near 1 means the groups are well separated, near 0 that the grouping explains nothing.
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, round(test_statistic, 4) AS r_statistic, p_value, number_of_groups FROM skbio.stats.anosim((SELECT b.id_1, b.id_2, b.distance, g.grp FROM skbio.diversity.beta_diversity((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',1),('s2','a',3),('s2','b',2),('s3','a',1),('s3','b',8),('s4','a',0),('s4','b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count))) AS b JOIN (VALUES ('s1','x'),('s2','x'),('s3','y'),('s4','y')) AS g(sample, grp) ON b.id_1 = g.sample))

example_queries.description: Recover the proportions behind D-1 additive log-ratios, restoring the reference part that alr divided everything by. Use the same ref_idx := you transformed with, or the parts come back permuted.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature, round(value, 6) AS value FROM skbio.stats.alr_inv((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1',1,0.1),('s1',2,-0.2),('s2',1,0.3),('s2',2,-0.1)) AS t(sample_id, coordinate, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature

example_queries.description: Turn 3-part compositions into 2 orthonormal coordinates — note the count drops from D to D-1, which is the point: unlike clr, the ilr coordinates are not linearly dependent, so a covariance matrix built from them is invertible and methods like PCA or LDA behave.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, component, round(value, 4) AS value FROM skbio.stats.ilr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, component

example_queries.description: Ordinate a count table with correspondence analysis, the chi-square counterpart of PCA for abundance data. Sorting by ca_1 orders the samples along the strongest compositional gradient, which is what the axis means for count data.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, round(ca_1, 4) AS ca_1, round(ca_2, 4) AS ca_2 FROM skbio.stats.ca((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',2),('s2','a',1),('s2','b',9),('s3','a',3),('s3','b',5)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value)), n_components := 2) ORDER BY ca_1

example_queries.description: Re-express each sample relative to the dataset's average composition rather than its own total: values above 1 are features enriched compared with the typical sample, below 1 depleted. This is the compositional equivalent of subtracting the mean before plotting.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(centered, 4) AS centered FROM skbio.stats.centralize((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

example_queries.description: Tips of a Newick tree
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.tip_count('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);')

example_queries.description: Build a rooted, ultrametric tree — every tip ends up equidistant from the root, so tree_height is the same for all of them. Reach for UPGMA when you want a clustering dendrogram to cut at a threshold, and for neighbor_joining when you want a phylogeny.
example_queries.sql: SELECT newick, skbio.tree.tip_count(newick) AS tips FROM skbio.tree.upgma((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','b',5),('a','c',9),('a','d',9),('b','c',10),('b','d',10),('c','d',8)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance)))

example_queries.description: Turn a pairwise distance matrix into an actual tree, then check it round-tripped by counting its tips. Neighbour joining is the default choice when the distances come from real data and no molecular clock can be assumed; feed it a beta_diversity matrix to get a sample dendrogram straight out of SQL.
example_queries.sql: SELECT newick, skbio.tree.tip_count(newick) AS tips FROM skbio.tree.neighbor_joining((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','b',5),('a','c',9),('a','d',9),('b','c',10),('b','d',10),('c','d',8)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance)))

example_queries.description: Build a minimum-evolution tree greedily, which is the one to reach for when the matrix is large enough that neighbour joining's cubic cost hurts. On a small matrix like this one it agrees with the others; the tip count confirms no taxa were dropped.
example_queries.sql: SELECT newick, skbio.tree.tip_count(newick) AS tips FROM skbio.tree.gme((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','b',5),('a','c',9),('a','d',9),('b','c',10),('b','d',10),('c','d',8)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance)))

example_queries.description: Build the balanced-minimum-evolution tree (the criterion FastME optimises), which is usually more accurate than greedy ME at a similar cost. Compare its output against neighbor_joining with robinson_foulds to see whether the method choice changed the topology at all.
example_queries.sql: SELECT newick, skbio.tree.tip_count(newick) AS tips FROM skbio.tree.bme((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','b',5),('a','c',9),('a','d',9),('b','c',10),('b','d',10),('c','d',8)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance)))

example_queries.description: Compare two trees on topology *and* branch lengths, so a pair that groups taxa identically but stretches a branch still scores non-zero. Use this rather than robinson_foulds when the lengths carry meaning — divergence times, substitution rates — and not just the grouping.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.weighted_robinson_foulds('((a:1,b:1):1,(c:1,d:1):1);', '((a:1,c:1):1,(b:1,d:1):1);') AS wrf_distance

example_queries.description: Measure how much evolutionary change a tree encodes in total. Over a tree pruned to one sample's features this is exactly Faith's PD, which makes it the way to compute phylogenetic diversity when you already hold the subtree rather than a feature table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.total_branch_length('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS branch_length

example_queries.description: Size a tree without leaving SQL — the quickest sanity check that a builder kept every taxon, and the denominator for anything you normalise per tip. Point it at a column of Newick strings to profile a whole table of trees.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.tip_count('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS tips

example_queries.description: Ask whether two trees group the same taxa together, ignoring branch lengths entirely: these two disagree on whether a pairs with b or with c, so the distance is non-zero. This is the standard way to check whether two reconstruction methods, or two bootstrap replicates, found the same shape.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.robinson_foulds('((a,b),(c,d));', '((a,c),(b,d));') AS rf_distance

example_queries.description: Read the deepest root-to-tip distance, i.e. how far back the tree reaches. On an ultrametric tree (anything from upgma) every tip sits at this height, so comparing it with a tip's own depth is a quick test of ultrametricity.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.tree_height('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS height

example_queries.description: Compare two trees by the tip-to-tip distances they imply, rather than by their splits. It answers the question that actually matters downstream — do these trees place the taxa at the same distances from each other? — and so reacts to the long branches in the second tree that robinson_foulds ignores.
example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.cophenetic_distance('((a:1,b:1):1,(c:1,d:1):1);', '((a:1,c:1):5,(b:1,d:1):5);') AS cophenetic_distance

Globally align the DNA read 'ACTGT' against the reference 'ACTGGT' and show the actual alignment. Return a single row with three columns: aligned_1 (the reference with alignment gaps), aligned_2 (the read with alignment gaps), and score.

Globally align the protein sequence 'MRIMK' against the reference 'MRITMK' and show the actual alignment. Return a single row with three columns: aligned_1 (the reference with alignment gaps), aligned_2 (the query with alignment gaps), and score.

Given the feature counts (1,'a',4), (1,'b',0), (1,'c',3) as (sample_id, feature_id, count) for sample 1, how many features are observed (have a non-zero count)? Return a single row with one integer column named richness.

Return a single row with six columns rounded to 4 decimal places: chao1, ace, singletons (features seen exactly once), doubletons (features seen exactly twice), chao1_lower and chao1_upper (the lower and upper bounds of the Chao1 confidence interval).

One sample has the feature counts (a,4), (b,2), (c,1), (d,1), (e,3), (f,7) as (feature_id, count). Return the OSD triple — observed richness, singletons, doubletons — as a single row with three columns named observed, singletons and doubletons.

One sample has the feature counts (a,4), (b,2), (c,1), (d,1), (e,3), (f,7) as (feature_id, count). How evenly is abundance spread across its features? Return a single row with five columns rounded to 4 decimal places: pielou, heip, simpson_e, mcintosh_e and gini.

One sample has the feature counts (a,4), (b,2), (c,1), (d,1), (e,3), (f,7) as (feature_id, count). Measure how much the community is dominated by its commonest features. Return a single row with six columns rounded to 4 decimal places: dominance, simpson, simpson_d, inv_simpson, enspie and berger_parker.

One sample has the feature counts (a,4), (b,2), (c,1), (d,1), (e,3), (f,7) as (feature_id, count). Return a single row with two columns rounded to 4 decimal places: mcintosh_d (McIntosh's dominance index) and strong (Strong's dominance index).

One sample has the feature counts (a,4), (b,2), (c,1), (d,1), (e,3), (f,7) as (feature_id, count). Return its entropy-family diversity as a single row with two columns rounded to 4 decimal places: shannon and brillouin.

One sample has the feature counts (a,4), (b,2), (c,1), (d,1), (e,3), (f,7) as (feature_id, count). Compute the three diversity metrics that take a diversity order q, all at q = 2. Return a single row with three columns rounded to 4 decimal places: hill, renyi and tsallis.

One sample has the feature counts (a,4), (b,2), (c,1), (d,1), (e,3), (f,7) as (feature_id, count). Return the sample-size-corrected richness indices as a single row with four columns rounded to 4 decimal places: margalef, menhinick, fisher_alpha and kempton_taylor.

One sample has the feature counts (a,4), (b,2), (c,1), (d,1), (e,3), (f,7) as (feature_id, count). How much of the community has been observed? Return a single row with four columns rounded to 4 decimal places: goods_coverage, robbins, esty_lower and esty_upper (the lower and upper bounds of Esty's coverage confidence interval).

From the feature table (s1,'a',4), (s1,'b',1), (s2,'a',3), (s2,'b',2), (s3,'a',0), (s3,'b',9) as (sample_id, feature_id, count), build the Bray-Curtis between-sample distance matrix. How many rows does the full matrix have? Return a single row with one column named n.

Given the feature table (s1,f1,1), (s1,f2,1), (s2,f3,1), (s2,f4,1), (s3,f1,1), (s3,f3,1) as (sample_id, feature_id, count) and the tree '((f1:0.1,f2:0.2):0.3,(f3:0.15,f4:0.25):0.35);', compute Faith's phylogenetic diversity of each sample, rounded to 4 decimals. Return columns sample_id and faith_pd, ordered by sample_id.

Given the feature table (s1,f1,1), (s1,f2,1), (s2,f3,1), (s2,f4,1), (s3,f1,1), (s3,f3,1) as (sample_id, feature_id, count) and the tree '((f1:0.1,f2:0.2):0.3,(f3:0.15,f4:0.25):0.35);', compute the unweighted UniFrac distance between every distinct pair of samples (exclude the diagonal and report each unordered pair once, with the alphabetically smaller id first). Return columns id_1, id_2 and distance rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by id_1 then id_2.

Rarefy the feature table (s1,'a',4), (s1,'b',2), (s1,'c',6), (s2,'a',10), (s2,'b',5), (s2,'c',5) as (sample_id, feature_id, count) to a common depth of 8 counts per sample, using the default seed. Return the rarefied table with columns sample_id, feature_id and count, ordered by sample_id then feature_id.

Given the feature table (s1,a,4), (s1,b,2), (s1,c,1), (s2,a,1), (s2,b,9), (s2,c,2) as (sample_id, feature_id, count), build the Bray-Curtis distance matrix and embed the samples on 2 principal coordinate axes. Return columns sample_id and pc_1 rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id.

Given the long feature table (s1,a,4), (s1,b,2), (s1,c,1), (s2,a,1), (s2,b,9), (s2,c,2) as (sample_id, feature_id, value), run a principal components analysis directly on the feature values (no distance matrix) with 2 components. Return columns sample_id and pc_1 rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id.

Given the long count table (s1,a,4), (s1,b,2), (s1,c,1), (s2,a,1), (s2,b,9), (s2,c,2) as (sample_id, feature_id, value), run a correspondence analysis with 2 axes. Return columns sample_id and ca_1 rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id.

Return a single row with two columns: pseudo_f, the test statistic rounded to 4 decimals, and n_groups, the number of distinct groups. Return columns sample_id, feature and value rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id then feature.

Given the long feature table (s1,a,1), (s1,b,2), (s1,c,3), (s2,a,4), (s2,b,5), (s2,c,6) as (sample_id, feature_id, value), apply the isometric log-ratio transform and then invert it back to a composition. Return columns sample_id, feature and value rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id then feature.

Return columns sample_id, feature and value rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id then feature.

Return columns sample_id, feature_id and centered rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id then feature_id.

Replace its zeros with small positive values by multiplicative replacement, keeping every non-zero ratio intact. Return columns sample_id, feature_id and value rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id then feature_id.

Apply the robust centred log-ratio transform, which handles the zeros without a pseudocount. Return columns sample_id, feature_id and rclr rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by sample_id then feature_id.

Return columns feature_1, feature_2 and vlr rounded to 4 decimals, ordered by feature_1 then feature_2.

Run the ANCOM differential-abundance test. Return one row per feature with columns feature_id, w and significant, ordered by feature_id.

Run the Dirichlet-multinomial t-test for differential abundance. Return one row per feature with columns feature_id, log2_fold_change rounded to 4 decimals, and significant, ordered by feature_id.
How many tips (leaves) are in the Newick tree '((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);'? Return a single row with one column named tips.

Build a neighbour-joining tree from the distance matrix (a,b,5), (a,c,9), (a,d,9), (b,c,10), (b,d,10), (c,d,8) given as (id_1, id_2, distance). Return a single row with two columns: newick, the tree in Newick format, and tips, the number of tips in it.

Return a single row with two columns rounded to 4 decimal places: total_length, the sum of all its branch lengths, and height, its maximum root-to-tip distance.

From the distance matrix (a,b,5), (a,c,9), (a,d,9), (b,c,10), (b,d,10), (c,d,8) given as (id_1, id_2, distance), build one tree with greedy minimum evolution and another with balanced minimum evolution, then compare them. Return a single row with one column named rf_distance holding the Robinson-Foulds distance between the two topologies.

Compare the two Newick trees '((a:1,b:1):1,(c:1,d:1):1);' and '((a:1,c:1):5,(b:1,d:1):5);' in the two branch-length-aware ways. Return a single row with two columns rounded to 4 decimal places: wrf, their weighted Robinson-Foulds distance, and cophenetic, their cophenetic distance.

schemas.name: alignment
schemas.comment: Pairwise sequence alignment: scores and aligned strings.

vgi.categories.name: score
vgi.categories.description: Optimal alignment score between two sequences.

vgi.categories.name: pairwise
vgi.categories.description: Aligned sequence pair (aligned strings + score).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Pairwise alignment of biological sequences. Reach here to score how similar two DNA or protein sequences are (optimal global-alignment score, per row) or to produce the actual alignment — the two sequences padded with gaps plus the score and aligned length — in global (Needleman-Wunsch) or local (Smith-Waterman) mode. Sequences are plain `VARCHAR` columns; a NULL or unparseable pair yields NULL rather than failing the query.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
### Sequence alignment

Align pairs of DNA or protein sequences:

- **Score** — optimal global-alignment score per row (a similarity measure)
- **Pairwise** — the aligned strings (gaps as `-`) plus score and length, global or local

Inputs are plain `VARCHAR` columns; malformed pairs degrade to NULL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Global alignment score of two DNA sequences
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.alignment.align_score_nucleotide('ACTGGT', 'ACTGT')

tags.vgi.title: Sequence Alignment

functions.name: pairwise_align_protein
functions.comment: Pairwise align two protein columns; emit aligned strings and score

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function performing pairwise alignment of two protein sequence columns and emitting the aligned strings, the score, and the aligned length, one row per input pair. The table arg is `(SELECT id?, seq1_col, seq2_col FROM ...)`; `seq1 :=`/`seq2 :=` name the two protein columns (default the first two non-id columns), `id :=` an optional carried id, and `mode :=` picks `global` (default) or `local`. Uses scikit-bio's default substitution matrix; gaps are `-`, and a NULL or non-protein pair yields NULL. Use `align_score_protein` for just the score.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**pairwise_align_protein** — align two protein columns, aligned strings + score.

- Table arg: `(SELECT id?, seq1, seq2 FROM ...)`; `seq1 :=`/`seq2 :=` the protein columns, `id :=` optional, `mode :=` `global` (default) or `local`
- Returns `(id?, aligned_1, aligned_2, score, length)`; gaps shown as `-`
- NULL/non-protein pairs yield NULL; `align_score_protein` returns just the score

vgi.example_queries.description: Align candidate protein sequences against their references and inspect the gapped alignment beside the score. Comparing an imperfect pair with an identical one shows what a 'good' score looks like for this substitution matrix, which a bare score column cannot tell you.

- Inputs: two `VARCHAR` DNA columns (case-insensitive)

Reach for this when you only need the number -- pairwise_align_nucleotide when you need to see where the gap fell.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.alignment.align_score_nucleotide('ACTGGT', 'ACTGT') AS score

schemas.name: diversity
schemas.comment: Community-ecology diversity from a long (sample, feature, count) table.

vgi.categories.name: alpha
vgi.categories.description: Per-sample diversity of one community, as aggregates.

vgi.categories.name: beta
vgi.categories.description: Between-sample community distances, as a matrix.

vgi.categories.name: phylogenetic
vgi.categories.description: Tree-aware diversity (Faith's PD, UniFrac).

vgi.categories.name: preprocessing
vgi.categories.description: Prepare a feature table (rarefaction).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Quantify community diversity from a long feature table — one row per (sample, feature, count), the shape a microbiome or OTU/ASV study naturally produces. Reach here to measure how diverse each individual sample is (alpha diversity, the full scikit-bio metric family computed as aggregates so a GROUP BY over the sample id yields one value per sample), how different samples are from one another (beta diversity, a between-sample distance matrix emitted in long form), and their tree-aware counterparts (Faith's phylogenetic diversity and UniFrac, which take a Newick tree argument). It also rarefies feature tables to a common depth. The distance matrix is the input other areas consume for ordination, group tests, and tree building.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
### Community diversity

From a long `(sample, feature, count)` feature table:

- **Alpha** — per-sample diversity (the full metric family), as aggregates you `GROUP BY sample_id`
- **Beta** — a between-sample distance matrix, emitted long for downstream ordination, group tests, and tree building
- **Phylogenetic** — Faith's PD and UniFrac (given a Newick tree)
- **Preprocessing** — rarefy each sample to a common depth

vgi.example_queries.description: Shannon diversity per sample
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.shannon(count) FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id

tags.vgi.title: Community Diversity

functions.name: unifrac
functions.comment: UniFrac phylogenetic distance matrix between samples (needs a tree)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function computing the UniFrac phylogenetic distance matrix between samples and emitting it long: one row per ordered sample pair. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3) and `tree :=` is a Newick tree whose tips are the feature ids. UniFrac measures how much evolutionary history two communities do NOT share; `weighted := true` weights branches by abundance (weighted UniFrac), otherwise presence/absence (unweighted, the default). Returns `(id_1, id_2, distance)` for the full matrix — feed it into `skbio.stats.pcoa` or `skbio.stats.permanova`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**UniFrac** — phylogenetic between-sample distance matrix.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3)
- `tree :=` — a Newick tree whose tips are the feature ids; `weighted :=` for weighted UniFrac (default unweighted)
- Returns the full matrix long: `id_1`, `id_2`, `distance` — feed to `pcoa`/`permanova`
- Measures unshared evolutionary history between communities

vgi.example_queries.description: Order sample pairs by how much evolutionary history they fail to share. Unlike Bray-Curtis, two samples holding different-but-closely-related features come out close together here, which is why UniFrac is the default beta metric for 16S data. Keep the full matrix (drop the filter) to feed pcoa or permanova.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id_1, id_2, round(distance, 4) AS distance FROM skbio.diversity.unifrac((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','f1',1),('s1','f2',1),('s2','f3',1),('s2','f4',1),('s3','f1',1),('s3','f3',1)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), tree := '((f1:0.1,f2:0.2):0.3,(f3:0.15,f4:0.25):0.35);') WHERE id_1 < id_2 ORDER BY distance

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: id_2
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Second sample id.

functions.name: subsample_counts
functions.comment: Rarefy each sample's feature counts to a fixed depth (long output)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function performing rarefaction: it subsamples each sample's feature counts down to a fixed depth (`depth :=`) so that every sample has the same total count — the standard way to remove sequencing-depth bias before comparing diversity. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3). Samples whose total is below `depth` are dropped. Sampling is without replacement by default (`with_replacement :=` to change) and uses a fixed `seed :=` for reproducibility. Returns the rarefied `(sample_id, feature_id, count)` table.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**subsample_counts** — rarefy each sample to a fixed depth.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3)
- `depth :=` — counts to draw per sample; samples below it are dropped
- `with_replacement :=` (default false), `seed :=` (fixed for reproducibility)
- Returns the rarefied `(sample_id, feature_id, count)` table (removes depth bias)

vgi.example_queries.description: Level two samples sequenced to different depths (12 and 20 counts) down to a common 8, so a later richness or diversity comparison measures biology rather than sequencing effort. Every sample's counts now sum to 8; run this before the alpha metrics, which are all depth-sensitive.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM skbio.diversity.subsample_counts((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',6),('s2','a',10),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',5)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), depth := 8) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

functions.name: faith_pd
functions.comment: Faith's phylogenetic diversity per sample (needs a tree)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function computing Faith's phylogenetic diversity (PD) of each sample: the total branch length of the sub-tree spanning the features present in that sample. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3) and `tree :=` is a Newick tree whose tip names are the feature ids. Unlike the non-phylogenetic richness metrics, PD credits samples for containing evolutionarily distinct features. Returns one `(sample_id, faith_pd)` row per sample; a feature missing from the tree raises an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**faith_pd** — Faith's phylogenetic diversity per sample.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3)
- `tree :=` — a Newick tree whose tips are the feature ids
- Returns `(sample_id, faith_pd)`: branch length spanned by each sample's features
- Rewards evolutionarily distinct features (unlike plain richness)

vgi.example_queries.description: Rank samples by how much evolutionary history they contain, not just how many features they have. s3 holds one feature from each clade and so spans more of the tree than s1 or s2, whose two features are siblings -- the distinction plain richness cannot make and the reason to pass a tree at all.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, round(faith_pd, 4) AS faith_pd FROM skbio.diversity.faith_pd((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','f1',1),('s1','f2',1),('s2','f3',1),('s2','f4',1),('s3','f1',1),('s3','f3',1)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), tree := '((f1:0.1,f2:0.2):0.3,(f3:0.15,f4:0.25):0.35);') ORDER BY faith_pd DESC

functions.name: beta_diversity
functions.comment: Between-sample distance matrix from a long feature table (long output)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function computing the between-sample beta-diversity distance matrix from a long feature table and emitting it long: one row per ordered sample pair. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3; override with `sample :=`, `feature :=`, `count :=`), and `metric :=` chooses the distance (default `braycurtis`; also `jaccard`, `euclidean`, `cityblock`, `canberra`, `cosine`, `hamming`, ...). The counts are pivoted to a samples x features abundance matrix (missing cells are 0) and every pairwise distance is computed. Returns `(id_1, id_2, distance)` for the full matrix (including the zero diagonal) — feed it straight into `skbio.stats.pcoa` or `skbio.stats.permanova`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Beta diversity** — between-sample distance matrix, long output.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default; override with `sample :=`/`feature :=`/`count :=`)
- `metric :=` — `braycurtis` (default), `jaccard`, `euclidean`, `cityblock`, `canberra`, `cosine`, `hamming`, ...
- Returns the full matrix long: `id_1`, `id_2`, `distance` (`DOUBLE`)
- Missing (sample, feature) cells count as 0; feed the output to `pcoa` / `permanova`

vgi.example_queries.description: Rank the sample pairs from most to least similar under Bray-Curtis. The id_1 < id_2 filter keeps one row per unordered pair (the function emits the full square matrix, diagonal included) — drop the filter when feeding pcoa, permanova, or a tree builder, all of which want the whole matrix.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id_1, id_2, round(distance, 4) AS distance FROM skbio.diversity.beta_diversity((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9),(3,'a',0),(3,'b',5)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count)), metric := 'braycurtis') WHERE id_1 < id_2 ORDER BY distance

functions.name: brillouin_d
functions.comment: brillouin_d alpha-diversity metric over one sample's feature counts

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Aggregate computing the **brillouin_d** alpha-diversity metric over one sample's feature abundance values. It is Brillouin's index, an entropy diversity for a fully-censused (not sampled) community. Pass the `count` column of a long feature table and `GROUP BY` the sample id, so each group yields one result; NULL rows are skipped and values are rounded to integers. Returns a single `DOUBLE` per sample.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**brillouin_d** — It is Brillouin's index, an entropy diversity for a fully-censused (not sampled) community.

- Input: the `count` column of a long `(sample, feature, count)` table
- Use `GROUP BY sample_id` to get one result per sample
- Returns a single `DOUBLE` per sample; NULL rows skipped, values rounded to integers

vgi.example_queries.description: Score two communities with brillouin_d in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is Brillouin's index, an entropy diversity for a fully-censused (not sampled) community. Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.brillouin_d(count) AS brillouin_d FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

arguments.name: abundance
arguments.description: Abundance value for one (sample, feature) cell

examples: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.brillouin_d(count) AS brillouin_d FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

functions.name: simpson_e
functions.comment: simpson_e alpha-diversity metric over one sample's feature counts

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Aggregate computing the **simpson_e** alpha-diversity metric over one sample's feature abundance values. It is Simpson's evenness, the inverse-Simpson diversity divided by richness, in [0, 1]. Pass the `count` column of a long feature table and `GROUP BY` the sample id, so each group yields one result; NULL rows are skipped and values are rounded to integers. Returns a single `DOUBLE` per sample.
