functions.comment: doubles alpha-diversity metric over one sample's feature counts

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Aggregate computing the **doubles** alpha-diversity metric over one sample's feature abundance values. It is the number of features observed exactly twice (doubletons). Pass the `count` column of a long feature table and `GROUP BY` the sample id, so each group yields one result; NULL rows are skipped and values are rounded to integers. Returns a single `DOUBLE` per sample.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**doubles** — It is the number of features observed exactly twice (doubletons).

- Input: the `count` column of a long `(sample, feature, count)` table
- Use `GROUP BY sample_id` to get one result per sample
- Returns a single `DOUBLE` per sample; NULL rows skipped, values rounded to integers

vgi.example_queries.description: Score two communities with doubles in a single GROUP BY: sample 1 spreads 7 counts over three features, sample 2 puts 9 of its 10 into one, and the metric is what separates them. It is the number of features observed exactly twice (doubletons). Being an aggregate rather than a table function is the point — one query scores every sample in the table.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.doubles(count) AS doubles FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

arguments.name: abundance
arguments.description: Abundance value for one (sample, feature) cell

examples: SELECT sample_id, skbio.diversity.doubles(count) AS doubles FROM (VALUES (1,'a',4),(1,'b',2),(1,'c',1),(2,'a',1),(2,'b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count) GROUP BY sample_id ORDER BY sample_id

schemas.name: sequence
schemas.comment: Analyze DNA, RNA, and protein sequences held in `VARCHAR` columns.

vgi.categories.name: transforms
vgi.categories.description: Derive a new sequence from a DNA input (complement, transcribe, translate).

vgi.categories.name: validation
vgi.categories.description: Check whether a string is a valid sequence of a given type.

vgi.categories.name: distance
vgi.categories.description: Compare two sequences position by position.

vgi.categories.name: composition
vgi.categories.description: Break a sequence into per-token counts (k-mers, residues).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Analyze biological sequences — DNA, RNA, or protein — stored one per row in ordinary `VARCHAR` columns. Reach for this area to derive new sequences (base complementation, transcription, codon translation), measure composition (GC fraction, k-mer and single-residue profiles as long token-count tables), compare reads to a reference, or validate that a string really is a sequence of a given alphabet. Inputs are case-insensitive and whitespace-tolerant; a NULL or malformed sequence yields NULL rather than failing the query, so the functions are safe over messy real-world reads.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
### Biological sequences

Work with DNA, RNA, and protein sequences directly in SQL — one sequence per `VARCHAR` cell.

- **Derive** new sequences (complementation, transcription, codon translation)
- **Measure** composition (GC fraction, k-mer and residue profiles)
- **Compare** reads and **validate** alphabets

Case-insensitive; malformed or NULL input degrades to NULL instead of erroring.

vgi.example_queries.description: GC content of a DNA sequence
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.gc_content('ATGCGGATTACAGG')

tags.vgi.title: Biological Sequences

functions.name: residue_frequencies
functions.comment: Count single residues (bases or amino acids) per sequence (long format)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function that counts single residues (nucleotide bases or amino acids) in each input sequence and emits them long: one row per distinct residue per sequence. The table arg is `(SELECT id_col, seq_col FROM ...)`; `sequence :=` names the string column (defaults to the single non-id column) and `id :=` an optional id carried onto each row. Uses scikit-bio's generic sequence, so DNA/RNA/protein all work. Returns `(id?, residue, count)` — the composition of each sequence; sum, or pivot to a wide base-count matrix. Equivalent to a 1-mer `kmer_frequencies`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Residue frequencies** — single base/amino-acid counts per sequence, long format.

- Table arg: `(SELECT id, seq FROM ...)`; `sequence :=` the string column, `id :=` an optional carried id
- Returns one row per distinct residue per sequence (plus the carried `id` if given):
  - `residue` — a single base or amino acid
  - `count` (`BIGINT`) — occurrences in that sequence
- Works for DNA/RNA/protein; the 1-mer case of `kmer_frequencies`

vgi.example_queries.description: Break each read down into its per-base counts, in alphabetical order so the two reads line up column-for-column. Reading the A/C/G/T counts side by side is how you spot a skewed or low-complexity read before it distorts a downstream analysis.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT read_id, residue, count FROM skbio.sequence.residue_frequencies((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('r1', 'ATGCGGATTACAGG'), ('r2', 'TTGCACGT')) AS reads(read_id, seq)), id := 'read_id') ORDER BY read_id, residue

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
#### Default -- no `id :=`

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `residue` | VARCHAR | A single residue (base or amino acid). |
| `count` | BIGINT | Number of occurrences in the sequence. |

#### With `id := 'read_id'` (a `VARCHAR` id column)

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read_id` | VARCHAR | The named id column, repeated on every row for that sequence. |
| `residue` | VARCHAR | A single residue (base or amino acid). |
| `count` | BIGINT | Number of occurrences in the sequence. |

The carried column takes the *name and type* of the input column named by `id :=`; the second variant shows the common case of a `VARCHAR` read id.

functions.name: translate_six_frames
functions.comment: Translate each DNA sequence in all six reading frames (long format)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function translating each input DNA sequence in all six reading frames — the three forward frames (+1, +2, +3, offset by 0/1/2 bases) and the three reverse-complement frames (-1, -2, -3) — and emitting them long: six rows per sequence. The table arg is `(SELECT id_col, seq_col FROM ...)`; `sequence :=` names the DNA column (defaults to the single non-id column) and `id :=` an optional id carried onto each row. Returns `(id?, frame, protein)` where a stop codon is `*`. Use it to scan for open reading frames when the coding frame/strand is unknown.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**translate_six_frames** — six-frame protein translation of DNA.

- Table arg: `(SELECT id, seq FROM ...)`; `sequence :=` the DNA column, `id :=` optional
- Returns six rows per sequence (plus the carried `id`):
  - `frame` — `+1`/`+2`/`+3` (forward) or `-1`/`-2`/`-3` (reverse complement)
  - `protein` — the amino-acid translation (stops as `*`)
- Scan for open reading frames when the coding strand/frame is unknown

vgi.example_queries.description: Translate a read in all six reading frames and surface the stop-codon-free ones first — the practical way to find the open reading frame when the coding strand and offset are unknown. The residue count shows how long each candidate peptide is.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT read_id, frame, protein, length(protein) AS residues FROM skbio.sequence.translate_six_frames((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('r1', 'ATGCGGATTACAGG')) AS reads(read_id, seq)), id := 'read_id') ORDER BY protein NOT LIKE '%*%' DESC, frame

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frame` | VARCHAR | Reading frame: +1/+2/+3 (forward) or -1/-2/-3 (reverse). |
| `protein` | VARCHAR | The amino-acid translation for that frame (stops as '*'). |

#### With `id := 'read_id'` (a `VARCHAR` id column)

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read_id` | VARCHAR | The named id column, repeated on every row for that sequence. |
| `frame` | VARCHAR | Reading frame: +1/+2/+3 (forward) or -1/-2/-3 (reverse). |
| `protein` | VARCHAR | The amino-acid translation for that frame (stops as '*'). |

The carried column takes the *name and type* of the input column named by `id :=`; the second variant shows the common case of a `VARCHAR` read id.

functions.name: kmer_frequencies
functions.comment: Count overlapping k-mers per sequence (long format)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function that counts overlapping k-mers (length-`k` subsequences) in each input sequence and emits them long: one row per distinct k-mer per sequence. The table arg is `(SELECT id_col, seq_col FROM ...)`; `sequence :=` names the string column (defaults to the single non-id column), `id :=` an optional id carried onto each row, and `k :=` the k-mer length (default 3). Uses scikit-bio's generic sequence, so DNA/RNA/protein all work. Returns `(id?, kmer, count)` where `count` is the overlapping occurrence count — pivot back to a wide k-mer matrix (a feature table for clustering/classification), or aggregate per k-mer across sequences.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**k-mer frequencies** — overlapping length-`k` token counts per sequence, long format.

- Table arg: `(SELECT id, seq FROM ...)`; `sequence :=` the string column, `id :=` an optional carried id, `k :=` the k-mer length (default 3)
- Returns one row per distinct k-mer per sequence (plus the carried `id` if given):
  - `kmer` — a length-`k` subsequence
  - `count` (`BIGINT`) — overlapping occurrences in that sequence
- Works for DNA/RNA/protein; `PIVOT` for a wide k-mer feature matrix

vgi.example_queries.description: Profile the 3-mer composition of each read, most frequent k-mer first. This is the building block of alignment-free comparison: the long (read, kmer, count) output PIVOTs straight into a feature matrix for clustering or taxonomic classification.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT read_id, kmer, count FROM skbio.sequence.kmer_frequencies((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('r1', 'ATGCGGATTACAGG'), ('r2', 'TTGCACGT')) AS reads(read_id, seq)), id := 'read_id', k := 3) ORDER BY read_id, count DESC, kmer

functions.name: translate
functions.comment: Translate a DNA sequence to protein (standard genetic code)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function translating a DNA sequence to its amino-acid sequence as a `VARCHAR`, reading successive codons from the first base with the standard genetic code (NCBI table 1); a stop codon is emitted as `*`. Pass one DNA column (case-insensitive). Trailing bases that do not complete a codon are ignored. NULL or non-DNA input returns NULL. Pair with `transcribe` for the RNA intermediate.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Translate** — DNA to protein via the standard genetic code.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` DNA column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: the amino-acid sequence as `VARCHAR` (stop codons as `*`)
- Reads codons from base 0; trailing partial codon ignored; NULL for NULL/non-DNA input

vgi.example_queries.description: Turn a coding sequence into its amino-acid sequence, reading codons from base 0 with the standard genetic code. Note the trailing base that does not complete a codon is simply dropped -- if the frame is unknown, use translate_six_frames instead of guessing this one.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.translate('ATGCGGATTACAGGT') AS protein

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.translate('ATGCGGATTACAGGT') AS protein

functions.name: reverse_transcribe
functions.comment: Reverse transcribe an RNA sequence to DNA (U -> T)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function reverse-transcribing an RNA sequence to DNA as a `VARCHAR`, replacing every uracil (U) with thymine (T) — the inverse of `transcribe`. Pass one `VARCHAR` RNA column (case-insensitive); NULL or non-RNA input returns NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**reverse_transcribe** — RNA to DNA (U becomes T).

- Input: one `VARCHAR` RNA column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: the DNA sequence as `VARCHAR` (NULL for NULL/non-RNA input)
- The inverse of `transcribe`

vgi.example_queries.description: Bring RNA-alphabet sequences (U instead of T) back into DNA space so they can be compared against a DNA reference or run through the DNA-only functions. It is the exact inverse of transcribe.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.reverse_transcribe('AUGCGGAUUACAGG') AS dna

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: An RNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.reverse_transcribe('AUGCGGAUUACAGG') AS dna

functions.name: reverse_complement
functions.comment: Reverse complement of a DNA sequence

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the reverse complement of a DNA sequence as a `VARCHAR`: the complement of each base (A<->T, G<->C) read 3'->5', i.e. the sequence of the opposite strand. Pass one DNA column (case-insensitive; whitespace ignored). Handles IUPAC degenerate codes and gaps; NULL or non-DNA input returns NULL. Use it to get the opposite-strand sequence, orient reads, or design/compare primers.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Reverse complement** — the opposite-strand sequence of DNA.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` DNA column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: a `VARCHAR` — complement of each base, reversed
- IUPAC degenerate codes and gaps supported; NULL for NULL/non-DNA input

vgi.example_queries.description: Read a sequence off the opposite strand. Sequencing gives reads in either orientation, so normalising with this is what lets two reads of the same locus be compared or deduplicated at all; it is also how a reverse primer is written down.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.reverse_complement('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS rc

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.reverse_complement('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS rc

functions.name: match_count
functions.comment: Number of agreeing positions between two equal-length sequences

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the number of positions at which two equal-length sequences agree, as a `BIGINT`. Pass two `VARCHAR` sequence columns (case-insensitive); NULL input or a length mismatch returns NULL. It is the complement of `mismatch_count` (the two sum to the length).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**match_count** — agreeing positions between two equal-length sequences.

- Inputs: two `VARCHAR` sequence columns of equal length
- Returns: a `BIGINT` match count (NULL if NULL or lengths differ)
- The complement of `mismatch_count`

vgi.example_queries.description: Count agreeing positions between two equal-length sequences — the complement of mismatch_count (the two always sum to the length). Divide by the length for percent identity, the number most similarity thresholds are quoted in.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.match_count('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS matches

arguments.name: seq1
arguments.description: First sequence

arguments.name: seq2
arguments.description: Second sequence (same length)

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.match_count('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS matches

functions.name: is_valid_dna
functions.comment: True if the string is a valid IUPAC DNA sequence

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar predicate returning `BOOLEAN` true when a string is a valid IUPAC DNA sequence — only the recognised nucleotide characters (A, C, G, T, the degenerate codes, and gap characters), case-insensitively. Pass one `VARCHAR` column. NULL input returns NULL; any other invalid content returns false. Use it to filter or flag non-DNA rows before calling the DNA transforms.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**is_valid_dna** — validate a DNA string.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: `BOOLEAN` (NULL for NULL input)
- Accepts IUPAC nucleotide + degenerate + gap characters only

vgi.example_queries.description: Screen a text column before running the DNA transforms over it. Contrasting a degenerate-but-valid read (N is a legal IUPAC code) with free text shows where the line is: use it in a WHERE clause so junk rows are filtered rather than silently turning into NULLs downstream.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_valid_dna('ATGCN') AS looks_like_dna, skbio.sequence.is_valid_dna('HELLO') AS looks_like_dna_too

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A candidate DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_valid_dna('ATGCN') AS looks_like_dna, skbio.sequence.is_valid_dna('HELLO') AS looks_like_dna_too

functions.name: count_subsequence
functions.comment: Count occurrences of a subsequence within a sequence

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning how many times a subsequence occurs within a sequence, as a `BIGINT`. Pass the sequence column first and the subsequence to search for second (both `VARCHAR`, case-insensitive); NULL input returns NULL. Handy for counting a motif or codon across reads.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**count_subsequence** — occurrences of a subsequence.

- Inputs: the sequence, then the subsequence to count (both `VARCHAR`)
- Returns: a `BIGINT` occurrence count (NULL for NULL input)
- Counts a motif/codon within each sequence

vgi.example_queries.description: Count how often a motif occurs in a sequence — here the ATG start codon, three times. This is the cheap way to screen a table of reads for a restriction site, primer binding site, or repeat before spending an alignment on them.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.count_subsequence('ATGCGATGCATG', 'ATG') AS start_codons

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: The sequence to search

arguments.name: subsequence
arguments.description: The subsequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.count_subsequence('ATGCGATGCATG', 'ATG') AS start_codons

functions.name: degap
functions.comment: Remove gap characters from a sequence

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function removing gap characters (`-` and `.`) from a sequence, returning the ungapped sequence as a `VARCHAR`. Works for any alphabet (DNA/RNA/protein). Pass one `VARCHAR` column; NULL input returns NULL. Use it to recover the original sequence from an aligned one.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**degap** — strip gap characters from a sequence.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` sequence column (any alphabet)
- Returns: the ungapped sequence as `VARCHAR` (NULL for NULL input)
- Removes `-` and `.`; recovers the sequence behind an alignment

vgi.example_queries.description: Recover the original sequence from an aligned one by dropping the gap characters an alignment inserted. Run it before length, composition, or k-mer calculations, all of which would otherwise count '-' as if it were a residue.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.degap('AC-GT--A') AS ungapped

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A sequence, possibly with gaps

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.degap('AC-GT--A') AS ungapped

functions.name: is_reverse_complement
functions.comment: True if the second DNA sequence is the reverse complement of the first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar predicate returning `BOOLEAN` true when the second DNA sequence is exactly the reverse complement of the first. Pass two `VARCHAR` DNA columns (case-insensitive); a NULL or non-DNA pair returns NULL. Use it to test whether two reads come from opposite strands.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**is_reverse_complement** — are two DNA sequences reverse complements?

- Inputs: two `VARCHAR` DNA columns (case-insensitive)
- Returns: `BOOLEAN` (NULL for NULL/non-DNA input)
- True when the second is the reverse complement of the first

vgi.example_queries.description: Decide whether two reads are the same sequence seen from opposite strands, in one predicate rather than reverse-complementing one side and comparing. Use it to collapse strand-duplicate reads or to check a primer pair points the right way.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_reverse_complement('ATGC', 'GCAT') AS same_locus

arguments.name: seq1
arguments.description: First DNA sequence

arguments.name: seq2
arguments.description: Second DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_reverse_complement('ATGC', 'GCAT') AS same_locus

functions.name: has_degenerates
functions.comment: True if the DNA sequence contains degenerate (ambiguity) codes

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar predicate returning `BOOLEAN` true when a DNA sequence contains at least one degenerate (ambiguity) code such as N, R, or Y — a base that stands for several possibilities. Pass one `VARCHAR` DNA column; NULL or non-DNA input returns NULL. Use it to flag reads with ambiguous bases.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**has_degenerates** — does DNA contain ambiguity codes?

- Input: one `VARCHAR` DNA column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: `BOOLEAN` (NULL for NULL/non-DNA input)
- True if any IUPAC degenerate code (N, R, Y, ...) is present

vgi.example_queries.description: Flag reads containing ambiguity codes (N, R, Y, ...), i.e. positions the basecaller could not resolve. Filtering these out is a standard quality step before variant calling or exact-match lookups, where an N would otherwise silently fail to match.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.has_degenerates('ACGTN') AS ambiguous_read, skbio.sequence.has_degenerates('ACGT') AS clean_read

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.has_degenerates('ACGTN') AS ambiguous_read, skbio.sequence.has_degenerates('ACGT') AS clean_read

functions.name: gc_frequency
functions.comment: Number of G/C bases in a DNA sequence

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the number of G and C bases in a DNA sequence as a `BIGINT` (the raw count behind `gc_content`). Pass one `VARCHAR` DNA column (case-insensitive); NULL or non-DNA input returns NULL. Divide by `length(seq)` for the fraction, or use `gc_content` directly.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**gc_frequency** — count of G/C bases in a DNA sequence.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` DNA column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: a `BIGINT` count (NULL for NULL/non-DNA input)
- The raw count behind `gc_content`

vgi.example_queries.description: Count G and C bases outright rather than as a fraction. The raw count is what you want when summing across reads or weighting by length; gc_content gives the same information already divided by the sequence length.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.gc_frequency('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS gc_bases

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.gc_frequency('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS gc_bases

functions.name: transcribe
functions.comment: Transcribe a DNA sequence to RNA (T -> U)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function transcribing a DNA sequence into its RNA transcript as a `VARCHAR`, replacing every thymine (T) with uracil (U). Pass one DNA column (case-insensitive). NULL or non-DNA input returns NULL. Chain with `translate` to go DNA -> protein, or use it to prepare RNA sequences for downstream analysis.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Transcribe** — DNA to RNA (T becomes U).

- Input: one `VARCHAR` DNA column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: the RNA transcript as `VARCHAR`
- NULL for NULL/non-DNA input

vgi.example_queries.description: Produce the RNA transcript of a DNA template (every T becomes U). Use it when a downstream tool or reference is written in RNA alphabet, or as the explicit middle step of the DNA -> RNA -> protein chain that translate otherwise does in one hop.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.transcribe('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS rna

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.transcribe('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS rna

functions.name: mismatch_count
functions.comment: Number of differing positions between two equal-length sequences

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the number of positions at which two equal-length sequences differ, as a `BIGINT` (the raw count behind the Hamming distance). Pass two `VARCHAR` sequence columns (case-insensitive); NULL input or a length mismatch returns NULL. Use `match_count` for the agreeing positions or `hamming_distance` for the fraction.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**mismatch_count** — differing positions between two equal-length sequences.

- Inputs: two `VARCHAR` sequence columns of equal length
- Returns: a `BIGINT` mismatch count (NULL if NULL or lengths differ)
- The count behind `hamming_distance`; see also `match_count`

vgi.example_queries.description: Count differing positions between a read and its reference as a whole number, which is what edit-distance thresholds are usually expressed in ('accept up to 2 mismatches'). hamming_distance gives the same comparison as a length-normalised fraction.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.mismatch_count('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS mismatches

arguments.name: seq1
arguments.description: First sequence

arguments.name: seq2
arguments.description: Second sequence (same length)

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.mismatch_count('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS mismatches

functions.name: hamming_distance
functions.comment: Hamming distance (fraction of differing positions) between two sequences

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the Hamming distance between two equal-length sequences as a `DOUBLE` in `[0, 1]`: the fraction of positions at which the characters differ. Pass two `VARCHAR` columns (case-insensitive; compared as generic sequences, so DNA/RNA/protein all work). Returns NULL if either value is NULL or the two sequences differ in length. Multiply by the length for a raw mismatch count; use it for read-vs-reference comparison or simple sequence similarity.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Hamming distance** — mismatch fraction between two equal-length sequences.

- Inputs: two `VARCHAR` sequence columns (case-insensitive)
- Returns: a `DOUBLE` in `[0, 1]`; NULL if either is NULL or lengths differ
- `* length` for a raw mismatch count

vgi.example_queries.description: Score how far a read has drifted from its reference as a length-normalised fraction, so reads of different lengths stay comparable. One substitution in eight bases gives 0.125; multiply by the length to recover the raw mismatch count. Requires equal lengths -- align first if there are indels.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.hamming_distance('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS distance

arguments.name: seq1
arguments.description: First sequence

arguments.name: seq2
arguments.description: Second sequence (same length as the first)

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.hamming_distance('ACGTACGT', 'ACGAACGT') AS distance

functions.name: has_gaps
functions.comment: True if the sequence contains gap characters

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar predicate returning `BOOLEAN` true when a sequence contains at least one gap character (`-` or `.`). Works for any alphabet. Pass one `VARCHAR` column; NULL input returns NULL. Use it to find aligned (gapped) rows or to filter them before `degap`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**has_gaps** — does a sequence contain gaps?

- Input: one `VARCHAR` sequence column (any alphabet)
- Returns: `BOOLEAN` (NULL for NULL input)
- True if any `-` or `.` is present

vgi.example_queries.description: Tell aligned sequences apart from raw ones in a mixed column — the gapped row is the one that came out of an alignment. Use it to decide which rows need degap before a length or composition calculation.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.has_gaps('AC-GT') AS aligned_row, skbio.sequence.has_gaps('ACGT') AS raw_row

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.has_gaps('AC-GT') AS aligned_row, skbio.sequence.has_gaps('ACGT') AS raw_row

functions.name: gc_content
functions.comment: GC content of a DNA sequence as a fraction in [0, 1]

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the GC content of a DNA sequence as a `DOUBLE` fraction in `[0, 1]` — the number of G and C bases divided by the sequence length (gaps excluded). Pass one `VARCHAR` column of DNA (case-insensitive; whitespace ignored). Rows that are NULL or not valid DNA (e.g. protein or free text) return NULL. Use it to profile read/contig composition, screen for GC-bias, or bin sequences by GC — multiply by 100 for a percentage.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**GC content** — fraction of G/C bases in a DNA sequence.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` DNA column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: a `DOUBLE` in `[0, 1]` (`* 100` for a percentage)
- NULL for NULL or non-DNA input; gaps are excluded from the denominator

vgi.example_queries.description: Profile a read's base composition as a single number in [0, 1]. GC content is the first thing to check when reads look odd: an outlier flags contamination or a different organism, and it drives PCR and melting behaviour. Multiply by 100 for the percentage people usually quote.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.gc_content('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS gc

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.gc_content('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS gc

functions.name: is_valid_protein
functions.comment: True if the string is a valid IUPAC protein sequence

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar predicate returning `BOOLEAN` true when a string is a valid IUPAC protein sequence — the 20 amino-acid codes plus the recognised ambiguity and gap characters, case-insensitively. Pass one `VARCHAR` column. NULL input returns NULL; other invalid content returns false. Note that pure-nucleotide strings can also be valid protein (A/C/G/T are amino-acid codes), so use `is_valid_dna` to distinguish DNA specifically.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**is_valid_protein** — validate a protein string.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: `BOOLEAN` (NULL for NULL input)
- Accepts the 20 amino acids + ambiguity/gap characters

vgi.example_queries.description: Check a column really holds amino-acid sequences before feeding the protein aligners. Beware the asymmetry this example hints at: a pure A/C/G/T string is *also* valid protein, so pair this with is_valid_dna when you need to tell the two alphabets apart.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_valid_protein('MRIT') AS looks_like_protein, skbio.sequence.is_valid_protein('ATGC1') AS looks_like_protein_too

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A candidate protein sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.is_valid_protein('MRIT') AS looks_like_protein, skbio.sequence.is_valid_protein('ATGC1') AS looks_like_protein_too

functions.name: complement
functions.comment: Complement of a DNA sequence (same 5'->3' order)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the base complement of a DNA sequence as a `VARCHAR` (A<->T, G<->C) in the same 5'->3' order — unlike `reverse_complement`, the sequence is not reversed. Pass one DNA column (case-insensitive). IUPAC degenerate codes and gaps are supported; NULL or non-DNA input returns NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Complement** — base-by-base complement of DNA, order preserved.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` DNA column (case-insensitive)
- Returns: a `VARCHAR`; use `reverse_complement` for the opposite strand
- NULL for NULL/non-DNA input

vgi.example_queries.description: Complement each base while keeping 5'->3' order — deliberately *not* the opposite strand. Compare it with reverse_complement on the same input to see the difference that trips people up: only the reversed form is what actually pairs with the original.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.sequence.complement('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS comp

arguments.name: seq
arguments.description: A DNA sequence

examples: SELECT skbio.sequence.complement('ATGCGGATTACAGG') AS comp

schemas.name: stats
schemas.comment: Ordination, distance-matrix hypothesis tests, and compositional transforms.

vgi.categories.name: ordination
vgi.categories.description: Embed samples in a low-dimensional space from a distance matrix.

vgi.categories.name: hypothesis-tests
vgi.categories.description: Test associations and correlations over distance matrices.

vgi.categories.name: composition
vgi.categories.description: Log-ratio transforms that move compositional data into real space.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Multivariate analysis of distance matrices and compositional data. Reach here to embed samples in a few interpretable dimensions — either from a distance matrix (principal-coordinates ordination) or directly from a feature table (principal components and correspondence analysis); to test whether a grouping or a second matrix explains between-sample distances (permutational and rank-based group tests, and matrix correlation); to move compositional feature data into ordinary real space with log-ratio transforms and their inverses; and to find differentially abundant features between groups (ANCOM and a Dirichlet-multinomial t-test). Distance-matrix inputs use the long (id_1, id_2, distance) shape the diversity area's beta-diversity matrix produces.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
### Multivariate statistics

Over distance matrices, feature tables, and compositions:

- **Ordination** — embed samples in low dimensions (from a distance matrix or feature table)
- **Hypothesis tests** — do groups or a second matrix explain the distances?
- **Composition** — log-ratio transforms (and inverses) into real space
- **Differential abundance** — which features differ between groups (ANCOM, Dirichlet-multinomial)

Distance inputs use the long `(id_1, id_2, distance)` shape from the beta-diversity matrix.

vgi.example_queries.description: PCoA of a distance matrix

tags.vgi.title: Multivariate Statistics

functions.name: rclr
functions.comment: rclr compositional transform of a long feature table

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function applying the **rclr** compositional operation to a long feature table `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3; override with `sample :=`, `feature :=`, `value :=`; `pseudocount :=` offsets zeros). It is the robust centred log-ratio: like CLR but it leaves zeros out of the geometric mean, so a pseudocount is usually unnecessary (leave `pseudocount :=` at 0).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**rclr** — It is the robust centred log-ratio: like CLR but it leaves zeros out of the geometric mean, so a pseudocount is usually unnecessary (leave `pseudocount :=` at 0).

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default)
- `pseudocount :=` — added to every value first to handle zeros

vgi.example_queries.description: Take log-ratios of a feature table without inventing a pseudocount: rclr excludes zeros from each sample's geometric mean instead of offsetting them. Reach for this rather than clr whenever the table is sparse, as microbiome count tables almost always are.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(rclr, 4) AS rclr FROM skbio.stats.rclr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Sample id.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: feature_id
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Feature id.

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Transformed value.

functions.name: power
functions.comment: Compositional power transform of a long feature table

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function applying the **power** compositional operation to a long feature table `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3; override with `sample :=`, `feature :=`, `value :=`; `pseudocount :=` offsets zeros). It raises each part of the closed composition to the exponent `power :=` and re-closes it (compositional scalar multiplication).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**power** — It raises each part of the closed composition to the exponent `power :=` and re-closes it (compositional scalar multiplication).

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default)
- `pseudocount :=` — added to every value first to handle zeros

vgi.example_queries.description: Sharpen a composition by squaring every part and re-closing it: the dominant features gain share and the rare ones lose it, while the result still sums to 1. An exponent below 1 does the opposite (flattens), which is how compositional data is up- or down-weighted without leaving the simplex.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(value, 4) AS value FROM skbio.stats.power((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value)), power := 2.0) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

functions.name: permanova
functions.comment: PERMANOVA test: does a grouping explain between-sample distances?

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Single-row table function running the **PERMANOVA** test: a permutational multivariate ANOVA that tests whether samples group by a categorical variable in distance space, comparing within- vs between-group distances. The table arg is `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance, group FROM ...)` where `group` is the group label of `id_1` (columns default to positional 1-4; override with `id_1 :=`, `id_2 :=`, `distance :=`, `group :=`), typically built by joining a group label onto a `beta_diversity` matrix. `permutations :=` sets the number of permutations for the p-value (default 999). Returns one row with the pseudo-F `test_statistic`, the `p_value`, and the sample/group/permutation counts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**PERMANOVA** — a permutational multivariate ANOVA that tests whether samples group by a categorical variable in distance space, comparing within- vs between-group distances.

- Table arg: `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance, group FROM ...)` — `group` is the label of `id_1` (positional 1-4 by default)
- `permutations :=` — permutation count for the p-value (default 999)
- Returns one row: `method`, `test_statistic` (pseudo-F), `p_value`, `sample_size`, `number_of_groups`, `permutations`
- Build the input by joining a grouping onto a `beta_diversity` distance matrix

vgi.example_queries.description: Test whether two groups of samples really are separated in community space, end to end: build the Bray-Curtis matrix, join each sample's group label onto id_1, and read off pseudo-F with its permutation p-value. The join is the pattern worth copying — a table function takes one input relation, so the grouping has to ride in as a fourth column rather than a second argument.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT method, round(test_statistic, 4) AS pseudo_f, p_value, number_of_groups FROM skbio.stats.permanova((SELECT b.id_1, b.id_2, b.distance, g.grp FROM skbio.diversity.beta_diversity((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',1),('s2','a',3),('s2','b',2),('s3','a',1),('s3','b',8),('s4','a',0),('s4','b',9)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, count))) AS b JOIN (VALUES ('s1','x'),('s2','x'),('s3','y'),('s4','y')) AS g(sample, grp) ON b.id_1 = g.sample))

functions.name: pcoa
functions.comment: Principal Coordinates Analysis of a distance matrix (per-sample coordinates)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function running Principal Coordinates Analysis (classical MDS) on a long distance matrix and returning each sample's coordinates on the leading axes. The table arg is `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance FROM ...)` — typically the output of `skbio.diversity.beta_diversity` (columns default to positional 1/2/3; override with `id_1 :=`, `id_2 :=`, `distance :=`). `n_components :=` sets how many principal-coordinate axes to return (default 3), fixing the output width at `(sample_id, pc_1, ..., pc_k)`. Use it to embed samples in a low-dimensional space for plotting or clustering; the axes are ordered by variance explained.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**PCoA** — principal coordinates (classical MDS) of a distance matrix.

- Table arg: `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance FROM ...)` (e.g. `beta_diversity` output; positional 1/2/3 by default)
- `n_components :=` — number of axes to return (default 3)
- Returns `(sample_id, pc_1, ..., pc_k)`; axes ordered by variance explained
- Feed a beta-diversity matrix in to embed samples for plotting/clustering

vgi.example_queries.description: Collapse a 3-sample distance matrix into two plottable coordinates and order the samples along the leading axis. Rounding keeps the output readable; sorting by pc_1 reads off the dominant gradient — which samples sit at the extremes of the largest source of variation.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, round(pc_1, 4) AS pc_1, round(pc_2, 4) AS pc_2 FROM skbio.stats.pcoa((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','a',0.0),('a','b',0.5),('a','c',0.7),('b','a',0.5),('b','b',0.0),('b','c',0.6),('c','a',0.7),('c','b',0.6),('c','c',0.0)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance)), n_components := 2) ORDER BY pc_1

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
#### `n_components := 2`

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sample_id` | VARCHAR | Sample id. |
| `pc_1` | DOUBLE | Coordinate on principal axis 1 (axes are ordered by variance explained). |
| `pc_2` | DOUBLE | Coordinate on principal axis 2 (axes are ordered by variance explained). |

#### `n_components := 3`

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sample_id` | VARCHAR | Sample id. |
| `pc_1` | DOUBLE | Coordinate on principal axis 1 (axes are ordered by variance explained). |
| `pc_2` | DOUBLE | Coordinate on principal axis 2 (axes are ordered by variance explained). |
| `pc_3` | DOUBLE | Coordinate on principal axis 3 (axes are ordered by variance explained). |

The pattern generalises: `n_components := k` returns `sample_id` plus `pc_1` through `pc_{k}` (default `k` = 3). Axes beyond what the data can support are returned as NULL.

functions.name: pca
functions.comment: Principal Components Analysis of a long feature table (per-sample scores)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function running Principal Components Analysis on a long feature table and returning each sample's scores on the leading components. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3; override with `sample :=`, `feature :=`, `value :=`). `n_components :=` sets how many principal-component axes to return (default 3), fixing the output width at `(sample_id, pc_1, ..., pc_k)`. - Works directly on feature values (no distance matrix needed, unlike `pcoa`)

functions.name: mantel
functions.comment: Mantel test: correlation between two distance matrices

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Single-row table function running the **Mantel test**: the correlation between two distance matrices measured over the same set of samples, with a permutation p-value. The table arg is `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance_x, distance_y FROM ...)` — the two `distance_*` columns are the corresponding entries of the two matrices for each id pair (columns default to positional 1-4; override with `id_1 :=`, `id_2 :=`, `distance_x :=`, `distance_y :=`). `method :=` picks `pearson` (default) or `spearman`, and `permutations :=` the permutation count (default 999). Returns one row: the `correlation`, `p_value`, sample count `n`, and permutation count. Use it to test whether two dissimilarities (e.g. genetic vs geographic distance) covary.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Mantel test** — correlation between two distance matrices.

- Table arg: `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance_x, distance_y FROM ...)` (positional 1-4 by default); the two `distance_*` columns are aligned entries of the two matrices
- `method :=` — `pearson` (default) or `spearman`; `permutations :=` — p-value permutations (default 999)
- Returns one row: `method`, `correlation`, `p_value`, `n`, `permutations`
- Tests whether two dissimilarities (e.g. genetic vs geographic) covary

vgi.example_queries.description: Test whether two dissimilarities measured over the same samples covary — community distance against geographic distance, say. Both matrices ride in as two aligned distance columns over the same id pairs, which is exactly what joining two beta_diversity results on (id_1, id_2) produces.

functions.name: dirmult_ttest
functions.comment: Dirichlet-multinomial t-test for differential abundance per feature

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function running scikit-bio's Dirichlet-multinomial t-test for differential abundance on a long count table with a per-sample grouping `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count, group FROM ...)`. It estimates, per feature, the log2 fold change between the two groups with a t-statistic, raw and Holm-adjusted p-values, and a significance flag. The two group labels are taken as reference and treatment in sorted order; the posterior is sampled with a fixed seed so results are reproducible. Build the input by joining a grouping onto a count table.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**dirmult_ttest** — Dirichlet-multinomial differential abundance per feature.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count, group FROM ...)` (positional 1-4)
- Returns per feature: `t_statistic`, `log2_fold_change`, `pvalue`, `qvalue`, `significant`
- Two group labels become reference/treatment (sorted); fixed seed for reproducibility

vgi.example_queries.description: Report an effect size and a multiple-testing-corrected q-value per feature, most significant first. Prefer this over ancom when you need a direction and magnitude (the log2 fold change) rather than just a ranked W statistic; the seed is fixed, so the numbers are reproducible.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_id, round(log2_fold_change, 4) AS log2_fold_change, round(qvalue, 4) AS qvalue, significant FROM skbio.stats.dirmult_ttest((SELECT s.sample_id, s.feature_id, s.count, g.grp FROM (VALUES ('s1','b1',12),('s1','b2',11),('s2','b1',9),('s2','b2',11),('s3','b1',1),('s3','b2',11),('s4','b1',22),('s4','b2',21),('s5','b1',20),('s5','b2',22),('s6','b1',23),('s6','b2',21)) AS s(sample_id, feature_id, count) JOIN (VALUES ('s1','x'),('s2','x'),('s3','x'),('s4','y'),('s5','y'),('s6','y')) AS g(sample, grp) ON s.sample_id = g.sample)) ORDER BY qvalue

functions.name: clr
functions.comment: Centred log-ratio (CLR) transform of a long feature table

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function applying the centred log-ratio (CLR) transform to each sample of a long feature table, returning the same long shape. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3; override with `sample :=`, `feature :=`, `value :=`). For each sample the values are closed to proportions and replaced by the log of each part divided by the geometric mean of the sample — moving compositional data into real space where ordinary statistics apply. Values must be positive; pass `pseudocount :=` (e.g. 1) to offset zeros before the log. Returns `(sample_id, feature_id, clr)`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**CLR** — centred log-ratio transform of compositional data.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default)
- Per sample: close to proportions, then `log(part / geometric_mean)`
- `pseudocount :=` — added to every value first to handle zeros (log 0 is undefined)
- Returns `(sample_id, feature_id, clr)` — same long shape as the input

vgi.example_queries.description: Move a feature table out of the simplex and into real space, where ordinary statistics (correlation, regression, distance) are meaningful again. A negative clr value means the feature is below its sample's geometric mean, positive above — the sign, not the raw count, is what carries the signal.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, feature_id, round(clr, 4) AS clr FROM skbio.stats.clr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, feature_id

functions.name: pairwise_vlr
functions.comment: Pairwise variance of log-ratios between features (long matrix)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function computing the variance of the log-ratio between every pair of features across the samples of a long feature table `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)`. A low variance means two features move together (are proportional); it is a compositionally-coherent measure of feature association. Returns the full feature-by-feature matrix long as `(feature_1, feature_2, vlr)`; `pseudocount :=` offsets zeros.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**pairwise_vlr** — variance of log-ratios between every pair of features.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)`; `pseudocount :=` offsets zeros
- Low variance = the two features are proportional (associated)
- Returns the feature-by-feature matrix long: `feature_1`, `feature_2`, `vlr`

vgi.example_queries.description: Rank feature pairs by how tightly they track each other across samples, smallest variance first — the pair at the top moves proportionally and is a candidate for co-occurring taxa. Filtering to feature_1 < feature_2 drops the zero diagonal and the mirrored half of the symmetric matrix.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_1, feature_2, round(vlr, 4) AS vlr FROM skbio.stats.pairwise_vlr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6),('s3','a',2),('s3','b',1),('s3','c',7)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) WHERE feature_1 < feature_2 ORDER BY vlr

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: feature_2
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Second feature id.

functions.name: ancom
functions.comment: ANCOM differential-abundance test per feature between groups

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function running the ANCOM (Analysis of Composition of Microbiomes) differential-abundance test on a long count table with a per-sample grouping. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count, group FROM ...)` where `group` is the label of the sample (columns default to positional 1-4). For each feature it reports the ANCOM `w` statistic (how many log-ratio sub-hypotheses were rejected) and whether it is declared significantly differentially abundant. Build the input by joining a grouping onto a feature-count table.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**ANCOM** — differential abundance of each feature between groups.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, count, group FROM ...)` (positional 1-4)
- Returns per feature: `w` (rejected sub-hypotheses) and `significant`
- Join a per-sample grouping onto a count table to build the input

vgi.example_queries.description: Find which features differ between two groups of samples, strongest evidence first. The join is the part worth copying: a table function gets one input relation, so the per-sample group label has to ride in as a fourth column rather than a second argument.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_id, w, significant FROM skbio.stats.ancom((SELECT s.sample_id, s.feature_id, s.count, g.grp FROM (VALUES ('s1','b1',12),('s1','b2',11),('s2','b1',9),('s2','b2',11),('s3','b1',1),('s3','b2',11),('s4','b1',22),('s4','b2',21),('s5','b1',20),('s5','b2',22),('s6','b1',23),('s6','b2',21)) AS s(sample_id, feature_id, count) JOIN (VALUES ('s1','x'),('s2','x'),('s3','x'),('s4','y'),('s5','y'),('s6','y')) AS g(sample, grp) ON s.sample_id = g.sample)) ORDER BY w DESC

functions.name: anosim
functions.comment: ANOSIM test: are within-group distances smaller than between-group?

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Single-row table function running the **ANOSIM** test: an analysis of similarities that tests whether distances within groups are smaller than distances between groups; the R statistic ranges from -1 to 1 (near 1 = strong separation). The table arg is `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance, group FROM ...)` where `group` is the group label of `id_1` (columns default to positional 1-4; override with `id_1 :=`, `id_2 :=`, `distance :=`, `group :=`), typically built by joining a group label onto a `beta_diversity` matrix. `permutations :=` sets the number of permutations for the p-value (default 999). Returns one row with the R `test_statistic`, the `p_value`, and the sample/group/permutation counts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**ANOSIM** — an analysis of similarities that tests whether distances within groups are smaller than distances between groups; the R statistic ranges from -1 to 1 (near 1 = strong separation).

- Table arg: `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance, group FROM ...)` — `group` is the label of `id_1` (positional 1-4 by default)
- `permutations :=` — permutation count for the p-value (default 999)
- Returns one row: `method`, `test_statistic` (R), `p_value`, `sample_size`, `number_of_groups`, `permutations`
- Build the input by joining a grouping onto a `beta_diversity` distance matrix

vgi.example_queries.description: Ask the same question as permanova but on ranked distances, which makes ANOSIM the more robust choice when the distances are skewed or the groups differ in spread. Its R statistic is directly interpretable on its own scale: near 1 means the groups are well separated, near 0 that the grouping explains nothing.

functions.name: ilr
functions.comment: Isometric log-ratio (ILR) transform of a long feature table (D-1 components)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function applying the isometric log-ratio (ILR) transform to each sample of a long feature table. Unlike CLR, ILR maps a D-part composition onto `D-1` orthonormal coordinates (no singular covariance), so it emits `(sample_id, component, value)` with `component` in `1..D-1`. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (columns default to positional 1/2/3; override with `sample :=`, `feature :=`, `value :=`). Values must be positive; pass `pseudocount :=` to offset zeros. Feature ids are sorted to give the components a stable basis across samples.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**ILR** — isometric log-ratio transform of compositional data.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default)
- Maps a D-part composition to `D-1` orthonormal coordinates (full-rank, unlike CLR)
- `pseudocount :=` — added to every value first to handle zeros
- Returns `(sample_id, component, value)` with `component` in `1..D-1`; features sorted for a stable basis

vgi.example_queries.description: Turn 3-part compositions into 2 orthonormal coordinates — note the count drops from D to D-1, which is the point: unlike clr, the ilr coordinates are not linearly dependent, so a covariance matrix built from them is invertible and methods like PCA or LDA behave.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, component, round(value, 4) AS value FROM skbio.stats.ilr((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',1),('s1','b',2),('s1','c',3),('s2','a',4),('s2','b',5),('s2','c',6)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value))) ORDER BY sample_id, component

functions.name: ca
functions.comment: Correspondence Analysis of a long feature (count) table (per-sample scores)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function running Correspondence Analysis on a long feature count table and returning each sample's scores on the leading axes. The table arg is `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default; override with `sample :=`, `feature :=`, `value :=`). `n_components :=` sets the number of axes (default 3), fixing the output at `(sample_id, ca_1, ..., ca_k)`. CA is the ordination of choice for count/abundance data with a unimodal (chi-square) response; values must be non-negative. Axes are ordered by inertia explained.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**CA** — correspondence analysis of a feature count table.

- Table arg: `(SELECT sample_id, feature_id, value FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default)
- `n_components :=` — number of axes to return (default 3)
- Returns `(sample_id, ca_1, ..., ca_k)`; values must be non-negative counts
- Chi-square ordination for abundance data; axes ordered by inertia explained

vgi.example_queries.description: Ordinate a count table with correspondence analysis, the chi-square counterpart of PCA for abundance data. Sorting by ca_1 orders the samples along the strongest compositional gradient, which is what the axis means for count data.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, round(ca_1, 4) AS ca_1, round(ca_2, 4) AS ca_2 FROM skbio.stats.ca((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('s1','a',4),('s1','b',2),('s2','a',1),('s2','b',9),('s3','a',3),('s3','b',5)) AS t(sample_id, feature_id, value)), n_components := 2) ORDER BY ca_1

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
#### `n_components := 2`

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sample_id` | VARCHAR | Sample id. |
| `ca_1` | DOUBLE | Score on correspondence axis 1 (axes are ordered by inertia explained). |
| `ca_2` | DOUBLE | Score on correspondence axis 2 (axes are ordered by inertia explained). |

#### `n_components := 3`

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sample_id` | VARCHAR | Sample id. |
| `ca_1` | DOUBLE | Score on correspondence axis 1 (axes are ordered by inertia explained). |
| `ca_2` | DOUBLE | Score on correspondence axis 2 (axes are ordered by inertia explained). |
| `ca_3` | DOUBLE | Score on correspondence axis 3 (axes are ordered by inertia explained). |

The pattern generalises: `n_components := k` returns `sample_id` plus `ca_1` through `ca_{k}` (default `k` = 3). Axes beyond what the data can support are returned as NULL.

functions.name: upgma
functions.comment: Build a upgma tree from a distance matrix (Newick output)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function building a phylogenetic tree from a long distance matrix and returning it as a single-row Newick string. UPGMA builds a rooted, ultrametric tree by repeatedly joining the closest clusters (average linkage); it assumes a molecular clock. The table arg is `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance FROM ...)` — typically a `beta_diversity` matrix (columns default to positional 1/2/3). Inspect the result with `tip_count` / `total_branch_length` / `tree_height` or compare trees with `robinson_foulds`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**upgma** — build a tree from a distance matrix.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
**gme** — build a tree from a distance matrix.

Greedy minimum evolution builds an unrooted tree by greedily minimising total tree length — fast for large matrices.

- Table arg: `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default)
- Returns one row: `newick` (a Newick-format `VARCHAR`)

vgi.example_queries.description: Build a minimum-evolution tree greedily, which is the one to reach for when the matrix is large enough that neighbour joining's cubic cost hurts. On a small matrix like this one it agrees with the others; the tip count confirms no taxa were dropped.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT newick, skbio.tree.tip_count(newick) AS tips FROM skbio.tree.gme((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','b',5),('a','c',9),('a','d',9),('b','c',10),('b','d',10),('c','d',8)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance)))

tags.vgi.doc_md:
**bme** — build a tree from a distance matrix.

Balanced minimum evolution builds an unrooted tree minimising a balanced tree-length criterion (the objective FastME optimises).

- Table arg: `(SELECT id_1, id_2, distance FROM ...)` (positional 1/2/3 by default)
- Returns one row: `newick` (a Newick-format `VARCHAR`)

vgi.example_queries.description: Build the balanced-minimum-evolution tree (the criterion FastME optimises), which is usually more accurate than greedy ME at a similar cost. Compare its output against neighbor_joining with robinson_foulds to see whether the method choice changed the topology at all.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT newick, skbio.tree.tip_count(newick) AS tips FROM skbio.tree.bme((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('a','b',5),('a','c',9),('a','d',9),('b','c',10),('b','d',10),('c','d',8)) AS d(id_1, id_2, distance)))

functions.name: weighted_robinson_foulds
functions.comment: Weighted Robinson-Foulds distance (branch-length aware) between two Newick trees

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the weighted Robinson-Foulds distance between two Newick trees as a `DOUBLE`: like the Robinson-Foulds distance but summing the branch-length differences of matched and unmatched splits, so it reflects both topology and branch lengths. Pass two `VARCHAR` Newick columns over the same taxa; 0 means identical. NULL or unparseable input returns NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**weighted_robinson_foulds** — branch-length-aware tree distance.

- Inputs: two `VARCHAR` Newick columns over the same taxa
- Returns: `DOUBLE` distance combining topology and branch lengths (0 = identical)
- NULL for NULL/unparseable input

vgi.example_queries.description: Compare two trees on topology *and* branch lengths, so a pair that groups taxa identically but stretches a branch still scores non-zero. Use this rather than robinson_foulds when the lengths carry meaning — divergence times, substitution rates — and not just the grouping.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.weighted_robinson_foulds('((a:1,b:1):1,(c:1,d:1):1);', '((a:1,c:1):1,(b:1,d:1):1);') AS wrf_distance

arguments.name: newick1
arguments.description: First Newick tree

arguments.name: newick2
arguments.description: Second Newick tree

examples: SELECT skbio.tree.weighted_robinson_foulds('((a:1,b:1):1,(c:1,d:1):1);', '((a:1,c:1):1,(b:1,d:1):1);') AS wrf_distance

functions.name: total_branch_length
functions.comment: Total branch length (sum of all branch lengths) of a Newick tree

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the total branch length of a Newick-format tree as a `DOUBLE`: the sum of every branch length. Pass one `VARCHAR` column of Newick strings. Branches without an explicit length count as zero; NULL or unparseable input returns NULL. This is Faith's phylogenetic-diversity measure when the tree spans a sample's features.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**total_branch_length** — sum of all branch lengths in a Newick tree.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` Newick column
- Returns: `DOUBLE` total length (NULL for NULL/unparseable input)
- Missing branch lengths count as 0; equals Faith's PD over a feature tree

vgi.example_queries.description: Measure how much evolutionary change a tree encodes in total. Over a tree pruned to one sample's features this is exactly Faith's PD, which makes it the way to compute phylogenetic diversity when you already hold the subtree rather than a feature table.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.total_branch_length('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS branch_length

arguments.name: newick
arguments.description: A Newick tree

examples: SELECT skbio.tree.total_branch_length('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS branch_length

functions.name: tip_count
functions.comment: Number of tips (leaves) in a Newick tree

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the number of tips (leaf nodes / taxa) in a Newick-format tree as a `BIGINT`. Pass one `VARCHAR` column of Newick strings (e.g. the output of a tree builder). NULL or unparseable input returns NULL. Use it to size trees stored per row without leaving SQL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**tip_count** — number of leaves in a Newick tree.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` Newick column
- Returns: `BIGINT` tip count (NULL for NULL/unparseable input)

vgi.example_queries.description: Size a tree without leaving SQL — the quickest sanity check that a builder kept every taxon, and the denominator for anything you normalise per tip. Point it at a column of Newick strings to profile a whole table of trees.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.tip_count('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS tips

arguments.name: newick
arguments.description: A Newick tree

examples: SELECT skbio.tree.tip_count('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS tips

functions.name: robinson_foulds
functions.comment: Robinson-Foulds topological distance between two Newick trees

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the Robinson-Foulds distance between two Newick trees as a `DOUBLE`: the number of bipartitions (splits) present in one tree but not the other — a purely topological distance ignoring branch lengths. Pass two `VARCHAR` Newick columns over the same taxa; 0 means identical topologies, larger means more different. NULL or unparseable input returns NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**robinson_foulds** — topological distance between two Newick trees.

- Inputs: two `VARCHAR` Newick columns over the same taxa
- Returns: `DOUBLE` split-difference count (0 = identical topology); ignores branch lengths
- NULL for NULL/unparseable input

vgi.example_queries.description: Ask whether two trees group the same taxa together, ignoring branch lengths entirely: these two disagree on whether a pairs with b or with c, so the distance is non-zero. This is the standard way to check whether two reconstruction methods, or two bootstrap replicates, found the same shape.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.robinson_foulds('((a,b),(c,d));', '((a,c),(b,d));') AS rf_distance

arguments.name: newick1
arguments.description: First Newick tree

arguments.name: newick2
arguments.description: Second Newick tree

examples: SELECT skbio.tree.robinson_foulds('((a,b),(c,d));', '((a,c),(b,d));') AS rf_distance

functions.name: tree_height
functions.comment: Height of a Newick tree (maximum root-to-tip branch-length distance)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the height of a Newick-format tree as a `DOUBLE`: the maximum branch-length distance from the root to any tip. Pass one `VARCHAR` column of Newick strings. Missing branch lengths count as zero; NULL or unparseable input returns NULL. For an ultrametric tree (e.g. from `upgma`) every tip is at this height.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**tree_height** — deepest root-to-tip distance in a Newick tree.

- Input: one `VARCHAR` Newick column
- Returns: `DOUBLE` height (NULL for NULL/unparseable input)
- For ultrametric trees (`upgma`) all tips sit at this height

vgi.example_queries.description: Read the deepest root-to-tip distance, i.e. how far back the tree reaches. On an ultrametric tree (anything from upgma) every tip sits at this height, so comparing it with a tip's own depth is a quick test of ultrametricity.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.tree_height('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS height

arguments.name: newick
arguments.description: A Newick tree

examples: SELECT skbio.tree.tree_height('((a:2,b:3):3,d:4,c:4);') AS height

functions.name: cophenetic_distance
functions.comment: Distance between two Newick trees based on tip-to-tip distances

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scalar function returning the cophenetic distance between two Newick trees as a `DOUBLE`: a distance derived from how much their tip-to-tip path-length distance matrices disagree over the shared taxa (0 means the trees imply identical pairwise distances, larger means more different). Unlike Robinson-Foulds it is branch-length sensitive. Pass two `VARCHAR` Newick columns; NULL or unparseable input returns NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**cophenetic_distance** — disagreement of two trees' tip-to-tip distances.

- Inputs: two `VARCHAR` Newick columns (shared taxa)
- Returns: `DOUBLE` distance (0 = identical pairwise distances); branch-length sensitive
- NULL for NULL/unparseable input

vgi.example_queries.description: Compare two trees by the tip-to-tip distances they imply, rather than by their splits. It answers the question that actually matters downstream — do these trees place the taxa at the same distances from each other? — and so reacts to the long branches in the second tree that robinson_foulds ignores.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT skbio.tree.cophenetic_distance('((a:1,b:1):1,(c:1,d:1):1);', '((a:1,c:1):5,(b:1,d:1):5);') AS cophenetic_distance

arguments.name: newick1
arguments.description: First Newick tree

arguments.name: newick2
arguments.description: Second Newick tree

examples: SELECT skbio.tree.cophenetic_distance('((a:1,b:1):1,(c:1,d:1):1);', '((a:1,c:1):5,(b:1,d:1):5);') AS cophenetic_distance

workers.title: scikit-learn
workers.tagline: scikit-learn for DuckDB/SQL — datasets, metrics, transforms, and a train/predict model registry, exposed as a VGI worker
workers.summary: scikit-learn datasets, metrics, transforms, and a train/predict model registry for DuckDB/SQL
workers.doc_md:
# scikit-learn for SQL

Exposes [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org) to DuckDB/SQL as VGI functions:

- **Datasets** — toy datasets and generators (`iris`, `make_classification`, ...)
- **Metrics** — regression/classification/clustering scores as aggregates
- **Transforms** — scalers, encoders, decomposition (fit-transform + stored)
- **Models** — `fit`/`predict`, typed `fit_<estimator>`, cross-validation, grid/randomized search, pipelines, and per-group modeling

Models and transformers are stored as reusable BLOBs in a registry.

example_queries.description: Load the built-in iris dataset.
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM sklearn.datasets.iris() LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Coefficient of determination over inline (actual, predicted) pairs.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sklearn.metrics.r2_score(actual, predicted) FROM (VALUES (3.0, 2.5), (5.0, 5.1), (7.0, 6.8)) AS t(actual, predicted);

example_queries.description: Fit a random-forest classifier on iris, then predict with the fitted model.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE iris_model = (SELECT model FROM sklearn.models.fit((SELECT * FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), estimator := 'random_forest_classifier', target := 'target'));
SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM sklearn.models.predict((SELECT * FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), model := getvariable('iris_model'), id := 'sample_id') LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Reduce iris to two principal components (fit-transform).
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM sklearn.preprocessing.pca((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), n_components := 2, id := 'sample_id') LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Three-fold cross-validated accuracy of a logistic-regression classifier on iris.
example_queries.sql: SELECT fold, score FROM sklearn.models.cross_val_score((SELECT * FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), estimator := 'logistic_regression', target := 'target', cv := 3);

example_queries.description: Average value by latitude band
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(latitude) AS lat, round(avg(target), 2) FROM sklearn.datasets.california_housing GROUP BY lat ORDER BY lat

example_queries.description: Target range
example_queries.sql: SELECT min(target), max(target), round(avg(target), 1) FROM sklearn.datasets.diabetes

example_queries.description: Class balance
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) FROM sklearn.datasets.breast_cancer GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Images per digit
example_queries.sql: SELECT target, count(*) FROM sklearn.datasets.digits GROUP BY target ORDER BY target

example_queries.description: Average alcohol per cultivar
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, round(avg(alcohol), 2) FROM sklearn.datasets.wine GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Row count per species
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) FROM sklearn.datasets.iris GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: 200 points in a two-moon shape
example_queries.sql: SELECT target, count(*) AS n FROM sklearn.datasets.make_moons(n_samples => 200, noise => 0.1) GROUP BY target

example_queries.description: Iris flowers with long petals
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, petal_length_cm, target_name FROM sklearn.datasets.iris() WHERE petal_length_cm > 5

example_queries.description: Mean petal length per species
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, avg(petal_length_cm) FROM sklearn.datasets.iris() GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Number of images per digit
example_queries.sql: SELECT target, count(*) AS n_images FROM sklearn.datasets.digits() GROUP BY target ORDER BY target

example_queries.description: 500 rows, 4 features, noisy target
example_queries.sql: SELECT corr(feature_0, target) AS r FROM sklearn.datasets.make_regression(n_samples => 500, n_features => 4, noise => 5.0)

example_queries.description: Mean tumour radius for malignant vs. benign samples
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, avg(mean_radius) AS mean_radius FROM sklearn.datasets.breast_cancer() GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Patients with the fastest disease progression
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, bmi, target FROM sklearn.datasets.diabetes() WHERE target > 250

example_queries.description: 200 points in two concentric rings
example_queries.sql: SELECT target, avg(sqrt(feature_0 * feature_0 + feature_1 * feature_1)) AS mean_radius FROM sklearn.datasets.make_circles(n_samples => 200, noise => 0.05) GROUP BY target

example_queries.description: Highest-value districts (downloads on first use)
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, medinc, target FROM sklearn.datasets.california_housing() WHERE target >= 5

example_queries.description: Mean alcohol content per wine cultivar
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, avg(alcohol) AS mean_alcohol FROM sklearn.datasets.wine() GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: 300 points in 4 clusters
example_queries.sql: SELECT cluster, avg(feature_0) AS x, avg(feature_1) AS y FROM sklearn.datasets.make_blobs(n_samples => 300, centers => 4) GROUP BY cluster

example_queries.description: Forward-chaining train/test splits over ordered rows
example_queries.sql: SELECT split, role, count(*) AS n_rows FROM sklearn.models.timeseries_split((SELECT sample_id FROM sklearn.datasets.iris() ORDER BY sample_id), id := 'sample_id', n_splits := 5) GROUP BY split, role ORDER BY split, role

example_queries.description: Class-balanced 5-fold for iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, fold FROM sklearn.models.stratified_kfold((SELECT sample_id, target FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), id := 'sample_id', label := 'target', n_splits := 5)

example_queries.description: Randomized-search a random forest on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_test_score, rank FROM sklearn.models.randomized_search((SELECT * FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_iter := 4, estimator := union_value(random_forest_classifier := {'n_estimators': [100, 200, 300], 'max_depth': [3, 5, 8]})) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Rank iris features by permutation importance for the stored 'iris_rf' model
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, importance_mean FROM sklearn.models.permutation_importance((SELECT * FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), model_name := 'iris_rf', target := 'target') ORDER BY importance_mean DESC

example_queries.description: Grid-search a random forest on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_test_score, rank FROM sklearn.models.grid_search((SELECT * FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', estimator := union_value(random_forest_classifier := {'n_estimators': [100, 300], 'max_depth': [3, 5]})) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Partial dependence of 'iris_rf' on petal length
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_value, class, partial_dependence FROM sklearn.models.partial_dependence((SELECT * FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), model_name := 'iris_rf', feature := 'petal_length_cm') ORDER BY feature_value

example_queries.description: Show one model's metadata
example_queries.sql: SELECT estimator, task, n_features, train_score FROM sklearn.models.model_info('iris_rf')

example_queries.description: List stored models, newest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, estimator, train_score FROM sklearn.models.list_models() ORDER BY created_at DESC

example_queries.description: Rows per fold in a 5-fold split of iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT fold, count(*) AS n_rows FROM sklearn.models.kfold((SELECT sample_id FROM sklearn.datasets.iris()), id := 'sample_id', n_splits := 5) GROUP BY fold
