functions.name: read_850
functions.comment: Shaped positional view of X12 transaction set 850

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Shaped, relational view of X12 transaction set 850 (read_850) — an 850 purchase order. The single `input` argument takes a file path or glob (e.g. '/data/*.850'), or inline `VARCHAR`/`BLOB` content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB prefix). Every row carries the five envelope keys (interchange_ctrl, group_ctrl, transaction_ctrl, transaction_type, source_path), then this set's positional columns — for example po1_line_number, po1_product_id, po1_quantity, po1_unit_price, n1_name. Columns are named by the PUBLIC segment ID and element position only (e.g. po1_quantity = PO102); raw codes are surfaced verbatim, so code-value translation needs your own licensed X12 reference. Each PO1 parent starts a logical row group; repeating children fan out to one row each sharing the parent's keys, so re-aggregate with GROUP BY on the parent id. Structural / positional only — no TR3 loop or code-set rules.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Shaped positional view of X12 `850` (an 850 purchase order). Carries the five envelope keys plus positional columns named by public segment ID and element position (e.g. po1_quantity = PO102) — such as po1_line_number, po1_product_id, po1_quantity, po1_unit_price, n1_name; raw codes verbatim. Reads a file path/glob, inline `VARCHAR` content, or a `BLOB`.

functions.name: envelope
functions.comment: One row per ST transaction: ISA/GS/ST envelope metadata + structural validity flags

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Summarize ANSI ASC X12 EDI file(s) as one row per ST transaction set — the routing / triage view. The single `input` argument is a file path/glob or inline content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB magic prefix). Columns expose the ISA interchange header (control number, sender/receiver qualifiers + IDs, date/time, version, P/T usage indicator), the GS functional group header (functional id, app sender/receiver, date, GS08 version), the ST header (control number, transaction type, impl reference), the actual ST..SE segment_count, and the structural validity flags se_count_ok / ge_count_ok / iea_count_ok / se_ctrl_match / ge_ctrl_match / iea_ctrl_match (NULL when the matching trailer is absent — e.g. a truncated interchange). This is structural validation only (segment counts + control-number matching) — no loop or code-set rules.

functions.name: read_837
functions.comment: Shaped positional view of X12 transaction set 837

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Shaped, relational view of X12 transaction set 837 (read_837) — an 837 health-care claim. The single `input` argument takes a file path or glob (e.g. '/data/*.837'), or inline `VARCHAR`/`BLOB` content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB prefix). Every row carries the five envelope keys (interchange_ctrl, group_ctrl, transaction_ctrl, transaction_type, source_path), then this set's positional columns — for example billing_provider_npi, subscriber_id, clm_total_charge, sv1_procedure. Columns are named by the PUBLIC segment ID and element position only (e.g. clm_total_charge = CLM02); raw codes are surfaced verbatim, so code-value translation needs your own licensed X12 reference. Each CLM parent starts a logical row group; repeating children fan out to one row each sharing the parent's keys, so re-aggregate with GROUP BY on the parent id. Structural / positional only — no TR3 loop or code-set rules.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Shaped positional view of X12 `837` (an 837 health-care claim). Carries the five envelope keys plus positional columns named by public segment ID and element position (e.g. clm_total_charge = CLM02) — such as billing_provider_npi, subscriber_id, clm_total_charge, sv1_procedure; raw codes verbatim. Reads a file path/glob, inline `VARCHAR` content, or a `BLOB`.

functions.name: segments_elements
functions.comment: Explode an X12 interchange into one row per element (component/repetition split)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Fully explode ANSI ASC X12 EDI file(s) into one row per element — the workhorse generic view. The single `input` argument is a file path/glob or inline content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB magic prefix). Each row carries the four envelope keys plus source_path, the segment_index, raw segment_id, the 1-based element_index (CLP02 is element_index 2), a component_index (NULL unless the element is a composite split on the sub-element separator), a repetition_index (NULL unless the element repeats on the repetition separator), and the raw value. Delimiters are sniffed per interchange from the ISA. Filter with WHERE segment_id = 'CLM' to pull specific segments.

functions.comment: Detect the transaction type (first ST01, or EDIFACT UNH02 message type) of inline content

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detect the transaction set type of inline X12 or UN/EDIFACT content without fully parsing the body: returns the first X12 ST01 transaction set identifier ('835', '837', '270', '271', '850', '997', '999', …) or, for an EDIFACT interchange, the UNH02 message type ('ORDERS', 'INVOIC', …). Useful for routing / triage. Returns NULL when no transaction header is found or the content is unrecognized (never an error). Pass the content from a column, e.g. via read_text().

functions.name: delimiters
functions.comment: Sniff the X12/EDIFACT delimiters from inline content into a STRUCT(element, segment, component, repetition)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Discover the delimiter bytes governing an inline X12 or UN/EDIFACT interchange and return them as a `STRUCT(element, segment, component, repetition)`, each a 1-char `VARCHAR`. For X12 the bytes are read deterministically from the fixed-width ISA (element = byte after 'ISA', component = ISA16, segment = byte after ISA16, repetition = ISA11 or NULL for the version-4010 'U' placeholder); for EDIFACT they come from the optional UNA service-string advice (or the EDIFACT defaults). `repetition` is NULL when no repetition separator is in use. Content that is not a recognizable interchange returns a NULL struct (never an error). Pass the content from a column, e.g. via read_text().
tags.vgi.doc_md: Sniff the EDI delimiters from inline content into a `STRUCT(element, segment, component, repetition)`; `repetition` is NULL when unused, and unrecognized content returns NULL.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT (x12.main.delimiters('ISA*00*          *00*          *ZZ*SENDER         *ZZ*RECEIVER       *240101*1200*^*00501*000000001*0*P*:~')).element AS element_sep;

workers.title: X.509 & TLS
workers.tagline: Parse X.509 certificates & inspect TLS endpoints for DuckDB (Go)
workers.summary: Parse X.509 certificates and inspect TLS endpoints
workers.doc_md:
# X.509 Certificate & TLS Inspection for DuckDB

**Parse X.509 certificates and inspect live TLS endpoints directly in SQL** — read subjects, issuers, validity windows, SHA-256 fingerprints, and subject alternative names (SANs) from PEM or DER certificates, and pull the certificate chain a TLS server presents, all without leaving DuckDB.

This is a defensive security and compliance toolkit for anyone who works with certificates at scale: SREs auditing certificate expiry across a fleet, security engineers triaging TLS configurations, and compliance teams reporting on certificate authorities, key algorithms, and signature algorithms. Instead of shelling out to `openssl` and parsing text by hand, you query certificates and endpoints as ordinary SQL columns and rows, then filter, join, and aggregate them like any other DuckDB data.

It is powered entirely by the Go standard library's battle-tested [`crypto/x509`](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/x509) and [`crypto/tls`](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/tls) packages — no third-party parsing code and no external services. The worker speaks the VGI protocol over Arrow, so DuckDB attaches it as a catalog and certificate parsing runs in-process at native speed. Certificate inputs are accepted as **PEM text** (`VARCHAR`) or **DER bytes** (`BLOB`); the format is sniffed from the content at runtime, so one query works for both.

## When to reach for it

Reach for this worker whenever certificates or TLS endpoints show up in your data and you want to treat them as structured columns rather than opaque blobs: auditing expiry windows across a fleet, pinning or comparing SHA-256 fingerprints, checking key and signature algorithms against a policy, expanding a certificate into a row per attribute for ad-hoc inspection, or pulling the chain a live server presents to confirm what it actually serves. Offline certificate parsing runs entirely in-process; live endpoint inspection **opens a network connection, so use it against AUTHORIZED endpoints only.**

## Typical uses

A few patterns recur. To flag soon-to-expire certificates, apply `cert_not_after` to a column of PEM or DER certificates and keep the rows whose expiry falls inside your renewal window, reporting each certificate's `cert_subject` alongside. To audit cryptographic hygiene across a fleet, group a certificate table by `cert_key_algorithm` and `cert_signature_algorithm` and count the weak ones. To confirm what a server actually serves, call the `tls_inspect` table function on an **authorized** `host:port` and read back the presented chain. Browse the `cert_fields` registry view to discover every attribute the worker can read and the scalar that returns each; ready-to-run, fully qualified statements live in the `x509.main` schema's example queries.

Learn more about the underlying library in the [Go `crypto/x509` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/x509) and the [Go source on GitHub](https://github.com/golang/go/tree/master/src/crypto/x509). Source for this worker lives at [github.com/Query-farm/vgi-x509](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-x509).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## x509.main

Defensive **X.509 certificate** parsing and **TLS endpoint** inspection, exposed as DuckDB SQL functions over Apache Arrow.

### Two ways to work

Scalar functions take one certificate and return a single field (subject, issuer, serial, key and signature algorithms, SHA-256 fingerprint, validity window, CA flag, or subject alternative names) — ideal for filtering, joining, and aggregating certificate columns. Table functions expand a certificate or endpoint into rows: one dumps every attribute of a certificate for ad-hoc inspection, the other connects to a live TLS endpoint (**AUTHORIZED endpoints only**) and returns the presented chain.

### Usage

Certificate inputs accept **PEM text** (`VARCHAR`) or **DER bytes** (`BLOB`); the content is sniffed at runtime. NULL certificate input yields NULL (scalars) or zero rows.

functions.name: cert_signature_algorithm
functions.comment: Certificate signature algorithm (Go crypto/x509 canonical name, e.g. ECDSA-SHA256)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the algorithm the issuing CA used to sign this certificate, as a `VARCHAR`. The value is Go crypto/x509's canonical name for the algorithm and is drawn from a fixed vocabulary: for RSA PKCS#1 v1.5, `SHA256-RSA`, `SHA384-RSA`, `SHA512-RSA` (and the legacy `SHA1-RSA`, `MD5-RSA`, `MD2-RSA`); for RSA-PSS, `SHA256-RSAPSS`, `SHA384-RSAPSS`, `SHA512-RSAPSS`; for ECDSA, `ECDSA-SHA256`, `ECDSA-SHA384`, `ECDSA-SHA512` (and legacy `ECDSA-SHA1`); for DSA, `DSA-SHA1`, `DSA-SHA256`; and the single-token `Ed25519`. An unrecognized OID yields `Unknown Signature Algorithm`. Note the ordering convention differs by family — RSA/DSA render as hash-then-key (`SHA256-RSA`) while ECDSA renders as key-then-hash (`ECDSA-SHA256`) — so match on the whole token, not a positional split. For a security audit, the SHA-1, MD5 and MD2 variants are considered weak/deprecated and are the ones worth flagging. Accepts PEM text (`VARCHAR`) or DER bytes (`BLOB`); NULL input yields NULL. Example: the committed fixture certificate is P-256 ECDSA and returns `ECDSA-SHA256`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Read the certificate signature algorithm as Go crypto/x509's canonical name (e.g. `ECDSA-SHA256`, `SHA256-RSA`, `Ed25519`). The value comes from a fixed vocabulary; the SHA-1/MD5/MD2 variants are weak and worth flagging in an audit.

functions.name: cert_key_algorithm
functions.comment: Public-key algorithm with size/curve (e.g. RSA-2048, ECDSA-P256, Ed25519)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the certificate's subject public-key algorithm together with its key size or curve, as a `VARCHAR` built by this worker (not Go's bare algorithm name). The value follows a fixed convention: RSA keys render as `RSA-<bits>` where <bits> is the modulus size, typically `RSA-2048`, `RSA-3072` or `RSA-4096`; ECDSA keys render as `ECDSA-<curve>` with the curve name stripped of its hyphen, i.e. `ECDSA-P256`, `ECDSA-P384`, `ECDSA-P521`; Edwards keys render as the single token `Ed25519`. Any other key type falls back to Go's public-key algorithm name (e.g. `DSA`). For a security audit, RSA moduli below 2048 bits are considered weak. Accepts PEM text (`VARCHAR`) or DER bytes (`BLOB`); NULL input yields NULL. Example: the committed fixture certificate carries a P-256 ECDSA key and returns `ECDSA-P256`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Read the public-key algorithm with its size or curve: `RSA-<bits>` (e.g. `RSA-2048`), `ECDSA-<curve>` (e.g. `ECDSA-P256`), or `Ed25519`. RSA moduli under 2048 bits are weak.

workers.doc_md:
# XSLT, XQuery & XPath for XML in SQL

![Saxonica SaxonC-HE logo](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/3630933?s=240&v=4)

Transform, query, and shred XML directly in DuckDB SQL with full **XSLT 3.0**, **XQuery 3.1**, and **XPath 3.1** support, powered by the production-grade Saxon processor.

This extension turns DuckDB into an XML processing engine. Instead of exporting data to a separate XSLT/XQuery toolchain, you can apply stylesheets, evaluate XPath expressions, run XQuery FLWOR programs, and explode XML documents into relational rows without ever leaving SQL. It is built for data engineers and analysts who land XML in columns -- SOAP/EDI payloads, RSS/Atom feeds, OOXML and SVG fragments, scientific and financial document formats -- and need to extract, reshape, or validate that markup at query time, row by row, with NULLs passed through cleanly.

## Key concepts

- **Per-row scalars vs. set-returning table functions.** Scalars compute one value per row (a string, boolean, number, or list); table functions and the array-plus-UNNEST pattern explode a single document into many rows -- the natural way to *shred* XML into a relational result.
- **Transform, query, and validate.** XSLT reshapes documents, XPath and XQuery pull values out of them, and a well-formedness check lets you filter malformed rows before processing.
- **NULL / invalid / error.** A NULL input yields NULL output (or no rows); malformed XML or a bad stylesheet/expression raises a clean DuckDB error, so bad data never crashes the worker.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker whenever XML lands in a DuckDB column and you need to read a value out of it, transform it into another shape, or normalize its repeated structure into rows for downstream SQL.

## Under the hood

The worker is backed by [SaxonC-HE](https://www.saxonica.com/), the free Home Edition of [Saxonica](https://www.saxonica.com/)'s Saxon processor -- the reference implementation for XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 -- via the [saxonche](https://pypi.org/project/saxonche/) Python bindings. A single native Saxon processor is booted once per worker and reused; compiled stylesheets and queries are cached on their source text, so a constant stylesheet applied down a column compiles once and transforms many rows. Note that SaxonC-HE is not schema-aware, so there is no XSD validation; the well-formedness check provides the strongest guarantee the free edition offers.

## Learn more

- [Saxonica homepage](https://www.saxonica.com/)
- [Saxon documentation](https://www.saxonica.com/documentation/index.html)
- [Saxon-HE source on GitHub](https://github.com/Saxonica/Saxon-HE)
- [`saxonche` on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/saxonche/)
- W3C specs: [XSLT 3.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-30/), [XPath 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-31/), [XQuery 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xquery-31/)

# main

XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 processing over XML, backed by SaxonC-HE.

The functions in this schema group into four capabilities:

- **Transform** an XML document with an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet.
- **Query** a document with XPath or XQuery to pull out a string, boolean, or numeric value.
- **Shred** a document into relational rows -- per row via an array you UNNEST, or via a set-returning table function.
- **Validate** that text is well-formed XML before you process it.

## saxon_info (table)

A single-row, directly-browsable table describing the SaxonC engine bundled with this worker — its version and edition, the XSLT/XQuery/XPath language levels it implements, and whether it is schema-aware.

**When to use:** learn the engine's capabilities before relying on them. The `schema_aware` column is the key signal: it is always false on the Home Edition, so there is no XSD validation. The table has no arguments and a single row of engine facts, so it is directly browsable.

**Columns:** `version`, `edition`, `xslt_version`, `xquery_version`, `xpath_version` (all `VARCHAR`) and `schema_aware` (`BOOLEAN`).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_nodes

Explode a single XML document into rows: emit **one `(seq, value)` row per XPath 3.1 match**, in document order.

**When to use:** shred one constant document into a relational result — turn `//item` matches into a numbered table you can join, filter, and aggregate. For shredding a *column* of documents instead, use the `xpath_array` scalar with `UNNEST`.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`; table-function named-argument syntax (`name := value`) is supported.

**Output columns:** `seq` (`BIGINT`, 1-based position) and `value` (`VARCHAR`, the match's string value).

**Behavior & edge cases:** no matches -> zero rows. Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xpath_nodes

Table function: one `(seq, value)` row per XPath 3.1 match in one document.

## Usage

Call `xslt.main.xpath_nodes(xml, expr)` in a `FROM` clause to expand each match into a numbered `(seq, value)` row.

## Notes

- Binds a single constant document; use `xpath_array` + `UNNEST` per row.
- `seq` is the 1-based document-order position of each match.
- Invalid XML/XPath raises an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xquery_rows

Run an **XQuery 3.1** query against one document and emit **one `(seq, value)` row per item** of the result sequence, in sequence order.

**When to use:** when the query yields a sequence (e.g. a FLWOR `for $x in //i return $x*2`) and you want each item as its own row to join, filter, or aggregate in SQL. Use the `xquery` scalar instead when you want the whole result serialized into one value.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document, bound as the context item) and `expr` (the XQuery 3.1 source). Both `VARCHAR`; named-argument syntax supported.

**Output columns:** `seq` (`BIGINT`, 1-based position) and `value` (`VARCHAR`, the item's string value).

**Behavior & edge cases:** an empty result sequence -> zero rows. Malformed XML or a malformed query raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:

Table function: one `(seq, value)` row per item in an XQuery 3.1 result sequence.

## Usage

## Notes

- One row per sequence item; `seq` is the 1-based position.
- Use the `xquery` scalar for a single serialized result.
- Invalid XML/query raises an error.

functions.comment: Transform an XML document with an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet; returns the serialized result

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xslt

Apply an **XSLT 3.0** stylesheet to an XML document and return the serialized transformation result as text.

**When to use:** reshape, rename, filter, or compute over XML — the full power of XSLT 3.0 (templates, `xsl:value-of`, `xsl:for-each`, modes, functions) — directly in SQL.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the source document) and `stylesheet` (the XSLT 3.0 source). Both are `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `VARCHAR` — the serialized result tree (often XML, but the stylesheet's `xsl:output` may select text/HTML/JSON).

**Behavior & edge cases:** a NULL in either argument yields NULL for that row. Malformed XML or a malformed stylesheet raises a clean DuckDB error. A constant stylesheet down a column compiles once and is reused. SaxonC-HE is not schema-aware, so schema-aware (validating) XSLT is unavailable.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xslt

Transform an XML document with an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet, returning the serialized result.

## Usage

Call `xslt.main.xslt(xml, stylesheet)` in any projection to transform a document column against a stylesheet.

## Notes

- Powered by SaxonC-HE (XSLT 3.0).
- NULL input -> NULL output.
- Invalid XML or stylesheet raises a DuckDB error.
- A constant stylesheet is compiled once and reused across rows.

functions.comment: Numeric (`DOUBLE`) value of the first XPath 3.1 match (NULL if non-numeric)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_number

Evaluate an **XPath 3.1** expression against an XML document and return its **numeric value** as a `DOUBLE`.

**When to use:** extract a number from XML and use it in SQL arithmetic — a measurement, a count (`count(//item)`), a sum (`sum(//price)`), or any numeric XPath computation.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `DOUBLE` — the numeric value of the first match, or NULL when the value is non-numeric (XPath NaN) or nothing matches.

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL. Wrap a path in `number(...)` to coerce a text node. Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xpath_number

Return the numeric (`DOUBLE`) value of the first XPath 3.1 match, or NULL.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT xslt.main.xpath_number('<r><n>42</n></r>', 'number(//n)');  -- 42.0
```

## Notes

- Non-numeric results (XPath NaN) come back as NULL.
- Use XPath aggregates like `count(...)` / `sum(...)` directly.
- NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/XPath raises an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xquery

Run an **XQuery 3.1** query against an XML document (bound as the context item) and return the serialized result.

**When to use:** richer querying than a single XPath — FLWOR expressions (`for`/`let`/`where`/`order by`/`return`), constructed elements, joins across parts of the document, and string/sequence functions like `string-join(//i, ',')`.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document, available as `.` and `/`) and `query` (the XQuery 3.1 source). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `VARCHAR` — the serialized query result (atomic text, or constructed XML, depending on the query).

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL. Use `xquery_rows` instead when you want one row per item of the result sequence. Malformed XML or a malformed query raises a clean DuckDB error.

## xpath_string

Evaluate an **XPath 3.1** expression against an XML document and return the **string value of the first match** (or NULL when nothing matches).

**When to use:** pull a single text value out of XML — an element's text, an attribute, or any atomic computed by XPath (`string(...)`, `concat(...)`, etc.).

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `VARCHAR` — the string value of the first node/atomic in document order, or NULL if the expression selects nothing.

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL. A malformed document or a malformed XPath raises a clean DuckDB error. Namespaces follow the document's in-scope bindings; use `//*:name` or `local-name()` predicates for namespace-agnostic matching.
tags.vgi.doc_md: # xpath_string Return the string value of the first XPath 3.1 match in a document, or NULL. ## Usage ```sql SELECT xslt.main.xpath_string('x', '//a'); -- 'x' ``` ## Notes - Returns the FIRST match only; use `xpath_array` to collect all matches. - NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/XPath raises an error. - Namespace-agnostic matching: `//*:tag` or `local-name() = 'tag'`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_boolean

Evaluate an **XPath 3.1** expression against an XML document and return its **effective boolean value** (EBV).

**When to use:** test a condition over XML inside a SQL `WHERE`/`CASE` — does a node exist (`boolean(//x)`), does a count match (`count(//a) = 1`), or any predicate that XPath can express.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `BOOLEAN` — the EBV of the expression (a non-empty node-set is true, an empty one is false; numeric/string EBV rules apply for atomics).

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL. Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# xpath_boolean

Return the effective boolean value of an XPath 3.1 expression over a document.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT xslt.main.xpath_boolean('<r><a/></r>', 'count(//a) = 1');  -- true
```

## Notes

- Follows XPath effective-boolean-value rules (existence, numbers, strings).
- NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/XPath raises an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_array

Evaluate an **XPath 3.1** expression against an XML document and return the string values of **all matches** as a `VARCHAR[]` list.

**When to use:** shred XML into rows. Apply this to a column of documents and `UNNEST(...)` the result to turn one document into many rows — the per-row counterpart to the `xpath_nodes` table function (which binds one constant document).

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression selecting many items). Both `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `VARCHAR[]` — the string value of every match, in document order; an empty list when nothing matches.

**Behavior & edge cases:** NULL in either argument yields NULL (not an empty list). Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md: # xpath_array Return the string values of ALL XPath 3.1 matches as a `VARCHAR[]` list. ## Usage ```sql SELECT UNNEST(xslt.main.xpath_array('ab', '//i')); ``` ## Notes - `UNNEST` the list to shred a column of documents into rows. - For a single constant document, the `xpath_nodes` table function is handier. - NULL input -> NULL output; invalid XML/XPath raises an error.

functions.name: is_well_formed
functions.comment: True if the text is well-formed XML; false if malformed (never an error)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## is_well_formed

Test whether a string is **well-formed XML** — returns `true` if it parses, `false` if it is malformed. **Never raises** (unlike the other functions).

**When to use:** validate or filter a column of candidate XML before transforming or querying it, e.g. `WHERE xslt.main.is_well_formed(doc)`, so malformed rows do not abort the scan.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the candidate text). `VARCHAR`.

**Output:** `BOOLEAN` — `true` for well-formed XML, `false` for malformed text; NULL input yields NULL.

**Behavior & edge cases:** this checks *well-formedness* (does it parse), not schema validity — SaxonC-HE is not schema-aware, so there is no XSD validation. Well-formedness is the strongest XML check the HE edition offers.
tags.vgi.doc_md: # is_well_formed Return `true` if the text is well-formed XML, `false` if malformed (never errors). ## Usage ```sql SELECT xslt.main.is_well_formed(''); -- true SELECT xslt.main.is_well_formed(''); -- false ``` ## Notes - Checks well-formedness only; there is no XSD/schema validation (HE limitation). - Safe to use in `WHERE` to filter out malformed rows. - NULL input -> NULL output.

workers.summary: Defensive YARA-X malware scanning: compile YARA rules and scan blobs/text for matches, all in SQL over Apache Arrow.
workers.doc_md:
# YARA Malware Scanning in SQL

![YARA-X logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/VirusTotal/yara-x/main/ls/editors/code/images/icon.png)

Scan blobs, files, and text columns for malware and indicators of compromise (IOCs) straight from DuckDB SQL by compiling and matching **YARA rules** — no external scanner, no native `libyara`, just functions you can call in a query.

This extension brings defensive YARA rule matching to the database, so security engineers, threat hunters, and data teams can triage suspicious files, hunt for signatures, and enforce detection rules over data they already have in DuckDB. Instead of exporting samples to a standalone tool, you write a YARA ruleset (or load one from a column) and let SQL fan it across millions of rows: filter a table of email attachments, label artifacts in an object store, or join scan verdicts back onto your metadata — all in one place.

Matching is powered by [YARA-X](https://github.com/VirusTotal/yara-x), VirusTotal's pure-Rust rewrite of the classic YARA engine, embedded directly in the worker so there is no C dependency to install or keep patched. Rules are compiled once per batch and reused, and scanning is *total*: untrusted, garbage, empty, or deliberately hostile data simply yields no matches rather than crashing the worker, so you can point it at live malware safely. The full YARA syntax — string, hex, and regex patterns, conditions, namespaces, tags, and the standard `pe`/`elf`/`hash`/`math` modules — is supported.

Two shapes of access are offered. Per-row scalar functions test a whole column of blobs or text against a ruleset, giving you a filter predicate, a match count, or the name of the rule that fired — ideal for triaging a table of samples or labelling artifacts in place. Table functions instead expand a single scan into detail rows, one per matching rule or per individual pattern hit (with byte offsets and the matched bytes), for forensics and drill-down. There is also a validation helper for checking that a ruleset compiles before you scan with it, and a `yara_modules` reference table listing the YARA-X modules (`pe`, `elf`, `hash`, `math`, …) a rule may import.

For rule-writing syntax and module reference see the official [YARA-X documentation](https://virustotal.github.io/yara-x/) and the [yara-x crate docs](https://docs.rs/yara-x).

# YARA — `main` schema

The single schema holding this worker's YARA rule-compilation and malware-scanning functions over Apache Arrow. The functions fall into a few groups:

- **Scanning** — per-row scalars that test a column of blobs or text against a ruleset (match predicate, matching-rule count, first matching rule).

Scanning is *total*: untrusted or hostile data yields no matches rather than crashing the worker; only an invalid rule source raises an error.

workers.doc_md:
## Yahoo Finance

Market data from Yahoo Finance, exposed as three keyless DuckDB table functions.

- **`history`** — OHLCV candles for one ticker over a named range or explicit date range.
- **`quote`** — a current-price snapshot (price, change, day & 52-week range, volume) for a list of tickers.
- **`search`** — resolve a company name or partial symbol to candidate tickers.

No secret or API key is required. Prices are delayed and provided for informational use only; review Yahoo's terms before redistribution. Intraday candles are only available for recent ranges.

example_queries.title: search_symbol
example_queries.description: Resolve a company name to candidate tickers
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, short_name FROM yfinance.main.search('apple') LIMIT 3;

example_queries.title: recent_history
example_queries.description: Fetch the last few daily candles for a ticker
example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, close FROM yfinance.main.history('AAPL', range := '5d') ORDER BY timestamp;

example_queries.description: Last month of daily candles for Apple
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM yfinance.main.history('AAPL')

example_queries.description: Current price for several megacaps at once
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, regular_market_price FROM yfinance.main.quote('AAPL,MSFT,GOOG')

example_queries.description: Find a ticker by company name
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, long_name FROM yfinance.main.search('vanguard')

example_queries.description: List the reference tickers for a given asset type
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, name, exchange FROM yfinance.main.symbol_reference WHERE asset_type = 'ETF' ORDER BY symbol

example_queries.description: Count the reference symbols grouped by asset type
example_queries.sql: SELECT asset_type, count(*) AS n FROM yfinance.main.symbol_reference GROUP BY asset_type ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: The five most recent daily closes and volumes for Apple
example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, close, volume FROM yfinance.main.history('AAPL', range := '1mo') ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: One year of weekly closes for Microsoft
example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, close, volume FROM yfinance.main.history('MSFT', range := '1y', bar := '1wk')

example_queries.description: The 52-week high and low for SPY, aggregated from daily candles
example_queries.sql: SELECT max(high) AS high_52w, min(low) AS low_52w FROM yfinance.main.history('SPY', range := '1y')

example_queries.description: Highest close over the last month for every ticker in a table, via LATERAL

## Market data functions

| Function | Returns | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `history` | OHLCV candles (time series) | charting, returns, backtests |
| `quote` | current snapshot per symbol | dashboards, watchlists |

## symbol_reference

A browsable, credential-free registry of well-known tickers. One row per symbol, naming the instrument, its asset type, its listing exchange, and the Yahoo symbol-format convention it illustrates. It resolves entirely inside DuckDB — no network, no key — so it is the safe first thing to look at. Once you have a `symbol`, pass it into `history`, `quote`, or `search`.

functions.name: history
functions.comment: Historical OHLCV candles for one symbol from Yahoo Finance (v8 chart API). Pick a named window (range := '1y') plus a candle width (bar := '1wk'), or an explicit start_date/end_date range. The symbol may be a column, so LATERAL history(t.sym) fetches candles for every row. Returns columns symbol, timestamp (UTC), open, high, low, close, adjclose, and volume.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Daily or intraday OHLCV candles for a single ticker over a chosen window. Use it for price history, charting, returns, and technical analysis. Pick a named range (range := '1y') with a candle width (bar := '1wk'), or an explicit start_date/end_date range. Thin or halted candles come back as NULL cells rather than failing the scan.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## history

Historical OHLCV candles for one ticker from Yahoo's chart feed. Choose a named `range` (e.g. `'6mo'`, `'1y'`, `'max'`) plus a `bar` candle width (`'1d'`, `'1wk'`, `'1mo'`, or an intraday width like `'5m'` on recent ranges), or pass an explicit `start_date`/`end_date` pair to override `range`. Emits one row per candle, ordered oldest-first; thin or halted candles come back with NULL price cells rather than failing the scan. Intraday bars are only retained by Yahoo for recent windows, so an intraday `bar` on a long `range` yields fewer rows than the range implies. `adjclose` falls back to `close` when Yahoo omits it.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, close, volume FROM yfinance.main.history('AAPL', range := '1mo') ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 5
vgi.example_queries.description: The five most recent daily closes and volumes for Apple

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, close, volume FROM yfinance.main.history('MSFT', range := '1y', bar := '1wk')
vgi.example_queries.description: One year of weekly closes for Microsoft

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT max(high) AS high_52w, min(low) AS low_52w FROM yfinance.main.history('SPY', range := '1y')
vgi.example_queries.description: The 52-week high and low for SPY, aggregated from daily candles

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT w.sym, max(h.close) AS high_close FROM (VALUES ('AAPL'), ('MSFT')) w(sym), LATERAL yfinance.main.history(w.sym, range := '1mo') h GROUP BY w.sym
vgi.example_queries.description: Highest close over the last month for every ticker in a table, via LATERAL

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A current market snapshot for one or more tickers: last price, change vs the previous close, day high/low, 52-week high/low, and volume. Keyless — one lightweight request per symbol. Use it for watchlists and dashboards; use `history` for a time series.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## quote

Current-price snapshot for a comma-separated list of tickers, one row per symbol. Backed by Yahoo's keyless chart-metadata plane, so `regular_market_change` and `regular_market_change_percent` are derived from the previous close, and market cap is not available. An unresolvable ticker is dropped rather than failing the batch, so the result may have fewer rows than symbols requested. Each symbol is fetched with its own lightweight request, in parallel, so a long watchlist stays responsive.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, regular_market_price, regular_market_change_percent FROM yfinance.main.quote('AAPL')
vgi.example_queries.description: Snapshot quote for Apple

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, regular_market_price FROM yfinance.main.quote('AAPL,MSFT,GOOG')
vgi.example_queries.description: Latest price for several symbols at once

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT w.sym, q.regular_market_price FROM (VALUES ('AAPL'), ('MSFT')) w(sym), LATERAL yfinance.main.quote(w.sym) q
vgi.example_queries.description: Latest price for every ticker in a table, via LATERAL

functions.name: search

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Resolve a company name or partial symbol to candidate ticker symbols, best matches first. Use it when you only know a name — take the resulting `symbol` and pass it to `history` or `quote`. Returns equities, ETFs, indices, and other instruments with their exchange and type.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## search

Ticker lookup over Yahoo's search endpoint. Returns up to `count` candidate symbols (news results are dropped), ranked by Yahoo's relevance score, best matches first. Take the resulting `symbol` and feed it into `history` or `quote`. The `count` argument caps how many candidates come back and is clamped to 1..50 (default 8).

vgi.example_queries.description: Find symbols matching 'apple'

vgi.example_queries.description: Up to 20 candidate symbols for a query

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.name, s.symbol FROM (VALUES ('apple'), ('microsoft')) c(name), LATERAL yfinance.main.search(c.name, count := 1) s
vgi.example_queries.description: Best-matching ticker for every company name in a table, via LATERAL
